.8# Zenith — Live Event Ticketing & Order Platform

> A production-shaped, backend-only distributed system built with Java 21 + Spring Boot.
> This document is the complete engineering plan: architecture, standards, and a
> task-by-task roadmap that takes someone with **no professional backend experience** to
> the technical depth of a strong 4–5 year engineer. Everything runs on one laptop.
>

## 0. Read this first — you are starting from zero

You know some Java. You know what an API is. You have not built or run a backend system
professionally. That is a perfectly good starting point and it is the starting point this
plan now assumes — but it changes four things, and skipping any of them is how people
abandon projects like this in week five.

### 0.1 The four things that change

**1. There is a foundations stage before the project starts.**
[Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) as written asks you to model a domain with DDD aggregates, wire up a hexagonal
architecture, map DTOs with MapStruct, and write Testcontainers integration tests. For
someone who has shipped Spring Boot for two years, that is an ordinary week. For you it is
six unfamiliar ideas arriving simultaneously, and you would spend the week fighting Maven
instead of learning design. So **[Stage F — Foundations](#stage-f--foundations-the-things-everything-else-assumes--63h--weeks-13)** (three weeks, at the start of [The roadmap](#7-the-roadmap)) now comes
first and teaches the Java, SQL, HTTP, Spring, Git, Docker, and testing that everything
afterwards silently assumes.

**2. The hours are now honest.**
The original 216-hour estimate assumed a working professional. You will be slower at
first — not because you are slow, but because a professional is pattern-matching against
things they have already built, and you have nothing to match against yet. That gap
closes fast. [The honest timeline](#02-the-honest-timeline) has the recalibrated plan.

**3. The order of difficulty is different for you.**
An experienced engineer finds [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) (database tuning) and [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) (concurrency) hardest. You
will find [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) hardest, because it is the first time all the pieces appear at once. That
is expected and it is temporary. [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) is deliberately the most expanded phase in this
document for exactly that reason.

**4. You are learning by asking AI, which is a real method with real failure modes.**
It can be faster than a bootcamp or dramatically worse than one, and the difference is
entirely in *how* you ask. [How to learn this by asking AI](#05-how-to-learn-this-by-asking-ai) is about that, and it is the most important section in this
document for you specifically. Read it before you write a line of code.

### 0.2 The honest timeline

| Stage | What it gives you | Hours | At 3 h/day, 6 days/week |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **[Stage F — Foundations](#stage-f--foundations-the-things-everything-else-assumes--63h--weeks-13)** | Java, SQL, HTTP, Spring, Git, Docker, testing | 63 | Weeks 1–3 |
| **Part A — Core backend** (Phases 0–6) | A real event-driven microservice system: REST, security, database tuning, caching, idempotency, Kafka, sagas | 208 | Weeks 4–15 |
| **Part B — Senior depth** (Phases 7–14) | Async jobs, files, WebSockets, Nginx, observability, **concurrency**, **Kubernetes**, capstone | 249 | Weeks 16–29 |
| **Total** | | **520** | **29 weeks ≈ 6.75 months** |

The 29 weeks hold 531 hours of budget against 520 hours of work. The 11-hour gap is
deliberate slack for the weeks where something breaks and swallows three evenings.
The arithmetic: weeks 1–3 are the one seven-day stretch of the plan — [Stage F — Foundations](#stage-f--foundations-the-things-everything-else-assumes--63h--weeks-13) runs
21 h/week, as the week-by-week map in [The roadmap](#7-the-roadmap) says explicitly — and every week from week 4
on is 18 h, so 3×21 + 26×18 = 531.

Part A on its own is already a stronger portfolio than most engineers have two years into
the job: seven services (the last two arrive in Part B), real database optimization work with query plans, a caching layer
with measured hit ratios, provable idempotency, and a compensating saga over Kafka.

The topics you specifically asked for that live in **Part B** — multithreading,
Kubernetes, WebSockets, observability — need the back half of the plan.

#### The midpoint checkpoint — end of week 15

The end of week 15 — about three and a half months in — is deliberately a natural stopping point. At that
moment you should have:

- A running system of seven services on your laptop, with REST APIs, OAuth2 security, Postgres, Redis, and Kafka.
- `docs/PERFORMANCE.md` with roughly a dozen measured before/after numbers you produced yourself.
- Around 15 ADRs, a C4 container diagram, and snapshot-tested OpenAPI specs.
- Provable no-oversell and no-double-charge behaviour, with concurrency tests that demonstrate it.
- Kafka carrying real events through a transactional outbox, with the compensating saga and the first CQRS read model complete ([Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) finishes in week 15).

That is a genuine portfolio and a genuine skill set. Treat it as a milestone to be proud
of rather than a halfway mark, and then decide about Part B from a position of strength
instead of exhaustion.

If three and a half months is already more than you have, read
[§0.3](#03-your-two-month-target-and-what-actually-fits-in-it) next — it sets out what a
genuinely good two-month version looks like and what it costs you.

### 0.3 Your two-month target, and what actually fits in it

You asked for a two-month project at three hours a day. That is about **144 hours**, and
the full plan is 520. The gap is not padding, and it is worth being blunt about where it
goes, because picking the wrong option now is how people end up in week seven on a plan
they did not realise they had changed.

A two-month version exists and it is a genuinely good project. What it is not is a project
that reads as four years of experience — because the things creating that impression
(measured optimisation, provable concurrency correctness, a saga with every failure branch
tested, an observability stack you can actually debug from) are each 12 to 18 hours on
their own, and there are eight of them. Cut them all and you have a competent CRUD service
with Kafka bolted on, which is what most two-year engineers build and what interviewers
see every week.

So choose one of these three deliberately:

| Option | Weeks | Hours | You finish with | Who it suits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A — Depth over breadth** | 9–10 | ~187 | [Stage F — Foundations](#stage-f--foundations-the-things-everything-else-assumes--63h--weeks-13), [Phase 0 — Repository, tooling, standards](#phase-0--repository-tooling-standards--15h-baseline), [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline), [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline), [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline). A properly layered REST service, real database optimization with saved query plans, and the reservation engine with provable no-oversell and idempotency. | You have interviews in two months and need something real and defensible *now*. |
| **B — The midpoint checkpoint** | 15 | 271 | Everything in A plus security, Redis, Kafka, the transactional outbox, the compensating saga, and CQRS. This is the checkpoint already described in [The honest timeline](#02-the-honest-timeline). | You can stretch to about four months and want the full distributed-systems story. |
| **C — The full plan** | 29 | 520 | Everything, including the 30-level concurrency track, observability, and Kubernetes. | You are treating this as a career investment rather than a deadline. |

**If you take option A**, the order is [Stage F — Foundations](#stage-f--foundations-the-things-everything-else-assumes--63h--weeks-13) → [Phase 0 — Repository, tooling, standards](#phase-0--repository-tooling-standards--15h-baseline) → [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) → [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) → [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline),
and two deliberate cuts make it fit: skip [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline) (security) and [Phase 4 — Redis and the caching layer](#phase-4--redis-and-the-caching-layer--12h-baseline) (Redis), and in
Phase 5 build three of the four reservation designs and *describe* the Redis-fronted
fourth, exactly as [the Descoping guide](#12-descoping-guide) allows.

That ordering is not arbitrary. [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) and [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) carry almost all of the interview weight in
this document: `EXPLAIN` output with before and after numbers you measured yourself, and a
concurrency test proving exactly zero oversell under 500 simultaneous buyers. A narrow
project with those two things in it out-interviews a wide project without them, reliably.
Be aware of the one honest cost: with [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline) skipped you have no authentication story, and
"how did you secure it?" is a guaranteed question. The correct answer is "I deliberately
descoped it to go deeper on concurrency — here is the design I would have built", not
silence.

**What you must not do** is attempt all 29 weeks in 8 and skim. Half of [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) is worse
than none of it, because an interviewer hearing "I did some multithreading" will ask a
follow-up, and a half-answer is a worse signal than an honest "I have not reached that yet;
here is what I did instead."

Everything from [What we are building and why this domain](#1-what-we-are-building-and-why-this-domain) onward is written for option C. If you are on A or B nothing changes
except where you stop — [the Descoping guide](#12-descoping-guide) is the cut list, and [How to present this credibly](#13-how-to-present-this-credibly) tells you how to describe a
deliberately scoped project without sounding apologetic about it.

### 0.4 What "4–5 years of experience" actually means

It is worth being precise about the target, because "4–5 years" is not a quantity of time,
it is a set of behaviours. When an interviewer probes for it, they are checking six things:

1. **Judgement under constraints.** Not "I used Kafka" but "I used Kafka here and a direct HTTP call there, and here is the trade-off I was making."
2. **Having seen things fail.** Specific failures, with causes and fixes. Deadlocks, cache stampedes, OOMs, restart loops.
3. **Knowing the alternatives you rejected.** A decision implies options. Someone who only knows one way has not made a decision, they have followed a tutorial.
4. **Operational instinct.** What breaks first under load, what you check first at 3 a.m., what a thread dump tells you.
5. **Measurement rather than belief.** Numbers with conditions attached, not adjectives.
6. **Explaining *why*, unprompted.** The strongest signal of all, and the hardest to fake.

**This project can genuinely give you all six**, because it is built around them: every
phase forces a trade-off, breaks something deliberately, and demands a measurement. That
is why it is structured as it is, and why the ADRs, postmortems, and performance report are
not optional decoration.

**Be equally clear about what it cannot give you**, because knowing the difference is
itself a maturity signal:

- Working inside a team: code review, disagreement, inherited conventions, shared ownership.
- Legacy archaeology — understanding 200,000 lines someone else wrote and left.
- Stakeholder pressure: shipping a compromise because the deadline is real.
- Production at genuine scale, with real users and real money, and the judgement that comes from being responsible for it.
- Being on call when it breaks and you did not cause it.

So the accurate claim is: **this gives you the technical depth of a strong 4–5 year
engineer on these specific topics, while you still have the organisational experience of a
junior.** That is a real and valuable position to be in, it is enough to compete for solid
mid-level roles, and stating it that way in an interview reads as self-awareness rather
than weakness. [How to present this credibly](#13-how-to-present-this-credibly) covers how to present it.

### 0.5 How to learn this by asking AI

This is your stated method, and it can genuinely work better than a course — AI will
explain the specific thing you are stuck on, at your level, at 1 a.m. But it has one
catastrophic failure mode: **it will cheerfully hand you working code you do not
understand**, and you will feel productive while learning nothing. An interviewer finds
that out in about ninety seconds. So treat the following as the method, not as advice.

#### The loop that works

For every task in this plan, in this order:

1. **Read the task's What / Why / Solves first.** Understand the *problem* before you see any solution. This is the single highest-leverage habit here, because a solution you meet before the problem is just trivia.
2. **Try it yourself for 30–45 minutes.** Get stuck. Being stuck is not wasted time; it is what makes the eventual answer stick. Information that arrives before the struggle does not get retained.
3. **Ask for the concept, not the code.** "Explain what a transactional outbox is and what problem it solves, as if I know Spring Boot but have never used Kafka." Not "write me an outbox implementation."
4. **Write the code yourself**, then ask for a review: "Here is my implementation. Review it like a senior engineer who is about to maintain it. What is wrong, what will break in production, and what did I not think about?"
5. **Ask what you still do not know.** "What are the three questions an interviewer would ask about this code that I would struggle to answer?" Then go answer them.
6. **Write it down in your own words** in `docs/journal.md` or the relevant doc. If you cannot write it without looking, you do not know it yet.
7. **Run it. Then break it.** Change a value, remove a lock, kill a container. Code you have only read is code you do not understand.

#### Prompts that teach you things

- "Explain X in simple terms, then show me a small example, then tell me what beginners usually get wrong about it."
- "What are the three ways to do X in Spring Boot, and what are the trade-offs of each?" — this is how you build the judgement from [What "4–5 years of experience" actually means](#04-what-45-years-of-experience-actually-means).
- "Review this code as a senior engineer. What will break under load or concurrency?"
- "Give me a deliberately broken version of this and let me find the bug." — outstanding for learning; almost nobody uses it.
- "Quiz me on X with five questions, hardest last, and do not give me the answers until I try."
- "Why would someone choose A over B here? When would that be the wrong choice?"
- "What does this error actually mean, and what are the three most likely causes?"
- "Show me what this looks like when it fails in production."

#### Prompts that quietly destroy your learning

- "Write the whole order service for me." You will get code, ship a phase, and be unable to answer one question about it.
- "Fix this" with a pasted stack trace and no attempt to read it yourself. Reading stack traces is a core skill ([Task F3.9 — Reading stack traces and using a debugger](#task-f39--reading-stack-traces-and-using-a-debugger--1h) teaches it); outsourcing it means you never acquire it.
- "Just give me the code." Sometimes legitimate for boilerplate you already understand — a `docker-compose.yml`, a Logback config. Never legitimate for anything you want to claim in an interview.
- Accepting the first answer without asking "why that way?"

#### Verify, always

AI is confidently wrong in predictable places, and these are exactly the places this
project lives:

- **Versions and APIs.** It will give you Spring Boot 2.x patterns, `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` (removed), or javax instead of jakarta imports. This document pins Spring Boot 4.1.x on Java 21 — check generated config against the official reference docs, which are genuinely excellent.
- **Configuration properties.** Invented or renamed YAML keys are extremely common. If a property does nothing, suspect it does not exist.
- **Anything involving a version-specific default.** Kafka, Hibernate, and Postgres defaults change between versions.
- **Performance claims.** Never take a number from AI. The entire point of [the Benchmarks to capture](#10-benchmarks-to-capture) is that you measure it yourself.

Rule of thumb: **if it compiles and the test passes, believe it. If it only sounds right,
check the docs.**

#### The explain test

Before marking any task done, do this: close your laptop and explain what you built, out
loud, to an empty room — what problem it solves, how it works, and what you would do
differently. Ninety seconds. If you stall, you have copied rather than learned, and you
should go back to step 3 of the loop.

This feels ridiculous. It is also the single best predictor of whether you will survive the
follow-up questions in an interview, because an interview *is* that exercise with someone
watching.

### 0.6 Five rules for not fooling yourself

1. **No code you cannot explain.** Not one line. If AI gave you something you do not understand, either understand it or delete it. This is the whole game.
2. **Run everything. Break everything.** The plan constantly asks you to break things on purpose — that is not filler, it is where the learning is.
3. **Write the number down before you optimise.** No baseline means no evidence and no story.
4. **One concept at a time when you are stuck.** If three things are broken, you changed three things. Revert to the last working state and move in single steps.
5. **Finish phases.** A finished Phase 3 beats half of Phases 3, 4, and 5. Partial knowledge collapses under questioning; complete knowledge compounds.

### 0.7 How to use this document

- **Work through it in order.** The dependencies are real: [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) needs [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline)'s locking, [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) needs the code you wrote in Phases 4–9 to audit.
- **Read one task at a time.** Do not read a whole phase ahead; it is demoralising and unnecessary.
- **Every task has the same parts in the same order** — nine in [Stage F — Foundations](#stage-f--foundations-the-things-everything-else-assumes--63h--weeks-13), eight in the phases (the worked code example exists only in Stage F) — described in [How every task below is written](#how-every-task-below-is-written). The most important of them is the **Checkpoint** — a short list of questions to answer out loud, from memory, before starting the next task. Those questions are not decoration. They are the mechanism that stops you mistaking "I followed the steps and it worked" for "I understand this".
- **Nothing is assumed known.** Every task lists what you must already know, and defines every new term in a **New words** table before using it. If a prerequisite is unfamiliar, go and learn it first — that is not falling behind, that is the plan working as designed.
- **This file is the only thing you need to read.** Every template, every explanation and every definition is in here. Everything under `docs/` is output *you* produce as tasks ask for it — [§16](#16-every-document-you-will-write-with-its-template) gives the template for each one. If you ever wonder "where was that explained?", it was here.
- **There is also a glossary**, at [§15](#15-glossary--every-acronym-and-term-in-plain-english). The per-task tables cover the words *that task* introduces; the glossary covers the vocabulary that turns up everywhere without ever being explained — API, p99, idempotent, SLO, bean, partition. **Read [§15.1](#151-the-acronyms-assumed-in-every-conversation) today, before [Stage F — Foundations](#stage-f--foundations-the-things-everything-else-assumes--63h--weeks-13).** It is about five minutes and it makes everything after it easier to read.
- **Every phase ends with an exit check.** A short tick-honestly list before you move on. If you cannot tick a box, the honest move is to go back, not forward — and nobody is watching, so there is nothing to gain by lying to yourself.
- **If a task still feels too big, split it yourself.** Ask AI: *"Break this task into smaller steps, and tell me the concepts I need to understand before each one."* Doing that is practice for the actual job, where nobody hands you a task list.
- **The checkboxes are real.** Tick them. Momentum matters more than you expect over 29 weeks.

#### Small things nobody tells freshers — answered once, here

Every big topic in this document gets a full explanation where it first appears. But there is a second category of question — the tiny, practical, "surely everyone knows this" kind — that experienced developers answer by reflex and therefore forget to write down. Those are collected here, once, so that when one of them hits you in week two you have somewhere to look instead of losing an evening to it. Skim this list now; come back to it whenever a task seems to assume something nobody taught you.

**The build failed and the screen is full of text. How do I actually read a Maven error?**
Do not read the bottom — the last twenty lines (`BUILD FAILURE`, "re-run with `-e`") are the summary, never the cause. Scroll up to the **first** line that starts with `[ERROR]`. It will be one of three kinds: a *compile error* (a file path with a line number — open that exact line; it is an ordinary Java mistake), a *test failure* (`Tests run: ..., Failures: 1` — the full story is in `target/surefire-reports/`, the folder you met in [Task F7.2 — Lifecycle, exceptions, and parameterised tests](#task-f72--lifecycle-exceptions-and-parameterised-tests--1h)), or a *plugin failure* (Spotless or Checkstyle naming a file and a rule — run the fix command from [Task 0.3](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h)). If the error contains a Java stack trace, read it the way [Task F3.9 — Reading stack traces and using a debugger](#task-f39--reading-stack-traces-and-using-a-debugger--1h) taught: top frame first, then the first frame in *your* package. [Task F1.5 — Understand the build and what a jar actually is](#task-f15--understand-the-build-and-what-a-jar-actually-is--1h) explains the phases the error happened inside.

**What is an IntelliJ "run configuration", and where do settings like `-Xmx512m` actually go?**
The first time you press run on a `main` method, IntelliJ silently creates a *run configuration* — a saved recipe saying which class to start, with which JVM options, environment variables, and working directory. It appears in the dropdown next to the run button. [§5.2](#52-your-machine-and-how-to-not-melt-it) tells you to give every service `-Xmx512m` in the IDE: open **Run → Edit Configurations**, pick the service, choose **Modify options → Add VM options**, and paste it there. It is saved with the project — set it once per service and forget it.

**From Phase 2 onward there are two or three services. How do I run them all at once?**
Each service is its own run configuration, and starting a second one does not stop the first — press run on `CatalogApplication`, then on `IdentityApplication`, and both are up. Each gets its own tab in the Run window, so their logs stay separate; when something misbehaves, check *which tab* you are reading before concluding anything. The infrastructure (Postgres, Redis, Kafka) stays in Docker via `make up` from [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h); only the Java services run from the IDE, exactly as [§5.2](#52-your-machine-and-how-to-not-melt-it) prescribes. Restart only the service you are editing — the others can keep running for days. This is the unstated mechanics behind [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h), where the gateway, catalog, and identity are all alive at the same time.

**I changed the code. Does the running application pick it up when I save?**
No. A JVM loads your compiled classes at startup and keeps running those; saving a file changes the source on disk, not the process. The normal loop is: stop the service (the red square in its Run tab), press run again — a few seconds. That cheap restart is what [§5.2](#52-your-machine-and-how-to-not-melt-it) means by keeping your "feedback loop at seconds" with the service on the host: the comparison is against a 40-second Docker image rebuild, not against some magic live-apply. A library called `spring-boot-devtools` can auto-restart on rebuild; it is optional and this plan never requires it — add it later if restarting by hand starts to annoy you.

**Which service listens on which port?**
Deliberately not pinned anywhere in this document — the numbers are yours to choose, and you make the choice concrete in [Task 2.3](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h), where the gateway's routes name every service's port. Two rules keep it painless. First, decide a scheme *once* and write it in the repo `README.md` — for example gateway on 8080 and one fixed port per service after it, in the order of the [§4.4 Quick reference](#44-quick-reference) table. Second, check for squatters before assigning: your infrastructure containers hold ports too (Postgres 5432, Redis 6379, Kafka 9092, and the Schema Registry conventionally sits on 8081), and `lsof -i :<port>` from [Task F1.4 — Read the startup log, then break things on purpose](#task-f14--read-the-startup-log-then-break-things-on-purpose--05h) tells you who is holding one. Set each service's port in its own `application.yml` ([Task F6.4](#task-f64--configuration-files-and-the-precedence-order--1h)).

**Where do test files physically live, and what must they be called?**
In `src/test/java`, mirroring `src/main/java` exactly, package for package: if `Money` lives at `src/main/java/com/zenith/common/money/Money.java`, its test lives at `src/test/java/com/zenith/common/money/MoneyTest.java`. The same-package trick is why a test can see things the outside world cannot. The `*Test` suffix is not a style choice — it is what Maven's test runner (a plugin called Surefire) matches, so a test class named `MoneyChecks` compiles happily and is silently never run. IntelliJ does the layout for you: with the class open, `⌘⇧T` creates or jumps to its test. The folders were laid out in [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h); what a test is worth is [Task F7.1](#task-f71--your-first-test-and-what-makes-a-test-worth-having--1h).

**Everyone keeps saying "check the official docs". Where are they?**
Bookmark these now: Spring Boot at `docs.spring.io/spring-boot` — its appendix lists **every configuration property that exists**, which is the cure for the invented YAML keys [§0.5](#05-how-to-learn-this-by-asking-ai) warns about; Spring Framework at `docs.spring.io/spring-framework`; Postgres at `postgresql.org/docs/17/`; Kafka at `kafka.apache.org/documentation`; Redis at `redis.io/docs`. One habit: every docs site has a version picker — check it matches the version pinned in [§5 — Technology stack](#5-technology-stack) before trusting a page, because a correct answer for the wrong version is still a wrong answer.

**The appendix mentions `./mvnw`. What is that?**
The *Maven wrapper* — a tiny script committed inside a project that downloads a specific Maven version and runs it, so everyone who clones the project builds with the identical Maven without installing anything. Projects generated by `start.spring.io` include it, which is why you will see `./mvnw` in other people's READMEs. You installed real Maven via SDKMAN in [Task F1.1](#task-f11--install-java-and-maven-and-understand-what-they-are--1h), so plain `mvn` is fine everywhere in this plan — the two are interchangeable, and seeing one where you expected the other means nothing is wrong.

**IntelliJ is covered in red after I edited a `pom.xml`. Is my code broken?**
Probably not. IntelliJ keeps its *own* model of the project and does not re-read your POMs on every change — after you add a dependency or a new module, it shows a small floating Maven reload icon (or use the Maven tool window → **Reload All Maven Projects**). Until you click it, imports from the new dependency stay red even though the code is correct. The rule: touched a `pom.xml` → reload before believing anything red. And when the IDE and the terminal disagree, the terminal wins — `mvn clean verify` is the truth, as [Task F1.5](#task-f15--understand-the-build-and-what-a-jar-actually-is--1h) established; the IDE run button is a convenience.

**What does a normal working day on this plan actually look like, end to end?**
Open: start the infrastructure for your current phase — `make up` with the right profile from the [§5.2](#52-your-machine-and-how-to-not-melt-it) table — then `git switch main && git pull` and create the task's branch, exactly as the task loop in [§6.4 — Definition of done](#64-definition-of-done-applies-to-every-task-in-this-plan) prescribes. Middle: the service runs from the IDE, you poke it with your `.http` file or Swagger UI, and you commit in small pieces as things work. Close: `make ci`, push, open the PR, self-review, merge — and one line in `docs/journal.md` saying what you learned. The containers can keep running overnight, or `make down` if the fans object. Nothing here is new — it is the same task loop laid out in wall-clock order, because seeing it that way once removes the "but what do I literally type first?" feeling on day one of Phase 1.

## 1. What we are building and why this domain

**Zenith** is the backend for a live-event ticketing and order platform: organizers publish
events with seat maps and pricing; customers browse, hold seats, pay, and receive
QR-coded tickets; gate staff scan tickets at the venue.

Every technology on your list is a *forced* requirement of this domain rather than a
bolt-on. That matters enormously, because in an interview the first question after
"what did you build" is "why did you need Kafka?" — and "because I wanted to learn Kafka"
is a failed answer.

| Requirement of the domain | Technology it forces |
| --- | --- |
| Tickets go on sale at a fixed minute; traffic goes from 50 to 50,000 req/s in seconds | Caching, rate limiting, load balancing, horizontal scaling, virtual waiting room |
| Two customers must never be sold the same seat | Transactions, row locking, optimistic concurrency, distributed locks |
| Payment networks time out and clients retry | Idempotency keys, inbox/outbox, exactly-once semantics |
| An order touches inventory, payment, ticketing, and email | Microservices, Kafka, saga with compensation |
| Browsing is 95% of traffic and is read-only | Redis cache, CQRS read models, read replicas, index design |
| Organizers upload 50 MB seat-map CSVs and 10 MB banners; customers download PDFs | Object storage, presigned URLs, streaming, range requests, Spring Batch |
| Customers watch the seat map change live and their queue position tick down | WebSockets, Redis pub/sub fanout |
| Reports, reconciliation, dunning (automatically chasing failed or overdue payments), scan-log rollups run nightly | Background jobs, distributed scheduling, partitioned parallel processing |
| 1M-row imports, fan-out to 3 pricing providers, 10k live connections | Thread pools, `CompletableFuture`, producer/consumer pipelines, virtual threads |
| On-call must know within 60 seconds that checkout is broken | Structured logging, metrics, tracing, SLOs, alerting |

If you would rather a different domain, the plan transfers with only the domain phases
changed: **freight/shipment orchestration** and **insurance claims processing** both have
the same shape (high-contention inventory → documents → payouts → notifications).

---

## 2. Target outcome

By the end of the roadmap you should have:

- **9 Spring Boot services** in a Maven monorepo, each with hexagonal architecture, >75% meaningful test coverage, and Testcontainers-backed integration tests.
- **A running local production-alike** — entirely on your laptop, no cloud account anywhere: Nginx → API gateway → services → Postgres (primary + replica) → Redis → Kafka → MinIO, all on Kubernetes (via `kind`, a tool that runs a real Kubernetes cluster inside Docker — see [the local-only: what replaces what](#51-local-only-what-replaces-what)), observed by Prometheus/Grafana/Loki/Tempo.
- **A 30-level concurrency lab** (`concurrency-lab/`) taking you from your first `Thread` to diagnosing a hung JVM from a thread dump, with JMH benchmark tables and a written audit of the concurrency bugs you found in your own earlier code.
- **A performance report** with measured before/after numbers you earned yourself: p99 latency, throughput, cache hit ratio, query plans, GC pauses, thread-pool behaviour under contention.
- **A documentation set**: C4 diagrams, ~22 ADRs, OpenAPI specs, runbooks, two postmortems, and `docs/concurrency.md` with JMH benchmark tables.
- **Deep, non-memorised answers** to: "how do you prevent double-charging?", "how do you scale WebSockets?", "what does your thread pool do when the queue is full?", "walk me through a slow query you fixed."

That last bullet is the actual deliverable. The code is the evidence.

### 2.1 What those deliverables actually mean

Those bullets use industry vocabulary that only makes sense once someone shows you the
thing. Here is each one in plain language: what it is, what problem it solves, what it
looks like, and why an interviewer cares. None of these are optional extras — they are a
large part of what makes the project read as professional work rather than a tutorial,
and each one is produced incrementally by the roadmap, so you never sit down to "write
the documentation" as a separate chore.

#### Hexagonal architecture from absolute zero — read this first

The next section builds hexagonal architecture carefully, with experiments, over nine
steps. It is the best thing in this document — but it moves fast if you have never heard
any of these words before. So this section exists to hand you the *one idea* first, three
times over, in increasing precision. Read this, then read the full explainer, and the
full explainer will feel like confirmation instead of a struggle.

##### First: what is a "layer" at all?

Forget software for a second. Think about any organisation that works — a hospital, a
bank branch, a restaurant. None of them lets everyone do everything. The person who
greets you is not the person who operates on you, and the surgeon does not answer the
front-desk phone. Work is split into groups, each group does one kind of job, and each
group talks only to the groups next to it.

A **layer** in software is exactly that — a group of classes that all do the same *kind*
of job, kept apart from classes doing a different kind of job. One layer talks to
customers (HTTP, JSON). One layer makes decisions. One layer deals with storage. The
classes inside a layer are teammates; classes in different layers are different
departments.

And one more word before the story, because everything turns on it. A **dependency** is
when one piece of code names another — so if the named one changes, the one naming it can
break. (The full explainer below makes this razor-sharp in its Step 1; for now, "A
depends on B" just means "A can be broken by B".)

Now the same idea, told three ways.

##### Telling 1 — a restaurant, start to finish

Picture a restaurant. One analogy, carried all the way through — every part of it maps
onto a part of your code, and we will not switch horses halfway.

**The chef is the business rules.** Everything the restaurant is actually *for* — the
recipes, the judgement that this fish is not fresh enough to serve, the rule that no
dessert leaves the kitchen without being tasted — lives with the chef. Lose the building,
lose the furniture, keep the chef, and you still have a restaurant. Lose the chef and you
have a room with tables.

**The waiter talks to customers.** Customers arrive speaking all sorts of "languages" —
one points at the menu, one orders in rapid French, one phones ahead. The waiter absorbs
all of that and turns every version into the *same* standard kitchen ticket: table 4,
one steak, medium. The chef reads tickets. The chef never hears the French.

**The supplier delivers ingredients.** The chef writes a shopping list — "2 kg salmon,
fresh, by 7 a.m." — and a supplier fulfils it. Which supplier? The chef genuinely does
not know and does not care. The restaurant switched fish suppliers last month and the
chef found out by overhearing it. Nothing about any recipe changed.

Now the three facts that make this *hexagonal*, rather than just a restaurant:

1. **The chef never talks to customers and never drives to the market.** All contact with
   the outside world goes through go-betweens — the waiter on the way in, the supplier on
   the way out. The chef is completely surrounded, and completely protected.
2. **The chef owns both pieces of paper.** The kitchen decided the ticket format, and the
   kitchen writes the shopping list. The waiter conforms to the kitchen's ticket; the
   supplier conforms to the kitchen's list. Imagine the opposite — every supplier
   dictating its own order form, the chef filling in whatever paperwork each one demands.
   Then switching suppliers means retraining the chef. Because the kitchen owns the
   paper, switching suppliers means retraining *nobody in the kitchen*.
3. **You can swap everything except the chef.** New waiters, a phone-ordering system, a
   different supplier, a different market — the recipes stay word-for-word the same.

That is the whole architecture. Now the names, each defined in one plain clause:

- The **domain** is the business rules themselves — the chef and the recipes.
- An **interface** is a Java file that lists method signatures with no code bodies — a
  contract saying *what* will be done, silent about *how*. It is the piece of paper.
- A **port** is an interface that sits at the edge of the business logic and is *owned by
  it* — the kitchen's ticket format (incoming work) and the kitchen's shopping list
  (outgoing needs).
- An **adapter** is a class that connects one specific outside technology to a port — the
  waiter (adapts customers to the ticket) and the supplier (adapts the market to the
  shopping list).

##### Telling 2 — the same story, as Zenith

Replace the restaurant with the `catalog-service` you will build in
[Phase 1](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline).

The chef's recipe is a pricing rule: *an event needs at least one price tier before it
can be published.* That rule lives in one plain Java class — the domain.

The waiter is the REST controller. Requests arrive as HTTP and JSON — the customer's
language — and the controller translates them into one standard method call, the
kitchen-ticket format the application layer published. Here is the part to sit with:
**the class holding the pricing rule has no idea whether the call came from a web request
or from a test.** Both walk in through the same door, as the same method call. That is
why, later, your domain tests will run in under a millisecond with no Spring and no
database — a test is just one more "customer", and the chef cannot tell customers apart.

The supplier is the persistence adapter. The business logic writes a shopping list — an
interface saying `findById`, `save` — and something on the outside fulfils it. **The
pricing rule does not know whether seats live in Postgres or in a `HashMap`.** In real
runs a JPA adapter fulfils the list against Postgres; in tests a twenty-line in-memory
class fulfils the same list from a map. The rule cannot tell, because the rule only ever
reads its own piece of paper.

##### Telling 3 — the same story, as code

Three tiny classes. This is a sketch, not the real Phase 1 code — but it is the complete
shape.

```java
// 1 — the DOMAIN: one class, one rule, zero imports from any framework.
public class Event {
    private final List<PriceTier> tiers;
    private EventStatus status;

    public void publish() {
        if (tiers.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("an event needs at least one price tier");
        }
        this.status = EventStatus.PUBLISHED;
    }
}
```
*Its job: hold the rule. This is the chef — the only class here that is genuinely yours.*

```java
// 2 — the PORT: an interface the business side owns. Note what is absent:
//     no SQL, no JPA, no mention of any database. Just needs.
public interface EventRepository {
    Optional<Event> findById(EventId id);
    void save(Event event);
}
```
*Its job: be the shopping list — the business logic's statement of what it needs,
written in its own package, in its own vocabulary.*

```java
// 3 — the ADAPTER: one class on the outside that fulfils the list. Today: a map.
public class InMemoryEventRepository implements EventRepository {
    private final Map<EventId, Event> store = new HashMap<>();

    public Optional<Event> findById(EventId id) { return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(id)); }
    public void save(Event event)               { store.put(event.id(), event); }
}
```
*Its job: be one supplier among many. Tomorrow a `JpaEventRepository` fulfils the same
interface against Postgres — and classes 1 and 2 do not change by a character.*

Count the direction of knowledge: the adapter names the interface, the interface serves
the domain, and the domain names nobody outside itself. All knowledge points inward,
toward the rule.

##### The one test of understanding

You understand hexagonal architecture when you can answer this honestly:

> **Could you swap Postgres for a plain text file and change zero lines of business
> code?** You would write one new adapter — a class that fulfils `EventRepository` by
> reading and writing a file — and touch nothing else. If yes, it is hexagonal. If the
> swap would force edits inside the rule classes, it is not — whatever the folder names
> say.

##### Why anyone bothers — one line

Your business rules are the only part of the system that is *yours*; everything else —
Postgres, Spring, Kafka, JSON — is replaceable machinery, so you arrange the code to
protect the one part that is yours from all the parts that are not.

##### New words from this section

| Word | Meaning in one line |
| --- | --- |
| **Layer** | A group of classes that all do the same kind of job, kept apart from other kinds |
| **Dependency** | A names B, so a change in B can break A |
| **Domain** | The business rules themselves — the chef and the recipes |
| **Interface** | A contract of method signatures with no bodies — *what*, never *how* |
| **Port** | An interface at the edge of the business logic, owned by the business logic |
| **Adapter** | A class connecting one outside technology (HTTP, Postgres, Kafka) to a port |

##### Now read the full explainer below — every step of it is this same idea, proven with experiments.

[The full explainer](#hexagonal-architecture-also-called-ports-and-adapters) takes
nothing on faith: it renames a database column and shows you exactly which files break
and why, it will recast "who protects whom" as a landlord and a tenant and as a factory
upstream of a village on a river — both are this section's chef, wearing different
clothes — and its
[Step 4](#step-4-the-trick--move-the-interface-not-just-create-one) names the single
precise mechanical move (*which package owns the interface* — the kitchen owns the
paper) that makes all of it real. Everything you just read is the map; the explainer
below is the territory. Go.
