#### Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command — 3h

**What:** Install the toolchain and get a one-command local infrastructure stack running.
**Why:** Every later phase assumes Postgres, Redis, Kafka, and MinIO are a `make up` away.
**Solves:** "works on my machine" drift, and the 20 minutes a day you would otherwise lose starting services by hand.

**Learn this first:** what a container is and is not (it is not a virtual machine — ask AI
to explain the difference in terms of the kernel); why a Compose file needs named volumes
if you want your data to survive a restart; the difference between a volume (Docker's
folder, for data the container owns) and a bind mount (your folder, for config files you
edit); what a healthcheck does and why `depends_on` without one is a common source of
flaky startup.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Image** | A frozen, read-only recipe for a program and everything it needs to run. `postgres:17-alpine` is an image. You download it once. |
| **Container** | A running copy of an image. You can start ten containers from one image, and they do not see each other's files. |
| **Volume** | A folder Docker manages that lives *outside* the container, so your database still has its data after the container is deleted. Without one, `docker compose down` throws your data away. |
| **Bind mount** | A folder or file on *your* machine mapped into a container. A volume is Docker-managed, for data the container owns; a bind mount is for files **you** need to edit on the host — the `nginx.conf` you will tune in Phase 10 and the Grafana dashboards you will edit in Phase 11 both reach their containers this way. |
| **Healthcheck** | A command Docker runs inside a container every few seconds to decide whether it is genuinely ready. A Postgres process that has started is not the same as a Postgres that will accept connections. |
| **`depends_on`** | Tells Compose to start B after A. On its own it waits only for the *process* to exist, not to be ready — which is why it causes flaky startup unless you pair it with a healthcheck. |
| **`.env` file** | A git-ignored `KEY=value` file Compose reads automatically. Writing `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` in the compose file makes Compose fill in the value from `.env`, so the credential never sits in a committed file. |
| **Restart policy** | What Docker does when a container exits. `restart: unless-stopped` brings it back after a crash, a Docker restart, or a reboot — unless you stopped it yourself. The default, `no`, never restarts anything, which is exactly right for a job that is supposed to run once and exit. |
| **Compose profile** | A label on a service so you can start a subset of them. `--profile core` brings up Postgres and Redis without the six other containers you do not need today. |
| **Makefile** | A file of named shortcuts. `make up` runs whatever commands you listed under `up:`. The recipe lines must begin with a real tab character, not spaces — this will bite you exactly once. |
| **KRaft** | Kafka's built-in way of managing its own cluster metadata. Older Kafka setups needed a separate ZooKeeper service; KRaft removes it, so you run one container instead of two. |
| **MinIO** | A program that speaks Amazon S3's API but runs on your laptop. Your code talks to it exactly as it would to real S3. |
| **Mailpit** | A fake SMTP server. It accepts email your app sends and shows it in a web page instead of delivering it to a real person. |
| **Schema Registry** | A small service that stores the agreed shape (schema) of every Kafka message, so programs writing and reading them cannot drift apart. Today you only need it to start; [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) teaches what it does. |
| **`mc`** | MinIO's command-line client. The bootstrap container runs it once at startup to create your first bucket. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** that **one command** brings the whole stack up from nothing. You will run this hundreds of times, and every second of friction here is multiplied by the twenty-five weeks that follow.
- **When it works you will see:** `make up` starting Postgres, Redis, Kafka, Schema Registry, MinIO and Mailpit, and `make reset` returning you to a clean slate.
- **Where people get stuck:** RAM. Six containers on a laptop is real memory pressure — check [§5.2 — Your machine, and how to not melt it](#52-your-machine-and-how-to-not-melt-it) before you start. If Docker keeps killing containers, raise its memory limit or run only the services the current phase needs.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Install Java and Maven through SDKMAN.**
    *What this step is:* SDKMAN is a small command-line tool that installs Java tools for you and lets you switch between versions. You will use it to install Java 21 and Maven, and then pin the exact Java version to this repository so the project always builds with the same Java — on your machine and on anyone else's. At the end of this step, `java` and `mvn` work in your terminal and the version is written down in the repo.
    *Builds on:* [Task F1.1 — Install Java and Maven, and understand what they are](#task-f11--install-java-and-maven-and-understand-what-they-are--1h) — you installed a JDK and Maven there and learned what each one is; this time you install them through a version manager so the exact version is pinned to this project instead of being whatever your machine happens to have.
    *Do this:*
    1. Install SDKMAN by running the one-line install command from sdkman.io, then open a fresh terminal so the `sdk` command exists.
    2. Run `sdk list java` and scan the list for the newest **21.x** build from **Temurin** (the vendor column shows `tem` — Temurin is a free, widely used build of Java).
    3. Run `sdk install java <that exact version>` — type the full version string exactly as the list shows it.
    4. Run `sdk install maven`.
    5. Create a file called `.sdkmanrc` in the root of the repo containing a line like `java=<that exact version>`. This pins the version **per-directory**: anyone who enters this folder and runs `sdk env` gets exactly this Java, no matter what else is on their machine.
    *You know it worked when:* `java -version` prints a 21.x version and `mvn -version` prints a Maven version that says it is running on that same Java.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Install Docker and the rest of the toolbox.**
    *What this step is:* You install the container runtime plus nine small command-line tools in one sitting. Several of them you will not touch for weeks — `kind` and `helm` not until [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline), and `async-profiler` not until [Phase 12 — the concurrency track](#phase-12-deliverables) — but you install them **now** so those phases are about the work, not about installation problems. At the end of this step every tool answers a version command.
    *Builds on:* [Task F1.2 — Install Docker, the IDE, and the small tools](#task-f12--install-docker-the-ide-and-the-small-tools--1h) — you installed Docker and a few small tools there; this step completes the full project toolbox.
    *Do this:*
    1. Install **OrbStack** (or Docker Desktop if you prefer) — this is what actually runs your containers on the Mac.
    2. Install the command-line tools, e.g. with Homebrew: `kind` (runs a whole Kubernetes cluster inside Docker — used in [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline)), `kubectl` (the command that talks to Kubernetes), `helm` (a package manager for Kubernetes apps — also Phase 13), `k6` (a load-testing tool that hammers your API on purpose), `jq` (slices JSON on the command line), `httpie` (a friendlier `curl`), `websocat` (like `curl`, but for WebSockets), `pgcli` (a nicer Postgres shell with autocomplete).
    3. Install `async-profiler` (a tool that shows you exactly where a running Java program spends its CPU — used in [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner)) by following its README; it is a download, not a brew formula, on most setups.
    *You know it worked when:* `docker ps` runs without an error, and each tool prints a version (`kind version`, `kubectl version --client`, `helm version`, `k6 version`, and so on).

- [ ] **Step 3 — Build the Compose file one service at a time.**
    *What this step is:* You write the single Compose file that defines all six infrastructure services this project runs on. The discipline that matters: add **one** service, start it, prove it works, and only then add the next. Adding all six at once and then debugging is the slow path. At the end of this step all six services start from one file.
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.9 — Compose, and your first Dockerfile](#task-f79--compose-and-your-first-dockerfile--15h) — you already wrote a small Compose file that started Postgres and Redis together with one command; this is the same idea grown to six services. [Task F7.8 — Docker: images, containers, ports, and volumes](#task-f78--docker-images-containers-ports-and-volumes--15h) — you learned there what images, containers, ports and volumes are; every line you write here uses those four ideas.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `deploy/compose/docker-compose.infra.yml`.
    2. Add **Postgres 17** first. Start it with `docker compose -f deploy/compose/docker-compose.infra.yml up -d` and prove you can connect (e.g. with `pgcli` or `psql`) before touching the file again.
    3. Add **Redis 7**. Start the stack again; `redis-cli ping` inside the container should answer `PONG`.
    4. Add **Kafka in KRaft mode** — KRaft (from the New words table above) means Kafka manages its own cluster metadata, so you run one Kafka container and **no** separate ZooKeeper container.
    5. Add **Schema Registry** — the small service that stores the agreed shape of every Kafka message so writers and readers cannot drift apart. Today it only needs to start; [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) teaches what it actually does.
    6. Add **MinIO** (speaks Amazon S3's API on your laptop) plus an **`mc` bootstrap container** — `mc` is MinIO's command-line client; this extra container runs once at startup to create your first bucket, then exits. That exit is normal.
    7. Add **Mailpit** — the fake SMTP server that catches every email your app sends and shows it on a local web page instead of delivering it to a real person.
    *You know it worked when:* `docker compose -f deploy/compose/docker-compose.infra.yml up -d` brings up all six services, `docker ps` shows them running, and the `mc` bootstrap container has exited with code 0 after creating the bucket.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Volumes, healthchecks, a network, and a restart policy for every service.**
    *What this step is:* Four settings that every service in the file gets, so the stack keeps its data, knows when it is genuinely ready, lets containers find each other by name, and comes back on its own after a crash. Each setting was defined in the New words table above — this step is where you actually apply them. At the end, the stack survives restarts without losing data or needing you.
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.8 — Docker: images, containers, ports, and volumes](#task-f78--docker-images-containers-ports-and-volumes--15h) — you learned there that a container's own filesystem is thrown away with the container, which is exactly why volumes exist.
    *Do this:*
    1. Give every service a **named volume** for its data, so `docker compose down` does not throw your database away.
    2. Give every service a **healthcheck** — a command Docker runs inside the container every few seconds to decide whether it is genuinely ready, not merely started.
    3. Put all services on one **fixed, explicitly named network**, so containers can reach each other by service name (your app will connect to host `postgres`, not an IP address).
    4. Set `restart: unless-stopped` on every long-running service — a stack you will lean on daily for the next twenty-five weeks should come back by itself after a crash, a Docker restart, or a reboot, instead of greeting every Monday with connection refused.
    5. **One exception:** leave the `mc` bootstrap container on the default `restart: no`. It runs once and exits on purpose, and a restart policy would turn a finished job into an infinite loop.
    *You know it worked when:* you create a throwaway table in Postgres, run `docker compose down` then `up -d`, and the table is still there; `docker ps` shows `(healthy)` next to each long-running service; and after restarting Docker itself, everything except `mc` comes back without you touching anything.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Make `make up` mean ready, not merely started.**
    *What this step is:* `depends_on` on its own only waits for the other container's *process* to exist — not for it to actually accept connections. The fix is to pair `depends_on` with the healthchecks from Step 4, using `condition: service_healthy`, so dependent services wait for genuine readiness. At the end of this step, nothing in the stack starts against a dependency that is not actually ready. (Until Step 9 gives you the Makefile, run the raw `docker compose -f deploy/compose/docker-compose.infra.yml ...` commands wherever this step says `make`.)
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.9 — Compose, and your first Dockerfile](#task-f79--compose-and-your-first-dockerfile--15h) — this is the F7.9 lesson (`depends_on` alone waits for a process to exist, not for it to be ready) applied to the real stack.
    *Do this:*
    1. Copy this shape for Postgres into your Compose file:

    ```yaml
    postgres:
      healthcheck:
        test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]   # use your POSTGRES_USER if you set one
        interval: 5s
        timeout: 3s
        retries: 10
    # Redis: redis-cli ping · Kafka: kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list
    schema-registry:
      depends_on:
        kafka:
          condition: service_healthy
    ```

    2. Now write the **Redis** equivalent yourself — the test command is `redis-cli ping`.
    3. Write the **Kafka** equivalent yourself — the test command is `kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list`.
    4. Make sure `schema-registry` depends on `kafka` with `condition: service_healthy`, exactly as in the block above — Schema Registry is the service most likely to crash against a Kafka that exists but is not ready yet.
    *You know it worked when:* a full teardown and cold start (`make reset && make up`, or the raw compose equivalents) comes up green every single time, with no service crash-looping while it waits for another.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Break it on purpose: Schema Registry versus an unready Kafka.**
    *What this step is:* You remove the readiness condition and watch the failure you just prevented actually happen, so you recognise it instantly the next time you see it in the wild. At the end of this step the condition is back in place and you have seen, with your own eyes, why it exists.
    *Builds on:* Step 5 above — the `condition: service_healthy` line you are about to delete is the one you just wrote there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Delete the `condition: service_healthy` line under `schema-registry` → `depends_on` → `kafka` (leave the rest in place).
    2. Run `make reset && make up` (or the raw compose equivalents until the Makefile exists in Step 9).
    3. Watch Schema Registry fall over against a Kafka that exists but is not ready yet — `docker compose logs schema-registry` shows the connection failures, and `docker ps` may show it restarting.
    4. Put the `condition:` line back and confirm a clean cold start again.
    *You know it worked when:* with the line deleted you saw Schema Registry fail at startup, and with the line restored the whole stack comes up cleanly from cold.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Rehearse bind mounts with a throwaway nginx proxy.**
    *What this step is:* A bind mount maps a file on *your* Mac into a container, so you can edit the file on the host and the container sees the change instantly — no rebuild, no copy step. You rehearse it now, with a five-minute throwaway web server, because [Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline) and [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline) silently depend on this exact edit-on-host, reload-in-container loop — you will tune this same `nginx.conf` in Phase 10 and edit Grafana dashboards (Grafana is the metrics-dashboard tool arriving in Phase 11) the same way. nginx itself is a small, very common web server and proxy — here it only has to return one line of text.
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.8 — Docker: images, containers, ports, and volumes](#task-f78--docker-images-containers-ports-and-volumes--15h) — you learned named volumes there (Docker's folder, for data the container owns); a bind mount is the other half of that pair (your folder, for files you edit).
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `deploy/compose/nginx/nginx.conf` containing one server block that returns a fixed text response — ask AI for the smallest valid one.
    2. Run a throwaway proxy with the file bind-mounted: `docker run -d --name proxy -p 8088:80 -v "$PWD/deploy/compose/nginx/nginx.conf":/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro nginx:alpine`
    3. `curl localhost:8088` and read the response text.
    4. Change the response text in the file **on your Mac**, in your normal editor.
    5. Run `docker exec proxy nginx -s reload` to tell nginx to re-read its config.
    6. `curl localhost:8088` again — the container sees your edit with no rebuild and no copy step.
    7. State the rule in `docs/local-setup.md` (create the file now if it does not exist — Step 11 fills it out properly): *named volume for data the container owns, bind mount for files you edit*.
    8. Clean up with `docker rm -f proxy`.
    *You know it worked when:* the second `curl` shows your edited text without any container rebuild or restart, and after cleanup `docker ps` no longer lists `proxy`.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Move every credential out of the compose file into `.env`.**
    *What this step is:* Passwords do not belong in a file that gets committed to git. Compose automatically reads a file named `.env` sitting next to the compose file, and fills in `${PLACEHOLDERS}` from it. At the end of this step the compose YAML contains no literal passwords, and the `.env` file holding them is git-ignored.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create a `.env` file beside the compose file containing `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev` plus the MinIO root user and password.
    2. In the compose YAML, replace each literal credential with a reference like `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}`.
    3. Make sure `.env` is listed in `.gitignore` so git never tracks it.
    4. Prove the substitution worked with `docker compose config` — it prints the fully rendered file, placeholders replaced with real values.
    5. Be honest about what this buys: `.env` keeps credentials out of git — it is **convenience, not secrecy**, because anyone with your laptop can read the file. The real secret stores arrive in [Task 2.4 — Application security hardening and auditing](#task-24--application-security-hardening-and-auditing--3h) — where secret and dependency scanning get wired into CI — and [Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies](#task-133--scaling-configuration-and-deployment-strategies--8h) — where Kubernetes-grade configuration handling arrives. And [Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h) adds a gitleaks scan — the net that catches the day you forget and paste a credential into a tracked file.
    *You know it worked when:* `docker compose config` prints the rendered file with real values filled in, the YAML itself contains only `${...}` placeholders, and `git status` never offers `.env` as a file to commit.

- [ ] **Step 9 — Add Compose profiles so daily work stays light.**
    *What this step is:* A profile is a label on a service that lets you start only a subset of the stack. Six containers on a laptop is real memory pressure, and most days you only need Postgres and Redis. At the end of this step you can choose how much of the stack to run. See [§5.2 — Your machine, and how to not melt it](#52-your-machine-and-how-to-not-melt-it) for the memory numbers on your machine.
    *Builds on:* Step 3 above — the six services you are now putting labels on.
    *Do this:*
    1. Define the profile names `core`, `events`, `media`, `observe`, `edge`, and `full` in the compose file.
    2. Assign today's services to the profiles that fit — `core` gets Postgres and Redis, `events` gets Kafka and Schema Registry, `media` gets MinIO and its `mc` bootstrap. `observe` and `edge` exist now but get their services in later phases; `full` means everything.
    3. Test it: `docker compose --profile core up -d` should start only Postgres and Redis.
    *You know it worked when:* starting with `--profile core` brings up exactly two containers, and starting with the full set brings up all six.

- [ ] **Step 10 — Write the Makefile: one short name per operation.**
    *What this step is:* A Makefile is a file of named shortcuts — `make up` runs whatever commands you listed under the `up:` target. You create one target per operation you will do daily, so nobody ever has to remember a long `docker compose -f ...` incantation. At the end of this step, every stack operation is one short command.
    *Builds on:* Steps 3–9 above — each target simply wraps the compose commands and profiles you have already proven work by hand.
    *Do this:*
    1. Before writing a single line, ask AI to explain Makefile tab-versus-space rules — recipe lines must begin with a real tab character, not spaces — so you hit this *before* your first "missing separator" error rather than after.
    2. Write targets: `up`, `down`, `reset` (down **and** wipe volumes), `logs`, `psql`, `redis-cli`, `topics`, `test`, `fmt` — plus `smoke` and `seed` as do-nothing placeholder targets for now.
    3. Make `up` accept an optional `profile=<name>` pass-through variable, forwarded as `docker compose --profile $(profile)`, so `make up profile=core` works.
    4. Know that `seed` will later take a `scale=<small|full>` variable (that arrives in [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h), where you generate millions of rows) — so the commands quoted in [§2.1 — What those deliverables actually mean](#21-what-those-deliverables-actually-mean) — `make up profile=core && make seed scale=full` — work as written.
    *You know it worked when:* `make up profile=core` starts only Postgres and Redis, `make psql` drops you into a database shell, and `make reset && make up` gives you a clean, healthy stack.

- [ ] **Step 11 — Understand that this Makefile grows with the project.**
    *What this step is:* Not a coding step — a mental-model step. The Makefile is the one place anyone (including future you) looks to find out how to run things, and over the next twenty-five weeks it keeps gaining targets. Keeping every operation behind a named target is exactly why `docs/local-setup.md` can stay short.
    *Builds on:* Step 10 above — the file whose future you are now mapping out.
    *Do this:*
    1. Read your Makefile top to bottom and say out loud what each target does.
    2. Note (a comment in the file is fine) which placeholders become real later: `smoke` becomes real in [Task 1.11 — The Testcontainers harness and test data builders](#task-111--the-testcontainers-harness-and-test-data-builders--1h), `ci` in [Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline](#task-04--git-workflow-the-remote-and-a-local-ci-pipeline--2h), `seed` in [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h), `cd` in [Task 13.4 — CI/CD pipeline](#task-134--cicd-pipeline--7h), and `demo` in [Task 14.3 — Demo path and interview preparation](#task-143--demo-path-and-interview-preparation--5h).
    *You know it worked when:* for any "how do I run X?" question about this project, your answer is `make <something>` — without opening the compose file to check.

- [ ] **Step 12 — Write `docs/local-setup.md`, then prove it from scratch.**
    *What this step is:* You write the setup document a brand-new teammate would follow on day one — and then you *become* that teammate: wipe everything and follow your own instructions with no memory allowed. If it does not work, the document is wrong, not you. At the end of this step the document is proven, not merely written.
    *Builds on:* Every step above — the document describes the stack and Makefile you just built, including the volume-versus-bind-mount rule you stated in Step 7.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write `docs/local-setup.md`: which tools to install (Steps 1–2), the one command that brings the stack up, and where to find each service.
    2. Wipe **all volumes** — `make reset` (or `docker compose down -v`).
    3. Follow your own document from the top, doing only what it says, resisting every urge to fill gaps from memory.
    4. Every time you hit a gap or a wrong instruction, fix the document, wipe, and start again.
    *You know it worked when:* following only the document, from wiped volumes, ends in a fully healthy stack — which is also most of this task's Done-when: `make reset && make up` healthy in under 90 seconds, and `make psql` opens a shell.

**Done when:** `make reset && make up` gives you a healthy stack in under 90 seconds, `make psql` opens a shell, and you can explain what each of the six services is for.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. What is the difference between an image, a container, and a volume? Which of the three survives `docker compose down`?
2. Why is `depends_on` on its own not enough to stop your application starting before Postgres can accept connections?
3. You run `make up` and Kafka never becomes healthy. Name the first three things you check, in order.
4. Why does this project run Kafka in KRaft mode rather than with ZooKeeper?
5. Someone deletes your `docker-compose.infra.yml`. Which six services would you have to put back, and what is each one for?
6. You edit `nginx.conf` on your Mac and the proxy container sees the change with no rebuild. What mechanism makes that work, and when is a named volume the right choice instead?
7. Why does the `mc` bootstrap container keep `restart: no` while the long-running services get `unless-stopped`?
8. Your database password lives in `.env`. Why is that fine for this repo and not for production — and which two later tasks hold the production answer?

#### Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton — 1.5h

**What:** A parent POM, shared `platform-*` modules, and one empty service that builds.
**Why:** A multi-module layout is how Java monorepos share code without publishing artifacts. Getting the shape right now means adding service #2 is a five-minute job.
**Solves:** copy-pasted utility classes drifting out of sync across services, and dependency versions differing between modules.

**Learn this first:** ask AI *"explain the difference between `dependencyManagement` and `dependencies` in a Maven parent POM, and what a BOM is"*. This single distinction causes more Maven confusion than anything else.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **POM** | `pom.xml`, the Project Object Model. The file where Maven reads what your project is called, what it depends on, and how to build it. |
| **Parent POM** | A POM other POMs inherit from. It has `<packaging>pom</packaging>` because it produces no jar of its own — it exists to hold shared settings. |
| **Module** | One sub-project inside the repository. `platform-common` and `catalog-service` are modules; the parent lists them and builds them together. |
| **`dependencies`** | The libraries this module actually uses. Each one ends up on the classpath. |
| **`dependencyManagement`** | A section that says "*if* anyone uses this library, use this version" — without adding it to the classpath. This is how you write a version number once instead of in nine modules. |
| **BOM (Bill of Materials)** | A published POM that is nothing but a big `dependencyManagement` block. Importing `spring-boot-dependencies` means Spring has already chosen mutually compatible versions of 400 libraries for you. |
| **Transitive dependency** | A library you did not ask for, pulled in because something you *did* ask for needs it. Most of your classpath is transitive. |
| **Reactor** | Maven's name for the multi-module build. It works out the order by reading which module depends on which — you never specify the order yourself. |
| **`-parameters`** | A compiler flag that keeps your method parameter names in the compiled `.class` file. Spring needs them later to match constructor arguments; without it you get confusing startup failures. |
| **`.editorconfig`** | A small file every mainstream editor reads, fixing indentation and line endings so a teammate's editor does not reformat your file. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** module boundaries and the fact that **dependencies point one way**. `platform-common` must never depend on a service. Getting this wrong now is painful to unwind in [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline), when services start sharing events.
- **When it works you will see:** `mvn -B clean verify` building three modules in dependency order, and `curl localhost:8080/actuator/health` returning `UP`.
- **Where people get stuck:** version numbers scattered across module POMs. Declare them once in the parent's `dependencyManagement` and never write a version in a child module again — drifting versions between services is a genuinely nasty class of bug.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Create the parent POM.**
    *What this step is:* You create one `pom.xml` at the root of the repository that every other module inherits from. It produces no jar of its own — its whole job is to hold shared settings and, crucially, dependency **versions**, written once instead of in nine modules. At the end of this step the root of the repo has a parent POM that Maven accepts.
    *Builds on:* [Task F1.5 — Understand the build and what a jar actually is](#task-f15--understand-the-build-and-what-a-jar-actually-is--1h) — you learned there what Maven's lifecycle phases do and what a jar is; this POM is where those phases now get configured. [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — the SDKMAN-installed Java 21 and Maven from there are what will run this build.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `pom.xml` at the repo root with `<packaging>pom</packaging>` — this marks it as a parent that builds no jar itself.
    2. Import the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM inside a `<dependencyManagement>` section (with `<type>pom</type>` and `<scope>import</scope>`). This is the move the Learn-this-first question was about: Spring has already chosen mutually compatible versions of about 400 libraries, and importing the BOM means you inherit all of those choices without putting a single extra library on the classpath.
    3. Set `<maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>` and the UTF-8 encoding property (`project.build.sourceEncoding`).
    4. Add the `-parameters` compiler flag to the compiler plugin configuration — it keeps your method parameter names inside the compiled `.class` files, and Spring needs them later to match constructor arguments; without it you get confusing startup failures.
    *You know it worked when:* `mvn -B clean verify` at the repo root runs and succeeds (it builds almost nothing yet — the point is that Maven parses and accepts your parent POM).

- [ ] **Step 2 — Create the two shared platform modules.**
    *What this step is:* You create the two modules every service will share: `platform-common` for shared value types and the error contract (the one agreed JSON shape every service returns when something goes wrong), and `platform-testing` for test base classes, fixtures, and the ArchUnit suite (ArchUnit is a library that writes unit tests over your architecture rules — it gets wired up in [Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h)). Both can be nearly empty today — what matters is that they exist, build, and sit in the right place. Remember the Focus rule: dependencies point **one way** — `platform-common` must never depend on a service.
    *Builds on:* Step 1 above — both modules declare the parent POM you just wrote as their parent, which is how they inherit its versions and settings.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `platform-common/` with its own small `pom.xml` that names the root POM as its `<parent>`.
    2. Create `platform-testing/` the same way.
    3. List both in the parent POM's `<modules>` section so Maven builds them as part of the repo.
    *You know it worked when:* `mvn -B clean verify` from the root now builds both platform modules without errors.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Create `catalog-service`, service 1 of nine.**
    *What this step is:* You create the first real service module, at `services/catalog-service`. This is **service 1 of nine**, and the one every later service is copied from — so take the structure seriously here: a sloppy layout now gets photocopied eight times. At the end of this step the module exists and is part of the build.
    *Builds on:* Step 1 above — it inherits the parent POM; Step 2 above — it depends on `platform-common` (one-way: the service depends on platform, never the reverse).
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `services/catalog-service/` with a `pom.xml` that names the root POM as its `<parent>` and declares a dependency on `platform-common` — with **no version number**, because the parent manages versions.
    2. Add `services/catalog-service` to the parent's `<modules>` list.
    3. Lay out the standard Maven source folders (`src/main/java`, `src/main/resources`, `src/test/java`) with a sensible base package.
    *You know it worked when:* `mvn -B clean verify` from the root lists `catalog-service` in the build and it compiles.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Make catalog-service a runnable Spring Boot app.**
    *What this step is:* You turn the empty module into an application that actually starts and can report its own health over HTTP. Nothing else yet — no endpoints, no database, no business logic. One running service with a health check is the whole deliverable.
    *Builds on:* [Task F1.3 — Your first Spring Boot application](#task-f13--your-first-spring-boot-application--15h) — you built a from-scratch Spring Boot app there; this is the same move, inside the multi-module build. Step 1 above — the imported BOM is why the next action needs no version numbers.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add `spring-boot-starter-web` and `spring-boot-starter-actuator` to `catalog-service`'s dependencies — **without version numbers**; the BOM you imported in Step 1 supplies them.
    2. Write the main class annotated with `@SpringBootApplication`.
    3. Start it (`mvn spring-boot:run` from the module, or run the main class from your IDE).
    4. In another terminal: `curl localhost:8080/actuator/health`.
    *You know it worked when:* the curl returns `{"status":"UP"}`.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Add editor and git hygiene files.**
    *What this step is:* Three small files that stop avoidable mess: `.editorconfig` fixes indentation and line endings so a teammate's editor does not reformat your files; `.gitattributes` tells git how to normalise line endings; `.gitignore` keeps build output and secrets out of version control. At the end of this step, git only ever sees files that belong in the repo.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — the git-ignored `.env` file holding your local credentials was created there, and this `.gitignore` is what keeps it out of the repo for good.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `.editorconfig` at the repo root (indentation style and size, line endings, final newline).
    2. Create `.gitattributes` (e.g. `* text=auto` to normalise line endings).
    3. Create `.gitignore` covering at least: `target/` (Maven's build output), IDE folders (such as `.idea/`), and `.env`.
    *You know it worked when:* `git status` shows none of `target/`, your IDE's folders, or `.env` — even right after a build.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Build everything and read the reactor order.**
    *What this step is:* The reactor is Maven's name for the multi-module build: it reads which module depends on which and works out the build order itself — you never specify the order anywhere. You run the full build and consciously read that order, because understanding *why* it is what it is cements the whole module-dependency picture.
    *Builds on:* Steps 1–4 above — the parent and three modules you just created are exactly what the reactor is about to order and build.
    *Do this:*
    1. Run `mvn -B clean verify` from the repo root.
    2. Find the "Reactor Summary" in the output and watch the module build order — the platform modules build before `catalog-service`, because it depends on them.
    3. Ask AI why Maven chose that order, and check its answer against what you just saw.
    *You know it worked when:* the build succeeds from the root, all three modules appear in the reactor summary in dependency order, and you can explain in one sentence what determined that order — which is this task's Done-when, minus the health-check curl you already proved in Step 4.

**Done when:** `mvn -B clean verify` succeeds from the repo root, builds three modules, and `curl localhost:8080/actuator/health` returns `UP`.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. What is the difference between `dependencyManagement` and `dependencies`? What happens if a library appears in both with different versions?
2. What is a BOM, and why does importing `spring-boot-dependencies` mean you stop writing version numbers?
3. Maven built your three modules in a specific order. What determined that order?
4. Why does `platform-common` not depend on `catalog-service`? What would break if you added that dependency?
5. What is a transitive dependency, and how would you find out why some library you never asked for is on your classpath?

#### Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build — 1.5h

**What:** Formatting, static analysis, coverage, and architecture rules wired into `mvn verify`.
**Why:** Gates added later are negotiated away ("we'll fix the warnings next sprint"). Gates added on day one are free, because there is no existing code to fix.
**Solves:** inconsistent formatting, silent coverage decay, and architecture erosion — the three things that make a two-year-old codebase unpleasant.

**Learn this first:** the difference between a *formatter* (rewrites your code — Spotless),
a *linter* (complains about style — Checkstyle), a *coverage tool* (measures which lines
tests executed — JaCoCo), and an *architecture test* (asserts structural rules — ArchUnit).
They are four different jobs and beginners routinely conflate them.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Formatter** | A tool that *rewrites* your code into a standard shape. Spotless with google-java-format. You stop having opinions about line breaks and get the time back. |
| **Linter** | A tool that *complains* without rewriting. Checkstyle. It catches things a formatter cannot, like a method with twelve branches. |
| **Coverage** | The percentage of your code that ran while the tests ran. JaCoCo measures it. It tells you what is definitely untested; it cannot tell you what is well tested. |
| **Line vs branch coverage** | Line coverage asks "did this line execute?". Branch coverage asks "did both the true *and* false sides of this `if` execute?". Branch is the harder and more honest number. |
| **Ratchet** | A threshold that can only go up. You start at 60% and raise it; the build fails if coverage drops below the best you have achieved. It stops slow decay without demanding a number you cannot hit yet. |
| **ArchUnit** | A library that writes tests about your *structure* rather than your behaviour — "nothing in `domain` may import Spring". Rules a human reviewer forgets, a test never does. |
| **Maven Enforcer** | A plugin that fails the build on environment problems: two copies of the same class, a Maven version that is too old, a snapshot dependency that should never have been committed. |
| **Build phase** | A named step in Maven's fixed sequence — `validate`, `compile`, `test`, `package`, `verify`, `install`. Binding a plugin to a phase means "run this tool at that point". |
| **Star import** | `import java.util.*;` instead of naming each class. Banned because it hides where a class came from and silently breaks when two packages gain a same-named class. |
| **Cyclomatic complexity** | A count of the independent paths through a method — roughly, one plus the number of branches. Above about 12 nobody can hold the method in their head, including you in a month. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** that a gate only works if it **fails the build**. A warning nobody reads is not a quality gate, and this is the difference between the habit being real and being decorative.
- **When it works you will see:** a deliberately badly-formatted file, an uncovered class, and a planted fake secret each turning the build red — you should *see* all three fail.
- **Where people get stuck:** setting a coverage target so high that you write meaningless tests to reach it. Pick a floor that stops regression, not a number that becomes theatre. And never add a blanket exclusion to make a gate pass.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Spotless: the formatter that fails the build.**
    *What this step is:* You wire Spotless — the *formatter* from the New words table, the tool that rewrites code into one standard shape using google-java-format — into Maven, so that badly formatted code fails `mvn verify` before anything even compiles. You bind it to the `validate` phase (the very first step in Maven's fixed build sequence — see *Build phase* in the New words table), so the failure is instant instead of arriving after a long test run. At the end you have a build that rejects wrong formatting and a one-word command that fixes it.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — you wrote the `Makefile` there, with `fmt` listed as a target; this step gives it its real job. [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — you created the parent `pom.xml` there; a plugin added to the parent applies to every module at once, which is why every gate in this task goes into the parent and never into an individual module.
    *Do this:*
    1. In the parent `pom.xml`, inside `<build><plugins>`, add the `spotless-maven-plugin` configured with `<googleJavaFormat/>`, and bind its `check` goal to the `validate` phase. Ask AI for the exact XML, then read it line by line until you can say what each element does.
    2. Run `mvn spotless:apply` once from the repo root — it rewrites every existing file into the standard shape. You stop having opinions about line breaks, and you get the time back.
    3. In the `Makefile`, make the `fmt` target run `mvn spotless:apply`, so fixing formatting is always just `make fmt`.
    4. Commit the whole-repo reformat **as its own commit** (for example `style: apply google-java-format to entire repo`). Never mix a reformat into a feature commit — it buries the real change under a thousand whitespace lines, and the diff becomes unreviewable.
    *You know it worked when:* you deliberately mangle the indentation of one Java file, `mvn verify` fails within seconds at the `validate` phase with Spotless naming that file, and `make fmt` followed by `mvn verify` is green again.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Checkstyle: a curated linter, not a shouting one.**
    *What this step is:* Checkstyle is the *linter* from the New words table — it complains about code without rewriting it, catching what a formatter cannot see, like a method with twelve branches. You give it a small, hand-picked ruleset. At the end, exactly four things fail the build, and nothing else makes noise.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — the parent `pom.xml` from there is where this plugin goes, so every module inherits it.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create a ruleset file at `config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml` containing exactly these rules: **no star imports** (`AvoidStarImport` — `import java.util.*;` is banned because it hides where a class came from and silently breaks when two packages gain a same-named class), **final parameters** (`FinalParameters` — method parameters must be `final`, so they cannot be quietly reassigned halfway through a method), **Javadoc requirement OFF** (do not enable any Javadoc rules — forced comments on every method produce boilerplate nobody reads), and **cyclomatic complexity ≤ 12** (`CyclomaticComplexity` with `max` set to 12 — past roughly 12 independent paths, nobody can hold the method in their head, including you in a month).
    2. Add the `maven-checkstyle-plugin` to the parent POM, point it at your ruleset file, configure it to **fail the build** on any violation, and bind its `check` goal into the build (the `verify` phase is fine).
    3. Resist the urge to enable everything. A gate that cries wolf gets disabled — four rules you always obey beat forty you learn to scroll past.
    *You know it worked when:* `mvn verify` passes on your current code, and temporarily adding `import java.util.*;` to any file turns the build red with a Checkstyle message naming `AvoidStarImport`. Revert the import.

- [ ] **Step 3 — JaCoCo: a coverage ratchet, not a coverage target.**
    *What this step is:* JaCoCo is the *coverage tool* from the New words table — it measures which percentage of your code actually ran while the tests ran. You set a **ratchet**: a threshold that can only ever go up. You start at 0.60 line coverage and 0.50 branch coverage (branch is the harder, more honest number — it asks whether both the true *and* false side of each `if` ran), raise them as your real coverage grows, and never lower them. The build fails if coverage ever drops below the floor.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — the parent `pom.xml` again, so the same floor applies to every module.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the `jacoco-maven-plugin` to the parent POM with two executions: `prepare-agent` (attaches the measuring agent while tests run) and `check` bound to the `verify` phase, with rules requiring **LINE covered ratio ≥ 0.60** and **BRANCH covered ratio ≥ 0.50**.
    2. Directly above those thresholds, write an XML comment in the POM explaining **why a ratchet beats a fixed target** — in your own words, roughly: a fixed "must be 80%" on day one makes you write meaningless tests just to hit a number; a ratchet starts where you honestly are and only forbids going backwards, so it stops slow decay without inviting theatre. End the comment with the rule: *raise these numbers as coverage grows; never lower them.*
    3. Never add a blanket exclusion to make this gate pass — excluding a package from coverage to go green is the gate lying to you.
    *You know it worked when:* `mvn verify` prints the JaCoCo coverage check and passes, and the ratchet comment is sitting in the parent POM where future-you will read it.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Maven Enforcer: fail on a broken environment.**
    *What this step is:* The *Maven Enforcer* plugin (New words table) fails the build on environment problems rather than code problems — things like two copies of the same class on the classpath, an ancient Maven, or a snapshot dependency (an unfinished `-SNAPSHOT` build of a library that can change under you) sneaking into the repo. At the end, three environment rules guard every build.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — the parent `pom.xml` is where the Enforcer lives.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the `maven-enforcer-plugin` to the parent POM with three rules: **ban duplicate classes** (needs the `extra-enforcer-rules` dependency — ask AI for the snippet), **require Maven ≥ 3.9**, and **ban snapshot dependencies** (the `requireReleaseDeps` rule).
    2. Prove one rule is live: temporarily change the required Maven version to `99.0`, run `mvn verify`, read the Enforcer's failure message, then change it back to `3.9`.
    *You know it worked when:* you have seen the Enforcer fail the build once (the fake `99.0` requirement) and `mvn verify` is green again with the real rules in place.

- [ ] **Step 5 — ArchUnit: the five architecture rules as tests.**
    *What this step is:* ArchUnit (New words table) writes tests about your code's *structure* instead of its behaviour — rules like "nothing in `domain` may import Spring". A human reviewer forgets such rules; a test never does. You will implement the five non-negotiable rules from [§6.2 — Per-service package structure](#62-per-service-package-structure-hexagonal--ports-and-adapters) — the section that defines the hexagonal package layout (`domain` / `application` / `adapter` / `config`) every service follows — as one reusable test suite that every service imports with a single line. The five rules, spelled out: (1) `domain` may not depend on `application`, `adapter`, `config`, Spring, Jakarta, or Hibernate; (2) `application` may not depend on `adapter`; (3) JPA entities may never leave `adapter.out.persistence` — no entity in a controller signature, ever; (4) no `@Autowired` field injection, constructor injection only; (5) no public mutable setters on aggregates — state changes go through intention-named methods (`event.publish()`, not `event.setStatus(PUBLISHED)`).
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — you created the `platform-testing` module there precisely to hold shared test machinery like this suite.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the `archunit-junit5` dependency to `platform-testing` (manage its version in the parent POM, as always).
    2. In `platform-testing`, write a base class — call it `ZenithArchitectureRules` — containing the five rules as `@ArchTest` fields (`@ArchTest` marks a field holding one structural rule; ask AI to show you rule (1) written with ArchUnit's fluent API, then write the other four yourself in the same shape).
    3. In `catalog-service`'s test folder, add the one-line subclass: a class annotated `@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.zenith.catalog")` (the annotation tells ArchUnit which packages to scan) that extends `ZenithArchitectureRules`. Every future service will copy this one line and nothing else.
    *You know it worked when:* `mvn verify` runs the ArchUnit tests inside `catalog-service` and they pass — and in Step 8 you will watch one of them fail on purpose, which is the real proof.

- [ ] **Step 6 — gitleaks: the secret scan.**
    *What this step is:* gitleaks is a scanner that reads your repository looking for strings shaped like credentials — AWS keys, API tokens, passwords — so that the day you absent-mindedly paste a real secret into a tracked file, a tool catches it before the internet does. At the end you have a `make secrets` command that scans the whole repo.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — the `Makefile` from there gets one more target, and the `.env` convention from that task is exactly the kind of credential this scan backstops.
    *Do this:*
    1. Install it: `brew install gitleaks`.
    2. Add a `secrets` target to the `Makefile` that runs `gitleaks detect`.
    3. Know where this is headed: [Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline](#task-04--git-workflow-the-remote-and-a-local-ci-pipeline--2h) folds this same scan into the `make ci` command it builds, and [Task 2.4 — Application security hardening and auditing](#task-24--application-security-hardening-and-auditing--3h) later adds this same scan to CI, so it also runs away from your laptop.
    *You know it worked when:* `make secrets` runs against your current repo and exits clean.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Break it on purpose: plant a fake secret.**
    *What this step is:* You have never seen the secret scan fail, so you do not actually know it is wired up. You plant an obviously fake AWS key, watch gitleaks go red, and revert. Thirty seconds of deliberate vandalism buys you certainty.
    *Builds on:* Step 6 — the `make secrets` target you just created.
    *Do this:*
    1. In any test file, add a string shaped like an AWS access key — `AKIA` followed by sixteen capital letters and digits (an invented one; never a real credential, not even an expired one).
    2. Run `make secrets` and read the failure: which file, which line, which rule matched.
    3. Revert the change (`git checkout -- <file>`), run `make secrets` again, and watch it go clean.
    *You know it worked when:* you saw the scan fail with the planted key named, and it passes again after the revert.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Break it on purpose: make every gate fail once.**
    *What this step is:* The whole point of this task is that each gate **fails the build** — a warning nobody reads is decoration, not a gate. So you now break each one deliberately, one at a time, and watch `mvn verify` go red three different ways. A gate you have never seen fail is a gate you do not know is wired up.
    *Builds on:* Steps 1–5 — every gate you are about to attack was wired up in this task; and [§6.2 — Per-service package structure](#62-per-service-package-structure-hexagonal--ports-and-adapters) — the `domain` package rule you will violate comes from there.
    *Do this:*
    1. **Break Checkstyle:** add a star import (`import java.util.*;`) to any class, run `mvn verify`, read the failure and note which plugin produced it, revert.
    2. **Break JaCoCo:** delete (or comment out) a test so coverage drops below the 0.60/0.50 floor from Step 3, run `mvn verify`, watch the coverage check fail, revert.
    3. **Break ArchUnit:** create a throwaway class in a `domain` package (make the package `com.zenith.catalog.domain` with one small class in it if it does not exist yet) and add `import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;` to it — importing Spring into `domain` violates rule (1) from Step 5. Run `mvn verify`, watch the ArchUnit test fail with a message naming the forbidden dependency, revert.
    4. After each failure, before reverting, say out loud which tool caught it and at which build phase — that is the mental map this task exists to build.
    *You know it worked when:* you have personally seen three distinct red builds — Checkstyle on the star import, JaCoCo on the dropped coverage, ArchUnit on the Spring import — plus the gitleaks failure from Step 7, which is exactly the "Done when" list for this task.

**Done when:** `mvn verify` fails for a star import, for dropped coverage, and for a Spring import inside `domain`, and `gitleaks detect` fails on the planted fake secret — and you have personally seen all four failures.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Four tools, four different jobs. Say in one sentence each what Spotless, Checkstyle, JaCoCo, and ArchUnit do.
2. What is the difference between line coverage and branch coverage, and which is easier to game with a bad test?
3. Why does a coverage ratchet beat a fixed target like "coverage must be 80%"?
4. You deliberately broke three gates. Pick one, and describe the failure message and which plugin produced it.
5. Why is it so much cheaper to add these gates now than in week 20?

#### Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline — 2h

**What:** A real hosted repository, trunk-based branching, conventional commits, the branch→push→PR→self-review→merge loop you will run for every task from here on, and a `make ci` script wired to a `pre-push` hook.
**Why:** CI from commit #1 means you never debug a 200-file "why is the build broken" merge; a pre-push hook makes a failing build physically unable to leave your machine; and working PR-by-PR against a protected `main` — even alone — is precisely the daily rhythm of a professional team. Six months of that rhythm is itself a credential: your contribution graph, your PR history and your commit messages become evidence no interview question can shake. It is also where the CV from [§13 — How to present this credibly](#13-how-to-present-this-credibly) gets its repo link.
**Solves:** the beginner pattern of committing broken code, the habit gap of not knowing what a real PR description contains, and a portfolio that exists only on one laptop — one disk failure from not existing at all.

**Learn this first:** ask AI *"explain trunk-based development versus git-flow and why most
companies moved to trunk-based"*, and *"what is a git hook and where do the scripts live?"*.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Trunk-based development** | Everyone commits to one long-lived branch (`main`), using branches that live hours or days rather than weeks. Merges stay small, so they stay easy. |
| **git-flow** | An older model with permanent `develop`, `release`, and `hotfix` branches. Most teams abandoned it because long-lived branches diverge and merging them becomes an event. |
| **Squash merge** | Collapsing all the commits on a branch into one commit on `main`. Keeps history readable; you lose the intermediate steps, which you rarely want anyway. |
| **Conventional commit** | A commit message in a fixed machine-readable shape: `feat(catalog): add event publish use case`. A tool can then generate a changelog and work out the next version number. |
| **Git hook** | A script git runs automatically at a given moment. They live in `.git/hooks/`, which is **not** cloned — so a hook is a personal safety net, not a team guarantee. That is why CI exists as well. |
| **`commit-msg` hook** | Runs after you write a message and can reject it. This is what enforces the conventional-commit format. |
| **`pre-push` hook** | Runs before git sends anything to a remote. Putting `make ci` here makes a failing build physically unable to leave your laptop. |
| **CI (continuous integration)** | Automatically building and testing every change. Yours runs twice from today: locally as a shell script called `make ci`, and on the forge as a GitHub Actions workflow running the same commands; [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline) grows this into a full build-and-deploy pipeline. |
| **Remote / `origin`** | A copy of your repository hosted elsewhere — here, on GitHub. `origin` is just the conventional name your local repo uses to refer to it. Pushing to a remote is what makes your work survive your laptop and visible to the world (and to interviewers). |
| **Forge** | The general word for a code-hosting service — GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket. This plan uses GitHub's free tier: hosting code costs nothing, forever, and is not a cloud subscription — every build, test and benchmark in this plan still runs on your own machine. |
| **Pull request (PR)** | A request to merge your branch into `main`, with a description, a diff viewer, and a place for review comments. On a team it is where review happens; solo, it is where *you* review you — and the habit is the same muscle. |
| **Self-review** | Opening your own PR's diff and reading every line as if a stranger wrote it, *before* merging. Reviewing your own work 24 hours later finds real bugs, and it is the honest solo substitute for review culture — [Task 14.4 — Behavioral rounds, and the AI question](#task-144--behavioral-rounds-and-the-ai-question--5h) turns this exact habit into an interview answer. |
| **Branch protection** | A forge rule that nobody — including you — can push directly to `main`; changes arrive only through a PR with green CI. It converts "I should use PRs" from intention into physics. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** two things. That CI is just your build, run automatically — once `make ci` is the same command the pipeline runs, "works on my machine" stops being possible. And that from this task onward, **every code task in this plan starts on a branch and ends with a pushed, self-reviewed, merged PR** — the task loop in [§6.4 — Definition of done](#64-definition-of-done-applies-to-every-task-in-this-plan) is the single place that sequence is written down, and today you rehearse it once end to end.
- **When it works you will see:** a pre-commit hook rejecting a badly formatted commit, `make ci` reproducing locally exactly what the pipeline runs, the same checks green in the Actions tab on GitHub, and a direct push to `main` refused by branch protection with your work arriving through a PR instead.
- **Where people get stuck:** hooks so slow you start using `--no-verify` — keep the pre-commit hook under a few seconds (formatting and a secret scan) and put the long checks in `make ci`. And treating the PR as a formality: clicking merge without reading the diff. The self-review is the entire point; skipping it quietly deletes the one review culture you have.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Create your GitHub account and an SSH key.**
    *What this step is:* GitHub is the *forge* (New words table) that will host your repository. To push code to it without typing a password every time, you create an SSH key — a pair of files where the private half stays on your laptop and the public half goes to GitHub, so GitHub can verify it is really you. At the end, your machine can talk to GitHub securely.
    *Do this:*
    1. Make a free GitHub account if you do not have one.
    2. Ask AI *"walk me through creating an SSH key and adding it to GitHub, and explain what the key actually is"* — follow it (typically `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`, then paste the contents of the `.pub` file into GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys). Do not skip the "explain" half; knowing what the key *is* matters more than the three commands.
    3. Verify the connection: `ssh -T git@github.com`.
    *You know it worked when:* `ssh -T git@github.com` replies with a greeting that contains your GitHub username.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Create the remote, once, and point your repo at it.**
    *What this step is:* Your repository currently exists only on one laptop — one disk failure from not existing at all. You create an empty repository on GitHub and connect your local repo to it as its *remote* (New words table — `origin` is just the conventional name your local repo uses for it). At the end, your code exists somewhere a laptop failure cannot reach.
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.6 — Git: the safety net and the daily loop](#task-f76--git-the-safety-net-and-the-daily-loop--05h) — the local git basics (staging, committing) you learned there are what you are now connecting to the outside world.
    *Do this:*
    1. On GitHub, create an empty repository named `zenith`. **Public is recommended** — the CV in [§13 — How to present this credibly](#13-how-to-present-this-credibly) links to it, public repos get every feature used in this plan for free, and an interviewer can only probe what they can see. Private works too if you prefer; you can flip it later.
    2. From inside your repo: `git remote add origin git@github.com:<you>/zenith.git`.
    3. Push: `git push -u origin main`. The `-u` links your local `main` to the remote one, so plain `git push` works from then on.
    4. Refresh the GitHub page and look at your code existing somewhere a laptop failure cannot reach.
    *You know it worked when:* the GitHub page shows your files and commit history, and a plain `git push` (no arguments) succeeds.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Adopt the branching rules: trunk, short-lived branches, squash merges.**
    *What this step is:* You adopt *trunk-based development* (New words table): one long-lived branch, `main`, plus short-lived `feat/*` branches that live hours or days, merged back with *squash merges* (all of a branch's commits collapsed into one commit on `main`, keeping history readable). Branch names carry the task id, so your git history reads like this plan. At the end, the convention is set and this task's own branch exists.
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.7 — Branching, merging, rebasing, and undoing](#task-f77--branching-merging-rebasing-and-undoing--05h) — you already know how to create, switch, and merge branches; this step decides *how you will use* that skill from now on.
    *Do this:*
    1. The rule from here on: `main` plus short-lived `feat/*` branches, squash merges, and the branch name carries the task id — `feat/p0-t4-git-workflow`, `feat/p3-t2-index-design`.
    2. In the GitHub repo → Settings → General → Pull Requests, make sure "Allow squash merging" is ticked (and untick the other merge styles if you want history to stay strictly one-commit-per-task).
    3. Start this task's own branch right now — `git switch -c feat/p0-t4-git-workflow` — and do the rest of this task's work on it, so it all arrives through your first real pull request at the end.
    *You know it worked when:* `git branch` shows you sitting on `feat/p0-t4-git-workflow`, and you can say without looking what the branch for [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline)'s index task would be called.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Turn on branch protection for `main`, then prove it is real.**
    *What this step is:* *Branch protection* (New words table) is a forge rule that nobody — including you — can push directly to `main`; changes arrive only through a pull request with green CI. It converts "I should use PRs" from intention into physics. At the end, a direct push to `main` is physically rejected.
    *Builds on:* Step 2 — the hosted repo whose settings you are now hardening.
    *Do this:*
    1. On GitHub → Settings → Branches, add a protection rule for `main` and tick **"Require a pull request before merging"**. (Solo, you approve your own PRs — so the setting to tick is "require a pull request", **not** "require approvals".)
    2. Also plan to tick **"Require status checks to pass"** with the CI check selected — GitHub only lists a check after it has run at least once, so the checkbox becomes tickable after your Actions workflow in Step 11 has its first run. Come back then and tick it; branch protection is not finished until you have.
    3. Prove it is real: make a trivial throwaway commit directly on `main` locally and try `git push origin main`. Read the rejection message. Then throw the local commit away with `git reset --hard origin/main`.
    4. Say the consequence out loud: from this moment, code reaches `main` only through the task loop in [§6.4 — Definition of done](#64-definition-of-done-applies-to-every-task-in-this-plan) — the section that spells out the branch→PR→merge sequence every task follows — which is exactly how every professional team you will ever join works.
    *You know it worked when:* the direct push is refused with a protected-branch error you have read, and your local `main` matches the remote again.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Conventional commits, enforced by a `commit-msg` hook.**
    *What this step is:* A *conventional commit* (New words table) is a commit message in a fixed machine-readable shape — `feat(catalog): add event publish use case` — a type, an optional scope in parentheses, a colon, a description. Because the shape is predictable, a tool can generate a changelog or compute the next version number from your history. You enforce it with a `commit-msg` hook — a script git runs after you write a message, which can reject it. Remember from the New words table: hooks live in `.git/hooks/`, which is **not** cloned, so this is a personal safety net, not a team guarantee — that is why CI exists as well.
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.6 — Git: the safety net and the daily loop](#task-f76--git-the-safety-net-and-the-daily-loop--05h) — you learned to write commit messages there; now you give them a machine-checkable shape.
    *Do this:*
    1. Learn the shape: `type(scope): description`, with types like `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`.
    2. Create `.git/hooks/commit-msg` — ask AI for a small shell script that rejects any message not matching `^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|test|chore)(\(.+\))?: .+` — and make it executable with `chmod +x .git/hooks/commit-msg` (a hook that is not executable is silently ignored; this bites everyone exactly once).
    3. Test it: try to commit with the message `stuff` and watch it be rejected; commit with `chore(repo): test commit-msg hook` and watch it pass.
    4. Ask AI *why machine-readable commit messages matter for changelogs and release automation* — the answer is the point of the convention.
    *You know it worked when:* the message `stuff` is rejected by your own hook and a properly shaped message goes through.

- [ ] **Step 6 — A fast `pre-commit` hook: format check plus secret scan.**
    *What this step is:* A `pre-commit` hook runs before each commit is recorded and can stop it. You put only the fast checks here — formatting and the secret scan — so a bad file never even enters history. Speed is the design constraint: a slow hook trains you to type `--no-verify` (git's bypass flag), and a bypassed hook protects nobody.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h) — Spotless (the formatter gate) and gitleaks (the secret scan behind `make secrets`) were both set up there; this hook just runs them earlier.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `.git/hooks/pre-commit` running `mvn spotless:check -q` and the gitleaks scan from Task 0.3, and `chmod +x` it.
    2. Time it. Keep it under a few seconds — if it is slower, trim it; the long checks belong in `make ci` (Step 9), not here.
    3. Test it: stage a deliberately mis-formatted file, try to commit, and watch the hook reject it; `make fmt`, stage, commit again, and watch it pass.
    *You know it worked when:* a badly formatted commit is blocked in under a few seconds, and a clean one goes through without you ever feeling tempted by `--no-verify`.

- [ ] **Step 7 — The PR template, where PRs actually live now.**
    *What this step is:* A *pull request* (New words table) is a request to merge your branch into `main`, with a description, a diff viewer, and a place for review comments. GitHub can pre-fill every PR description from a template file, so every PR you open arrives pre-structured, exactly as on a team. At the end, opening a PR automatically presents four headings waiting to be filled in.
    *Builds on:* Step 2 — the file lives in the hosted repo, under a magic path GitHub looks for.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `.github/pull_request_template.md` with four headings — *What changed / Why / How I tested it / Risk and rollback* — nothing else is required; the structure is the value.
    2. Note the division of labour: keep writing the heavier schema-change plans into `docs/changes/` ([Task 3.5 — Partitioning, read replicas, and zero-downtime migrations](#task-35--partitioning-read-replicas-and-zero-downtime-migrations--6h) uses those for its zero-downtime migration plans); the PR template is the everyday sibling.
    *You know it worked when:* after this branch is merged, the next PR you open shows the four headings in the description box without you typing them.

- [ ] **Step 8 — The self-review checklist, written into the template.**
    *What this step is:* *Self-review* (New words table) is opening your own PR's diff and reading every line as if a stranger wrote it, *before* merging — the honest solo substitute for review culture. You embed the checklist inside the PR template as a markdown comment (text wrapped in `<!-- -->`, visible while editing the description but invisible in the rendered PR), so the questions confront you on every single PR.
    *Builds on:* Step 7 — the template file you just created.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add an HTML comment to `.github/pull_request_template.md` containing the checklist: *read the whole diff top to bottom as a stranger; for each file ask — would I approve this name? is anything dead or commented-out? where is the test for this line? did anything sneak in that the title does not mention?*
    2. Set the expectation now: finding one real fix per self-review is normal, and each one is proof the habit works — not proof you were careless.
    *You know it worked when:* the checklist is in the template, invisible in a rendered PR but staring at you whenever you edit a PR description.

- [ ] **Step 9 — `make ci`: your local pipeline in one command.**
    *What this step is:* *CI* (New words table) is just your build, run automatically. You write it first as a plain local command: `make ci` runs the exact gate sequence a hosted CI would, so "works on my machine" stops being possible — the machine and the pipeline run the same thing. **This is your fast local gate for the whole plan**; [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline) extends it into a full build-and-deploy pipeline rather than replacing it.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — that task left `ci` as a promised Makefile target; this is where it becomes real. [Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h) — every gate `make ci` runs (Spotless, Checkstyle, the JaCoCo threshold, the ArchUnit suite, gitleaks) was wired up there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a `ci` target to the `Makefile` running the exact gate sequence a hosted CI would: `spotless:check`, `checkstyle`, `mvn -B verify` (which executes the JaCoCo threshold and the ArchUnit suite, because [Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h) bound them into `verify`).
    2. Include the `make secrets` gitleaks scan — [Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h) promised that "Task 0.4 folds it into `make ci`", and this is that moment.
    3. Run `make ci` once end to end and note how long it takes — this is the price you pay per push, and knowing it stops you resenting it.
    *You know it worked when:* `make ci` goes green in one command on clean code, and goes red if you re-break any single gate from [Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h).

- [ ] **Step 10 — Wire `make ci` into a `pre-push` hook, then prove it blocks you.**
    *What this step is:* A `pre-push` hook (New words table) runs before git sends anything to the remote. Putting `make ci` there makes a failing build physically unable to leave your laptop. Then — because a gate you have never seen fail is a gate you do not know is wired up — you verify it by trying to push broken code.
    *Builds on:* Step 9 — the `make ci` command the hook runs; Step 5/6 — the same `.git/hooks/` mechanics.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `.git/hooks/pre-push` containing `make ci`, and `chmod +x` it.
    2. Break it on purpose: add a deliberately failing test (assert that 1 equals 2), commit it on your branch (with a conventional message — your Step 5 hook insists), and run `git push`. Watch the hook run `make ci`, fail on the test, and refuse to send anything.
    3. Revert the failing test, push again, and watch it go through.
    *You know it worked when:* you have seen a `git push` of broken code die on your own laptop before reaching GitHub.

- [ ] **Step 11 — Mirror `make ci` into GitHub Actions.**
    *What this step is:* GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in CI runner: a YAML file in your repo tells it what to run on every push and PR (free on public repos; generous free minutes on private ones). Because it runs the *same* `make ci`, this is the two-layer setup real teams run: the hook is *your* fast feedback, Actions is the *team-visible* truth that branch protection trusts — and the layer that still works when someone (you, tired, at midnight) bypasses a hook with `--no-verify`.
    *Builds on:* Step 9 — the `make ci` being mirrored; Step 4 — the branch-protection rule waiting to require this check.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml` that triggers on every push and PR, checks out the code, sets up Java 21 (Temurin) and gitleaks, and runs the same `make ci`. Ask AI for a minimal workflow file, then read every line until none of it is magic.
    2. Push your branch and watch your first green run in the Actions tab — it is the same screenshot a company pipeline produces.
    3. Go back to Step 4's unfinished business: in the branch-protection rule, tick "Require status checks to pass" and select this CI check, now that GitHub has seen it run.
    *You know it worked when:* the Actions tab shows the same `make ci` green that your laptop shows, and branch protection now lists the check as required.

- [ ] **Step 12 — Rehearse the full task loop once, end to end.**
    *What this step is:* The task loop in [§6.4 — Definition of done](#64-definition-of-done-applies-to-every-task-in-this-plan) is the single place the branch→push→PR→self-review→merge sequence is written down, and **every code task in this plan from here on starts and ends with it**. Today you run it twice: once for real, to land this task's own branch, and once as a timed rehearsal on a trivial change, so the mechanics become muscle memory before they ever carry real code.
    *Builds on:* every step above — the loop is those pieces working together.
    *Do this:*
    1. Land this task first: push `feat/p0-t4-git-workflow`, open the PR (the template appears by itself), fill in all four headings, **self-review the whole diff as a stranger** and leave at least one comment on your own code, squash-merge when CI is green, delete the branch.
    2. Now the timed rehearsal on a trivial change — add one line to the README: `git switch main && git pull` → branch → commit → push → PR (template appears by itself) → self-review the diff → squash-merge → delete the branch → `git switch main && git pull`.
    3. Time it. The loop should cost under five minutes of overhead per task — that price buys you a professional history: six months of PRs, descriptions, and self-reviews that no interview question can shake.
    *You know it worked when:* your first squash-merged PR exists on GitHub with the template filled in and a self-review comment on your own diff, and the rehearsal loop came in under five minutes.

**Done when:** a direct push to `main` is rejected by branch protection, a `git push` of broken code is rejected by your own pre-push hook, the same `make ci` is green both locally and in the Actions tab, and your first squash-merged PR exists on GitHub with the template filled in and a self-review comment on your own diff.
