1. What is trunk-based development, and what specific problem with long-lived branches does it avoid?
2. Where do git hooks live, and why does a teammate cloning your repository not get them?
3. Why would a team want commit messages to be machine-readable?
4. Your `pre-push` hook rejected a push. Walk through exactly which checks ran and in what order.
5. A hook is easy to bypass with `--no-verify`. So what is the point of one — and what catches what the hook cannot?
6. Recite the task loop from [§6.4 — Definition of done](#64-definition-of-done-applies-to-every-task-in-this-plan), command by command, and say what each step is *for*.
7. Why run the same checks twice — in a local hook *and* in Actions? What does each layer give you that the other cannot?

#### Task 0.5 — Architecture Decision Records — 1h

**What:** Five ADRs recording the decisions you have already made, each naming a rejected alternative.
**Why:** Undocumented decisions are what make a codebase unexplainable six weeks later — including to you. ADRs are also the single cheapest artifact that signals senior behaviour in an interview.
**Solves:** "why is it built this way?" having no answer, and re-litigating settled decisions every time someone new reads the code.

**Learn this first:** re-read the [ADR explanation in §2.1](#adrs--architecture-decision-records). The format matters less than the honesty: an ADR with no "consequences" section and no rejected option is marketing, not a decision record.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **ADR** | Architecture Decision Record. A short markdown file recording one significant decision: what the situation was, what you considered, what you chose, and what it costs you. |
| **Context** | The first section: the forces and constraints at the time. Written so a reader in a year understands why the obvious answer today was not obvious then. |
| **Options considered** | The alternatives you rejected, each with its failure mode. This is the section that proves you made a decision rather than followed a tutorial. |
| **Consequences** | What becomes true now — including the bad parts. An ADR with only benefits is marketing. |
| **Superseded** | The status you give an old ADR when a later one replaces it. You never delete or edit the original; the trail of changed minds is the valuable part. |
| **Immutable record** | ADRs are append-only. Changing a decision means writing a new ADR, not rewriting history. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** the **Options considered** section. Your code already records what you did; nothing else records what you rejected, and that is the part a future reader actually needs. ADR-0000 is the most important one you will write.
- **When it works you will see:** five short files in `docs/adr/`, each naming a specific rejected alternative and at least one negative consequence you accept.
- **Where people get stuck:** writing ADRs with no downsides. If you cannot name a cost, you have not finished thinking — and a reviewer reads a one-sided ADR as marketing. Also: writing them months later. Write at the moment of deciding or do not bother.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Create the ADR folder and template.**
    *What this step is:* An ADR (Architecture Decision Record) is a short markdown file — one page, maximum — that records a single significant decision: the situation, the options you considered, what you chose, and what that choice costs you. In this step you set up the place these files live and a reusable template, so writing each ADR is a copy-and-fill job. At the end you will have `docs/adr/` in your repository with a `template.md` inside it.
    *Builds on:* [the ADR explainer in §2.1](#adrs--architecture-decision-records) — the full format, with a worked example (the transactional-outbox ADR), lives there; re-read it now before you write anything.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create the folder `docs/adr/` at the root of your `zenith` repository.
    2. Pick one of two ways to get a template — both are fine. Either install `adr-tools` (a small command-line tool that creates numbered ADR files for you — on a Mac: `brew install adr-tools`), or — simpler — create `docs/adr/template.md` by hand with exactly these four sections, copied from [the ADR example](#adrs--architecture-decision-records):
        ```markdown
        # ADR-NNNN — <the decision, in one line>

        **Status:** Accepted · **Date:** YYYY-MM-DD · **Supersedes:** —

        ## Context
        <the forces and constraints at the time of deciding>

        ## Options considered
        <each alternative, numbered, with its failure mode>

        ## Decision
        <which option, and the one-sentence reason>

        ## Consequences
        <what becomes true now — including the bad parts>
        ```
    3. For every ADR below, copy `template.md` to a new file named `docs/adr/NNNN-short-title.md` (for example `docs/adr/0000-microservices-over-modular-monolith.md`) and fill it in.
    *You know it worked when:* `docs/adr/template.md` exists and contains the four headings Context, Options considered, Decision, Consequences.

- [ ] **Step 2 — ADR-0000: microservices rather than a modular monolith.**
    *What this step is:* Your first and most important ADR. It records the single biggest decision in this project: building Zenith as nine separate services instead of one application. A *modular monolith* is the main alternative — one deployable application whose internal packages keep strict boundaries, so it stays well-organised without being split into separate programs. Write this one first, and take it seriously: the honest truth is that at this scale — nine services for a system with no users — the modular monolith is the right call on pure engineering merit, and your ADR must say exactly that. At the end you will have `docs/adr/0000-microservices-over-modular-monolith.md`, the highest-value page in the repository.
    *Builds on:* [the ADR explainer in §2.1](#adrs--architecture-decision-records) — the format and the rule that rejected options are the most valuable section.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/adr/0000-microservices-over-modular-monolith.md` from your template.
    2. In **Context**, state the real reason plainly: you are deliberately buying exposure to distributed failure modes — *partial failure* (one service is down while the others are up), *eventual consistency* (different services briefly disagree about the data until events catch up), and *distributed debugging* (following one request across several programs) — because a monolith cannot teach you any of those, and learning them is the goal of this project. Say exactly that; do not dress it up as a scaling need you do not have.
    3. In **Options considered**, record the two rejected alternatives with their failure modes *for your goal*: (a) a modular monolith with enforced package boundaries — technically the right answer at this scale, but the wrong answer for the goal, because it removes the distributed problems you are here to practise; (b) service-per-team — splitting services along team ownership lines — rejected because there is no team, just you.
    4. In **Consequences**, be blunt: every operational cost in [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline), [Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline), and [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline) is self-inflicted by this decision — name them as such (event delivery you must make reliable yourself, load balancing and resilience machinery a monolith would not need, and cross-service logging, metrics and tracing just to see what is happening).
    5. Read it back once as a hostile interviewer. "Why nine services?" is the first challenge any experienced interviewer will put to this project — answering "at this scale it should have been a modular monolith, and here is what I bought by not doing that" converts the project's most obvious weakness into the strongest evidence of judgement you have.
    *You know it worked when:* ADR-0000 names both rejected alternatives, states the real (learning) motivation in the Context section, and its Consequences section explicitly calls the [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) / [Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline) / [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline) costs self-inflicted.

- [ ] **Step 3 — ADR-0001: use a Maven monorepo.**
    *What this step is:* A short ADR recording a decision you have already physically made — keeping all nine services and the shared modules in one repository with one parent `pom.xml` (a *monorepo*), rather than giving each service its own repository. At the end you will have `docs/adr/0001-maven-monorepo.md`.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — where you built exactly this: a parent POM, `platform-common`, `platform-testing`, and `catalog-service` in one repository.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/adr/0001-maven-monorepo.md` from your template.
    2. In **Options considered**, record the rejected alternative: one repository per service. Note its failure mode for a solo project — every change to shared code (like `platform-common`) would mean publishing a new version and bumping it in nine separate repositories.
    3. In **Consequences**, record the cost you accept: **no independent versioning** — all modules share one version number, so you can never release one service at version 2.0 while the others stay at 1.0. Everything versions and ships together.
    *You know it worked when:* ADR-0001 names "repo per service" as the rejected option and "no independent versioning" as an accepted negative consequence.

- [ ] **Step 4 — ADR-0002: hexagonal architecture per service.**
    *What this step is:* An ADR recording that every service's internal structure will be *hexagonal* — the domain code in the middle declares interfaces (ports), and the web and database code (adapters) depend inward on the domain, never the other way round. The rejected alternative is the *classic layered* structure (controller → service → repository, where the business logic ends up depending on the database layer). At the end you will have `docs/adr/0002-hexagonal-architecture.md`.
    *Builds on:* [the hexagonal architecture explainer in §2.1](#hexagonal-architecture-also-called-ports-and-adapters) — the full walkthrough of ports, adapters, and who depends on whom; skim it again if "dependencies point inward" is not crisp in your head.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/adr/0002-hexagonal-architecture.md` from your template.
    2. In **Options considered**, record the rejected alternative: classic layered architecture, with its failure mode — the domain ends up shaped by, and welded to, the persistence and web frameworks.
    3. In **Consequences**, record the cost you accept: **more mapping code** — because the domain refuses to know about web or database shapes, you write conversion code at every boundary (domain object ↔ database row, domain object ↔ JSON body).
    *You know it worked when:* ADR-0002 names classic layered as the rejected option and "more mapping code" as an accepted negative consequence.

- [ ] **Step 5 — ADR-0003: Postgres as the system of record.**
    *What this step is:* An ADR recording that Postgres — the relational database you already run — is where the authoritative copy of Zenith's data lives (that is what *system of record* means). The rejected alternative is MongoDB, a document database that stores JSON-like documents without a fixed schema. At the end you will have `docs/adr/0003-postgres-system-of-record.md`.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — Postgres 17 is already running in your compose stack, so this ADR records a choice you have already acted on. [Module F5 — SQL and relational data modelling](#module-f5--sql-and-relational-data-modelling--9h) — where you learned the things this decision buys: constraints the database enforces, and multi-row transactions ([Task F5.8 — Transactions, ACID, and isolation](#task-f58--transactions-acid-and-isolation--15h)).
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/adr/0003-postgres-system-of-record.md` from your template.
    2. In **Options considered**, record the rejected alternative: MongoDB, with its failure mode for a ticketing system — bookings and payments need multi-row transactions and hard constraints, which is relational home turf.
    3. In **Consequences**, record the cost you accept: **schema migrations are mandatory** — every change to a table's shape must be written as a versioned migration script that runs before the new code does (Flyway, the migration tool from [Task F5.11 — JPA, the SQL log, and Flyway](#task-f511--jpa-the-sql-log-and-flyway--1h), is how this project does it).
    *You know it worked when:* ADR-0003 names MongoDB as the rejected option and mandatory schema migrations as an accepted negative consequence.

- [ ] **Step 6 — ADR-0004: Kafka as the event backbone.**
    *What this step is:* An ADR recording that Kafka — the event log you already run — is how services will tell each other what happened (the *event backbone*: the one shared channel every cross-service event flows through). Two alternatives get rejected: RabbitMQ, a traditional message broker that hands each message to a consumer and then deletes it, and database polling, where you write events into a table and every interested service queries that table over and over. At the end you will have `docs/adr/0004-kafka-event-backbone.md`.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — Kafka (in KRaft mode) and the Schema Registry are already in your compose stack. [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) is where you will actually pay the costs this ADR records.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/adr/0004-kafka-event-backbone.md` from your template.
    2. In **Options considered**, record both rejected alternatives with a failure mode each: RabbitMQ (messages vanish once consumed, so a new service cannot replay history), and database polling (constant query load, and latency decided by how often you poll).
    3. In **Consequences**, record the two costs you accept: **operational complexity** (one more stateful piece of infrastructure to run, monitor, and understand), and **at-least-once semantics you must handle** — Kafka guarantees a message is delivered *at least* once, which means duplicates are possible, so every consumer you ever write must cope with seeing the same event twice.
    *You know it worked when:* ADR-0004 names both RabbitMQ and database polling as rejected options, and lists both operational complexity and at-least-once delivery as accepted negative consequences.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Break it on purpose: the no-downside audit.**
    *What this step is:* A final pass over all five ADRs, reading only the Consequences sections, hunting for the classic failure — an ADR that lists only benefits. An ADR with no bad consequences is marketing, not a decision record: every real decision costs something, and if you cannot name the cost, you have not finished thinking about the decision. At the end, every one of your five ADRs names at least one negative consequence you accept.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline](#task-04--git-workflow-the-remote-and-a-local-ci-pipeline--2h) — the branch → push → PR → self-review → merge loop you now run for every task; ship these ADRs through it.
    *Do this:*
    1. Open each of the five ADRs and read only its **Consequences** section. For each, ask: is there at least one line that makes this decision look worse, which I am accepting anyway?
    2. Where a Consequences section is all sunshine, stop and write the downside now — the table above each decision in Steps 2–6 gives you the minimum one, but add any others you genuinely believe.
    3. Commit the five ADRs and the template through your normal PR loop. During self-review, read each ADR as a sceptical stranger and check the Options considered section names a *specific* alternative, not a vague "other approaches".
    *You know it worked when:* all five files in `docs/adr/` name a specific rejected alternative and at least one negative consequence — and you can say each ADR's downside out loud without opening the file.

**Done when:** `docs/adr/` has five records, each naming a specific rejected alternative and at least one negative consequence you accept.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. What are the four sections of an ADR, and which one do people most often skip?
2. Why is an ADR that lists no downsides a warning sign?
3. Pick one of your five ADRs. State the option you rejected and the specific reason.
4. You change your mind in [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) about something you decided in Phase 0. What exactly do you do to the original ADR?
5. Why is "we chose Postgres" not an ADR, but "we chose Postgres over MongoDB because we need multi-row transactions, accepting mandatory schema migrations" is?

#### Task 0.6 — OOP in practice: entities, value objects, and immutability — 1h

**What:** Write, by hand, the small object-design vocabulary the entire domain model depends on.
**Why:** You asked for in-depth OOP. The part that actually matters day to day is not inheritance trees — it is knowing when a thing has an identity and when it is just a value, and defending invariants in constructors.
**Solves:** the anemic-model failure mode where every class is a bag of getters and setters and the rules live scattered across "service" classes.

**Learn this first:** ask AI *"explain the difference between an entity and a value object
in domain-driven design, with a worked example, and explain how `equals` should differ
between them"*. Then ask it to critique your own answer.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Entity** | An object with an identity that persists while its contents change. An `Event` whose title you edit is still the same event. Two entities are equal when their IDs match. |
| **Value object** | An object that *is* its contents, with no identity. ₹500 is ₹500; there is no "which one". Two value objects are equal when every field matches. |
| **Invariant** | A rule that must be true at all times, not just when someone remembers to check. "Money is never negative." The constructor is where you enforce it. |
| **Immutability** | Having no way to change an object after construction — no setters, final fields. Immutable objects are automatically safe to share between threads, which is why [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) keeps coming back to this. |
| **Compact constructor** | A Java `record`'s short constructor form where you validate arguments before they are assigned. The natural home for an invariant. |
| **`record`** | A Java class whose only job is to hold values. You get the constructor, `equals`, `hashCode`, and `toString` generated, with value-based equality — exactly what a value object needs. |
| **Sealed interface** | An interface that names the only types allowed to implement it. The compiler can then prove your `switch` covers every case, so adding a new one becomes a compile error rather than a production bug. |
| **Primitive obsession** | Passing `BigDecimal amount` and `String currency` around as two loose parameters instead of one `Money`. This is how someone eventually adds dollars to rupees. |
| **Anemic domain model** | Classes that are only getters and setters, with all the real rules living in `*Service` classes. It is the default thing people build, and the thing this task exists to prevent. |
| **SOLID** | Five design principles. The two that matter most here are the Single Responsibility Principle and the Dependency Inversion Principle, which [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h) — one class per use case, depending only on interfaces it declares itself — is built around. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** the distinction between a thing with **identity** (an `Event` that changes over time and is still the same event) and a thing that is purely a **value** (`Money(500, "INR")`). Every modelling decision in [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) starts here.
- **When it works you will see:** a `Money` value object that cannot be constructed negative and whose equality is value-based, and an `Event` entity whose identity survives every field changing.
- **Where people get stuck:** giving value objects an id "because the database needs one". That is the database's concern, not the model's. The persistence adapter maps it; the domain should not know.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Write SOLID down, with a Zenith example per principle.**
    *What this step is:* SOLID is five classic design principles (Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion). In this step you write a short document — one paragraph per principle, in your own words — where every paragraph names something from *Zenith* (this project), not a textbook shape. At the end you will have `docs/design-principles.md`: five paragraphs you could speak aloud in an interview.
    *Builds on:* [Task F2.6 — Interfaces, abstract classes, and polymorphism](#task-f26--interfaces-abstract-classes-and-polymorphism--1h) — where you wrote the `PricingRule` interface with flat and tiered implementations; that hierarchy is your example here. [Task F2.7 — Inheritance, overriding, and why you will usually prefer composition](#task-f27--inheritance-overriding-and-why-you-will-usually-prefer-composition--15h) — the habits SOLID formalises. [The hexagonal architecture explainer in §2.1](#hexagonal-architecture-also-called-ports-and-adapters) — where `port/out` interfaces (interfaces the domain declares for things it needs from the outside world, like saving data) were introduced; that is your Dependency Inversion example.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/design-principles.md` with five headings: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion.
    2. Under each, write **one paragraph in your own words** — copy-pasting an AI answer defeats the task — anchored to a Zenith example. Two are prescribed: for **Liskov Substitution** (any implementation of an interface must be usable wherever the interface is expected, without surprises), describe a violation *risk* in a `PricingRule` hierarchy — for example, a new rule that throws for quantities every other rule handles would break every caller that treats all `PricingRule`s alike. For **Dependency Inversion** (high-level code depends on interfaces it owns, not on low-level detail), describe how a `port/out` interface realises it: the domain declares "something that saves events", and the database adapter implements it — so the dependency arrow points *into* the domain.
    3. Invent your own Zenith-flavoured example for the remaining three principles.
    *You know it worked when:* `docs/design-principles.md` has five paragraphs, each naming a Zenith class or interface — and none of them reads like a textbook definition.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Build `Money`, `Slug`, and `SeatCoordinate` as value objects.**
    *What this step is:* You implement the three value objects the whole domain model will lean on, in the shared `platform-common` module. A value object *is* its contents — ₹500 is ₹500, there is no "which one" — so each is a `record` (immutable, value-based equality for free) whose compact constructor refuses to ever let an invalid instance exist. At the end you will have three small records in `platform-common` that cannot be constructed in an invalid state, with no setters anywhere.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — where you created `platform-common`, the shared module for value types that every service may use. [Task F3.6 — Records, and objects that cannot hold invalid data](#task-f36--records-and-objects-that-cannot-hold-invalid-data--1h) — where you wrote `record Money(long amountInPaise, String currency)` with a compact constructor; this step is that idea, done for real. [Task F4.6 — JSON and serialisation](#task-f46--json-and-serialisation--1h) — where `BigDecimal` (Java's exact decimal number type, the correct type for money) replaced the whole-paise workaround. [Task F3.8 — Immutability and defensive copying](#task-f38--immutability-and-defensive-copying--1h) — why no-setters matters. [Task F2.8 — `equals`, `hashCode`, and the contract collections rely on](#task-f28--equals-hashcode-and-the-contract-collections-rely-on--15h) — the equality contract records satisfy for you.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `platform-common`, create `record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency)` with a compact constructor that rejects a null or negative `amount` and a currency that is not a valid ISO-4217 code (the three-letter standard like `INR` or `USD` — `Currency.getInstance(currency)` throws for invalid ones, which is validation you get for free).
    2. Create `record Slug(String value)` — a slug is the URL-friendly identifier for an event, like `coldplay-mumbai-2026` — whose compact constructor rejects anything that is not lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens.
    3. Create `record SeatCoordinate(String row, int number)` whose compact constructor rejects a blank row and a number below 1.
    4. Write no setters, and no mutable fields — records make both impossible, which is the point. Do not hand-write `equals`/`hashCode`: the record generates value-based versions (two `Money`s are equal when amount and currency both match), which is exactly what a value object needs.
    5. Note what you did **not** add: an `id` field. Giving a value object an id "because the database needs one" is the classic mistake — the database's id is the persistence adapter's concern, and the domain should not know about it.
    *You know it worked when:* all three records compile in `platform-common`, constructing any of them with bad input throws, and `new Money(new BigDecimal("500"), "INR").equals(new Money(new BigDecimal("500"), "INR"))` is `true`.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Sketch the `Event` entity, as the contrast.**
    *What this step is:* An entity is the opposite of a value object: it has an *identity* that persists while its contents change — an `Event` whose title you edit is still the same event. You sketch one (a rough illustrative class, not the production version — [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) builds that properly) to make the contrast physical: identity-based equality, and state that can only change through *intention methods* — methods named after a business action, like `publish()`, that enforce the rules of that action — never through a bare setter like `setStatus()`. At the end you will have a small `Event` class whose identity survives every field changing.
    *Builds on:* [Task F3.6 — Records, and objects that cannot hold invalid data](#task-f36--records-and-objects-that-cannot-hold-invalid-data--1h) — whose "where people get stuck" warned that a thing with identity and a lifecycle should be a class, not a record; this is that thing. [Task F2.8 — `equals`, `hashCode`, and the contract collections rely on](#task-f28--equals-hashcode-and-the-contract-collections-rely-on--15h) — where you learned to base `equals` on exactly the fields that define sameness; for an entity, that is the ID alone.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write a plain class `Event` with a `private final UUID id`, mutable fields such as `title` and `status`, and `equals`/`hashCode` implemented **on the id only** — two `Event` objects with the same id are the same event, even if every other field differs.
    2. Expose state change only through intention methods: write `publish()`, which checks the event is in a publishable state before changing `status` — and deliberately do **not** write `setStatus()`. A setter says "anyone may put anything here"; an intention method says "this business action, with its rules, happened".
    3. Add a comment at the top: `// sketch — the real Event aggregate is built in Phase 1`.
    *You know it worked when:* two `Event` instances with the same id but different titles are `.equals()`, changing the title changes neither equality nor `hashCode`, and there is no `setStatus` method to call.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Write the failing-case tests first.**
    *What this step is:* Tests that attack your value objects with invalid input and demand an exception. The rule being proven: a value object that *can* be constructed in an invalid state is not a value object — the constructor is the gate, and these tests are you rattling it. Write each test before you trust the validation it covers. At the end you will have a test class in which every invariant from Step 2 has a test that constructs a bad instance and expects a throw.
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.2 — Lifecycle, exceptions, and parameterised tests](#task-f72--lifecycle-exceptions-and-parameterised-tests--1h) — where you learned `assertThrows`, the JUnit way of asserting that code throws. [Task F7.1 — Your first test, and what makes a test worth having](#task-f71--your-first-test-and-what-makes-a-test-worth-having--1h) — what a test is for in the first place.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `platform-common`'s test folder, write the headline test: `assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> new Money(new BigDecimal("-1"), "USD"))` — `new Money(new BigDecimal("-1"), "USD")` **must throw**.
    2. Add one failing-case test per invariant: `Money` with a null amount and with a nonsense currency, `Slug` with uppercase letters and with spaces, `SeatCoordinate` with a blank row and with seat number 0.
    3. Add the positive equality test: two `Money` objects built from the same values are `.equals()` and share a `hashCode`.
    4. **Break it on purpose:** comment out one validation line in `Money`'s compact constructor, run the tests, and watch the matching test go red — that red is proof the test actually guards something. Put the line back and watch it go green.
    *You know it worked when:* `mvn test` is green with the validation in place, and goes red the moment you comment a validation line out.

- [ ] **Step 5 — A sealed result type instead of null or exceptions.**
    *What this step is:* You model "what happened when we tried to hold seats" as a closed set of outcomes the compiler knows about: `sealed interface HoldResult permits Granted, Rejected, PartiallyGranted`. A sealed interface names the only types allowed to implement it, so a `switch` over a `HoldResult` can be *exhaustive* — the compiler proves every case is handled, and adding a fourth outcome later becomes a compile error at every switch instead of a production bug. At the end you will have the sealed interface, its three record implementations, and one exhaustive switch over them.
    *Builds on:* [Task F3.7 — Sealed interfaces, pattern matching, and text blocks](#task-f37--sealed-interfaces-pattern-matching-and-text-blocks--1h) — where sealed interfaces and switch pattern matching were taught; this is their first real Zenith use.
    *Do this:*
    1. Next to your value objects, declare:
        ```java
        sealed interface HoldResult permits Granted, Rejected, PartiallyGranted {}
        record Granted(List<SeatCoordinate> seats) implements HoldResult {}
        record Rejected(String reason) implements HoldResult {}
        record PartiallyGranted(List<SeatCoordinate> granted, List<SeatCoordinate> refused) implements HoldResult {}
        ```
    2. Write a small method (a test is fine) that takes a `HoldResult` and handles it with a pattern-matching `switch` covering all three cases — and **no `default` branch**, because `default` is what silently swallows the fourth case you add next year.
    3. **Break it on purpose:** delete one `case` and recompile — the compiler refuses, because the switch is no longer exhaustive. That refusal is the entire value of `sealed`. Put the case back.
    4. Ask AI: *"why is a sealed result type like HoldResult better than returning null or throwing an exception for a seat-hold outcome?"* — expect the answer to land on: null and exceptions hide the outcome set from the compiler, while a sealed type forces every caller to handle every outcome, visibly. Write the one sentence you found most convincing into your notes.
    *You know it worked when:* removing any `case` from the switch is a compile error, and you can explain in one sentence why that beats a `null` return.

**Done when:** `Money` cannot be constructed negative, `equals` is value-based and tested, and you can explain entity-versus-value-object out loud in 60 seconds without notes.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Define entity and value object, and give one Zenith example of each.
2. How should `equals` differ between an entity and a value object, and why?
3. Why does `Money` validate inside its own constructor rather than in the service that builds it?
4. What is an anemic domain model, and why is it a problem rather than just a style preference?
5. What does `sealed` give you that a plain interface does not? Answer in terms of what the compiler can prove.

#### Task 0.7 — The design pattern register — 1h

**What:** A living document mapping each design pattern to the real class in your codebase that uses it.
**Why:** Patterns learned as a glossary evaporate within a month. Patterns tied to code you wrote stick for years.
**Solves:** the interview failure mode of naming a pattern but being unable to say what problem it solved in your code — which is worse than not naming it at all.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Design pattern** | A named, repeatable solution to a problem that keeps recurring. The name is useful only because it lets two engineers skip a ten-minute explanation. |
| **GoF** | "Gang of Four", the four authors of the 1994 book that named most of the classic patterns. You will hear the term in interviews. |
| **Pattern register** | Your `docs/patterns.md` — a table tying each pattern to the actual class in your code that uses it and the problem it solved there. |
| **Pattern fever** | Reaching for a pattern because you know it rather than because the problem needs it. A `StrategyFactoryBuilder` wrapping one `if` is the classic symptom. |
| **Singleton** | A pattern guaranteeing one instance of a class. Listed here as one you deliberately do **not** write, because Spring already manages bean lifecycle for you. |
| **Visitor** | A pattern for adding operations to a fixed set of types. Rejected here because Zenith has no stable element hierarchy worth the indirection. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** starting the register **empty**. You fill a row only when a real problem forced the pattern. A register filled in advance is a list of patterns you will then go looking for excuses to use.
- **When it works you will see:** a `docs/patterns.md` with twelve named patterns and the "where used" column deliberately blank.
- **Where people get stuck:** pattern fever — reaching for a pattern because you know it. A `StrategyFactoryBuilder` wrapping a single `if` is the classic symptom and it reads as inexperience, not sophistication.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Create the register file with its four columns.**
    *What this step is:* The pattern register is one markdown table that will live for the whole project, tying each design pattern (a named, reusable solution to a recurring problem) to the real class in your code that uses it. In this step you only create the file and its table header. At the end you will have `docs/patterns.md` with four columns and no rows yet.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/patterns.md` containing a markdown table with exactly these columns: *Pattern · Where used · What problem it solved · What I would do differently*.
    2. Add one line of prose above the table saying what the register is for — future-you will thank present-you. Note while you write it: the **last** column is the one interviewers find interesting, because "what I would do differently" is the column only someone who actually used the pattern can fill.
    *You know it worked when:* `docs/patterns.md` exists and its table header shows all four column names.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Seed the twelve patterns, honestly, with "where used" blank.**
    *What this step is:* You add a row for each of the twelve patterns you will most plausibly meet in this project and in interviews — but you deliberately leave the "where used" column **empty**. A register filled in advance is a list of patterns you will then go hunting for excuses to use (that is *pattern fever*, and a `StrategyFactoryBuilder` wrapping one `if` is its classic symptom). A row gets filled only when a real problem forces the pattern. At the end you will have twelve named rows, all with a blank "where used".
    *Builds on:* [Task F2.6 — Interfaces, abstract classes, and polymorphism](#task-f26--interfaces-abstract-classes-and-polymorphism--1h) — where you already wrote a Strategy (the `PricingRule` interface with flat and tiered rules) chosen by a factory method; resist filling those rows now — fill them when the *Zenith* code earns them.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add one row each for: Builder, Factory Method, Strategy, Template Method, Adapter, Facade, Decorator, Proxy, Observer, Chain of Responsibility, State, Specification. For each, add a one-line plain-English meaning in your own words in the "what problem it solved" column prefixed with "(expected:)" — so the row teaches you something even while unfilled — or keep that column blank too if you prefer the stricter discipline; the one hard rule is that **"where used" stays blank** until real code exists.
    2. Be honest with yourself about the last two rows. **Chain of Responsibility** (a line of handlers where each either deals with a request or passes it on) shows up in this plan as chains you *configure* — the gateway filters of [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline) and the Kafka error handlers of [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) — not chains you design from scratch. And no task in this plan actually makes you write a **Specification** (an object representing a reusable business rule you can combine with and/or). Mark both rows "understood, not written" — that is a legitimate register entry, and claiming more than that is exactly the dishonesty this register exists to prevent.
    *You know it worked when:* the table has twelve rows, every "where used" cell is empty, and the Chain of Responsibility and Specification rows carry "understood, not written".

- [ ] **Step 3 — Add the same-commit rule to your definition of done.**
    *What this step is:* A standing rule that keeps the register alive: whenever you apply a pattern in code, the register row is added **in the same commit** as the code. In week 20, backfilling this document would be both painful (you will not remember which class used what, or why) and dishonest (a backfilled "what problem it solved" is a guess dressed as a record). At the end, the rule is written where you will actually re-read it.
    *Builds on:* [§6.4 — Definition of done](#64-definition-of-done-applies-to-every-task-in-this-plan) — the checklist every task in this plan must pass before you call it finished; this step extends it. [Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline](#task-04--git-workflow-the-remote-and-a-local-ci-pipeline--2h) — the branch → commit → PR → self-review → merge loop every change now travels through, which is why "same commit" is an enforceable idea at all.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write the rule into your own copy of the definition of done (wherever you keep your per-task checklist — your notes file or the PR template's self-review comment from [Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline](#task-04--git-workflow-the-remote-and-a-local-ci-pipeline--2h)): *"applied a pattern → added its `docs/patterns.md` row in the same commit."*
    2. Add the same check to your self-review habit: when reviewing your own PR diff, if a diff introduces a Builder, Strategy, or any other register pattern, confirm the `docs/patterns.md` change is sitting in the same diff.
    *You know it worked when:* you can point at the written rule, and your self-review checklist mentions the register.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Record two patterns you will deliberately not use.**
    *What this step is:* Knowing when *not* to reach for a pattern is the senior signal, so the register also records rejections. You add a short section naming two patterns this project consciously avoids, each with its reason. At the end, `docs/patterns.md` has a "deliberately not used" section with two entries.
    *Builds on:* [Task F6.3 — Bean scopes, duplicate beans, and beans you do not own](#task-f63--bean-scopes-duplicate-beans-and-beans-you-do-not-own--05h) — where you saw that Spring beans are singleton-scoped by default: the framework already guarantees one instance per application, which is the whole reason the first rejection below exists.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a section *Deliberately not used* to `docs/patterns.md`.
    2. Entry one — **Singleton** (the hand-written pattern guaranteeing one instance of a class, usually via a private constructor and a static `getInstance()`): rejected because Spring already manages bean scope and lifecycle for you; hand-rolling a singleton inside a Spring app duplicates the framework's job and makes testing harder.
    3. Entry two — **Visitor** (a pattern for adding new operations to a fixed, rarely-changing set of types without editing those types): rejected because Zenith has no stable element hierarchy worth that indirection — the pattern's cost only pays off when the set of types is frozen and operations keep multiplying, which is not this project.
    *You know it worked when:* both rejections appear in the file with a one-sentence reason each, specific enough that you could defend them out loud.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Collect one real over-application story.**
    *What this step is:* Pattern fever is easier to avoid once you have seen its wreckage, so you gather concrete examples of patterns being over-applied and keep the most convincing one. At the end, your notes hold one named example of a pattern that made real code worse, plus the simpler alternative.
    *Do this:*
    1. Ask AI: *"give me three examples of design patterns being over-applied in Java codebases and what the simpler alternative was"*. Expect answers like a factory hierarchy wrapping a single `new`, or an Observer setup where one direct method call would do.
    2. Pick the example that most convinces you, and add it to your notes in your own words — the pattern, what it cost, and the simpler alternative that was available.
    *You know it worked when:* you can tell the story in under a minute: which pattern, why it was overkill there, and what the simpler code looked like.

**Done when:** `docs/patterns.md` exists with a "where used" column you have committed to maintaining, and two explicitly rejected patterns with reasons.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Why does the register record "what problem it solved" rather than just the pattern name?
2. Name the two patterns you decided *not* to use, and the reason for each.
3. What rule did you add to your definition of done about patterns, and why does backfilling in week 20 not work?
4. Give an example of a design pattern being over-applied, and say what the simpler alternative was.

**Phase 0 exit check — tick honestly:**

- [ ] `make reset && make up` works from a cold start, following only `docs/local-setup.md`.
- [ ] `mvn -B clean verify` passes, and I have *seen* each quality gate fail on purpose.
- [ ] A `git push` of failing code is blocked by my own pre-push hook.
- [ ] I have five ADRs, each with a rejected alternative and an accepted downside.
- [ ] I can explain entity versus value object, and why `Money` validates in its constructor.
- [ ] (after [Task 0.8 — Low-level design: from a blank page to classes](#task-08--low-level-design-from-a-blank-page-to-classes--4h), which follows below) I have three timed low-level-design attempts committed under `lld-practice/`, each with my own written critique.

**Phase 0 interview talking points:** why a monorepo; what ArchUnit prevents that code
review does not; what an ADR is and which one you later regretted; why a coverage ratchet
beats a coverage target.

#### Task 0.8 — Low-level design: from a blank page to classes — 4h

**What:** Practise the interview round where you are handed a problem statement and 45 minutes to produce classes, responsibilities and a skeleton that runs.
**Why:** Almost every backend hiring loop has an LLD or machine-coding round, scored separately from system design and from DSA. You already have the raw skills from [Task 0.6 — OOP in practice: entities, value objects, and immutability](#task-06--oop-in-practice-entities-value-objects-and-immutability--1h) and [Task 0.7 — The design pattern register](#task-07--the-design-pattern-register--1h) — what you do not yet have is the **format and the clock**, and those are what people actually fail on.
**Solves:** freezing in front of a blank page, over-engineering a 45-minute problem, and the specific failure of designing data instead of behaviour.

**Learn this first:** [Task 0.6 — OOP in practice: entities, value objects, and immutability](#task-06--oop-in-practice-entities-value-objects-and-immutability--1h) and [Task 0.7 — The design pattern register](#task-07--the-design-pattern-register--1h). From [Stage F — Foundations](#stage-f--foundations-the-things-everything-else-assumes--63h--weeks-13): [Task F2.2](#task-f22--classes-and-objects-the-thing-everything-else-is-made-of--15h) (classes and constructors), [Task F2.6](#task-f26--interfaces-abstract-classes-and-polymorphism--1h) (interfaces), [Task F2.7](#task-f27--inheritance-overriding-and-why-you-will-usually-prefer-composition--15h) (composition over inheritance), [Task F2.11](#task-f211--enums-that-carry-behaviour--1h) (enums).

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **LLD** | Low-Level Design. A round where you design the classes for **one bounded problem** — a parking lot, a rate limiter, a lift. Not architecture, not algorithms. Class names, responsibilities, relationships, interfaces. |
| **HLD vs LLD** | HLD is boxes and arrows *between* services; LLD is classes *inside* one box. They are usually separate rounds, and answering one in the other's language is a common and costly mistake. |
| **Machine coding** | The same exercise with a compiler: running code plus tests in 90–120 minutes. Judged heavily on whether it actually runs. |
| **Class responsibility** | The one reason a class exists. If you cannot state it in a sentence without the word "and", it is doing too much. |
| **Association / aggregation / composition** | Three strengths of "has-a". Association: knows about. Aggregation: holds, but the part survives independently. Composition: owns, and the part dies with it. Interviewers do ask you to distinguish these. **Note the word clash:** in SQL ([Task F5.6 — Grouping, aggregates, and CTEs](#task-f56--grouping-aggregates-and-ctes--05h), where it means `COUNT`/`SUM`/`GROUP BY`) "aggregation" means something unrelated — `COUNT`, `SUM` and `GROUP BY`. |
| **Anaemic model** | Classes that are only data with getters, and all the behaviour in a service. The most common reason an LLD answer scores badly. |
| **Driver** | A tiny `main` demonstrating the flow end to end. In machine coding, a design that does not run scores below a simpler one that does. |
| **Over-engineering tell** | An interface, a factory and a config layer for a problem with three concrete types. Reads as inexperience, not sophistication. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** producing something **coherent and running** in 45 minutes. A complete simple design scores far above an elegant half-finished one, every time.
- **When it works you will see:** three timed attempts committed under `lld-practice/`, each with real classes, a driver that runs, and your own written critique of it.
- **Where people get stuck:** designing data instead of behaviour. A `Ticket` with six getters and no methods, and all the logic in a `ParkingLotService`, is an anaemic model — and it is the single most common reason candidates fail this round. Put the behaviour on the class that owns the data.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Memorise the shape of the round.**
    *What this step is:* An LLD round is not a free-form chat — it has a standard rhythm, and interviewers quietly score you on whether you follow one. Before you practise anything, learn the five-step sequence and the minutes each step gets, so when the clock starts you never face a blank page wondering what to do first. At the end of this step the sequence is written on a physical card sitting next to your keyboard.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write this on an index card or sticky note, word for word: **clarify requirements (5 min) → list the nouns and pick the real entities (5 min) → assign responsibilities and define interfaces (15 min) → write the core classes (15 min) → driver, plus the edge cases you consciously skipped (5 min)**. (A *driver*, from the New words table above, is the tiny `main` method that runs the whole flow end to end.)
    2. Keep that card next to you for all three practice runs in this task — and for every rep after it.
    *You know it worked when:* you can recite all five steps and their minutes out loud without looking at the card.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Practice 1: a parking lot, 45 minutes on the clock.**
    *What this step is:* Your first full timed attempt, on deliberately the most boring classic there is: a parking lot. You design vehicle types, spot types, a pricing strategy, and a ticket. Nothing looked up — no search, no AI, no notes except your card from Step 1. At the end you have a folder of real Java classes and a driver, finished or not.
    *Builds on:* [Task F2.2 — Classes and objects: the thing everything else is made of](#task-f22--classes-and-objects-the-thing-everything-else-is-made-of--15h) — where you learned to write a class with fields and a constructor; [Task F2.11 — Enums that carry behaviour](#task-f211--enums-that-carry-behaviour--1h) — vehicle types and spot types are a natural fit for the enums-with-behaviour you wrote there; [Task 0.6 — OOP in practice: entities, value objects, and immutability](#task-06--oop-in-practice-entities-value-objects-and-immutability--1h) — the entity-versus-value-object vocabulary you use to decide what each class is.
    *Do this:*
    1. Set a real timer for 45 minutes and start it before you re-read the problem.
    2. Work through the card in order: clarify the scope to yourself in writing, list the nouns and pick the real entities, assign responsibilities and interfaces, write the core classes, then the driver.
    3. **Stop at 45 minutes even if it is unfinished** — running out of time is part of what you are practising.
    *You know it worked when:* the timer rang, you actually stopped, and a folder of `.java` files with a `main` method exists — a half-finished design counts, as long as the stop was honest.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Review your own attempt, in writing.**
    *What this step is:* You now grade Practice 1 the way an interviewer would. **The review is where the learning happens, not the attempt** — skipping it turns the 45 minutes into wasted typing.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.6 — OOP in practice: entities, value objects, and immutability](#task-06--oop-in-practice-entities-value-objects-and-immutability--1h) — where you learned why behaviour belongs on the class that owns the data (the anaemic-model trap in the New words table above); [Task 0.7 — The design pattern register](#task-07--the-design-pattern-register--1h) — where you learned to spot "pattern fever", reaching for a pattern the problem never asked for.
    *Do this:*
    1. Answer these three questions **in writing**, naming your actual classes: does any class have more than one reason to change? Did you model *behaviour*, or data with getters? Did you add an abstraction the problem did not ask for?
    2. Save the answers as a short critique file inside the attempt's folder.
    *You know it worked when:* the critique names at least one specific class of yours under each of the three questions — "all fine" on a first attempt means you have not looked hard enough.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Practice 2: an in-memory rate limiter, 45 minutes.**
    *What this step is:* A second timed attempt, closer to real backend work. A rate limiter is an object that decides whether to allow or reject each incoming request based on how many came recently — "at most 100 requests per minute per user", say. You must support **at least two** limiting algorithms (for example a fixed-window counter — allow at most N per clock minute — and a token bucket — a budget that refills steadily) **behind one interface**. This exact design comes back twice: [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) uses it as the gateway's in-memory limiter, and [Task 4.4 — Redis as a data structure server](#task-44--redis-as-a-data-structure-server--3h) rebuilds it backed by Redis and a Lua script. Designing it well today pays off twice.
    *Builds on:* [Task F2.6 — Interfaces, abstract classes, and polymorphism](#task-f26--interfaces-abstract-classes-and-polymorphism--1h) — this reuses the Strategy pattern you wrote there: each algorithm variant behind one interface, chosen at runtime.
    *Do this:*
    1. Set the 45-minute timer and follow the card again.
    2. Define one interface (something like `RateLimiter` with an `allow(userId)` method) and at least two implementing algorithms behind it.
    3. Write a driver that hammers both implementations and shows requests being allowed, then rejected.
    4. Stop at 45 minutes, then repeat the Step 3 written review on this attempt.
    *You know it worked when:* two different algorithms sit behind one interface, and the driver demonstrably rejects a request once the limit is hit.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Practice 3: a cut-down Zenith, from a blank page, 45 minutes.**
    *What this step is:* Your third timed attempt is a throwaway sketch of the very system this plan builds: events, seats, holds (a seat reserved for a few minutes while someone pays), and bookings. You are about to spend eleven tasks doing this properly in [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) — doing a cold, throwaway version first makes every one of those tasks clearer, and comparing the two afterwards is genuinely instructive about what careful modelling buys you.
    *Do this:*
    1. Set the 45-minute timer. From memory only, design classes for events, seats, holds, and bookings, following the card.
    2. Write the driver, stop at 45 minutes, and run the Step 3 written review once more.
    3. Leave the attempt untouched — at the end of [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline), come back and compare it to the real domain model, and note what the careful version got right that this one missed.
    *You know it worked when:* the attempt exists, the review is written, and you have a reminder (a journal line is enough) to compare it against the real model at the [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) exit.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Commit all three attempts with an honest note.**
    *What this step is:* The three attempts and their reviews become permanent, visible history in your repository, each ending with one honest sentence: *what I would change given another fifteen minutes.* That note is exactly what you say out loud in a real round when the time goes — practising writing it is practising saying it.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline](#task-04--git-workflow-the-remote-and-a-local-ci-pipeline--2h) — you commit these the same branch-and-PR way you set up there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `lld-practice/` at the repository root, with one subfolder per attempt (`parking-lot/`, `rate-limiter/`, `zenith-sketch/`).
    2. In each subfolder, alongside the code and the written review, add the short note: *what I would change given another fifteen minutes.*
    3. Commit and push.
    *You know it worked when:* `git log` shows the commits, and each of the three folders contains code, a review, and the fifteen-minutes note.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Read the canon list once, and set up the drip.**
    *What this step is:* Across most companies this round is drawn from a small, stable set of problems. Reading the list once means the problem shapes stop being surprises. You will **not** practise them all today, and you should not try — you practise them at a steady drip instead, and this step is where you learn the schedule.
    *Do this:*
    1. Read the canon list: parking lot, elevator bank, Splitwise (an expense-sharing ledger — who owes whom after a trip), BookMyShow-style ticket booking (you are literally building one), an LRU cache (a cache that evicts its least-recently-used entry when full), a logger framework, a vending machine, chess, a notification dispatcher, a URL shortener, an ATM, a meeting-room scheduler.
    2. Learn the schedule: **every phase exit from [Phase 1](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) through [Phase 11](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline) adds one new timed 45-minute problem from this list** — [§11 — Weekly cadence and how to not fall behind](#11-weekly-cadence-and-how-to-not-fall-behind) places it in the day-7 weekly review slot, so it costs none of your budgeted build hours.
    3. Add up what that buys you: three attempts today, one per phase exit through [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline), and one cold re-run in [Task 14.3 — Demo path and interview preparation](#task-143--demo-path-and-interview-preparation--5h) — roughly fifteen timed reps by the end of the plan, which is what "comfortable in this round" actually takes. Reps, not brilliance, are what this round rewards.
    *You know it worked when:* you can name at least half the canon problems from memory and say exactly when your next rep happens (the day-7 slot of the [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) exit).

- [ ] **Step 8 — Learn the two sentences that rescue a real round.**
    *What this step is:* Two short sentences handle the two scariest moments of a live round — the start, and running out of time. Both read as experience. Silence and quiet guessing do not.
    *Do this:*
    1. Memorise sentence one, for the start: *"Let me clarify the scope before I start designing."*
    2. Memorise sentence two, for when the clock beats you: *"I am deliberately not handling X — here is what I would add for it."*
    3. Say each one out loud once, in context: the first before your next practice run, the second at its 45-minute mark.
    *You know it worked when:* you can produce both sentences from memory and say which moment of a round each belongs to.

- [ ] **Step 9 — Ask AI to run a mock round and critique you.**
    *What this step is:* You turn the whole exercise into something you can repeat forever without this document. An AI can generate a fresh problem and then grade your design the way an interviewer would — which makes this the most repeatable interview exercise in the whole plan.
    *Builds on:* [§0.5 — How to learn this by asking AI](#05-how-to-learn-this-by-asking-ai) — the rules for asking AI to teach rather than to do the work for you.
    *Do this:*
    1. Ask AI: *"Give me a 45-minute LLD problem statement. Let me design it, then critique my classes the way an interviewer would, focusing on responsibilities, on anaemic models, and on anything I over-engineered."*
    2. Do the full cycle once — timed design, then the critique — and write down one weakness the critique found.
    3. Repeat this whenever you have a spare evening.
    *You know it worked when:* you have completed one full AI-critiqued cycle and can name the specific weakness it caught in your design.

**Done when:** three timed attempts are committed, you can recite the five-step sequence
from memory, and you can name the specific over-engineering you caught in your own first
attempt.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. What is the difference between an HLD round and an LLD round? Name one thing that is out of scope in each.
2. Recite the five-step sequence and the minutes you give each step.
3. What is an anaemic model, and why does it score badly when the code still works?
4. In your parking lot, which class owns the pricing rule, and why not the one next to it?
5. Ten minutes left, three features unbuilt. What do you say out loud?
6. Distinguish association, aggregation and composition, using your own classes as the examples.

### Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service — 17h baseline

**Scheduled:** Weeks 5–6

**Goal:** `catalog-service` as the reference implementation every later service copies:
DDD aggregates, hexagonal layering, a REST API with grown-up HTTP semantics, and a real
test pyramid.

**Why this phase exists:** you will build eight more services. Getting the first one
genuinely right — and then templating it — is worth triple the time it costs. Every
shortcut you take here you will take ten more times.

**Before you start — the shape of what you are building.** Everything in this phase is an
answer to one question: *where does each kind of code live, and what is it allowed to
know about?* Hexagonal architecture ([explained in §2.1](#hexagonal-architecture-also-called-ports-and-adapters))
is the answer. The four rings, inside out:

| Ring | Package | Knows about | Never knows about |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Domain** | `domain/` | Plain Java only | Spring, JPA, HTTP, Kafka |
| **Application** | `application/` + `port/` | Domain, its own port interfaces | Any concrete adapter |
| **Adapters (in)** | `adapter/in/web`, `adapter/in/messaging` | Application input ports | Persistence details |
| **Adapters (out)** | `adapter/out/persistence`, `adapter/out/messaging` | Application output ports | Each other |

Ask AI: *"I have a Spring Boot service using hexagonal architecture. Walk me through
exactly which classes a single `POST /events` request touches, in order, from the
controller to the database and back — and tell me which direction each dependency points."*
Draw that call chain on paper before you write any code. If you cannot draw it, the rest
of this phase will feel arbitrary.

**Services you create in this phase:** none — you fill in `catalog-service`, which you
created as a skeleton in [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) and which is **service 1 of nine**. Every other service
in this plan begins as a copy of what you build here, so the structure matters more than
the feature.

**New to you in this phase:** DDD vocabulary, MapStruct, RFC 9457, keyset pagination,
ETags, Flyway, JPA mapping, Testcontainers. Returning from [Stage F — Foundations](#stage-f--foundations-the-things-everything-else-assumes--63h--weeks-13): Bean Validation
([Task F6.8 — Validation, one error shape, and a request log](#task-f68--validation-one-error-shape-and-a-request-log--1h)), Mockito ([Task F7.4 — Mockito in practice, and the over-mocking trap](#task-f74--mockito-in-practice-and-the-over-mocking-trap--05h)), `@WebMvcTest` ([Task F7.5 — Testing a Spring application with slices](#task-f75--testing-a-spring-application-with-slices--1h)).

---

#### Task 1.1 — Event-storm the domain and draw the context map — 1.5h

**What:** Discover the business before modelling it. List every business event, group the events into bounded contexts, and draw how the contexts talk.
**Why:** Microservice boundaries drawn from technical nouns ("the database service", "the util service") are the number-one cause of distributed monoliths. Boundaries drawn from business invariants hold up for years.
**Solves:** the chatty, transaction-spanning service split you would otherwise discover in week 15 and be unable to undo without rewriting everything.

**Learn this first:** ask AI *"explain bounded context in DDD using a concrete example
where the same word means two different things in two contexts"*. For Zenith that word is
"ticket" — in Catalog it is a price tier, in Orders it is a line item, in Access Control it
is a scannable credential. Three different models, deliberately.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Event storming** | A discovery technique: list every business event in past tense ("OrderPlaced", "TicketScanned") before designing anything. Events are easier to agree on than nouns, which is why you start there. |
| **Bounded context** | A boundary inside which one word has exactly one meaning. Not the same thing as a microservice — a context is about language and consistency; a service is a deployment choice that usually follows it. |
| **Ubiquitous language** | The vocabulary shared by the code and the business, inside one context. If the business says "hold" and the code says "reservation", you will pay for that difference for years. |
| **Context map** | A diagram of your contexts and, crucially, the *kind* of relationship between each pair. The relationships carry more information than the boxes. |
| **Customer/supplier** | A relationship where the downstream context's needs genuinely influence what the upstream one publishes. |
| **Anti-corruption layer** | A translation layer that converts another context's model into yours, so their vocabulary never leaks into your code. You build a real one in [Task 6.4 — Service decomposition: extract payment-service](#task-64--service-decomposition-extract-payment-service--5h). |
| **Shared-nothing** | Two contexts with no shared database and no shared classes, communicating only by events. The loosest and most durable coupling available. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** drawing boundaries from **business invariants**, not from technical nouns. A "database service" or "utils service" is the number-one cause of a distributed monolith.
- **When it works you will see:** a context map on paper where you can justify every boundary with a consistency argument — "these two facts must be true at the same instant, so they live together".
- **Where people get stuck:** splitting by layer (a controller service, a data service) instead of by capability. That gives you all the cost of microservices and none of the independence, because every change touches all of them.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — List every business event, 40 or more.**
    *What this step is:* Event storming starts with a brain-dump, not a design. A *business event* is something that happened and mattered to the business, written in past tense — "OrganizerSignedUp", "EventPublished", "SeatHeld", "PaymentCaptured", "TicketScanned". Past-tense facts are easy to agree on; class names are not — which is exactly why you start with the facts. At the end of this step you have a long, unfiltered, roughly time-ordered list.
    *Do this:*
    1. On paper or in a plain text file, list **every** business event in Zenith's life, from "organizer signs up" at one end to "ticket scanned at the gate" at the other, in rough time order.
    2. Write each one in past tense, as a fact that happened.
    3. Aim for **40 or more**. Do not filter, do not group, do not judge — quantity first, structure later.
    *You know it worked when:* the list has 40+ entries, each a past-tense fact, and you resisted the urge to organise them while writing.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Group the events into bounded contexts.**
    *What this step is:* Now you sort the pile. A *bounded context* (from the New words table above) is a boundary inside which one word has exactly one meaning. The grouping heuristic is the single most important sentence in this task: **events that always happen together in one transaction belong in one context** — a transaction being one all-or-nothing database write, as you met it in [Module F5 — SQL and relational data modelling](#module-f5--sql-and-relational-data-modelling--9h). "SeatHeld" and "HoldExpired" must be consistent with each other at every instant, so they live together; "EventPublished" and "PaymentCaptured" never need to commit in the same instant, so they do not.
    *Builds on:* [§4 — Service catalog](#4-service-catalog) — the chapter that describes Zenith's services (identity, catalog, inventory, order, payment, media, notification, realtime) and the jobs each one owns; your groups should land roughly on those contexts, and where they do not, that is worth a note, not a silent fix.
    *Do this:*
    1. Go through your 40+ events and ask of each pair that feels related: "must these two facts become true in the same instant?" If yes, same group.
    2. Sort every event into exactly one group, and give each group a business name ("Catalog", "Inventory", "Orders", ...), matching the contexts described in [§4 — Service catalog](#4-service-catalog).
    *You know it worked when:* every event sits in exactly one group, and for any two groups you can name a pair of events that do **not** need to be transactionally consistent with each other.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Hunt the words that change meaning between groups.**
    *What this step is:* The clearest evidence of a real boundary is a word that means different things on each side of it. You already met the flagship example in "Learn this first" above: "ticket" is a price tier in Catalog, a line item in Orders, and a scannable credential in Access Control — three different models, deliberately. Each such word you find is a boundary confirmed.
    *Do this:*
    1. Read your groups side by side and write down every word that appears in more than one group with a different meaning — start with "ticket", then look for others (candidates: "event", "seat", "customer").
    2. For each word, write one line per context stating what it means *there*.
    *You know it worked when:* you have a written list of at least two or three such words, "ticket" among them, each with its per-context meanings spelled out.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Draw the context map in Mermaid.**
    *What this step is:* You turn the groups into a diagram-as-code file: a *context map*, where the boxes are your contexts and — crucially — every arrow is labelled with the *kind* of relationship, because the relationships carry more information than the boxes. Mermaid is the text-based diagram language that GitHub and VS Code render natively; you first saw it in the [C4 diagrams](#c4-diagrams) explanation in [What those deliverables actually mean](#21-what-those-deliverables-actually-mean).
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — the repository you created there is where this file lives.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/architecture/context-map.md` and draw the map in a Mermaid block, one node per context.
    2. Label **every** relationship between contexts as exactly one of: **shared-nothing + events** (no shared database, no shared classes, they only exchange events), **customer/supplier** (the downstream context's needs genuinely influence what the upstream one publishes), or **anti-corruption layer** (a translation layer that converts the other context's model into yours — you build a real one in [Task 6.4 — Service decomposition: extract payment-service](#task-64--service-decomposition-extract-payment-service--5h)). The shape is:

    ```mermaid
    graph LR
      Catalog -- "shared-nothing + events" --> Orders
    ```

    3. Preview the file (VS Code's markdown preview, or push and view on GitHub) and fix it until it renders.
    *You know it worked when:* the map renders as a diagram — not as raw text — and every single arrow carries one of the three relationship labels.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Justify every boundary with a consistency sentence.**
    *What this step is:* The final pass is the honesty check. For each boundary on the map you write one sentence in a fixed template: *"these are separate because ___ does not need to be transactionally consistent with ___."* If you cannot finish that sentence for a boundary, the boundary is wrong — it was drawn from a technology instinct ("the database service") rather than a business invariant, which is exactly the distributed-monolith trap this task exists to avoid.
    *Do this:*
    1. Under the diagram in `docs/architecture/context-map.md`, write the template sentence once per boundary, filling both blanks with concrete business facts ("the published event description does not need to be transactionally consistent with the count of seats currently held").
    2. Strike out and redraw any boundary whose sentence you cannot honestly complete.
    *You know it worked when:* every edge on the map has its sentence, and none of the sentences mentions a technology — only business facts and whether they must be true at the same instant.

**Done when:** you can justify every service boundary in [§4 — Service catalog](#4-service-catalog) with a consistency argument rather than a technology one, and the context map renders.

2. Give the Zenith example of one word meaning three different things, and name all three meanings.
3. What is the heuristic for deciding two events belong in the same context?
