#### Task 1.7 — REST adapter, part 1: resources, DTOs, and validation — 1.5h

**What:** Controllers, request/response DTOs, mapping, and input validation at the edge.
**Why:** This is the surface reviewers judge first. It is also where the most common beginner mistake lives: returning JPA entities or domain objects straight out of a controller.
**Solves:** API responses that change shape whenever you refactor a database column, and lazy-loading exceptions thrown during JSON serialization.

**Learn this first:** ask AI *"why is it a bad idea to return JPA entities directly from a
Spring controller? Give me four distinct reasons."* The answers (coupling, lazy-loading
exceptions, accidental data exposure, unversionable contract) are all things you need to be
able to say.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **DTO** | Data Transfer Object. A record whose only job is to be the shape of one request or response. Separate from both your domain model and your database rows, on purpose. |
| **MapStruct** | A library that generates the boring DTO↔domain mapping code at compile time, so there is no reflection cost and no hand-written copying to forget a field in. |
| **Bean Validation** | The `@NotBlank` / `@Positive` annotation standard. Spring checks them when you put `@Valid` on a controller parameter and rejects bad input before your code runs. |
| **Custom constraint** | Your own annotation plus a validator class, for rules the built-ins cannot express — `@FutureDateRange` spanning two fields. Writing one teaches you how the validation SPI fits together. |
| **Test slice** | `@WebMvcTest` boots only the web layer — controllers, JSON, validation — and none of your database or services. Fast, and it fails for web reasons only. |
| **Idempotent verb** | An HTTP method where sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once. `PUT` and `DELETE` are; `POST` is not, which is the entire reason [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) exists. |
| **`Location` header** | On a 201 response, the URL of the thing you just created. Clients should follow it rather than constructing the URL themselves. |
| **JSON Merge Patch** | A `PATCH` format where the body is a partial object and `null` means "remove this field". Worth knowing by name because the alternative, JSON Patch, is a different and more awkward standard. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** that a DTO is a separate thing from a domain object **on purpose**. They will look almost identical at first and you will be tempted to merge them; the whole point is that your API does not change when your model does.
- **When it works you will see:** a request body validated and rejected with a 400 listing the exact offending fields, before any domain code runs.
- **Where people get stuck:** exposing the entity to save mapping code. Six weeks later you rename a domain field and silently break every client. The duplication is the feature — [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) asks you to justify it honestly in ADR-0006.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Request and response DTO records.**
    *What this step is:* A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a record whose only job is to be the shape of one request or one response — deliberately separate from both your domain model and your database rows. You will create one record per request body and one per response body, and make controllers speak *only* in these. At the end, nothing inside your service can change the API's shape by accident.
    *Builds on:* [Task F3.6 — Records, and objects that cannot hold invalid data](#task-f36--records-and-objects-that-cannot-hold-invalid-data--1h) — records, the one-line immutable classes DTOs are made of. [Task 1.4 — The domain layer: aggregates with real behaviour](#task-14--the-domain-layer-aggregates-with-real-behaviour--2h) — the domain objects you must *not* expose here. [Task F4.6 — JSON and serialisation](#task-f46--json-and-serialisation--1h) — how a Java object becomes JSON, which is what happens to these records on the wire.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `catalog-service`, create the package `adapter/in/web/dto` and write request **records** (`CreateEventRequest`, `UpdateEventRequest`, ...) and response **records** (`EventResponse`, ...).
    2. Make every controller method accept and return only these records — **never JPA entities, never domain objects, in either direction**. They will look almost identical to the domain objects at first; that duplication is the feature, not a smell.
    *You know it worked when:* a search of the `web` package finds no domain type and no JPA entity in any controller signature — the task's Done-when checks exactly this.

- [ ] **Step 2 — MapStruct mappers, with a test that every field maps.**
    *What this step is:* MapStruct is a library that generates the boring DTO-to-domain copying code at compile time — no reflection cost, no hand-written copying to forget a field in. You add it, declare mapper interfaces, and then write the test that catches MapStruct's one failure mode: a field it silently didn't map.
    *Builds on:* Step 1's DTO records and [Task 1.4 — The domain layer: aggregates with real behaviour](#task-14--the-domain-layer-aggregates-with-real-behaviour--2h) — the domain objects on the other side of the mapping.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the MapStruct dependency and its annotation processor to the `catalog-service` POM.
    2. Declare `@Mapper` interfaces that convert DTO ↔ domain in both directions; MapStruct generates the implementations at compile time.
    3. Write a test asserting **every field maps**: build a domain object with every single field populated, map it to the DTO, and assert each DTO field carries the value. An unmapped field is a silent `null` in production — this test is the only thing standing between you and that.
    4. Prove the test earns its keep: temporarily break one mapping, watch the test fail, restore it.
    *You know it worked when:* the field-coverage test passes — and failed when you deliberately broke a mapping.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Bean Validation, plus a hand-written `@FutureDateRange`.**
    *What this step is:* Bean Validation is the `@NotBlank` / `@Positive` annotation standard: you annotate the request record, put `@Valid` on the controller parameter, and Spring rejects bad input before your code runs. The built-ins check one field at a time, so you will also write one custom class-level constraint — a rule that looks at two fields together — by hand, because writing one teaches you how the validation SPI (Service Provider Interface — the extension seam the standard gives you to plug in your own rules) fits together.
    *Builds on:* [Task F6.8 — Validation, one error shape, and a request log](#task-f68--validation-one-error-shape-and-a-request-log--1h) — where you first used `@Valid` to reject invalid input. [Task 1.3 — Value objects and domain events](#task-13--value-objects-and-domain-events--3h) — the date-range idea this constraint guards at the edge.
    *Do this:*
    1. Annotate the request records' fields with the built-ins — `@NotBlank` on required text, `@Positive` on counts and amounts — and put `@Valid` on each controller's request-body parameter.
    2. Write the custom class-level `@FutureDateRange` constraint **by hand** — the annotation type itself, plus a `ConstraintValidator` class that reads both date fields of the request and checks the range lies in the future with start before end. No library shortcut, no copy-paste: the point is seeing how the SPI's pieces connect.
    *You know it worked when:* `POST`-ing an invalid body returns a 400 that names the exact offending fields, before any domain code runs — put a breakpoint in the use case and watch it never get hit.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Keep the domain re-checking its own invariants.**
    *What this step is:* You now validate at the edge **and** the domain still enforces the same rules itself. That looks like duplication — this step is where you convince yourself it is correct rather than redundant. The short version: edge validation is a courtesy to clients and can be bypassed (another use case, a message consumer, a bug); the domain invariant is the actual guarantee.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.2 — Aggregates, invariants, and consistency boundaries](#task-12--aggregates-invariants-and-consistency-boundaries--15h) — the written rules each aggregate must never violate. [Task 1.4 — The domain layer: aggregates with real behaviour](#task-14--the-domain-layer-aggregates-with-real-behaviour--2h) — the aggregates that enforce those rules by throwing domain exceptions.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write a test that calls a use case **directly** — skipping the controller and all Bean Validation — with input the edge would have rejected, and assert the domain still refuses it with a domain exception.
    2. Ask AI: *"I validate requests at the REST edge and my domain aggregates re-check the same invariants. Why is that duplication correct rather than redundant?"* — and make sure you can give the answer from memory; the Checkpoint asks for it.
    *You know it worked when:* the direct-call test proves bad input dies in the domain even with no controller anywhere in sight.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Correct verbs and status codes on every endpoint.**
    *What this step is:* Each HTTP method carries a promise, and your endpoints must keep it. You wire up all four write operations with the exact verb, status code, and header the standard expects. Remember from the New-words table: an *idempotent* verb is one where sending the same request twice has the same effect as once — `PUT` and `DELETE` are, `POST` is not, which is the entire reason [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) exists.
    *Builds on:* [Task F4.2 — Methods, and the promise each one makes](#task-f42--methods-and-the-promise-each-one-makes--1h) — choosing between `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE`. [Task F4.3 — Status codes, and the ones beginners get wrong](#task-f43--status-codes-and-the-ones-beginners-get-wrong--1h) — which code means what.
    *Do this:*
    1. `POST /events` → **201** with a **`Location` header** containing the URL of the event you just created; clients follow that header rather than constructing the URL themselves.
    2. `PUT` → an **idempotent full replacement**: the body is the complete new state, and sending it twice leaves the resource exactly as sending it once.
    3. `PATCH` via **JSON Merge Patch**: the body is a partial object, `null` means "remove this field", and the content type is `application/merge-patch+json`.
    4. `DELETE` → **204**, and **idempotent on repeat** — deleting the same event a second time returns 204 again, not an error.
    *You know it worked when:* exercising each verb with `curl -i` shows exactly those codes and headers, and repeating the same `PUT` or `DELETE` changes nothing.

- [ ] **Step 6 — `@WebMvcTest` slice tests: happy path and every validation failure.**
    *What this step is:* `@WebMvcTest` boots only the web layer — controllers, JSON converters, validation — and none of your use cases or database, so these tests run in about a second and fail for web reasons only. You write one happy-path test per endpoint and one test per validation rule.
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.5 — Testing a Spring application with slices](#task-f75--testing-a-spring-application-with-slices--1h) — recall from there what `@WebMvcTest` loads and what it deliberately does not. [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h) — the inbound port interfaces your controller calls are exactly the beans you mock out here. [Task 1.8 — REST adapter, part 2: one error contract for the whole platform](#task-18--rest-adapter-part-2-one-error-contract-for-the-whole-platform--1h) — when that task adds your `@RestControllerAdvice`, notice that this slice includes it, so your error-shape assertions run here too.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write `@WebMvcTest(EventController.class)` tests, replacing each inbound port the controller needs with `@MockitoBean`, and drive requests through `MockMvc`.
    2. One **happy-path** test per endpoint, asserting status, headers (the 201 `Location`!), and body fields via `jsonPath`.
    3. One test per **validation failure**, asserting the 400 and that the response names the offending field.
    *You know it worked when:* the whole slice suite passes in about a second with no database container running.

**Done when:** `POST /events` returns 201 with a `Location` header, invalid input returns 400, and no JPA entity appears anywhere in the `web` package.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Give four distinct reasons not to return a JPA entity directly from a controller.
2. You validate at the edge and the domain re-checks the same rules. Why is that correct rather than redundant duplication?
3. Which HTTP verbs are idempotent, and what does idempotent mean precisely in this context?
4. What does `@WebMvcTest` load, and what does it deliberately not load?
5. `POST /events` succeeded. What status code did you return, what header did you set, and what is in it?

#### Task 1.8 — REST adapter, part 2: one error contract for the whole platform — 1h

**What:** A single, machine-readable error format produced by a `@RestControllerAdvice`, used by all nine services.
**Why:** Clients need to distinguish retryable from fatal, and user-fixable from bug, without string-matching your error messages. This is also where accidental information disclosure happens.
**Solves:** clients that cannot handle errors programmatically, and stack traces leaking database schema to the internet.

**Learn this first:** read RFC 9457 (`application/problem+json`) — it is short. Ask AI
*"explain RFC 9457 problem details and what each standard field is for, then show me a good
and a bad error response for a validation failure."*

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **RFC 9457** | The standard that defines `application/problem+json`: an error body with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, and `instance`. Using a standard means client libraries already understand you. |
| **`@RestControllerAdvice`** | A class that catches exceptions thrown anywhere in your controllers and turns them into responses. Putting it in `platform-common` is how all nine services get the same error shape for free. |
| **`code`** | Your own stable, documented string like `EVENT_ALREADY_PUBLISHED`. Machines branch on this. It must never change once published. |
| **`detail`** | The human-readable sentence. Humans read this. You may reword it freely, which is exactly why machines must not depend on it. |
| **Information disclosure** | Leaking internals — stack traces, SQL, class names, table names — in an error response. It is a genuine security finding, not untidiness: it hands an attacker your schema and your framework versions. |
| **`traceId`** | A single identifier attached to one request as it crosses services, so a support ticket quoting it leads you straight to the right logs. Added now, made genuinely useful in [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline). |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** **one** error shape across all nine services. Decide it now, in the first service, because retrofitting a consistent error contract across nine services later is miserable work nobody enjoys.
- **When it works you will see:** every failure — validation, not-found, conflict, unexpected — returning the same JSON structure with a stable `type` field.
- **Where people get stuck:** leaking internals in the message. Stack traces, SQL fragments, class names and internal hostnames in an error body are both an information leak and a sign of an unfinished handler.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — The shared `@RestControllerAdvice` in platform-common.**
    *What this step is:* A `@RestControllerAdvice` is a class that catches exceptions thrown anywhere in your controllers and turns them into HTTP responses. You build **one**, in the shared module, producing the RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` format from this task's Learn-this-first — so all nine future services inherit the identical error shape for free instead of nine teams inventing nine shapes.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — `platform-common`, the shared module every service depends on; this handler is exactly the kind of thing it exists for. [Task F6.8 — Validation, one error shape, and a request log](#task-f68--validation-one-error-shape-and-a-request-log--1h) — you already built a single error shape for one small app there; this step promotes that idea to the whole platform, on the standard format.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `platform-common`, create the exception-handling class annotated `@RestControllerAdvice`, producing bodies with the five RFC 9457 fields — `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance` — and the content type `application/problem+json`. Spring's built-in `ProblemDetail` class maps onto this standard directly.
    2. Confirm `catalog-service` picks it up through its existing dependency on `platform-common` — no copy of the handler in the service itself, ever. That placement is the entire mechanism by which all nine services get the same contract.
    *You know it worked when:* an exception thrown inside `catalog-service` comes back with `Content-Type: application/problem+json`, even though the class that produced it lives in `platform-common`.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Map every kind of failure deliberately.**
    *What this step is:* Each class of failure gets a deliberately chosen status code and the same JSON structure. The hard part is the 409-vs-422 decision for domain exceptions — and the requirement is not just to decide, but to **write the rule down** so the next exception maps itself.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.4 — The domain layer: aggregates with real behaviour](#task-14--the-domain-layer-aggregates-with-real-behaviour--2h) — the `DomainException` hierarchy your aggregates throw; Task 1.4 promised they would be mapped to HTTP here. [Task 1.7 — REST adapter, part 1: resources, DTOs, and validation](#task-17--rest-adapter-part-1-resources-dtos-and-validation--15h) — the Bean Validation failures that need the 400 branch.
    *Do this:*
    1. Domain exceptions → **409 or 422** — decide which, **per exception**, and write the rule down (for example: 409 when the request conflicts with the resource's *current state*, like publishing an already-published event; 422 when the request can never be processed regardless of state). The Checkpoint asks for the rule, not the list.
    2. Validation failures → **400** with a structured **`errors[]` array** naming each offending field, so a client can highlight the right form inputs.
    3. Anything unexpected → **500** carrying **only** a `traceId` — no message, no exception name, nothing that describes your internals.
    *You know it worked when:* triggering one failure of each kind — a domain conflict, a validation error, an unexpected crash — returns the same JSON structure with the status you chose and a stable `type` field.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Add the stable, documented `code` field.**
    *What this step is:* Alongside the human-readable `detail` sentence, every error carries a `code` — your own stable string like `EVENT_ALREADY_PUBLISHED`. Machines branch on `code`; humans read `detail`. The split matters because `detail` may be reworded freely at any time — which is exactly why no client must ever string-match on it.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a `code` field to the error body, one documented value per distinct failure (e.g. `EVENT_ALREADY_PUBLISHED`), alongside the human-readable `detail`.
    2. Keep a documented list of codes, with the rule written at the top: **a `code` never changes once published** — clients are branching on it.
    *You know it worked when:* the same failure always returns the same `code`, two different failures return different `code`s, and the list is written down.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Write the never-leak test.**
    *What this step is:* Information disclosure — stack traces, SQL, class names, table names in an error body — is a genuine security finding, not untidiness: it hands an attacker your schema and your framework versions. You write one test that scans every error response and fails if anything internal appears. This test guards every service forever.
    *Builds on:* Step 2's handler — the thing this test is pointed at.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write a test that exercises your error paths and asserts **no stack trace, no SQL, and no class name ever appears** in a response body — in practice: assert the body never contains strings like `Exception`, `java.`, `at `, `SELECT`, or your own package name.
    2. Run it against every failure kind you mapped in Step 2, not just one.
    *You know it worked when:* the test passes for every currently mapped error path — and you understand it is supposed to *fail* the moment any future handler gets sloppy.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Break it on purpose: throw a `NullPointerException`.**
    *What this step is:* Proof that Step 4's test actually protects you. A `NullPointerException` from [Task F2.3 — `null`, `==`, and `.equals()`](#task-f23--null--and-equals--1h) is the archetypal *unexpected* failure — nobody wrote a handler for it, so it falls through to your catch-everything branch. You throw one deliberately and watch the safety net hold.
    *Do this:*
    1. Temporarily add `throw new NullPointerException();` as the first line of a controller method.
    2. Call that endpoint and confirm the client receives a 500 `application/problem+json` body carrying **only** a `traceId` and a generic title — no `NullPointerException`, no class name, no stack frames — and confirm the Step-4 test still passes (and fails if you make the handler echo the exception message, which is worth trying once).
    3. Remove the deliberate throw.
    *You know it worked when:* during the experiment the response body contained nothing that names the exception or any class — just the standard problem body with a `traceId`.

- [ ] **Step 6 — `traceId` in every error response, from day one.**
    *What this step is:* A `traceId` is one identifier attached to a request, so a support ticket quoting it leads straight to the right logs. Real distributed tracing — the same id crossing all nine services — arrives in [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline); you put the field in the contract **now**, because retrofitting a new field into the error shape later means touching every service.
    *Do this:*
    1. Generate a `traceId` per request — a small request filter that creates a random UUID at the start of each request and stashes it where the error handler can read it is enough for now.
    2. Include it in **every** error body — including the 500s from Step 2, where it is the *only* payload.
    3. Log the same id alongside the server-side error, so a reported `traceId` actually finds the log line.
    *You know it worked when:* every error body carries a `traceId`, two separate failing requests show two different ids, and grepping your log for a response's id finds the matching server-side entry.

**Done when:** every error path returns `application/problem+json` with a `code` and a `traceId`, and a test proves internals never leak.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. What fields does problem+json define, and what is each one for?
2. Why do clients branch on `code` and never on `detail`?
3. Which of your domain exceptions map to 409 and which to 422? State the rule you wrote down, not just the list.
4. Why is a stack trace in a response body a security problem rather than just sloppy?
5. You throw an unexpected `NullPointerException` in a controller. Exactly what does the client receive?

#### Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract — 1.5h

**What:** Keyset pagination, ETags with conditional requests, and a snapshot-tested OpenAPI spec.
**Why:** These three are the clearest "this person has operated an API at scale" signals in the whole phase. Offset pagination and missing ETags are what junior APIs look like.
**Solves:** pages that silently duplicate or skip rows under concurrent inserts, expensive re-fetching of unchanged data, and breaking clients by accident.

**Learn this first:** ask AI *"explain why `OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20` gets slower as the offset
grows, and how keyset (cursor) pagination avoids both the performance problem and the
duplicate-row problem."* Make sure you understand **both** problems — most explanations
cover only performance.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Offset pagination** | `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000`. The database must walk and discard 10,000 rows first, so later pages get slower; and if a row is inserted between requests, every subsequent page shifts. |
| **Keyset pagination** | Also called cursor or seek pagination. "Give me 20 rows after *this* sort position." Constant speed at any depth, and immune to inserts shifting the window. |
| **Opaque cursor** | Base64 of the sort key, handed back to the client as a meaningless string. Opaque on purpose: you can change what is inside it later without breaking any client. |
| **ETag** | A short fingerprint of a response, usually derived from the row's version. The client stores it and sends it back next time. |
| **`If-None-Match` → 304** | The client says "I already have the version with this ETag". If it still matches, you return `304 Not Modified` with an empty body and the client reuses what it has. |
| **`If-Match` → 412** | The client says "only apply this update if the resource is still at this version". If it has changed, you return `412 Precondition Failed` — optimistic concurrency control at the HTTP layer. |
| **OpenAPI** | A machine-readable description of your API. springdoc generates it from your code, and Swagger UI turns it into a page you can click — which is your only UI on this project. |
| **Snapshot test** | Committing the generated spec to the repository and failing the build when it changes. You can still change the API; you just cannot do it by accident. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** **cursor-based** pagination rather than offset. `OFFSET 50000` makes the database count and discard fifty thousand rows on every page, and it is one of the most common avoidable slow queries there is.
- **When it works you will see:** an OpenAPI spec generated from your code, and a snapshot test that fails when you change the contract accidentally.
- **Where people get stuck:** returning `Object` or `Map<String, Object>` from a controller. A generated spec is only as good as your types, and those document nothing at all.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Build keyset pagination on the list endpoint.**
    *What this step is:* You will change `GET /events` so it pages with a **cursor** — a bookmark that says "give me the next rows after this exact sort position" — instead of an offset that says "skip the first N rows". The database never counts and discards rows, and a row inserted while someone is paging cannot shift the pages. At the end of this step the list endpoint accepts `?cursor=<opaque base64 of (startsAt,id)>&limit=`, caps `limit` at 100, and every page of results carries a `nextCursor` the client sends back to get the following page.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.7 — REST adapter, part 1: resources, DTOs, and validation](#task-17--rest-adapter-part-1-resources-dtos-and-validation--15h) — the `EventController` and response DTOs you built there are what you are adding the cursor parameters to. [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h) — the `SearchEventsQuery` port and the `InMemoryEventRepository` fake from there are what actually run the query for now; real Postgres takes over in [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h).
    *Do this:*
    1. Fix the sort order the cursor is built from: `(startsAt, id)` — `startsAt` orders events by time, and `id` is the tie-breaker so two events starting at the same instant still have exactly one unambiguous order. Without a tie-breaker, "the next row after this one" is not well defined.
    2. Add `cursor` and `limit` query parameters to the list endpoint. Enforce the cap: `limit` is never allowed to exceed 100, whatever the client asks for — an uncapped limit is an invitation to fetch a million rows in one request.
    3. Make the cursor **opaque**: to produce `nextCursor`, take the last row of the page's `(startsAt, id)`, join them into a small string, and Base64-encode it (Base64 is a standard way to turn any bytes into a safe, copy-pasteable ASCII string — `java.util.Base64` does it in one line). The client sees only gibberish, and that is the point — clients cannot read it, so they cannot depend on what is inside, so you can change its contents later without breaking any client.
    4. When a request arrives with a cursor, Base64-decode it back into `(startsAt, id)` and return the next `limit` rows strictly **after** that position in the sort order. Put the fresh `nextCursor` in the response; when no rows are left, omit it so the client knows it is done.
    *You know it worked when:* you can walk the entire event list page by page with `curl`, feeding each response's `nextCursor` into the next request, no row ever appears twice, and a request with `limit=5000` returns at most 100 rows.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Break it on purpose: offset duplicates a row, keyset does not.**
    *What this step is:* One test that proves *why* Step 1 was worth doing — and the story you tell in an interview. You will simulate the real-world race: a client is reading page 1, somebody inserts a new row that sorts into page 1, and the client then asks for page 2. With offset pagination every later row shifts down one position, so the last row of page 1 shows up again on page 2 — a silent duplicate. With keyset pagination the cursor pins an absolute position, so nothing shifts.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h) — the `InMemoryEventRepository` fake from there is the data store this test drives, so no database is needed.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write a test that inserts around 30 events with distinct `startsAt` values.
    2. First, the **offset** version: read page 1 as "skip 0, take 20"; now insert one new event whose `startsAt` sorts it *into* page 1 (earlier than page 1's last row); read page 2 as "skip 20, take 20". Assert that the last row of page 1 appears **again** on page 2 — the duplicate, caught red-handed.
    3. Then the **keyset** version: read page 1 with no cursor; insert a new row into page 1's range exactly as before; read page 2 using page 1's `nextCursor`. Assert the two pages share **no** row.
    *You know it worked when:* the test is green with both assertions in it — one proving the offset duplicate exists, one proving the keyset pages do not overlap. If you delete the mid-read insert, the offset assertion should fail, which proves the test is really testing the race.

- [ ] **Step 3 — ETag and 304 on `GET /events/{id}`.**
    *What this step is:* You will give every single-event response a fingerprint (the `ETag` header) derived from the aggregate's version number, and teach the endpoint to answer `304 Not Modified` — an empty-body "you already have the latest" — when the client sends that fingerprint back in `If-None-Match`. At the end of this step a repeat fetch of an unchanged event costs almost no bytes.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h) — the `InMemoryEventRepository` fake from there already carries a simple version counter that increments on every save; that counter is where the version comes from for now. If your fake does not have the counter yet, add it in this step. In [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) this same version becomes a real database column.
    *Do this:*
    1. On `GET /events/{id}`, set the `ETag` response header from the aggregate's version — e.g. version 7 becomes `ETag: "7"` (the quotes are part of the HTTP ETag format).
    2. When a request arrives with `If-None-Match`, compare it to the current version's ETag. If they match, return `304 Not Modified` with an **empty body**; if not, return `200` with the full body and the new ETag.
    3. Verify the round trip by hand: `curl -i` the event and note the `ETag` value, then `curl -i -H 'If-None-Match: "<that value>"'` the same URL and watch the 304 come back. Then save the event (so the version increments) and watch the same conditional request return 200 with a fresh ETag.
    *You know it worked when:* the second `curl` returns `304` with no body, and after any write to the event the same `If-None-Match` value gets a `200` again.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Measure the bytes a 304 saves, and record it.**
    *What this step is:* A 304 is only worth bragging about with a number attached. You will measure how many response bytes the conditional request avoids and write that number into the project's benchmark table, where every performance claim in this project lives.
    *Builds on:* [10. Benchmarks to capture](#10-benchmarks-to-capture) — the standing table of measurements this project fills in phase by phase; row 32 is reserved for exactly this number.
    *Do this:*
    1. Fetch the event twice with `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{size_download}\n'` — once plainly (full 200 body) and once with the matching `If-None-Match` header (304, empty body). The difference between the two printed sizes is your bytes saved per request.
    2. Note the result in row 32 of the [§10 benchmark table](#10-benchmarks-to-capture) ("Bytes saved by ETag/304 on event detail"), including the conditions — which endpoint, which payload — as that section demands.
    *You know it worked when:* row 32 of the benchmark table contains a real measured number, not a guess.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Require `If-Match` on `PUT`, reject stale writes with 412.**
    *What this step is:* The mirror image of Step 3, protecting writes instead of reads. A client doing a `PUT` (a full replacement of the resource, from [Task 1.7 — REST adapter, part 1: resources, DTOs, and validation](#task-17--rest-adapter-part-1-resources-dtos-and-validation--15h)) must say which version it thinks it is replacing, via the `If-Match` header. If the resource has moved on since the client read it, you answer `412 Precondition Failed` instead of silently overwriting someone else's change. This is **optimistic concurrency control** — let everyone work freely, detect the conflict at write time — done at the HTTP layer.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.8 — REST adapter, part 2: one error contract for the whole platform](#task-18--rest-adapter-part-2-one-error-contract-for-the-whole-platform--1h) — the 412 response body must come out in the same problem+json error shape your `@RestControllerAdvice` produces for every other error. [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — the version compared here becomes a real JPA `@Version` column there, so this exact behaviour gets re-proven against the database later.
    *Do this:*
    1. On `PUT /events/{id}`, require the `If-Match` header. A `PUT` without it gets rejected (a 428 "Precondition Required" or a 400 with a clear message — pick one and be consistent); a `PUT` whose `If-Match` does not equal the current version's ETag gets `412 Precondition Failed`.
    2. Prove the conflict by hand: `GET` the event and note its ETag, `PUT` with that ETag and watch it succeed (version increments), then `PUT` again with the **old** ETag and watch the 412.
    *You know it worked when:* the second `PUT` with the stale ETag returns 412 in your standard problem+json shape, and a `PUT` with the fresh ETag succeeds.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Generate the OpenAPI spec with springdoc, with real descriptions.**
    *What this step is:* You will add the `springdoc-openapi` dependency so your controllers, DTO records, and validation annotations generate a machine-readable API description at `/v3/api-docs` and a clickable Swagger UI page at `/swagger-ui.html`. Since this project has no frontend, that page **is** your manual-testing UI from now on. At the end of this step every endpoint carries a genuine description and example — not the auto-generated stubs.
    *Builds on:* [OpenAPI specs in §2.1](#openapi-specs) — the full explanation of what the spec is, why it cannot drift out of date, and why it doubles as your manual-testing UI. [Task 1.7 — REST adapter, part 1: resources, DTOs, and validation](#task-17--rest-adapter-part-1-resources-dtos-and-validation--15h) — the concrete DTO records you built there are what makes the generated spec meaningful; an endpoint returning `Object` or `Map<String, Object>` documents nothing at all.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the `springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui` dependency to catalog-service and start the app; confirm `/v3/api-docs` serves JSON and `/swagger-ui.html` serves the clickable page.
    2. Go endpoint by endpoint and add genuine `@Operation` summaries/descriptions and example values on every endpoint and DTO — write them for a stranger who has never seen the service. Cover the behaviours you just built: the `cursor`/`limit` parameters, the `ETag` response header, the 304, the `If-Match` header, and the 412.
    3. Use the "Try it out" button in Swagger UI to send one real request per endpoint — this is you adopting your new manual-testing UI.
    *You know it worked when:* a colleague (or you, squinting) could drive every endpoint from `/swagger-ui.html` alone, without reading the code, and no endpoint in the spec shows a bare `Object` schema.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Snapshot the generated spec and make CI fail on accidental contract changes.** *(Do the setup now; the box is ticked after [Task 1.11 — The Testcontainers harness and test data builders](#task-111--the-testcontainers-harness-and-test-data-builders--1h) — see "Done when".)*
    *What this step is:* A **snapshot test** — you commit the generated spec file to the repository, and a test compares the freshly generated spec against the committed copy and fails when they differ. You can still change your API whenever you like; you just cannot do it *by accident*, because any contract change turns into a red build until you deliberately update the snapshot. At the end of this step, renaming a response field without touching the snapshot makes CI go red.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline](#task-04--git-workflow-the-remote-and-a-local-ci-pipeline--2h) — the `make ci` pipeline and pre-push hook from there is what will catch the failing snapshot test. [OpenAPI specs in §2.1](#openapi-specs) — explains why treating the spec as a tested contract, not just nice docs, is the senior move. [Task 1.11 — The Testcontainers harness and test data builders](#task-111--the-testcontainers-harness-and-test-data-builders--1h) — the test that regenerates the spec needs the integration-test harness built there, which is why this box waits.
    *Do this:*
    1. Save the generated spec into `contracts/openapi/catalog-v1.json` and commit it.
    2. Write a test that generates the current spec and compares it byte-for-byte (or JSON-equal) against the committed file, failing with a readable diff when they differ. Add a one-line documented way to deliberately refresh the snapshot when a change is intentional.
    3. Prove it: rename one response field in a DTO, push, and watch CI go red. Then make the change "on purpose" the correct way — update the snapshot in the same commit — and watch CI go green. Revert both if the rename was only an experiment.

#### Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping — 1h

**What:** A versioned schema, JPA entities kept separate from the domain model, and an adapter that maps between them.
**Why:** The schema is the longest-lived artifact in the system — it outlives the code. And separating the JPA entity from the aggregate is what lets you optimise the database in [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) without touching business rules.
**Solves:** schema drift between environments, and a domain model whose shape is dictated by what JPA finds convenient.

**Learn this first:** ask AI *"explain what `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto` does and why
using `update` in production is dangerous"*, then *"what problem do database migration
tools like Flyway solve?"*

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Migration** | A numbered SQL file describing one schema change. `V1__catalog_baseline.sql`. The set of files applied so far *is* the schema version, recorded in a table Flyway owns. |
| **`ddl-auto`** | A Hibernate setting for what to do with the schema at startup. `update` silently alters your tables and can never drop or rename safely; `validate` only checks that the code and schema agree and fails loudly if not. Use `validate`. |
| **Optimistic locking** | A `version` column that increments on every update. If two people read and then write, the second write finds the version has moved and fails instead of silently overwriting. |
| **UUIDv4** | A completely random UUID. Random keys scatter inserts across the whole B-tree index, dirtying many pages instead of a few. |
| **UUIDv7** | A UUID with a timestamp in the high bits, so new keys sort near each other. Inserts stay in the same few index pages, which is measurably faster — [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) makes you prove it. |
| **LAZY vs EAGER** | Whether a related entity is loaded with the parent or on first access. `EAGER` quietly turns one query into many, which is how N+1 problems are born; always start `LAZY`. |
| **`open-in-view`** | A Spring default that keeps the database session open through rendering, so a lazy field accessed in the controller silently fires another query. Set it to `false` so those mistakes fail fast in the right layer. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** keeping the JPA entity **separate** from the domain aggregate, with a mapper between. It costs real effort and you should be able to say honestly what it buys.
- **When it works you will see:** Flyway applying migrations at startup, and a domain object saved and reloaded without JPA annotations appearing anywhere in the domain package.
- **Where people get stuck:** `@Data` from Lombok on an entity. It generates `equals`/`hashCode` over every field including the generated id, so an entity added to a `HashSet` before saving is lost the moment the id is assigned. You met this exact bug in [Task F2.8 — `equals`, `hashCode`, and the contract collections rely on](#task-f28--equals-hashcode-and-the-contract-collections-rely-on--15h), where you watched a `HashSet` lose an object whose hash changed after insertion.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Write `V1__catalog_baseline.sql`, the first Flyway migration.**
    *What this step is:* You will write the first numbered migration file — the SQL that creates catalog-service's tables — and hand the schema over to Flyway's ownership forever. From now on the database's shape is defined only by the stack of committed `V<n>__*.sql` files, never by Hibernate guessing it from your classes. At the end of this step the service starts, Flyway applies the migration, and the tables exist with every constraint deliberately named.
    *Builds on:* [Task F5.11 — JPA, the SQL log, and Flyway](#task-f511--jpa-the-sql-log-and-flyway--1h) — where you first put a schema under Flyway's control and saw it record applied migrations in its own history table. [Task F5.2 — Design and create your first tables](#task-f52--design-and-create-your-first-tables--1h) — where you learned to pick sensible Postgres types and write `CREATE TABLE`. [Task 1.2 — Aggregates, invariants, and consistency boundaries](#task-12--aggregates-invariants-and-consistency-boundaries--15h) — the aggregates you drew there tell you which tables this service needs.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `catalog-service/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__catalog_baseline.sql` — the default folder Flyway scans, as you saw in [Task F5.11 — JPA, the SQL log, and Flyway](#task-f511--jpa-the-sql-log-and-flyway--1h).
    2. Write the `CREATE TABLE` statements for the catalog aggregates (the event table and its children, such as price tiers). Follow the conventions and never deviate: **snake_case** column and table names, **singular** table names (`event`, not `events`), and a **surrogate UUID primary key** — "surrogate" means a made-up key that exists only to identify the row, instead of reusing a business value like a name that might change.
    3. Name every constraint **explicitly** — `CONSTRAINT pk_event PRIMARY KEY (id)`, `CONSTRAINT fk_price_tier_event FOREIGN KEY ...` — instead of letting Postgres invent a name. The payoff comes months later: a violation error that says `fk_price_tier_event` tells you instantly what broke, and a future migration can drop a constraint it can actually name.
    4. Give every table `created_at` and `updated_at` timestamp columns, and a `version` column (a plain integer) for optimistic locking — the two-people-edited-the-same-row protection Step 5 wires up and [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h) already exposed to clients as the ETag/`If-Match` version.
    *You know it worked when:* the service starts, the log shows Flyway applying `V1__catalog_baseline`, and `select * from flyway_schema_history;` in `psql` shows one applied row.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Use UUIDv7, not UUIDv4, for primary keys.**
    *What this step is:* Both are UUIDs, but UUIDv4 is completely random while UUIDv7 starts with a timestamp, so freshly generated v7 keys sort next to each other. Postgres stores the primary-key index as a B-tree — a sorted structure of fixed-size pages — and random keys land all over that tree, dirtying many pages per batch of inserts, while time-ordered keys keep landing in the same few pages. At the end of this step every new id the service generates is a UUIDv7, and you have the explanation written down.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.4 — The domain layer: aggregates with real behaviour](#task-14--the-domain-layer-aggregates-with-real-behaviour--2h) — the static factory `Event.draft(...)` from there is where new ids are born, so that is where the generator plugs in.
    *Do this:*
    1. Ask AI: *"why do random UUIDv4 primary keys hurt B-tree insert performance and page locality, and how does UUIDv7 avoid it?"* Write the answer down in your own words — [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) makes you **measure** this, so future-you wants the prediction on record.
    2. Make whatever code creates new ids generate UUIDv7 (a small generator utility, or a tiny library — `java.util.UUID.randomUUID()` is v4, so it is exactly what you are moving away from). Route all new-id creation through it so there is one place to look.
    *You know it worked when:* two ids generated a moment apart agree in their leading characters and sort adjacently — print ten in a row and watch them come out already ordered.

- [ ] **Step 3 — JPA entities in the adapter, mapped to the domain by `EventPersistenceAdapter`.**
    *What this step is:* You will write a **second** set of classes for persistence — JPA `@Entity` classes living in `adapter/out/persistence/entity` — kept deliberately separate from the domain aggregates, plus an adapter that converts between the two and implements the repository port. This is the hexagonal promise kept: the domain stays plain Java, and everything JPA wants (annotations, no-arg constructors, mutable fields) stays in the adapter where it cannot dictate your model's shape.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h) — the `EventRepository` port declared there is the interface this adapter now implements, and the `InMemoryEventRepository` fake from there is what it replaces as the production bean (keep the fake for use-case tests). [Task 1.4 — The domain layer: aggregates with real behaviour](#task-14--the-domain-layer-aggregates-with-real-behaviour--2h) — the plain-Java `Event` aggregate from there is one side of the mapping, and its `Builder` for the many-argument reconstruction case was built precisely for this adapter to use. [Task F5.11 — JPA, the SQL log, and Flyway](#task-f511--jpa-the-sql-log-and-flyway--1h) — where you first mapped an entity and queried through a repository.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create the entity classes under `adapter/out/persistence/entity` — e.g. `EventEntity` — mapping exactly the columns from `V1__catalog_baseline.sql`.
    2. Write `EventPersistenceAdapter` in `adapter/out/persistence`: it implements the `EventRepository` port, uses a Spring Data repository internally, and maps entity ↔ aggregate in both directions (aggregate → entity on save; entity → aggregate on load, via the aggregate's `Builder`).
    3. Register the adapter as the production bean in place of the in-memory fake; keep the fake on the test side for fast use-case tests.
    *You know it worked when:* a domain `Event` saved through the port comes back equal after a reload from real Postgres, and `grep -r "jakarta.persistence" catalog-service/src/main/java/**/domain/` finds nothing — no JPA annotation anywhere in the domain package.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Write ADR-0006: one model per layer, costs included.**
    *What this step is:* You now maintain three near-identical shapes of the same concept — DTO, domain aggregate, JPA entity — and that duplication is a *decision*, so it gets an Architecture Decision Record. An honest ADR names what the duplication buys (each layer can change without dragging the others along) **and** what it costs: three classes to touch every time a field is added.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.5 — Architecture Decision Records](#task-05--architecture-decision-records--1h) — where you learned the ADR format and wrote the first five. [Task 1.7 — REST adapter, part 1: resources, DTOs, and validation](#task-17--rest-adapter-part-1-resources-dtos-and-validation--15h) — the DTO↔domain duplication from there is the first of the two duplications this ADR must justify; the entity↔domain one from Step 3 is the second.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write `ADR-0006` ("One model per layer") in your ADR folder, in the same format as ADR-0000 through ADR-0005: context, options considered, decision, consequences.
    2. Justify **both** duplications — DTO↔domain and entity↔domain — name the rejected alternative (one shared class across all layers) and why it was rejected, and state the cost plainly: adding one field means touching three classes and two mappers.
    *You know it worked when:* a stranger reading ADR-0006 could argue both sides of the trade-off, and the cost sentence is in there verbatim, not glossed over.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Configure the four settings that prevent the classic traps.**
    *What this step is:* Four small configurations, each blocking a famous production bug: `@Version` for optimistic locking, `LAZY` on every association, `open-in-view: false`, and `ddl-auto: validate`. Each was explained in this task's "New words" table; this step turns them on. At the end, the classic JPA foot-guns fail fast and loudly instead of silently misbehaving.
    *Builds on:* [Task F6.4 — Configuration files and the precedence order](#task-f64--configuration-files-and-the-precedence-order--1h) — where you learned to write the `application.yml` these settings live in. [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h) — the HTTP-layer version check from there (`If-Match` → 412) is what the `@Version` column now backs with a real database guarantee.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a `@Version`-annotated field to each entity, mapped to the `version` column from Step 1. Now, if two transactions load the same row and both write, the second write fails with an optimistic-lock exception instead of silently overwriting the first.
    2. Put `fetch = FetchType.LAZY` on **every** association (`@ManyToOne` is `EAGER` by default — the trap). `EAGER` quietly turns one query into many, which is how N+1 problems are born.
    3. In `application.yml`, set `spring.jpa.open-in-view: false` — so a lazy field touched after the transaction ends throws immediately in the right layer instead of silently firing an extra query from the controller.
    4. In `application.yml`, set `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: validate` — Hibernate now only *checks* that entities and schema agree at startup and fails loudly on a mismatch; it never alters tables itself, because Flyway owns the schema now.
    *You know it worked when:* the app boots clean with `validate` on, and a quick test that loads one `Event` in two "sessions" and saves both gets an `OptimisticLockingFailureException` on the second save.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Never put Lombok's `@Data` on an entity — and know why.**
    *What this step is:* A rule you obey *and* can explain. `@Data` generates `equals`/`hashCode` over every field including the database-generated id, so an entity added to a `HashSet` before saving is lost the moment the id gets assigned — its hash changed after insertion, exactly the contract violation you watched in [Task F2.8 — `equals`, `hashCode`, and the contract collections rely on](#task-f28--equals-hashcode-and-the-contract-collections-rely-on--15h). It also generates a `toString` over every field, which touches lazy associations and triggers surprise queries.
    *Builds on:* [Task F2.8 — `equals`, `hashCode`, and the contract collections rely on](#task-f28--equals-hashcode-and-the-contract-collections-rely-on--15h) — where you built the mental model of why a hash that changes after insertion makes collections lose objects; this is that exact bug wearing JPA clothes.
    *Do this:*
    1. Check no entity class carries `@Data` (or `@EqualsAndHashCode`/`@ToString` over all fields). If you want `equals`/`hashCode` on an entity at all, base them on the id only, with the null-id case handled deliberately.
    2. Ask AI: *"what exactly does Lombok's `@Data` break on a JPA entity — equals/hashCode with lazy proxies and generated ids, and toString triggering lazy loads?"* — then say the two failure modes out loud in your own words, so you can explain the rule rather than just obey it.
    *You know it worked when:* you can name both breakages without notes — the checkpoint below asks for exactly this.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Break it on purpose: make `ddl-auto: validate` catch schema drift.**
    *What this step is:* Proof that the safety net from Step 5 actually catches the mistake it exists for — adding a field to an entity and forgetting the migration. You will commit the mistake deliberately and watch startup refuse to proceed. At the end of this step you have *seen* the failure, so when it happens for real in week 14 you will recognise it in two seconds.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a new field to `EventEntity` — say `private String color;` — and do **not** write a migration for it.
    2. Start the service and read the failure: Hibernate's schema validation aborts startup, naming the entity and the missing column.
    3. Revert the field (or keep it and write the proper `V2__*.sql` migration — either way the entity and the migrations must agree again) and confirm the service starts clean.
    *You know it worked when:* you saw startup fail with a schema-validation error that names the missing column, and after fixing the mismatch the service boots normally.

**Done when:** the schema is fully Flyway-managed, no domain class has a JPA annotation, and an entity/migration mismatch fails startup.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Why is `ddl-auto: update` dangerous in production, and what does `validate` do instead?
2. Why UUIDv7 rather than UUIDv4 for primary keys? Answer in terms of B-tree pages.
3. What does `open-in-view: false` prevent, and where will the error now appear instead?
4. What exactly does Lombok's `@Data` break on a JPA entity? Name two things.
5. You added a field to an entity and forgot the migration. What happened at startup, and which setting caused it?

#### Task 1.11 — The Testcontainers harness and test data builders — 1h

**What:** The reusable integration-test base class and fixture builders the whole repository will use for the next twenty weeks.
**Why:** This is leverage. Every service, every phase, inherits it. Done well, writing an integration test later costs two minutes; done badly, it costs an afternoon each time.
**Solves:** false confidence from testing against an in-memory database that behaves differently from production.

**Learn this first:** re-read [the Testcontainers explanation in §2.1](#testcontainers-backed-integration-tests). The key insight is that H2 does not have Postgres' query planner, types, locking semantics, or `SKIP LOCKED` — and you depend on every one of those from [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) onward.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Testcontainers** | A library that starts real Docker containers from inside your tests, so you test against actual Postgres instead of a substitute. |
| **H2** | An in-memory database often used to make tests fast. It has a different query planner, different types, and no `SKIP LOCKED` — all of which this plan depends on from [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) onward. |
| **Container reuse** | Keeping one container alive across test runs instead of starting a fresh one each time. The difference between a suite you run constantly and one you avoid. |
| **`@DynamicPropertySource`** | A Spring hook for setting properties at runtime. Needed because the container's port is assigned when it starts, so you cannot write it in a config file ahead of time. |
| **Test isolation** | How you stop test A's rows from breaking test B. Either roll back a transaction after each test, or truncate the tables between tests. Each has trade-offs; pick one deliberately. |
| **Test fixture** | A known starting state for a test. `EventFixtures.aPublishedEvent()`. |
| **Object Mother** | The pattern of a single named place that builds ready-made test objects, so a test reads as behaviour rather than twelve lines of construction. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** making integration tests **fast enough to actually run**. With container reuse they start in seconds; without it they take thirty and you will quietly stop running them.
- **When it works you will see:** a real Postgres in Docker for your tests, a warm start under ten seconds, and the golden-path test green via `make smoke`.
- **Where people get stuck:** tests that pass alone and fail together. That is a data isolation problem — pick transactional rollback or truncate-between-tests, write down which, and apply it consistently.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Write the `PostgresIntegrationTest` base class in `platform-testing`.**
    *What this step is:* One abstract class that every integration test in this repository will extend for the next twenty weeks. It starts a single real Postgres container (via Testcontainers) once per JVM, keeps it alive for reuse across runs, and tells Spring the container's randomly assigned connection details. The shape is subtle and the subtlety is the whole point: the popular `@Testcontainers`/`@Container` annotations manage the container's lifecycle *per test class* and stop it when the class finishes — which silently defeats `withReuse(true)` with no error, just a fresh container and the full cold start on every run. So you deliberately do NOT use them; you own the lifecycle yourself with a plain `static` field and a `static` initializer.
    *Builds on:* [Testcontainers-backed integration tests in §2.1](#testcontainers-backed-integration-tests) — the full explanation of why real Postgres beats H2 here, with this exact class shape spelled out. [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — the `platform-testing` module you created there is where this class lives, so every service can import it.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `platform-testing`, create the abstract base class exactly in the shape from [What those deliverables actually mean](#21-what-those-deliverables-actually-mean):

    ```java
    @SpringBootTest
    abstract class PostgresIntegrationTest {

      // A plain static singleton, started once for the whole JVM — deliberately NOT
      // annotated with @Container, and no @Testcontainers on the class.
      static final PostgreSQLContainer<?> POSTGRES =
          new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17-alpine").withReuse(true);

      static { POSTGRES.start(); }

      @DynamicPropertySource
      static void datasourceProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.datasource.url", POSTGRES::getJdbcUrl);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.password", POSTGRES::getPassword);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.username", POSTGRES::getUsername);
      }
    }
    ```

    2. Note why `@DynamicPropertySource` is there: the container's port is assigned the moment it starts, so you cannot write the JDBC URL into a config file ahead of time — this Spring hook injects it at runtime instead.
    3. Write one throwaway test extending the class that runs `SELECT 1` through the datasource, just to prove the wiring.
    *You know it worked when:* the throwaway test is green, and `docker ps` while it runs shows a real `postgres:17-alpine` container that your test started.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Turn on container reuse and measure the warm-start difference.**
    *What this step is:* Reuse has two halves — the unmanaged-singleton class shape from Step 1, and a one-line opt-in on your machine — and missing either half makes every run silently pay the full cold start, which is exactly how teams end up not running their integration tests. The measurement is your proof that reuse is actually on: it is the gap between tests you run constantly and tests you avoid.
    *Builds on:* Step 1's `withReuse(true)` singleton — the class-side half that this machine-side half completes.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create (or edit) `~/.testcontainers.properties` in your home directory and add the line `testcontainers.reuse.enable=true`.
    2. Run the integration test twice and time both runs (`time mvn -pl catalog-service test -Dtest=YourIntegrationTest` works). The first run pays the cold start; the second should start in seconds, because the container from run one is still alive and gets found again.
    3. If the second run is as slow as the first, reuse is silently off — one of the two halves is missing. Check both: the class must be the plain unmanaged singleton (no `@Testcontainers`, no `@Container`), and the properties file must exist with the exact line above.
    4. Write both timings down — this number comes back in this task's "Done when" (warm start under 10 seconds) and in the checkpoint.
    *You know it worked when:* the second run is dramatically faster than the first, and `docker ps` between runs shows the Postgres container still running.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Choose and implement a test-isolation strategy, and write it down.**
    *What this step is:* With one shared container, test A's rows can break test B — the infamous "passes alone, fails together" suite, which is miserable to debug. You prevent it by choosing one of two strategies deliberately: **transactional rollback** (each test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back afterwards — fast, but you never see committed data, so anything testing commit-time behaviour is out of its reach) or **truncate-between-tests** (empty the tables before or after each test — slightly slower, but tests see real commits). Either works; what does not work is choosing by accident.
    *Do this:*
    1. Pick one. For rollback: put `@Transactional` on the base class (or the tests), and Spring rolls back after each test automatically. For truncate: write a small helper that truncates all application tables, and call it from an `@BeforeEach` in the base class.
    2. Write down which you chose and *why*, where the next person will find it — a comment block on `PostgresIntegrationTest` plus a line in `docs/local-setup.md` is enough. Include the characteristic failure mode of the option you rejected, because the checkpoint asks for it.
    3. Prove the isolation: write two tests that each insert a row with the same unique value, and run them in the same suite — both must pass, in either order.
    *You know it worked when:* the full suite passes, any single test passes alone, and running the suite twice in a row passes both times — no leftover rows from a previous run can break anything.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Test-data builders: `EventFixtures`, the Object Mother.**
    *What this step is:* A single named place that hands tests ready-made objects — `EventFixtures.aPublishedEvent().withTier(...)` — combining the Builder pattern with the Object Mother pattern (both defined in this task's "New words" table). The rule is absolute: **never** construct a 12-field object inline in a test, because then the test is about construction rather than behaviour, and every added field breaks fifty tests.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.4 — The domain layer: aggregates with real behaviour](#task-14--the-domain-layer-aggregates-with-real-behaviour--2h) — the `Event` aggregate and its `Builder` from there are what the fixtures construct under the hood. [Task 0.7 — The design pattern register](#task-07--the-design-pattern-register--1h) — Builder and Object Mother are two more rows for the pattern register you keep there.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `platform-testing` (or the service's test-fixtures source set), create `EventFixtures` with named starting points — `anUnpublishedEvent()`, `aPublishedEvent()` — each returning a builder pre-filled with sensible defaults, so a test only states what it *cares* about: `EventFixtures.aPublishedEvent().withTier(premium()).build()`.
    2. Go back through the tests you have written so far in Phase 1 and replace any inline multi-field construction with a fixture call.
    *You know it worked when:* no test in the repository constructs an `Event` field by field, and a new test's setup reads as one self-explanatory line.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Write two real integration tests, and time the second.**
    *What this step is:* The harness's acceptance test is economic: writing integration test number two must take under five minutes, or the harness has failed at its one job — making integration tests cheap enough that you actually write them. You write the first real test, then a second, with a clock running on the second.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — the `EventPersistenceAdapter` built there is the natural subject: it is the first code whose correctness genuinely depends on real Postgres. Steps 1–4 — the base class, reuse, isolation, and fixtures this test gets for free.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write the first real integration test: extend `PostgresIntegrationTest`, use `EventFixtures` for data, save an `Event` through the repository port, reload it, and assert it round-trips intact.
    2. Now start a timer and write a second integration test (any other adapter behaviour — reloading by a query, updating a field, whatever is next on your list). Stop the timer when it is green.
    3. If the second test took more than five minutes, the harness is the problem, not you — find the friction (slow start? fiddly setup? missing fixture?) and fix the harness *now* rather than paying that tax on every test for twenty weeks.
    *You know it worked when:* both tests are green against real Postgres and your timed second test came in under five minutes.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Write the golden-path test, and wire it to `make smoke`.**
    *What this step is:* One test, the journey from [§3.5 Walkthrough: buying a ticket, end to end](#35-walkthrough-buying-a-ticket-end-to-end): create an event → publish it → read it back. Right now that is all the system can do, and that is the point — it starts trivial and grows one assertion at a time as the project grows, as the table in [the standing rule](#the-standing-rule-it-must-still-run-at-the-end-of-every-phase) lays out. From here on, **this test passing is the definition of "the project still works"**, and every phase exit check asks for it.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — the Makefile from there already reserves a `smoke` target with a note that it "becomes real in Task 1.11"; this is that moment. [The standing rule](#the-standing-rule-it-must-still-run-at-the-end-of-every-phase) — the project-wide promise this test enforces.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write the golden-path test on the harness: through the real HTTP layer, `POST` a new event, publish it, then `GET` it back and assert what came back is what went in.
    2. Wire the Makefile's `smoke` target to run exactly this test (starting whatever it needs first), so `make smoke` is one command from cold to verdict.
    3. Run `make smoke` from a cold start — stack down, nothing warm — and watch it go green.
    *You know it worked when:* `make smoke` on a cold machine finishes green with no manual steps in between, and you understand that from now on this command is the project's heartbeat.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Document the harness where the next person will look.**
    *What this step is:* Two small documentation updates so the harness is discoverable: the patterns you just applied go into the pattern register, and the harness itself gets a note in the local-setup guide.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.7 — The design pattern register](#task-07--the-design-pattern-register--1h) — `docs/patterns.md` and its *Pattern · Where used · What problem it solved* columns live there. [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — `docs/local-setup.md`, the one place anyone looks to find out how to run things, was written there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the Testcontainers rows to `docs/patterns.md` — the singleton reusable container, and the Builder + Object Mother fixtures — each with the real class name in "where used" and the problem it solved.
    2. Note the harness in `docs/local-setup.md`: that integration tests need Docker running, that reuse requires the `~/.testcontainers.properties` line, and which isolation strategy the suite uses.
    *You know it worked when:* a stranger could read those two files and run the integration suite, with reuse on, without asking you anything.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Go back and finish [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h)'s two deferred checks.**
    *What this step is:* [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h) deliberately left two boxes unticked because they needed the harness you have just built: the OpenAPI snapshot test, and the ETag/`If-Match` checks re-run against a real database version column instead of the in-memory counter. This step closes that loop — the one place the task order crosses the test harness.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h) — where the snapshot test and the ETag/412 behaviour were specified and the two boxes were marked "ticked after Task 1.11". [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — the real JPA `@Version` column from there now backs the version the ETag and `If-Match` checks compare.
    *Do this:*
    1. Finish the OpenAPI snapshot test from [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h): the committed `contracts/openapi/catalog-v1.json`, the test that fails on an undeliberate change, and the proof — rename a response field, watch CI go red, then revert or update the snapshot deliberately.
    2. Re-run the ETag/304 and `If-Match`/412 tests as integration tests on the harness, against real Postgres, so the version being compared is the real `@Version` column — then watch it increment in the database after a successful `PUT`.
    3. Go back to [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h) and tick its two deferred boxes, and the matching line in its "Done when".
    *You know it worked when:* [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h) has no unticked boxes left, you have personally seen its snapshot test fail CI on a renamed field, and a stale `If-Match` gets its 412 from a test running against real Postgres.

**Done when:** integration tests run against real Postgres in a container, start in under 10 seconds warm, and a new integration test takes you under five minutes to write.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Name three ways H2 behaves differently from Postgres that would actually matter later in this plan.
2. Which isolation strategy did you choose, and what is the characteristic failure mode of the other one?
3. What does `@DynamicPropertySource` do that a static `application-test.yml` cannot?
4. Why does a test-data builder make a test more readable than constructing the object inline?

**Phase 1 deliverables:** `catalog-service` serving a documented, paginated, validated,
ETag-aware API; a reusable Testcontainers harness; the first seven ADRs (ADR-0000 through ADR-0006); a populated pattern
register.

**Phase 1 exit check — tick honestly:**

- [ ] `make up && make smoke` passes from a cold start, with the new assertions for this phase.
- [ ] I can draw the full call path of one `POST /events` request, naming every class and the direction of every dependency.
- [ ] My domain tests run with no Spring context in under a second.
- [ ] I have a test that proves offset pagination duplicates a row and keyset does not.
- [ ] Every error response is problem+json with a stable `code` and a `traceId`, and a test proves no internals leak.
- [ ] Writing a new integration test takes me under five minutes.
- [ ] Task 1.9's two deferred checks are ticked: the OpenAPI snapshot test exists and I have seen it fail on a renamed field, and ETag/`If-Match` are proven against the real `@Version` column.
- [ ] I could rebuild this service's structure from an empty directory without re-reading this document.

**Phase 1 pitfalls:** leaking JPA entities into controllers; `@Transactional` on
controllers; calling `Instant.now()` in the domain; defaulting to offset pagination;
`@Data` on entities; mapping DTOs by hand and forgetting a field.

**Phase 1 interview talking points:** entity versus value object; why your domain tests
need no Spring context; how keyset pagination avoids duplicates *and* stays fast; what RFC
9457 buys a client; why the port interface lives in the application layer and not the
adapter.
