### Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway — 16h baseline

**Scheduled:** Weeks 7–8

**Goal:** real authentication and authorization, multi-tenant data isolation, an API
gateway in front, and a first rate limiter — deliberately in-memory for now; it moves to Redis in Phase 4, once Redis has been taught.

**Why this phase exists:** you listed many things but not security, and security is the
single most common reason a senior candidate is marked down. "How does a request get
authorized?" and "how do you stop tenant A reading tenant B's data?" are asked in almost
every backend loop.

**Services you create in this phase:** `identity-service` (Task 2.1) and `edge-gateway`
(Task 2.3) — services 2 and 3 of nine. Both start as a copy of the `catalog-service`
template you built in Phase 1.

#### Task 2.1 — identity-service: OAuth2 authorization server — 3h

**What:** Issue and rotate JWTs with Spring Authorization Server; model users, orgs, roles, permissions.
**Why:** Hand-rolled "login returns a JWT I signed with HS256 and a hardcoded secret" is the classic junior signature. A real authorization server with asymmetric keys and a JWKS endpoint is the senior one.
**Solves:** secret sharing across services, inability to rotate keys, and no standards-based path to third-party clients.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **OAuth2** | A standard describing how one program gets permission to act for a user, without ever seeing the user's password. It is about *delegation*; it is not a login screen. |
| **Authorization server** | The service that checks credentials and issues tokens. Here, `identity-service`. There is exactly one in the system. |
| **Resource server** | Any service that *accepts* a token and decides what the holder may do. Every other service in Zenith is one. |
| **JWT** | JSON Web Token. A signed blob of JSON. Anyone can read it — **it is not encrypted** — but nobody can alter it without the signing key. Never put a secret in one. |
| **Claim** | One field inside the token: `sub` (who), `org_id` (which tenant), `exp` (when it dies), `roles`, `scope`. |
| **JWKS** | JSON Web Key Set — a public URL (`/.well-known/jwks.json`) publishing the *public* half of your signing keys. Services fetch it to verify signatures, so the private key never leaves the authorization server. |
| **Service template** | The shape of `catalog-service` from [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) — hexagonal packages, error contract, ArchUnit suite, Flyway setup. Every new service starts as a copy of it, which is why Phase 1 was worth the time. |
| **`kid`** | Key ID, a header naming which key signed this token. It is what makes rotation possible: publish the new key, sign with it, keep accepting the old one until the last token signed with it has expired. |
| **HS256 vs RS256** | HS256 signs with one shared secret, so every service that can *verify* a token can also *forge* one. RS256 signs with a private key and verifies with a public one. The difference is why hand-rolled HS256 auth reads as junior. |
| **PKCE** | Proof Key for Code Exchange. The client invents a random secret, sends its hash up front, and reveals the original when redeeming the code — so a stolen authorization code is useless on its own. |
| **`client_credentials`** | The OAuth2 flow for service-to-service calls, where there is no user at all. `order-service` uses it to call `payment-service` in [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline), where services call each other with no user present. |
| **Refresh token rotation** | Each time a refresh token is used it is invalidated and a new one issued. If an old one is ever presented again, someone has a stolen copy — that is *reuse detection*, and the correct response is to kill the whole session family. |
| **Argon2id** | A deliberately slow, memory-hard password hashing algorithm. Slowness is the feature: it makes brute-forcing a stolen database expensive. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** using a **real** authorization server with asymmetric keys. A hand-rolled "login returns a JWT I signed with a hardcoded secret" is the single clearest junior signature in a backend project.
- **When it works you will see:** a token obtained via `client_credentials`, pasted into jwt.io, with every claim explainable — and the signing key rotated without any downtime.
- **Where people get stuck:** putting anything secret in the JWT. It is signed, not encrypted: anyone can base64-decode it and read everything. Also, long-lived access tokens — if revocation takes an hour, you have no revocation.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Create `identity-service` from the service template.**
    *What this step is:* You are creating the second microservice of the project — a brand-new Spring Boot service called `identity-service`, whose only job will be to check credentials and hand out tokens. You do not design it from scratch: you copy the shape of `catalog-service`, the service you finished in Phase 1, and rename things. At the end of this step you have a second service that compiles, starts, passes the same architecture tests, and runs its own database migrations — but does nothing interesting yet.
    *Builds on:* [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) — where you built `catalog-service`, the template you are now copying. [Task 1.8 — REST adapter, part 2: one error contract for the whole platform](#task-18--rest-adapter-part-2-one-error-contract-for-the-whole-platform--1h) — the shared Problem-Details error format every service must speak, including this one. [Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h) — the reusable ArchUnit suite (the tests that check code *structure*, like "domain imports no Spring") that the new service must import and pass. [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — Flyway, the tool that runs numbered SQL files to build your schema; this service gets its own set. [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — the Docker Compose file that starts your whole local stack; the new service joins it.

Create a new Maven module `identity-service` next to `catalog-service` in the monorepo (add it to the parent POM from [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h)), with the same hexagonal package layout: `domain/`, `application/`, `adapter/in/web/`, `adapter/out/persistence/`, `config/`.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Turn it into a real authorization server.**
    *What this step is:* You add the `spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server` dependency and configure the two token-issuing flows the platform needs. Flow one: `authorization_code` + PKCE — the flow for *humans*: the user is sent to a login page, logs in, and the client application gets a one-time code it exchanges for tokens; PKCE (the client invents a random secret, sends its hash up front, reveals the original when redeeming the code) makes a stolen code useless on its own. Flow two: `client_credentials` — the flow for *machines*: one service presents its own id and secret and gets a token with no user involved at all. At the end of this step both flows hand out signed JWTs.
    *Builds on:* Step 1 — the `identity-service` skeleton you just created; everything here is configuration and registered-client records inside it.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the Spring Authorization Server dependency and a `SecurityFilterChain` configuration enabling the authorization server endpoints.
    2. Register two clients: a public client using `authorization_code` with PKCE **required** (for users), and a confidential client using `client_credentials` (for service-to-service calls).
    3. Obtain a token with each flow: for `client_credentials`, a single `curl -u client:secret -d grant_type=client_credentials http://localhost:<port>/oauth2/token`; for `authorization_code` + PKCE, walk the browser redirect once and watch the code-for-token exchange.
    *You know it worked when:* both flows return an access token, and pasting one into jwt.io shows a decoded JWT (remember — readable by anyone, forgeable by no one without the key).

- [ ] **Step 3 — Refresh tokens with rotation and reuse detection.**
    *What this step is:* Access tokens will be short-lived (10 minutes — Step 6), so clients need a *refresh token* to get a new access token without logging in again. You configure **rotation**: every time a refresh token is used it is invalidated and a brand-new one is issued. That buys you **reuse detection** for free — if an already-used refresh token is ever presented again, there are now two parties holding tokens from the same session, which means one of them stole it. The correct response is to kill the whole session family (every token descended from that login), and that is what you implement.
    *Builds on:* Step 2 — the authorization server that is now issuing tokens; this step changes what happens on the `refresh_token` grant.
    *Do this:*
    1. Enable the `refresh_token` grant for the user-facing client with rotation turned on (each refresh invalidates the old refresh token and issues a new pair).
    2. Implement reuse detection: when a refresh token that was already consumed is presented, revoke every token belonging to that session family, not just the one token.
    3. Test the attack by hand: refresh once (works), then replay the *old* refresh token (must be rejected), then try the *new* one too — it must also be dead, because reuse detection killed the family.
    *You know it worked when:* replaying a used refresh token is rejected **and** takes the rest of its session family down with it.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Asymmetric signing keys from a keystore, published as JWKS.**
    *What this step is:* You replace the server's default throwaway signing key with a real RSA or EC key pair loaded from a keystore file — a password-protected file format (`.p12`/`.jks`) that Java uses to store keys. The *private* half signs tokens and never leaves `identity-service`; the *public* half is published at `/.well-known/jwks.json`, the standard URL every other service will fetch to verify signatures. This is the whole point of RS256 over HS256: verifiers can check tokens but can never forge them. At the end of this step your tokens are signed by a key you generated, and the public half is one `curl` away.
    *Builds on:* Step 2 — the authorization server whose signing key you are now replacing with your own.
    *Do this:*
    1. Generate an RSA (or EC) key pair into a keystore file with `keytool`, and keep the keystore **out of git** — add it to `.gitignore` and load its path and password from environment variables or an untracked local config file.
    2. Configure the authorization server to load its `JWKSource` from that keystore, giving the key a `kid` (the key-id header that names which key signed a token).
    3. `curl http://localhost:<port>/.well-known/jwks.json` and read what you published: the public key material and the `kid` — and nothing private.
    *You know it worked when:* the JWKS endpoint returns your public key, a freshly issued token's header carries your `kid`, and `git status` shows no keystore anywhere near the repo.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Document and perform key rotation with overlapping `kid`s.**
    *What this step is:* Keys must be replaceable — that is the senior move this task exists for. You cannot simply swap the key, because tokens signed with the old key are still out there and must stay verifiable until they expire. The procedure: *add* a new key with a new `kid` alongside the old one, publish **both** in JWKS, start signing new tokens with the new key, and only remove the old key after every token signed with it has expired. You write this procedure down as a short runbook and then actually perform it.
    *Builds on:* Step 4 — the keystore and JWKS endpoint; rotation is adding and later removing keys there. Step 6's 10-minute access-token lifetime is what makes the overlap window short.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write `docs/runbooks/key-rotation.md`: generate new key → publish both `kid`s in JWKS → sign with new `kid` → wait out the longest-lived token signed by the old key → remove the old key.
    2. Perform it once for real: mint a token with the old key, rotate, mint a token with the new key, and verify **both** tokens validate against the JWKS endpoint during the overlap — no restart of any consuming service, no downtime.
    *You know it worked when:* during the overlap, two tokens with different `kid`s both verify, and after retirement the old-key token (now expired anyway) is the only thing rejected.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Design what goes inside the token.**
    *What this step is:* You decide, deliberately, the claims — the JSON fields — your access tokens carry: `sub` (who the user is), `org_id` (which customer organization they belong to — the field the whole multi-tenancy story in [Task 2.2 — Resource-server authorization and multi-tenancy](#task-22--resource-server-authorization-and-multi-tenancy--5h) will hang off), `roles`, `permissions`, `scope`, and a short `exp` of **10 minutes** for access tokens. Short, because a JWT cannot be un-issued: once signed it is valid until `exp`, so the lifetime *is* your revocation latency. And nothing secret ever goes in — a JWT is signed, not encrypted; anyone can base64-decode it.
    *Builds on:* Step 2 — the token issuing you are now customising with a claims customizer.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a token customizer that writes `org_id`, `roles`, `permissions`, and `scope` into the access token, and set the access-token time-to-live to 10 minutes.
    2. Decode a fresh token on jwt.io and check every claim: for each one, say out loud what it is for and which service will read it. If you cannot explain a claim, remove it.
    *You know it worked when:* a decoded token shows exactly your designed claim set, `exp` minus `iat` is 600 seconds, and nothing in the payload would hurt you if printed on a billboard.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Write ADR-0007: JWT vs opaque tokens.**
    *What this step is:* An Architecture Decision Record capturing *why* you chose self-contained JWTs over opaque tokens (random strings the resource server must phone home to check). The real trade-off: JWTs give you **revocation latency** (a logged-out user's token stays valid until `exp`) in exchange for no per-request **introspection cost** (no network call to `identity-service` on every request). Your mitigation, which goes in the ADR: the short 10-minute TTL from Step 6, plus a **deny-list** for forced logout — a list of revoked token ids every service checks before trusting a token. The deny-list is in-memory for now; it moves to Redis in [Phase 4 — Redis and the caching layer](#phase-4--redis-and-the-caching-layer--12h-baseline) (specifically [Task 4.4 — Redis as a data structure server](#task-44--redis-as-a-data-structure-server--3h)), along with the Redis version of the rate limiter you will first build in-memory at the gateway in [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h).
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.5 — Architecture Decision Records](#task-05--architecture-decision-records--1h) — where you set up the ADR format and wrote the first five; this is the same template, numbered 0007.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write `docs/adr/0007-jwt-vs-opaque-tokens.md` in your established ADR format: context, the decision (JWT), the rejected alternative (opaque + introspection) and *why*, the consequence (revocation latency), and the mitigation (short TTL + deny-list, in-memory now, Redis in [Phase 4 — Redis and the caching layer](#phase-4--redis-and-the-caching-layer--12h-baseline)).
    2. Implement the minimal in-memory deny-list: forced logout adds the token id, token validation consults it.
    *You know it worked when:* the ADR names a real rejected alternative with an honest cost, and a force-logged-out user's still-unexpired token is rejected because the deny-list caught it.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Store passwords with Argon2id and lock out brute force.**
    *What this step is:* Passwords are never stored — only a slow, salted hash of them, so a stolen database does not hand over working credentials. You use Argon2id, a deliberately slow and memory-hungry hashing algorithm (slowness is the feature: it makes guessing billions of passwords expensive) — or bcrypt with cost factor 12 or higher if Argon2id is unavailable. You also throttle login attempts and lock accounts with exponential backoff: each consecutive failure doubles the wait before the next attempt is allowed.
    *Builds on:* Step 2 — the `authorization_code` flow's login step is where this password check runs.
    *Do this:*
    1. Configure the `PasswordEncoder` as `Argon2PasswordEncoder` (or `BCryptPasswordEncoder` with strength ≥ 12).
    2. Track failed attempts per account; after each failure double the lockout wait (exponential backoff) before another attempt is accepted.
    3. Test it: hammer a login with wrong passwords and watch the allowed-retry time double; then log in correctly after the window and watch the counter reset.
    *You know it worked when:* the stored column holds an Argon2id/bcrypt hash (never plaintext), and the fifth rapid wrong-password attempt is rejected for *being too soon*, not just for being wrong.

- [ ] **Step 9 — The identity schema, with a local-only seeded admin.**
    *What this step is:* The database tables that model who exists and what they may do: `users`, `organizations` (the customer companies — the tenants), `memberships` (which user belongs to which organization, since one user can belong to several), `roles`, `permissions`, and `api_keys` (for partner integrations, filled in properly in [Task 2.2 — Resource-server authorization and multi-tenancy](#task-22--resource-server-authorization-and-multi-tenancy--5h)). You also seed one admin user so you can actually log in locally — via a Flyway migration that is **guarded to run only in the local profile**, because a seeded admin reaching any real environment is a breach waiting to happen.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — the Flyway habit (numbered, immutable SQL migrations) this schema is written in. Step 8 — the admin's seeded password is an Argon2id hash, not plaintext.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write the Flyway migration creating `users`, `organizations`, `memberships`, `roles`, `permissions`, and `api_keys`, with foreign keys linking them.
    2. Add the admin seed as a migration that only applies under the local profile (for example via Flyway locations or a placeholder that resolves differently per profile), inserting the admin with a pre-computed Argon2id hash.
    3. Start the service with the local profile — admin exists; check the migration set used by any non-local profile does not include the seed.
    *You know it worked when:* you can log in as the seeded admin locally, and the seed migration provably does not run outside the local profile.

- [ ] **Step 10 — `[stretch]` TOTP MFA with recovery codes.**
    *What this step is:* Optional extra if you have time. TOTP (time-based one-time password) is the six-digit code from an authenticator app: server and app share a secret, both derive the current code from the secret plus the clock. You add enrolment (show a QR code, verify one code), a second login step for enrolled users, and single-use recovery codes (stored hashed, like passwords) for when the phone is lost.
    *Builds on:* Step 8 — the login flow this adds a second factor to; Step 9 — the `users` table gains the TOTP secret and hashed recovery codes.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add TOTP enrolment: generate a secret, render the `otpauth://` QR, require one valid code to activate.
    2. Require the code at login for enrolled users; generate ten single-use recovery codes, store only their hashes, and consume one on use.
    *You know it worked when:* login with a wrong TOTP code fails, a correct one succeeds, and a recovery code works exactly once.

**Done when:** you can obtain a token with `client_credentials`, decode it, rotate the signing key without downtime, and a revoked refresh token is rejected on reuse.
