### Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization — 21h baseline

**Scheduled:** Weeks 8–10

**Goal:** go from "it works" to "it works at 10× data volume", with measurements.

**Why this phase exists:** DB optimization is the most frequently claimed and least
frequently demonstrated skill on CVs. The deliverable here is not "I added indexes"; it
is a document with query plans and latency numbers before and after, which almost no
candidate has.

#### Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline — 2h

**What:** Generate millions of rows and record a baseline you can be judged against.
**Why:** Optimization without a baseline is superstition. Also, almost every performance bug is invisible at 1,000 rows.
**Solves:** tuning the wrong thing, and having no number to put in your performance report.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Baseline** | The measurement you take *before* changing anything. Without it, every later claim is an opinion. This is the single most skipped step in performance work. |
| **p50 / p95 / p99** | Percentile latencies. p99 = 1% of requests were slower than this. Averages hide the problem entirely — one user in a hundred having a terrible time is invisible in a mean. |
| **RPS** | Requests per second the system actually completed. Always quote it together with the latency it was achieved at; either number alone is meaningless. |
| **Skew** | Uneven distribution — one mega-event holding 20% of all seats. Real data is always skewed, and skew is where performance problems hide. Evenly generated test data makes systems look faster than they are. |
| **`pg_stat_statements`** | A Postgres extension that records every query shape with its call count and total time. Your primary tool for finding what is actually slow, rather than what you assume is slow. |
| **`auto_explain`** | A Postgres extension that writes the query plan to the log automatically whenever a query exceeds a time threshold. It catches slow queries in the act, including ones you never thought to test. |
| **`total_exec_time` vs `mean_exec_time`** | Total points at a cheap query called constantly — a caching candidate. Mean points at an individually slow query — an indexing candidate. Two different problems needing two different fixes. |
| **`COPY`** | Postgres's bulk-load command. Dramatically faster than row-by-row `INSERT` for seeding 10M rows. |
| **k6** | A load-testing tool where scenarios are written in JavaScript. Your only client for the whole project, since there is no frontend. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** that **a baseline you did not measure is not a baseline**. Every optimisation claim in the rest of this plan is meaningless without the before number recorded here.
- **When it works you will see:** a million rows of realistic data, and a saved k6 report with p50/p95/p99 under stated conditions in `docs/benchmarks/baseline.md`.
- **Where people get stuck:** testing with a thousand rows. Everything is fast on a thousand rows — sequential scans, N+1 queries, missing indexes all look fine. The whole point is a dataset big enough for bad decisions to hurt.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Build the data generator that makes Postgres sweat.**
    *What this step is:* You will write a small program under `tools/seed` that fills your database with production-sized data: 5k events, 2k venues, 10M seats, 2M orders, and 20M scan records (a scan record is one row written each time a ticket's QR code is checked at the venue gate). The point of the volume: every performance sin — missing index, N+1, sequential scan — is invisible at a thousand rows and painful at ten million. The data must also be *skewed*: one deliberately chosen mega-event holds 20% of all the seats, because skew is where real problems hide — evenly spread test data makes systems look faster than they are. At the end of this step you can fill the database from scratch, fast.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — the Docker Compose stack whose Postgres this fills, and the `make psql` shortcut you will use to check it. [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — Flyway, the tool that owns your schema through numbered SQL migration files; `V1__catalog_baseline.sql` created the event and venue tables there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Open a database shell with `make psql` and run `\dt` to list your tables. Events and venues exist from [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h)'s baseline migration. For any table the generator needs that does not exist yet (seats, orders, scan records), first add a Flyway migration creating it, following the [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) conventions — snake_case, singular table names, UUIDv7 primary keys, explicitly named constraints.
    2. Create `tools/seed` — a small standalone Java program is fine. Generate in dependency order so foreign keys always point at rows that exist: venues → events → seats → orders → scan records.

    4. Build the skew in deliberately: pick one mega-event and give it 20% of the 10M seats (~2M rows), and weight orders and scan records toward it the same way.

    *What this step is:* You will connect your generator to the `make seed` command so the whole dataset is reproducible — every later benchmark must start from the same data, or the numbers cannot be compared. The target takes a `scale=` argument: `small` for daily development (minutes, not hours), `full` for benchmarking (the complete 10M-seat dataset).

- [ ] **Step 3 — Turn on Postgres's two always-on profilers.**
    *What this step is:* You will enable `pg_stat_statements` (records every query shape with its call count and total time — your tool for finding what is *actually* slow) and `auto_explain` (writes the query plan to the log whenever a query exceeds a time threshold — it catches slow queries in the act, including ones you never thought to test). Both live in the Postgres service definition inside the Compose file.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — `deploy/compose/docker-compose.infra.yml`, the file where your Postgres container is defined; that is "the compose Postgres config" this step edits.
    *Do this:*
    1. Both are extensions that must be loaded at server start, so add them to the Postgres service's startup command in the compose file, with `auto_explain` set to `min_duration = 200ms` and `analyze = on`:

    ```yaml
    postgres:
      command:
        - postgres
        - "-c"
        - "shared_preload_libraries=pg_stat_statements,auto_explain"
        - "-c"
        - "auto_explain.log_min_duration=200ms"
        - "-c"
        - "auto_explain.log_analyze=on"
    ```

    2. Recreate the container (`make down && make up` — your data lives in the named volume, so it survives), then in `make psql` run `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;` — the preload makes the extension *available*; this makes its view *queryable*.

This file is the "before" that every optimisation in Phase 3 and [Phase 4 — Redis and the caching layer](#phase-4--redis-and-the-caching-layer--12h-baseline) will be judged against.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — k6 was installed there with the rest of the toolchain. [Task 1.7 — REST adapter, part 1: resources, DTOs, and validation](#task-17--rest-adapter-part-1-resources-dtos-and-validation--15h) and [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h) — the catalog endpoints these scenarios hit. [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) — all traffic now flows through the gateway you built there, so point k6 at it, the way a real client would arrive.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write one script per flow in the repo's `load/` directory: `load/event-search.js`, `load/event-detail.js`, `load/availability.js`, `load/order-create.js`. Start from k6's basic shape (a `default function` doing an HTTP call, an `options` block setting virtual users and duration) — ask AI for a minimal example and build up.
    2. Make the traffic realistic, not uniform: weight requests toward the mega-event from Step 1, because flash-sale traffic is never evenly spread — and neither is yours.
    3. Run each scenario against `make seed scale=full` data, discard the warmup, and record p50/p95/p99 and RPS per scenario into `docs/benchmarks/baseline.md` — together with the date, the dataset size, and your machine's specs, because a benchmark number without its conditions is worthless.
    *You know it worked when:* `docs/benchmarks/baseline.md` contains a table of all four scenarios with p50/p95/p99 and RPS each, plus the date and dataset size — and you could rerun any scenario from its saved command alone.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Clear [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline)'s TODO: prove the rate limiter is accurate at 500 VUs.**
    *What this step is:* Back in [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline) you proved your gateway's rate limiter *works* using two parallel curl loops, and left a written TODO to prove it is *accurate* once you had a real load tool — a curl loop cannot generate 500 simultaneous clients, so it can never show whether the limiter admits exactly the configured number of requests or quietly over-admits under pressure. Now you have k6. A VU is a "virtual user" — one simulated client running your script in a loop; 500 VUs means 500 of them hammering the gateway at once.
    *Builds on:* [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) — the in-memory token-bucket rate limiter behind your own `RateLimiter` port, the 429-with-`Retry-After` behaviour, and the TODO this step deletes.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write `load/rate-limit.js`: 500 VUs against a rate-limited endpoint through the gateway for a fixed window, using a k6 `Counter` to count responses that were admitted (2xx) versus rejected (429).
    2. Assert in the script that the admitted count matches the configured limit for that window — this is the accuracy proof the curl loops could not give you. If it over-admits, you have found a real concurrency bug in the bucket; fix it before moving on.
    3. Delete the TODO from [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline) and note the result next to your other numbers in `docs/benchmarks/baseline.md`.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Capture the top-10 query tables — your optimisation shopping list.**
    *What this step is:* You will pull two top-10 lists out of `pg_stat_statements`: the queries costing the most *total* time, and the queries slowest *per call*. These point at two different problems — the top offender by `total_exec_time` is usually a cheap query called constantly (a caching candidate, [Phase 4 — Redis and the caching layer](#phase-4--redis-and-the-caching-layer--12h-baseline)'s business), while the top by `mean_exec_time` is an individually slow query (an indexing candidate, the very next task's business). This list is what stops you optimising the wrong thing.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) Step 3 of this task — the `pg_stat_statements` extension you enabled there is what has been silently recording every query since.
    *Do this:*
    1. Reset the statistics so old noise does not pollute the list: `SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();` in `make psql`, then re-run your four k6 scenarios from Step 4 so the view holds exactly your baseline traffic.
    2. Pull both lists:

    ```sql
    SELECT left(query, 80) AS query, calls,
           round(total_exec_time) AS total_ms,
           round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS mean_ms
    FROM pg_stat_statements
    ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;
    -- then run it again ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC
    ```

    3. Paste both tables into `docs/benchmarks/baseline.md`, and add the note the bullet demands: which query is your cache candidate (top by total — cheap but called constantly) and which is your index candidate (top by mean — individually slow).
    *You know it worked when:* `docs/benchmarks/baseline.md` contains both top-10 tables and one sentence each naming the cache candidate and the index candidate — which is exactly the shopping list the next task starts from.

**Done when:** `docs/benchmarks/baseline.md` has numbers and the top-10 query table, with the date and dataset size recorded.

1. What does p99 actually mean, and why report it instead of the average?
2. Why does this task insist on skewed data rather than evenly distributed rows?
3. A query is top of the list by total time; a different one is top by mean time. What different action does each suggest?
4. Why is a benchmark number worthless without the hardware, dataset size, and date recorded next to it?
5. You have your baseline. What is the rule about when you are allowed to start optimising?

#### Task 3.2 — Index design and reading query plans — 4h

**What:** Learn to read `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and design indexes deliberately.
**Why:** This is the single highest-leverage database skill, and it is directly testable in an interview with a whiteboard query.
**Solves:** sequential scans on 10M-row tables, redundant indexes slowing writes, and unused indexes consuming cache.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **B-tree** | The default index structure: a sorted, balanced tree. Sorted is why it serves ranges and `ORDER BY`, and why column order in a composite index matters so much. |
| **Seq Scan** | Postgres reading the whole table. Correct for small tables, a red flag on ten million rows. |
| **Index Scan** | Using the index to find matching rows, then visiting the table to fetch the other columns. |
| **Index Only Scan** | Answering entirely from the index because it already contains every column needed. The fastest option, and what `INCLUDE` is for. |
| **`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`** | `EXPLAIN` shows the plan; `ANALYZE` actually runs it and shows real timings; `BUFFERS` shows how many pages came from cache versus disk. Always use all three. |
| **Estimated vs actual rows** | The planner's guess against reality. A large gap means the statistics are stale, and a planner working from bad numbers will choose a bad plan — so you fix the statistics, not the query. |
| **`shared hit` vs `shared read`** | Pages found in Postgres's cache versus pages fetched from disk. A high read count is where your latency went. |
| **Leftmost prefix rule** | A composite index on `(a, b, c)` can serve queries filtering on `a`, or `a,b`, or `a,b,c` — but not on `b` alone. This single rule explains most "why is my index not used?" questions. |
| **Covering index** | An index carrying extra columns via `INCLUDE` purely so the query never has to touch the table. |
| **`Heap Fetches: 0`** | The line in a plan proving an index-only scan truly avoided the table. Anything above zero means it did not. |
| **Partial index** | An index over only the rows matching a condition (`WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED'`). Smaller, so more of it stays cached. |
| **GIN** | An index type for values containing many searchable items — full-text documents, JSONB, arrays. |
| **`pg_trgm`** | A trigram extension that makes `ILIKE '%text%'` indexable by breaking strings into three-character chunks. |
| **Selectivity** | What fraction of rows a condition keeps. Highly selective conditions (few rows) belong first in a composite index; `status = 'ACTIVE'` matching 90% of the table is barely worth indexing alone. |
| **Index bloat** | Dead space accumulating in an index after many updates and deletes, making it larger and slower until it is rebuilt. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** reading `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` unaided. This is the highest-value single skill in the phase and it is directly testable in an interview.
- **When it works you will see:** a query plan going from `Seq Scan` to `Index Scan`, with buffer reads dropping by orders of magnitude, both plans saved.
- **Where people get stuck:** adding indexes without measuring. Each one slows every write, and an index the planner never chooses is pure cost. Also: column *order* in a composite index matters enormously, and getting it wrong means the index sits unused.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Read the plans for your five worst queries.**
    *What this step is:* You will take the five worst queries from your top-10 lists and read their execution plans with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` — `EXPLAIN` shows the plan Postgres chose, `ANALYZE` actually runs the query and shows real timings, `BUFFERS` shows how many pages came from cache versus disk; always use all three together. At the end of this step you can look at a plan and point at where the time went, which is the single highest-value skill in this phase.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — the `pg_stat_statements` top-10 tables you saved in `docs/benchmarks/baseline.md` are where your "five worst queries" come from, and the 10M-row dataset is what makes their plans honest.
    *Do this:*
    1. Pick the five worst queries from your two top-10 tables (overlap is fine — take five distinct ones). For each, run it in `make psql` prefixed with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.
    2. In each plan, hunt for these six smells and annotate every one you find:
        - `Seq Scan` on a large table — Postgres reading all ten million rows because no index helps; correct for small tables, a red flag here.
        - `Rows Removed by Filter` — rows fetched and then thrown away; a big number means the index (or lack of one) is not doing the filtering.
        - a large gap between `estimated` and `actual` rows — the planner's guess versus reality; a big gap means stale statistics, and the fix is `ANALYZE <table>;` (refresh the stats), not rewriting the query.
        - `Nested Loop` with a high loop count — the inner side executed once per outer row; thousands of loops is thousands of repeated work.
        - a `Sort` with `Sort Method: external merge  Disk: ...` — the sort did not fit in memory and spilled to disk.
        - high `shared read` versus `shared hit` in the `BUFFERS` line — `hit` is pages found in Postgres's cache, `read` is pages fetched from disk; a high read count is where your latency went.
    *You know it worked when:* for each of the five plans you can point at the most expensive node and name which of the six smells it shows — out loud, without notes.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Composite index column order, proven with plans.**
    *What this step is:* A composite index is one index over several columns, and the *order* of those columns decides whether it gets used at all — the leftmost prefix rule: an index on `(a, b, c)` can serve queries filtering on `a`, or `a,b`, or `a,b,c`, but never on `b` alone. You will build the index both ways on the real query "upcoming events for one organisation" and prove with plans why one order works and the reverse does not. At the end you can answer the most common "why is my index not used?" question from first principles.
    *Builds on:* [Task 2.2 — Resource-server authorization and multi-tenancy](#task-22--resource-server-authorization-and-multi-tenancy--5h) — every tenant-scoped query filters on the `org_id` column you added there, which is why it leads the index. [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — the event table and its `starts_at` start-time column from the baseline migration.
    *Do this:*
    1. Take the query shape `WHERE org_id = ? AND starts_at >= ? ORDER BY starts_at, id` and build `CREATE INDEX ON event (org_id, starts_at, id);`. Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and save the plan — you should see an index scan with no separate `Sort` node, because a B-tree is sorted and this order matches filter *then* sort.
    2. Drop it, build the reverse — `(starts_at, org_id, id)` — and run the same query. Save that plan too: the equality filter on `org_id` can no longer use the index's leftmost column, so the plan is worse or ignores the index entirely.
    3. Write it up (a short note alongside the plans is enough): why equality columns go first, range/sort columns after — selectivity plus the leftmost prefix rule in your own words. Restore the correct index.
    *You know it worked when:* you have both saved plans, the correct order shows an Index Scan with no separate Sort, and you can state the leftmost prefix rule from memory.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Covering index: never touch the table at all.**
    *What this step is:* A normal index scan finds matching rows in the index, then visits the table to fetch the other columns. A *covering* index carries those extra columns inside the index itself via `INCLUDE`, so the query is answered entirely from the index — an **index-only scan**, the fastest option there is. The plan line that proves it is `Heap Fetches: 0` ("heap" is Postgres's word for the table file); anything above zero means the table was touched after all.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — the 10M-row seat table and the availability query from your k6 baseline, this project's canonical example of a query worth covering.
    *Do this:*
    1. Take a hot query that reads only a few columns — the per-section availability aggregate is ideal: it filters on `event_id` and `status` and reads `section`. Save its before plan.
    2. Build the covering index: `CREATE INDEX ON seat (event_id, status) INCLUDE (section);` — filter columns in the key, the merely-read column in `INCLUDE`.
    3. Re-run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and find two things in the after plan: the node type `Index Only Scan`, and the line `Heap Fetches: 0`.
    *You know it worked when:* the after plan says `Index Only Scan` with `Heap Fetches: 0`, and the buffer counts dropped by orders of magnitude against the before plan.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Partial index: index only the rows you query.**
    *What this step is:* A partial index covers only the rows matching a condition — here `WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED'` — instead of the whole table. Smaller index, so more of it stays in cache, and writes to rows outside the condition never touch it. You will build one and compare it honestly against the full-table equivalent.
    *Do this:*
    1. Build two indexes on the event table: one plain, one with `WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED'` appended.
    2. Compare their sizes — `SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('<index_name>'));` for each — and write both numbers down.
    3. Run a published-only query (`WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED' AND ...`) with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and confirm the planner chooses the partial index. Then try a query *without* the status condition and notice the partial index cannot serve it — that asymmetry is the trade-off you are buying.
    *You know it worked when:* the partial index is measurably smaller than the full one, and the plan for the published-only query names the partial index.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Make `ILIKE '%x%'` searchable: GIN and `pg_trgm`.**
    *What this step is:* A B-tree is a *sorted* structure, so it can only help a text search anchored at the start of the string — `'abc%'` works, `'%abc%'` cannot, because rows matching a middle-of-string pattern are scattered everywhere in sort order. The fixes are GIN (an index type for values containing many searchable items) plus `pg_trgm` (an extension that breaks strings into three-character chunks so substring matches become indexable), or `tsvector` full-text search (word-based matching). You will build event-name autocomplete and compare all three approaches.
    *Do this:*
    1. Save the before plan: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on `SELECT ... FROM event WHERE name ILIKE '%tour%';` — a Seq Scan over 5k events, and understand why no B-tree could help.
    2. `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;` then `CREATE INDEX ON event USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);`. Re-run the same query and save the plan — now a bitmap index scan via trigrams.
    3. Build the `tsvector` variant (full-text search over the name), query it with `@@`, and save that plan too. Note the difference in kind: trigram matches *substrings* ("our" matches "tour"), full-text matches *words and their stems* — autocomplete usually wants trigram; searching descriptions usually wants full-text.
    *You know it worked when:* you have three saved plans — unindexed `ILIKE` (Seq Scan), trigram (index used), `tsvector` — and can say in one sentence each when trigram versus full-text is the right tool.

- [ ] **Step 6 — JSONB: flexible metadata, indexed — and when it is the wrong answer.**
    *What this step is:* JSONB is Postgres's binary JSON column type: it lets one column hold free-form structured data (per-event extras like door policies or sponsor blurbs) without a migration per new field, and a GIN index makes containment queries over it fast. You will add it, index it, query it with `@>` (the containment operator: "does this JSON contain this JSON?") — and write down the rule for when *not* to use it.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — schema changes go through a numbered Flyway migration, never by hand.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a `metadata jsonb` column to the event table via a new Flyway migration, and have the seed generator (or a quick update) populate it with varied shapes.
    2. `CREATE INDEX ON event USING gin (metadata);` then query with containment — e.g. `WHERE metadata @> '{"all_ages": true}'` — and confirm with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` that the GIN index is used.
    3. Write the rule down where you keep your notes: anything you filter or join on *constantly* belongs in a real column with a real index, not inside JSONB — JSONB is for data whose shape varies and which you query occasionally, and reaching for it to avoid designing the schema is how databases rot.
    *You know it worked when:* the `@>` query's plan shows the GIN index, and your write-up contains the one-sentence rule for when JSONB is the wrong answer.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Drop the dead weight: unused and redundant indexes.**
    *What this step is:* Every index slows every write to its table — each `INSERT`/`UPDATE` must maintain it — and takes cache space; an index the planner never chooses is pure cost. Postgres keeps the receipts in `pg_stat_user_indexes`, whose `idx_scan` column counts how many times each index was actually used. You will find the zeros, drop them, and *measure* the write-throughput win — plus understand index bloat (dead space accumulating in an index after many updates and deletes, making it larger and slower until it is rebuilt) and the tool for it, `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` (a rebuild that does not block writes while it runs).
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — the k6 scenarios there are the realistic load that populates `idx_scan`; an index unused after that traffic is genuinely unused.
    *Do this:*
    1. Run your k6 scenarios so the counters reflect real traffic, then query `SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes ORDER BY idx_scan;` — every `idx_scan = 0` row is a candidate. Also hunt *redundant* indexes: an index on `(a)` when another on `(a, b)` exists is dead weight, because the composite already serves `a` alone (Step 2's leftmost prefix rule).
    2. Measure write throughput before — time a batch of inserts, e.g. re-run a slice of the seed — then `DROP INDEX` the unused and redundant ones and measure again. Record the gain.
    3. Write a short note explaining index bloat and when `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` is the answer: after heavy update/delete churn an index keeps its dead space; `CONCURRENTLY` rebuilds it clean without locking out writers, at the cost of taking longer.
    *You know it worked when:* at least one index is gone with a before/after write-throughput number recorded, and you can explain bloat and `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` out loud.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Save the evidence into `docs/benchmarks/plans/`.**
    *What this step is:* Every before/after plan pair from this task becomes a saved file. This is the artifact almost no candidate has — "I added indexes" is a claim; a directory of plans with latency deltas is proof, and it is what the phase's deliverable and your interview stories are built from.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — `docs/benchmarks/` is the home your baseline already lives in; plans get their own subdirectory.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/benchmarks/plans/` and save each before/after pair as plain-text files with honest names — e.g. `availability-before-seqscan.txt` / `availability-after-covering-index.txt` — covering at minimum the three queries the Done-when names.
    2. Next to each pair, note the measured latency delta and the one-line change that caused it (the index DDL).
    *You know it worked when:* `docs/benchmarks/plans/` holds a before/after pair plus latency delta for each of the three named queries that moved from seq scan to index (or index-only) scan.

**Done when:** three named queries moved from seq scan to index (or index-only) scan with recorded latency deltas, and you can read a plan unaided.


**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Walk through an `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output and name five specific things you look at, in order.
2. Why does `(org_id, starts_at, id)` serve your query when `(starts_at, org_id, id)` does not? Name the rule.
3. What makes an index-only scan possible, and which line in the plan proves you got one?
4. Estimated rows say 50, actual rows say 500,000. What is wrong, and what do you do about it?
5. Why can a normal B-tree not serve `ILIKE '%foo%'`, and what are your two alternatives?
6. Indexes make reads faster. Name two concrete costs they impose.
7. You found an index with `idx_scan = 0` after a week of load. What does that mean and what do you do?

#### Task 3.3 — Fixing ORM pathologies — 3h

**What:** Hunt down N+1 queries, over-fetching, and accidental lazy loading; introduce projections.
**Why:** Hibernate makes it trivially easy to issue 500 queries for one endpoint, and spotting that is a standard interview question.
**Solves:** endpoints whose latency scales linearly with page size.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **N+1 query** | One query to fetch 50 events, then one more per event to fetch its price tiers — 51 queries for one endpoint. Latency then grows linearly with page size, which is why it is invisible in development and fatal in production. |
| **`JOIN FETCH`** | A JPQL instruction to load the association in the same query. The most direct fix, but it interacts badly with pagination. |
| **`@EntityGraph`** | A declarative way to say which associations to load for a given query, without rewriting the JPQL. |
| **`default_batch_fetch_size`** | Tells Hibernate to load lazy associations for many parents in one `IN (...)` query. Turns 51 queries into 2 without touching any query, which is why it is the best default. |
| **Projection** | Selecting only the columns you need directly into a DTO, rather than loading whole entities and mapping afterwards. Less memory, less garbage, no lazy-loading risk. |
| **Over-fetching** | Loading twenty columns and five associations to render three fields. |
| **`LazyInitializationException`** | Thrown when you touch a lazy association after the database session has closed. The symptom of mapping outside the transaction. |
| **JDBC batching** | Sending many statements to the database in one network round trip instead of one at a time. |
| **`reWriteBatchedInserts`** | A Postgres JDBC setting that rewrites many single-row inserts into one multi-row `INSERT`. Often a several-fold throughput gain from one URL parameter. |
| **Query-count assertion** | A test that fails if an endpoint issues more queries than you allow. This is what converts N+1 from something you notice in production into something that breaks the build. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** a **query-count assertion** in CI. Spotting one N+1 is useful; making it impossible for a new one to merge is the senior move.
- **When it works you will see:** a test that fails with "expected 2 queries, got 11" when someone reintroduces lazy loading in a loop.
- **Where people get stuck:** fixing N+1 by making everything `EAGER`. That loads your entire object graph on every query — you have traded many small queries for one enormous one, which is usually worse.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Make query counts a test assertion.**
    *What this step is:* You will add a counter that records every SQL statement your application sends during a test, then write tests that *assert* on that count — "GET /events?limit=50 must issue ≤ 3 queries". This is the step that turns N+1 (one query for the list, plus one more per row — taught and seen with your own eyes in the Foundations) from something you notice in production into something that fails the build before it merges. That conversion is the professional move, and it is the single most important thing in this task.
    *Builds on:* [Task F6.11 — Relationships, lazy loading, and the N+1 problem](#task-f611--relationships-lazy-loading-and-the-n1-problem--1h) — where you counted twenty-one statements for twenty events by reading the SQL log; this step automates that counting. [Task 1.11 — The Testcontainers harness and test data builders](#task-111--the-testcontainers-harness-and-test-data-builders--1h) — the test setup that runs a real Postgres in Docker, which these tests run against. [Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline](#task-04--git-workflow-the-remote-and-a-local-ci-pipeline--2h) — `make ci` runs the test suite, so a failing query-count assertion blocks the merge, which is the whole point.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a test-scoped statement counter. Two good options: **datasource-proxy** (a library that wraps your `DataSource` and counts every statement passing through it) or **Hibernate statistics** (`hibernate.generate_statistics: true` in the test profile, then read the counts from `SessionFactory` statistics). Pick one; datasource-proxy counts *everything*, including plain JDBC, which makes it the more honest witness.
    2. Write assertions for your hottest read endpoints, starting with: GET `/events?limit=50` must issue ≤ 3 queries. The test calls the endpoint, reads the counter, and fails with the actual number if the budget is exceeded.
    3. Run `make ci` and confirm the new tests are part of it.
    *You know it worked when:* you temporarily make an association load lazily inside a mapping loop and the test fails with a message like "expected ≤ 3 queries, got 51" — then revert and it goes green again.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Break it on purpose: reproduce the N+1 at real volume.**
    *What this step is:* Before fixing N+1 three ways, you will manufacture one deliberately and watch what it costs at Phase 3 data volume. The signature: latency grows *linearly with page size* — which is precisely why N+1 is invisible in development (tiny pages, tiny data) and fatal in production.
    *Builds on:* [Task F6.11 — Relationships, lazy loading, and the N+1 problem](#task-f611--relationships-lazy-loading-and-the-n1-problem--1h) — the same bug at toy scale: twenty-one statements for twenty events. [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — the seeded 10M-row dataset that makes the cost real instead of theoretical.
    *Do this:*
    1. On an events-list endpoint, make the mapping touch a lazy association per element (for example, read each event's venue name while looping over the loaded entities). This is the mistake every codebase contains somewhere.
    2. Hit GET `/events?limit=50` and read your Step 1 counter: 51 statements — one for the list, one per row.
    3. Measure latency at `limit=10` and `limit=50` and note that it scales roughly linearly with the limit. Write the two numbers down — they are your before.
    *You know it worked when:* the counter reports 51 queries for a 50-row page and your Step 1 assertion is red.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Fix the N+1 three ways and document when each is right.**
    *What this step is:* There are three standard fixes, and a senior engineer can say when each applies: `JOIN FETCH` (a JPQL instruction to load the association in the same query), `@EntityGraph` (a declarative annotation naming which associations to load for a given repository method, without rewriting the JPQL), and `hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` (a global setting telling Hibernate to load lazy associations for many parents in one `IN (...)` query — it turns 51 queries into 2 without touching any query, which is why it is the best default). You will apply each in turn, compare, and write up the trade-offs — including the famous trap where `JOIN FETCH` meets pagination.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.3 — Fixing ORM pathologies](#task-33--fixing-orm-pathologies--3h) Step 2 of this task — the deliberately broken endpoint and its before numbers.
    *Do this:*
    1. Fix one: a `@Query` with `join fetch` on the association. Counter should read 1. Note the catch before moving on: combine `JOIN FETCH` on a collection with `Pageable` and Hibernate logs its in-memory-pagination warning (`HHH000104`, "firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory") — the join multiplies rows, so Hibernate cannot ask the database for "page 2" and instead fetches *everything* and paginates in Java. The actual danger: a request for 50 rows quietly loads the whole table into memory. What to do instead: two queries — page the parent *ids* first, then fetch associations for just those ids — or use one of the next two fixes.
    2. Fix two: revert, then `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = ...)` on the repository method. Same count check. This shines when the *same* query needs different loading shapes in different use cases.
    3. Fix three: revert, then set `hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` in configuration and watch the counter read 2 — one query for the page, one `IN (...)` for all the venues at once. No query was touched, and pagination works correctly, which is why this is the best default.
    4. Document in your notes when each is right: batch size as the safe global default; `@EntityGraph` for per-use-case loading; `JOIN FETCH` for single-object or non-paginated fetches — never under pagination.
    *You know it worked when:* all three variants turn the Step 1 assertion green, and your write-up answers "why does `JOIN FETCH` plus pagination warn, and what do you do instead?" in your own words.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Replace entity loading with DTO projections on read-heavy endpoints.**
    *What this step is:* Loading a full entity to render three fields is over-fetching — twenty columns and five associations hydrated, tracked by the persistence context, then thrown away after mapping. A *projection* selects only the needed columns straight into a DTO (a plain data-carrying record): less memory, less garbage for the JVM to collect, and no lazy associations left to trip over. You will convert your read-heavy endpoints and measure the difference.
    *Builds on:* [Task F5.10 — Java talks to Postgres: raw JDBC and JdbcClient](#task-f510--java-talks-to-postgres-raw-jdbc-and-jdbcclient--1h) — `JdbcClient`, Spring's thin SQL wrapper, is one of the projection options here and the reason this project keeps plain SQL for hot paths. [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — the k6 scenarios you re-run to measure the latency difference.
    *Do this:*
    1. Pick your read-heavy endpoints (event search and event detail are the obvious ones) and replace entity loading with one of: a Spring Data *interface projection* (a small interface whose getters name the columns), a *constructor projection* (JPQL `select new ...` into a record), or `JdbcClient` with a row mapper for full SQL control.
    2. Measure the difference, before and after: latency via the matching [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) k6 scenario, and allocation via the simplest honest proxy — Hibernate statistics' entity-load count for the endpoint drops to zero, because no entities are hydrated at all.
    3. Record both deltas in your notes; keep entities for the *write* paths, where their behaviour and optimistic locking earn their cost.
    *You know it worked when:* the endpoint returns the same JSON as before, the entity-load count for it is zero, and a latency delta is written down.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Write-path batching: many rows, one round trip.**
    *What this step is:* By default Hibernate sends one `INSERT` per row — one network round trip each. JDBC batching groups many statements into one round trip, and `reWriteBatchedInserts=true` (a Postgres JDBC driver setting, switched on in the connection URL) goes further by rewriting the batch into a single multi-row `INSERT` — often a several-fold throughput gain from one URL parameter. You will switch it all on and prove the gain with a benchmark.
    *Do this:*
    1. In configuration set `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size` (a few dozen is typical), plus `hibernate.order_inserts: true` and `hibernate.order_updates: true` — Hibernate can only batch *consecutive identical* statements, and ordering groups them so batches actually form.
    2. Append `reWriteBatchedInserts=true` to the JDBC URL (`jdbc:postgresql://...?reWriteBatchedInserts=true`).
    3. Benchmark 10k inserts before and after — a small test or a `tools/seed` slice both work; same data, same machine, only the settings changed. Expect a large multiple, and record both numbers.
    *You know it worked when:* the before/after throughput for 10k inserts is documented and the after is a multiple of the before.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Kill lazy-loading surprises for good.**
    *What this step is:* A `LazyInitializationException` is thrown when code touches a lazy association after the database session has closed — the symptom of mapping entities to responses *outside* the transaction. The project already made the deliberate choice that exposes this early: `spring.jpa.open-in-view: false` (on, this Spring default keeps the session open through JSON rendering, silently firing queries during serialisation and hiding the bug). This step verifies the setting still holds and that no such exception can escape anywhere.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — where `spring.jpa.open-in-view: false` was set (the "already set" this bullet refers to). [Task F6.11 — Relationships, lazy loading, and the N+1 problem](#task-f611--relationships-lazy-loading-and-the-n1-problem--1h) — where you triggered the exception on purpose and adopted the project rule this step enforces: map entities to response records *inside* the transactional service method; controllers receive records, never entities.
    *Do this:*
    1. Confirm `spring.jpa.open-in-view: false` is still in the configuration — and keep it that way; convenience that hides work is the worst kind.
    2. Audit the read paths: no controller returns or touches an entity, every entity→DTO mapping happens inside the `@Transactional` service method. Steps 4's projections already removed most of the risk — this closes the rest.
    3. Exercise everything — the full test suite plus a k6 run over the endpoints — and search the logs for `LazyInitializationException`.
    *You know it worked when:* zero `LazyInitializationException` anywhere in test and load-run logs, with `open-in-view` still `false`.

- [ ] **Step 7 — `[stretch]` Introduce jOOQ for the two most complex reporting queries.**
    *What this step is:* Optional stretch goal. jOOQ is a library that generates Java classes from your database schema so you write SQL *as type-checked Java code* — a renamed column becomes a compile error instead of a runtime surprise. You will port your two gnarliest reporting queries to it and write down the honest trade-off against the simpler tool you already know.
    *Builds on:* [Task F5.10 — Java talks to Postgres: raw JDBC and JdbcClient](#task-f510--java-talks-to-postgres-raw-jdbc-and-jdbcclient--1h) — `JdbcClient`, the SQL-in-a-string approach jOOQ is being compared against.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add jOOQ with its code generator pointed at your Flyway-managed schema, and port the two most complex reporting queries (the ones with the most joins and aggregates).
    2. Verify both return results identical to the originals.
    3. Note the trade-off versus `JdbcClient` in your notes: jOOQ buys compile-time safety against schema drift and composable query-building, at the cost of a code-generation step and a build dependency; `JdbcClient` stays simpler and keeps the SQL literal. For two queries the honest answer may be "not worth it" — writing that down is the point.
    *You know it worked when:* both jOOQ queries return the same results as the SQL versions, and the trade-off note exists.

**Done when:** query-count assertions guard your three hottest endpoints, and batch insert throughput is documented before/after.


**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. What is an N+1 query, and how would you spot one with no tooling at all?
2. Three ways to fix N+1. Describe each and say when it is the right choice.
3. Why does `JOIN FETCH` combined with pagination produce an in-memory-pagination warning, and what is the actual danger?
4. What does a DTO projection avoid that loading the entity and mapping it does not?
5. What does `reWriteBatchedInserts=true` change about what is sent over the wire?
6. Your query-count assertion fails after a refactor that "changed nothing". Why is that test earning its keep?

#### Task 3.4 — Transactions, MVCC, locking, and connection pooling — 6h

**What:** Isolation levels, MVCC (the mechanism Postgres actually isolates with), write skew and what SERIALIZABLE actually does about it, pessimistic vs optimistic locking, deadlocks, `@Transactional` propagation made observable, and HikariCP sizing.
**Why:** The reservation engine in [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) depends entirely on this, and "explain isolation levels", "why don't readers block writers?", "name an anomaly REPEATABLE READ still allows" and "how do you prevent lost updates" are top-5 interview questions.
**Solves:** lost updates, phantom oversell, write skew that nobody notices until an invariant is broken in production, audit rows that vanish with the very rollback they were supposed to record, deadlocks under load, pool exhaustion, and tables that stay huge after you delete half their rows.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **ACID** | Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Isolation is the one with levels and the one that causes arguments. |
| **Lost update** | Two transactions read 10, both add 1, both write 11. One update vanished. This is the oversell bug in miniature, which is why [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) depends on this task. |
| **Non-repeatable read** | Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values, because someone committed in between. |
| **Phantom read** | Re-running the same query in one transaction and finding *new rows* that were not there before. |
| **READ COMMITTED** | Postgres's default. You only see committed data — but it does **not** prevent lost updates, and assuming it does is a very common and very expensive mistake. |
| **REPEATABLE READ** | Your transaction sees a consistent snapshot from its start. In Postgres this also prevents phantoms. |
| **SERIALIZABLE** | Behaves as if transactions ran one after another. Strongest and slowest; it can abort your transaction, so you must be prepared to retry. |
| **MVCC** | Multi-Version Concurrency Control — *the* mechanism behind everything else in this table. Postgres never changes a row in place: an `UPDATE` writes a **new version** of the row and marks the old one as expired, and each transaction reads whichever version was current when its snapshot was taken. This is why readers never block writers and writers never block readers — they are not touching the same physical thing. Ask an interviewer's favourite question of yourself now: "why don't readers block writers in Postgres?" — the answer is this row. |
| **Row version / `xmin`, `xmax`** | Every Postgres row carries two hidden columns you can actually select: `xmin` (the transaction that created this version) and `xmax` (the one that expired it, if any). They are the version bookkeeping of MVCC made visible — `SELECT xmin, xmax, * FROM seat` works on any table, and watching `xmin` change after an `UPDATE` is the fastest way to believe that updates write new rows. |
| **Dead tuple** | An expired row version that no transaction can see any more. It does not vanish — it sits in the table taking space until VACUUM reclaims it. A table whose rows are updated all day ([Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline)'s `seat_hold` table will flip statuses all day) manufactures dead tuples continuously. This is also where [Task 3.2 — Index design and reading query plans](#task-32--index-design-and-reading-query-plans--4h)'s "index bloat" actually comes from. |
| **VACUUM** | The cleanup command that marks dead tuples' space as reusable. Plain `VACUUM` runs alongside normal traffic but does **not** shrink the file on disk — the space is recycled internally. `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the whole table and *does* give the disk back, but takes an exclusive lock for the duration, which is why you almost never run it on a live table. |
| **autovacuum** | The background process that runs VACUUM for you when a table accumulates enough dead tuples. Usually invisible; the classic production incident is an update-heavy table where autovacuum falls behind and the table quietly triples in size. It also protects against transaction-ID wraparound — a rare, fatal condition where the 32-bit transaction counter would overflow; you only need one sentence on it, but that sentence marks you as someone who has read about real Postgres operations. |
| **Bloat** | The accumulated dead space in a table or index after heavy updates and deletes. The symptom: row count unchanged, disk size tripled, cache full of garbage. The cure: VACUUM keeps it bounded; `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` ([Task 3.2 — Index design and reading query plans](#task-32--index-design-and-reading-query-plans--4h), where you learned to rebuild an index without blocking writes) rebuilds a bloated index. |
| **Visibility map** | Postgres's per-page record of "every row version here is visible to everyone". VACUUM maintains it — and it is the quiet reason the `Heap Fetches: 0` index-only scan from [Task 3.2 — Index design and reading query plans](#task-32--index-design-and-reading-query-plans--4h) — the covering-index exercise where the planner skipped the table entirely — was possible at all: the planner may skip the table only for pages the map vouches for. |
| **Optimistic locking** | Assume conflicts are rare: check a version on write and fail if it moved. Best when contention is low. |
| **Pessimistic locking** | Assume conflicts are likely: take the lock up front with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. Best when contention is high and retries would thrash. |
| **`SKIP LOCKED`** | "Give me rows nobody else has locked, and do not wait." The key to multiple workers consuming one queue table without blocking or duplicating. |
| **Deadlock** | Two transactions each holding what the other needs. The database kills one. The general fix is always the same: acquire locks in a consistent order. |
| **Self-invocation** | Calling a `@Transactional` method from another method in the same class. The annotation does nothing, because Spring's proxy was bypassed entirely. Catches almost everyone once. |
| **Pool exhaustion** | Every connection is checked out, so new requests queue and then time out. Usually caused by long transactions, not by too small a pool. |
| **`statement_timeout`** | Postgres kills any query running longer than this. Your last line of defence against one bad query holding resources indefinitely. |
| **`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`** | Kills connections that opened a transaction and then went quiet — which otherwise hold locks forever. |
| **Write skew** | The anomaly `REPEATABLE READ` still allows. Two transactions each **read the same data**, each **write something different** based on what they read, both commit cleanly — and the combined result breaks a rule that neither transaction broke on its own. The classic: two cleanup jobs each check "at least one active hold remains", each expires a *different* hold, and together they expire both. No row was written by both, so no lock ever fired — the snapshots were each telling the truth. |
| **SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation)** | How Postgres `SERIALIZABLE` actually works. It does not take more locks and it does not make transactions queue: it lets both run optimistically on their snapshots, watches for dangerous read-write patterns between them, and **aborts one at commit time** with a `serialization_failure`. The consequence lands on you — code that runs under `SERIALIZABLE` must be written to retry. |
| **SQLSTATE `40001`** | The error code of that abort (`serialization_failure`). Seeing 40001 means "nothing is broken — run the transaction again". A bounded retry loop around the transaction is the standard, expected response, not a workaround. |
| **Propagation** | The rule a `@Transactional` method uses to decide what to do about a transaction that may already be open in its caller: join it, suspend it and start a fresh one of its own, or refuse to run without one. Until now this attribute has existed in the plan only as a word — this task makes each behaviour observable with row counts. |
| **`REQUIRED`** | The default propagation: join the caller's transaction if there is one, otherwise start a new one. Everything inside lives and dies with that single transaction — if the outer method rolls back, the inner method's writes vanish with it. |
| **`REQUIRES_NEW`** | Suspend the caller's transaction and open a brand-new one that commits or rolls back **independently**. The audit-log propagation: the audit row must survive even when the business transaction around it is rolled back. |
| **`MANDATORY`** | "I refuse to run outside a transaction." If no transaction is open when the method is called, Spring throws immediately instead of letting the method silently run in autocommit. A guard-rail for methods that must never do half a job. |
| **`rollbackFor`** | The attribute that fixes the rule [Task F6.10 — Spring Data JPA: repositories, transactions, and the persistence context](#task-f610--spring-data-jpa-repositories-transactions-and-the-persistence-context--1h) taught you: by default Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions and **commits** on checked ones. `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)` makes checked exceptions roll back too — the explicit fix for methods where a checked failure means the work must not stand. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** two things. Causing a **deadlock on purpose**, reading it in the Postgres log, and understanding the lock-ordering rule that prevents it — very few candidates have done this deliberately. And being able to say **why readers never block writers** (MVCC): it is the mechanism underneath every isolation behaviour you reproduce in this task, and the follow-up question behind most of the others.
- **When it works you will see:** two transactions deadlocking, Postgres killing one, and you finding the exact statements in the log; and, in the bloat lab, a table tripling in size under updates while its row count never changes — then autovacuum quietly cleaning up after you switch it back on.
- **Where people get stuck:** sizing the connection pool by guesswork, or large. A bigger pool is frequently *slower* — more connections contend for the same CPUs and disks. You should be able to defend your number with a measurement.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Reproduce the three classic anomalies yourself.**
    *What this step is:* An *anomaly* is a way two simultaneous transactions can interfere and produce a result neither of them intended. Before you trust any isolation level, you make each anomaly happen with your own hands: the lost update, the non-repeatable read, and the phantom read. Each test uses **two separate database connections**, because every anomaly here is two transactions interleaving — something a single connection can never show you. At the end you will have three passing tests and a written table of which Postgres isolation level prevents which anomaly.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.11 — The Testcontainers harness and test data builders](#task-111--the-testcontainers-harness-and-test-data-builders--1h) — the harness that gives every integration test a real Postgres in Docker; [Task F5.8 — Transactions, ACID, and isolation](#task-f58--transactions-acid-and-isolation--15h) — where you first ran `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` by hand and met the isolation level names.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create an integration test class (e.g. `IsolationAnomalyTest`) that opens **two raw JDBC connections** to the same Testcontainers Postgres and sets `setAutoCommit(false)` on both — each connection is now one transaction you control by hand.
    2. **Lost update:** seed a row with the value 10. On both connections: `SELECT` the value (both read 10), add 1 in Java, `UPDATE` it to 11, commit both. Assert the final value is **11, not 12** — one increment silently vanished, and READ COMMITTED (the default) did nothing to stop it. Then rerun with both transactions at `REPEATABLE READ` and watch Postgres abort the second `UPDATE` with a serialization error — that is the level that refuses to lose the update.
    3. **Non-repeatable read:** connection 1 begins and `SELECT`s a row; connection 2 updates that row and commits; connection 1 `SELECT`s the same row again. Under READ COMMITTED the value changed mid-transaction. Rerun with connection 1 under `REPEATABLE READ` — the value stays the same.
    4. **Phantom read:** connection 1 runs `SELECT count(*) ... WHERE ...`; connection 2 inserts a new matching row and commits; connection 1 reruns the exact same query. Under READ COMMITTED the new row appears out of nowhere; under `REPEATABLE READ` in Postgres it does not (Postgres is stricter here than the SQL standard requires).
    5. Prove the default: run `SHOW default_transaction_isolation;` and record that it prints `read committed` — Postgres's default is READ COMMITTED, **not** READ UNCOMMITTED. (If you ask Postgres for READ UNCOMMITTED it quietly gives you READ COMMITTED anyway — it does not implement dirty reads at all.)
    6. Write the summary as a small table — one row per anomaly, one column per isolation level, prevented yes/no.
    *You know it worked when:* all three tests pass, each shows the anomaly happening at one isolation level and not happening at a stricter one, and you have the `read committed` output and the summary table saved.

- [ ] **Step 2 — See the mechanism behind it: MVCC.**
    *What this step is:* You just watched anomalies; now you watch the machinery that decides what each transaction sees. MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) means Postgres never changes a row in place — an `UPDATE` writes a **new version** of the row, and every transaction keeps reading whichever version was current when its snapshot was taken. You will watch a reader and a writer work on "the same row" at the same moment without either one waiting, then look at the hidden version-bookkeeping columns with your own eyes. At the end you will own the answer to a top-tier interview question instead of having memorised it.
    *Builds on:* [Task F5.8 — Transactions, ACID, and isolation](#task-f58--transactions-acid-and-isolation--15h) — running transactions by hand in `psql`; [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — which seeded the `seat` table you will poke at here.
    *Do this:*
    1. Open two `psql` sessions against your compose Postgres (run `docker compose exec postgres psql -U <user> <db>` in two terminals).
    2. Session 1: `BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;` then `SELECT` one seat row by id.
    3. Session 2: `UPDATE` that exact row and commit — and note that the `UPDATE` returned immediately. **It never waited for session 1.**
    4. Back in session 1: `SELECT` the row again — still the old value. You have just watched a reader and a writer work on "the same row" without blocking each other, because they were never on the same physical thing: the `UPDATE` wrote a new row version, and your snapshot kept reading the old one.
    5. Make the invisible visible: run `SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, * FROM seat WHERE id = ...` before and after an update (`xmin` = the transaction that created this row version, `xmax` = the one that expired it, `ctid` = where it physically sits). Watch the bookkeeping change after the update — proof that the update wrote a *new* row rather than editing the old one.
    6. Close the loop in one written sentence in your own words: *readers do not block writers (and vice versa) because every transaction reads its own snapshot of row versions.*
    *You know it worked when:* session 2's `UPDATE` returned without waiting, session 1 kept seeing the old value until its transaction ended, you watched `xmin` change across an update, and your one-sentence explanation is written down.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Pay MVCC's bill: the bloat lab.**
    *What this step is:* Those old row versions from Step 2 do not vanish — they become **dead tuples** (expired row versions no transaction can see any more) that sit in the table taking space until VACUUM reclaims them. This step makes you manufacture bloat deliberately, measure it, clean it up, and understand who normally does that for you. At the end you will have before/after size numbers recorded and a working mental model of VACUUM, `VACUUM FULL`, and autovacuum.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.2 — Index design and reading query plans](#task-32--index-design-and-reading-query-plans--4h) — where you met index bloat and the `Heap Fetches: 0` index-only scan, both of which this step finally explains; [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — which created `docs/benchmarks/`, where you will record the numbers; [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) — whose real `seat_hold` table will flip statuses all day and behave exactly like this lab.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create a scratch table `hold_lab(id uuid primary key, event_id uuid, status text)` and fill it with ~100k rows (a quick `INSERT ... SELECT` over `generate_series` is fine).
    2. Turn off the automatic cleaner for this one table so you can watch the mess accumulate: `ALTER TABLE hold_lab SET (autovacuum_enabled = false);`
    3. Record the starting size: `SELECT pg_total_relation_size('hold_lab');`
    4. `UPDATE` **all** rows three times (e.g. flip `status` back and forth). Each update writes a full new version of every row.
    5. Check `pg_stat_user_tables` for `hold_lab`: `n_dead_tup` has exploded, and `pg_total_relation_size` shows the table is roughly **triple** its starting size — while `SELECT count(*)` is completely unchanged. Same rows, three times the disk.
    6. Run plain `VACUUM hold_lab;` and measure again: the dead space is now *reusable* but the file on disk did **not** shrink — Postgres recycles the space internally rather than giving it back. Understand why that is usually fine: future updates reuse the holes instead of growing the file.
    7. Write one note on what `VACUUM FULL` would do instead — rewrite the whole table and actually shrink the file — and what it costs: an exclusive lock for the whole duration, which is why you almost never run it on a live table.
    8. Re-enable autovacuum (`ALTER TABLE hold_lab SET (autovacuum_enabled = true);`), run the update churn again gently, and watch autovacuum take over the cleanup without you.
    9. Connect it to what you already know, in three written sentences: this dead-tuple churn is where the index bloat from [Task 3.2 — Index design and reading query plans](#task-32--index-design-and-reading-query-plans--4h) actually comes from; it is why [Task 3.5 — Partitioning, read replicas, and zero-downtime migrations](#task-35--partitioning-read-replicas-and-zero-downtime-migrations--6h) deletes history by detaching whole partitions instead of running a mass `DELETE` (a mass delete just manufactures millions of dead tuples); and the **visibility map** VACUUM maintains (the per-page record of "every row version here is visible to everyone") is what made your `Heap Fetches: 0` index-only scan possible at all.
    10. Record the before/after table sizes in `docs/benchmarks/`.
    *You know it worked when:* you have a saved before/after size comparison showing the table roughly tripling under updates with its row count unchanged, then recovering reusable space after `VACUUM`, and your three connect-the-dots sentences are written down.

- [ ] **Step 4 — The fourth anomaly: write skew.**
    *What this step is:* The lost update and non-repeatable read were fights over a single row, and even the phantom was one transaction writing rows the other's query could see. Write skew is sneakier: two transactions each **read the same data**, each **write something different** based on what they read — no single row is touched by both — and both commit cleanly, jointly breaking a rule neither broke alone. This is the anomaly `REPEATABLE READ` *cannot* stop, and you will reproduce it by hand. At the end you will have watched a business invariant break with no error, no block, and no lock fired.
    *Builds on:* Step 3's `hold_lab` scratch table — you stage the anomaly on it; [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) — which builds a hold-cleanup job exactly like the one you are about to simulate.
    *Do this:*
    1. On `hold_lab`, set up exactly **2 active holds** for one event, and adopt the business rule: *"at least one active hold must remain for this event."*
    2. Open two `psql` sessions. In **both**, run `BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;`
    3. In each session, count the active holds for that event. Both see 2 — so both conclude it is safe to expire one.
    4. Session 1 expires hold A (`UPDATE ... SET status = 'expired' WHERE id = <A>`); session 2 expires hold B. Both commit. No block, no error — and **zero** active holds remain. The rule is broken, and neither transaction broke it alone.
    5. Write down *why* nothing fired: each session wrote a row the other never touched, so no row lock ever collided; and each snapshot honestly showed 2 active holds — it was telling the truth at the moment it was taken. This is MVCC from Step 2 working **exactly as designed**, which is what makes write skew so dangerous.
    *You know it worked when:* starting from 2 active holds and a "keep at least one" rule, both REPEATABLE READ transactions committed without any error and the active count is 0 — and you can explain in one breath why no lock and no snapshot caught it.

- [ ] **Step 5 — SERIALIZABLE aborts; your code must retry.**
    *What this step is:* Now you run the identical write-skew dance under `SERIALIZABLE` and watch Postgres catch it — not by blocking, but by **aborting one transaction at commit time**. That is SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation): both transactions run optimistically on their snapshots, Postgres watches for dangerous read-write patterns between them, and cancels one at the finish line. The bill lands on your code — anything running under SERIALIZABLE must be written to retry. At the end you will have a Java retry loop and a 20-attempt concurrency test proving the invariant holds.
    *Builds on:* Step 4's write-skew setup on `hold_lab` — you rerun the exact same two-session dance, only the isolation level changes.
    *Do this:*
    1. Reset `hold_lab` to 2 active holds. Rerun Step 4's two sessions, but both now begin with `BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;`
    2. Observe: neither session blocks while working — but at commit, Postgres aborts one with `ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`, SQLSTATE `40001`. Read that code as "nothing is broken — run the transaction again."
    3. Write a **bounded retry loop in Java** around the transaction: catch the serialization failure (SQLSTATE `40001` / Spring's serialization-failure exception), back off briefly **with jitter** — a small random extra delay, so two retriers that collided once do not retry in lockstep and collide again — and re-run the *whole* transaction from the top, up to a fixed maximum number of attempts.
    4. Write a test that hammers the "at least one active hold remains" rule with **20 concurrent attempts** through that retry loop, and assert two things: the invariant holds at the end, and every aborted attempt either eventually succeeds or gives up cleanly after its bounded retries — no attempt hangs, none errors out uncaught.
    5. Close with one sentence in your own words: *Postgres SERIALIZABLE does not block — it aborts, and code that uses it must retry.*
    *You know it worked when:* you have seen the `40001` abort in `psql`, the 20-attempt concurrency test passes with the invariant intact, and your closing sentence is written down.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Optimistic locking with @Version and retries.**
    *What this step is:* Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: every row carries a version number, every write says "update where version = what I read", and if someone else got there first the write fails instead of silently overwriting. JPA does this for you with the `@Version` annotation. Your job is to handle the failure properly — retry a bounded number of times, then give the client an honest `409 Conflict`. At the end you will have an endpoint that survives concurrent edits without losing either one silently.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — where you added the `@Version` column to your entities; [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h) — where the same idea appeared at the HTTP layer as `If-Match`/412.
    *Do this:*
    1. Pick an update path on a `@Version`-carrying entity and write a two-thread test that makes both threads read the same entity, modify it, and save — one save succeeds, the other throws `OptimisticLockingFailureException`.
    2. Handle it with a **bounded retry**: either `@Retryable` (note: that annotation comes from the separate **spring-retry** library, not Spring core — you must add the dependency) or simply a manual loop with jitter, re-reading the entity fresh on each attempt.
    3. After the retries are exhausted, return HTTP **409** to the caller — a truthful "someone else changed this; your edit did not apply" — never a silent overwrite and never a 500.
    *You know it worked when:* the concurrent-edit test shows one winner, the loser retrying, and — when you force every retry to collide — a clean 409 response after exhaustion.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Pessimistic locking and the SKIP LOCKED queue.**
    *What this step is:* Pessimistic locking is the opposite bet: conflicts are *likely*, so take the lock up front with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and make everyone else wait. The star of this step is the variant `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` — "give me rows nobody else has locked, and do not wait" — which is the key to several workers consuming one queue table without blocking or duplicating each other. At the end you will have a multi-threaded test proving exactly that.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.11 — The Testcontainers harness and test data builders](#task-111--the-testcontainers-harness-and-test-data-builders--1h) — the real-Postgres test harness this concurrency test needs (an in-memory database would not lock like Postgres does).
    *Do this:*
    1. First feel plain `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`: lock a row in one `psql` session, try to lock it in a second, and watch the second session *hang* until the first commits. That hang is the cost of pessimism.
    2. Create a small work-queue table (id, payload, a `claimed_by` column) and seed it with jobs.
    3. Write the consumer query: `SELECT ... FROM work_queue ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1` — each worker grabs an unclaimed, unlocked row; rows locked by other workers are silently skipped instead of waited on.
    4. Write a test with **20 threads** consuming that work table concurrently, asserting: every job is processed **exactly once** (no duplicates) and no thread ever blocks waiting on another.
    *You know it worked when:* the 20-thread test passes — total processed count equals the number of seeded jobs, no job appears twice, and the test completes without lock-wait stalls.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Break it on purpose: cause a deadlock.**
    *What this step is:* A deadlock is two transactions each holding a lock the other needs — neither can ever proceed, so Postgres kills one. Very few candidates have caused one *deliberately*, read the database's own account of it, and fixed it. You will do all three. At the end you will have a written postmortem, which is a genuinely great interview story.
    *Builds on:* Step 7 — you now know what it feels like when a transaction waits on a row lock; a deadlock is two of those waits pointing at each other.
    *Do this:*
    1. Open two `psql` sessions and two rows (A and B). Session 1: `BEGIN;` then `UPDATE` row A. Session 2: `BEGIN;` then `UPDATE` row B. Now session 1 updates row B (it waits — session 2 holds it), and session 2 updates row A (it would wait on session 1 — the circle is closed).
    2. Within about a second, Postgres detects the cycle and kills one session with `ERROR: deadlock detected`. The other proceeds.
    3. Read the deadlock report in the Postgres log (`docker compose logs postgres`, or the log file): it names both processes, both locks, and **the exact statements** that collided. Find yours.
    4. Fix it the way it is always fixed: make every transaction acquire its locks **in a consistent order** (e.g. always lock the lower id first). Rerun the dance in that order and observe plain waiting instead of a deadlock.
    5. Document the whole thing — what the two transactions were doing, what the log said, the lock-ordering rule that fixed it — as a short postmortem. This is a great interview story; write it like one.
    *You know it worked when:* you have the `deadlock detected` error on your screen, the matching entry found in the Postgres log, and the postmortem written — and the re-ordered version of the same workload no longer deadlocks.

- [ ] **Step 9 — The @Transactional traps that catch everyone.**
    *What this step is:* Four well-known ways `@Transactional` quietly does not do what you think. You will prove the worst one with a test (self-invocation — the annotation silently doing *nothing*), and write down the other three as working knowledge. At the end you will have a failing-then-passing test and three documented rules.
    *Builds on:* [Task F6.10 — Spring Data JPA: repositories, transactions, and the persistence context](#task-f610--spring-data-jpa-repositories-transactions-and-the-persistence-context--1h) — where you first met Spring's proxy-based transactions and the self-invocation trap in theory.
    *Do this:*
    1. **Self-invocation, proven:** in one service class, have public method `a()` (not annotated) call `this.b()` where `b()` is `@Transactional`. Write a test showing no transaction is active inside `b()` (e.g. `TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive()` returns false, or a forced rollback that fails to roll anything back). The reason: Spring wraps your bean in a proxy, and `this.b()` bypasses the proxy entirely — the annotation never runs. Move `b()` to a separate bean and watch the same test pass.
    2. **`readOnly = true`:** mark your pure-read service methods with it and note the benefits you get: Hibernate skips dirty-checking (cheaper), and — crucially for [Task 3.5 — Partitioning, read replicas, and zero-downtime migrations](#task-35--partitioning-read-replicas-and-zero-downtime-migrations--6h) — it is the exact flag replica routing will key on.
    3. **`REQUIRES_NEW` for audit writes:** note the one legitimate everyday use — an audit row that must survive even when the business transaction around it rolls back. You will *prove* this with row counts in Step 10.
    4. **Never call a remote service inside a transaction:** write down the rule and the reason — the transaction holds its locks and its pooled connection for the entire remote call, so one slow downstream service makes you hold-the-lock-over-the-network and starves everyone else. Audit your own code for violations.
    *You know it worked when:* the self-invocation test fails inside the same class and passes from a separate bean, and the three written rules (readOnly, REQUIRES_NEW-for-audit, no-remote-calls-in-transactions) are in your notes with one-line justifications.

- [ ] **Step 10 — Make propagation observable: the two-method experiment.**
