#### Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling — 4h

**What:** Spring Kafka producers and consumers with retries, backoff, DLQ, and idempotent processing.
**Why:** The happy path takes 20 minutes; everything that matters is in the failure path, which is also what gets asked about.
**Solves:** poison-pill messages that block a partition forever, infinite retry loops, and duplicate side effects.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Manual acknowledgement** | Committing the offset yourself, after the work succeeded. With auto-commit, Kafka may record a message as processed while your handler is still running — or has already failed. |
| **Poison pill** | A message that fails every time it is processed, often because it cannot even be deserialised. Without special handling the consumer retries it forever and that partition stops dead. |
| **`ErrorHandlingDeserializer`** | Wraps deserialisation so a malformed record becomes a handled error rather than an exception that kills the container and starts the poison-pill loop. |
| **Retryable vs non-retryable** | Timeouts, 5xx and deadlocks may succeed on a second attempt. Validation failures and business rejections never will. Retrying the second kind just wastes time and delays the alert. |
| **Blocking retry** | Retrying inside the listener with a sleep. Simple, but it stalls the whole partition behind the failing message — everything else waits for one bad record. |
| **Non-blocking retry** | `@RetryableTopic` republishes the failure to `-retry-1s`, `-retry-10s`, `-retry-1m` topics, so the main partition keeps flowing. The cost is that the retried message is now out of order relative to its siblings, which is unacceptable for some workloads. |
| **DLQ** | Dead-letter queue — where a message goes after retries are exhausted, so a human can inspect and replay it. A DLQ with no alert and no replay tool is just a bin. |
| **Idempotent consumer** | A `processed_event(consumer_group, event_id)` table with a unique constraint, written inside the processing transaction. This is what makes at-least-once delivery safe, and it is required regardless of broker guarantees. |
| **Consumer concurrency** | How many threads a listener runs. Useful up to the partition count and pointless beyond it, since a partition is only ever assigned to one thread. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** the **DLQ**, and that consumers must be idempotent because at-least-once delivery means duplicates are not an edge case but a certainty.
- **When it works you will see:** a poison message landing in the DLQ without stalling its partition, and the same event replayed twenty times producing exactly one side effect.
- **Where people get stuck:** infinite retry on a message that can never succeed. It blocks the partition forever and everything behind it stops. Bounded retries plus a DLQ is the only sane default.

The cost: the retried message is now out of order relative to its partition siblings.
    *Builds on:* [Task 6.1 — Kafka fundamentals, hands-on](#task-61--kafka-fundamentals-hands-on--3h) — a partition is the ordered lane; one stuck record blocks everything behind it. [Task 6.2 — Event contract design and schema evolution](#task-62--event-contract-design-and-schema-evolution--2h) — the topic naming convention these retry topics extend.
    *Do this:*
    1. Annotate the listener with `@RetryableTopic`, configured for backoff delays of 1 s, 10 s and 1 m with suffixes that produce `zenith.orders.v1.order-placed-retry-1s`, `-retry-10s`, `-retry-1m`, and a dead-letter suffix producing `zenith.orders.v1.order-placed.dlq`. Exclude the Step 3 non-retryable exceptions so they go straight to the `.dlq`.
    2. List topics with the [Task 6.1 — Kafka fundamentals, hands-on](#task-61--kafka-fundamentals-hands-on--3h) CLI and confirm the retry and DLQ topics were created.

Write both costs into `docs/kafka-notes.md`: blocking retries stall the whole partition behind one bad record; non-blocking retries sacrifice ordering — and name a workload where that loss is unacceptable (for example, a retried `order-placed` must never be processed after the same order's `order-cancelled`), which is when you accept blocking retries or design the consumer to tolerate reordering.

The consumer-side fix is a `processed_event(consumer_group, event_id)` table with a unique constraint, checked and inserted **inside the processing transaction**: a duplicate then fails the insert and becomes a harmless no-op. You will prove it by replaying one event 20 times and asserting exactly one side effect.

[Task 5.5 — Transactional outbox](#task-55--transactional-outbox--3h) — where you learned that at-least-once is the deal and consumers must cope, and where sleeps died: an eventual assertion uses Awaitility with a deadline, never a sleep.     *What this step is:* A record the consumer cannot even deserialise fails *before* your listener code runs, so none of your error handling sees it — the container throws, restarts, meets the same record again, and the partition stops dead. That is the poison-pill loop. You will cause it deliberately, then fix it, so you recognise both halves forever.
    *Builds on:* [Task 6.1 — Kafka fundamentals, hands-on](#task-61--kafka-fundamentals-hands-on--3h) — the console producer you will use to write garbage onto a real topic.
    *Do this:*
    1. First, the break: with the plain Avro deserializer configured, use the [Task 6.1 — Kafka fundamentals, hands-on](#task-61--kafka-fundamentals-hands-on--3h) console producer to write `this-is-not-avro` onto `zenith.orders.v1.order-placed`. Watch the log: the same deserialization exception repeats endlessly, the partition's lag stops falling, and no later record gets through — an infinite poison-pill loop.
    2. Now the fix: wrap the deserializer in `ErrorHandlingDeserializer` — set the consumer's value deserializer to it, with `spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class` pointing at the real Avro deserializer. A malformed record now becomes a handled `DeserializationException` instead of a container-killing crash — and deserialization failures are on your Step 3 non-retryable list, so the record is recovered to the DLQ.
    3. Repeat the garbage write: the bad record lands in the `.dlq`, and the next good record processes normally.
    *You know it worked when:* the same garbage record that froze the partition now lands in the DLQ while consumption continues behind it.

    *Builds on:* [Task 6.2 — Event contract design and schema evolution](#task-62--event-contract-design-and-schema-evolution--2h) — headers: when Spring Kafka dead-letters a record, it stamps the original topic, partition, offset, and the exception message into the record's headers, which is exactly what `inspect` reads and `replay` routes by.

    1.     2. Expose a `kafka_dlq_depth` gauge through Micrometer — the metrics library Spring Boot ships; dashboards for it arrive in [Task 11.2 — Metrics that answer real questions](#task-112--metrics-that-answer-real-questions--3h), but the number is already useful in tests and logs today. Compute it from the DLQ topic's end offsets minus an inspection group's committed offsets.

[Task 11.4 — SLOs, alerting, and runbooks](#task-114--slos-alerting-and-runbooks--2h) wires every entry in that file — you are leaving future-you a shopping list, not skipping the alert.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Consumer concurrency: the partition count is the ceiling.**
    *What this step is:* A listener's `concurrency` setting is how many consumer threads it runs. Each thread owns whole partitions, so setting concurrency above the partition count buys nothing — the extra threads sit idle, the same law as the idle fourth consumer you saw in [Task 6.1 — Kafka fundamentals, hands-on](#task-61--kafka-fundamentals-hands-on--3h). And within one partition you must not parallelise: fanning a partition's records out to a worker pool reorders them, destroying the only ordering guarantee Kafka gives you.
    *Builds on:* [Task 6.1 — Kafka fundamentals, hands-on](#task-61--kafka-fundamentals-hands-on--3h) — a partition goes to exactly one consumer in a group (here: one listener thread), and members beyond the partition count idle.
    *Do this:*
    1. Set the listener's `concurrency` equal to the topic's partition count from `docs/architecture/topics.md` — via `spring.kafka.listener.concurrency` or `factory.setConcurrency(...)`.
    2. Log the thread name inside the listener and produce keyed messages across all partitions: each partition's records always appear on the same thread.
    3. Write both rules into `docs/kafka-notes.md`: concurrency above the partition count means idle threads; and never process a single partition's records in parallel — do not hand them to an executor — because that reorders them (do not).
    *You know it worked when:* with 3 partitions and `concurrency=3`, the logs show three listener threads each owning a stable set of partitions, and your notes say why you set the number no higher.

**Done when:** a poison pill lands in the DLQ without stalling the partition, a transient failure succeeds on retry, and a 20× replay produces one side effect.

2. Blocking versus non-blocking retries: what does each cost you, and when is the ordering loss unacceptable?
3. How do you classify an exception as retryable or not, and why send non-retryable failures straight to the DLQ?
4. How does your consumer stay idempotent, and what does the 20× replay test actually prove?
5. Why is there no point setting consumer concurrency above the partition count?

#### Task 6.4 — Service decomposition: extract payment-service — 5h

**What:** Pull payments out of `order-service` into its own service, properly — then pin the new boundary down with a consumer-driven contract test, so the two halves can never silently break each other again.
**Why:** "I split a monolith" is a far stronger claim than "I started with microservices", and doing the extraction teaches you the hard parts: data ownership, anti-corruption layers, and contract testing.
**Solves:** a shared database and shared deployment between a money-critical component and a workflow component — and the follow-on problem every split creates: two codebases that can now break each other's assumptions without either one's build going red.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Seam** | The line you cut along: which tables, which use cases, which events move. The test of a good seam is that no single transaction needs to cross it. |
| **Data ownership** | Exactly one service may write a given table. Shared write access to one database is the defining feature of a distributed monolith, and it removes every benefit of splitting. |
| **Anti-corruption layer** | A translation layer at your boundary converting their model into yours. Without it, their vocabulary and their changes propagate straight into your core. |
| **Contract test** | A test that pins down the exact requests and responses two services have agreed on. Crucially, it is owned by the *consumer* — the service doing the calling — because only the consumer knows which fields it actually reads. An integration test asks "does my service work?"; a contract test asks "do our two services still agree?", and it runs in each service's own build, with no shared test environment needed. |
| **Consumer-driven** | The direction the agreement flows: the consumer writes down what it needs, and the provider must prove it can satisfy every consumer's recorded needs before it ships. This flips the usual power balance on purpose — the provider stays free to change anything no consumer depends on, and is physically prevented from changing anything a consumer does. |
| **Pact file** | The JSON artifact of that agreement — the exact request the consumer will send and the exact response shape it expects — generated by running the consumer's contract test. Big teams exchange pact files through a broker service; locally you simply commit the file to the repo, which does the same job with zero extra infrastructure. |
| **Distributed monolith** | Services that must be deployed together to work. All the operational cost of microservices with none of the independence — the outcome you are specifically avoiding here. |
| **Graceful degradation** | Losing a non-essential dependency and continuing with reduced function instead of returning 500s. |
| **`client_credentials`** | The service-to-service OAuth2 flow from [Task 2.1 — identity-service: OAuth2 authorization server](#task-21--identity-service-oauth2-authorization-server--3h) (where you configured it in Spring Authorization Server), used here so `order-service` can authenticate to `payment-service` without a user being involved. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** performing a **real extraction** rather than claiming you could. The hard parts are data ownership, the anti-corruption layer, and proving the new boundary with a consumer-driven contract — not moving the files.
- **When it works you will see:** payments running as their own service with its own schema, the order flow still working end to end, and a provider change that would break the consumer failing the provider's build before it can deploy.
- **Where people get stuck:** two services writing the same table. That is the defining feature of a distributed monolith — all the operational cost of microservices with none of the independence. Exactly one service may write a given table.

    2. Write the one-off data-move script: an `INSERT INTO ... SELECT ...` that copies the existing payment rows from `order-service`'s schema into the new one. This script is a migration like any other — versioned, committed, run once by Flyway.
    3. In a later `order-service` migration, drop the old payment tables from its schema. Not "stop using them" — drop them, so a leftover code path that still writes them fails loudly instead of silently splitting the truth across two places.
    *You know it worked when:* both services start clean against their own schemas, the row counts in the new payment tables match what the old ones held, and the old payment tables no longer exist in `order-service`'s schema — so no code anywhere *can* write payment data except `payment-service`.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Define the boundary contract: async writes, sync reads.**
    *What this step is:* You decide, and write down, exactly how the two services talk from now on. Two channels: for the order workflow (things that change state — authorize this payment, payment captured, payment failed), commands and events flow **asynchronously** over Kafka; for support queries ("what is the payment status of order 123?"), `payment-service` exposes one thin **synchronous** read endpoint, `GET /payments/{orderId}`. At the end of this step the split exists in code and the reasoning exists in writing.
    *Builds on:* [Task 6.1 — Kafka fundamentals, hands-on](#task-61--kafka-fundamentals-hands-on--3h) and [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) — the Kafka producers and consumers with retries, DLQ, and idempotent processing that the async channel rides on.
    *Do this:*
    1. Route the workflow through topics: `order-service` publishes the command/event messages that used to be method calls, and `payment-service` consumes them (and publishes its outcomes back), using the [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) machinery.
    2. Implement `GET /payments/{orderId}` in `payment-service` — thin means it returns the payment's current state and nothing else; no side effects, no workflow logic.
    3. Document why the split goes this way (in `NOTES.md` or the ADR you write in Step 12): **writes are async** because checkout must not stall or fail just because `payment-service` is slow or briefly down — the event waits in Kafka and the workflow resumes; **reads are sync** because a support person asking a question needs the answer now, and a stale or failed read is annoying but harmless — no money moves on a read.
    *You know it worked when:* the end-to-end order flow still completes with the two services running as separate processes, and `curl` of `GET /payments/{orderId}` on `payment-service`'s port returns the payment state for a real order.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Build the anti-corruption layer in `order-service`.**
    *What this step is:* An anti-corruption layer is a thin translation layer at your boundary that converts *their* model into *yours*. When `order-service` consumes a payment event, it immediately maps it into its own vocabulary — its own small classes, named in order terms — instead of letting `payment-service`'s types spread through its core. Without this, every payment-side rename ripples straight into order code. The rule has a sharp edge you can enforce: `order-service` never imports a `payment-service` class. The **only** thing the two services share is the Avro schema module — nothing else.
    *Builds on:* [Task 6.2 — Event contract design and schema evolution](#task-62--event-contract-design-and-schema-evolution--2h) — the Avro schemas in `contracts/avro/` with generated classes and the schema registry; that shared schema module *is* the agreed contract for the async channel.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `order-service`, write a small mapper at the consuming edge: it takes the Avro-generated payment event and produces an `order-service`-owned object (its own enum for payment outcome, its own value types) before anything else touches it. Everything inward of the mapper speaks only order vocabulary.
    2. Check the Maven dependencies: `order-service` may depend on the shared Avro schema module and on nothing else from the payment side. Add an ArchUnit rule (the architecture-test library you wired in [Task 0.3 — Quality gates that fail the build](#task-03--quality-gates-that-fail-the-build--15h)) forbidding imports from `payment-service` packages, so the boundary cannot erode silently.
    *You know it worked when:* the ArchUnit rule passes — and when you temporarily add a `payment-service` import to an `order-service` class, the build goes red.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Secure and harden the service-to-service call.**
    *What this step is:* The synchronous `GET /payments/{orderId}` call is a remote call between two services with no human involved, so it needs three things: authentication (prove who is calling), trace propagation (so one request can be followed across both services), and resilience (so a slow or dead `payment-service` cannot drag `order-service` down with it). At the end of this step the call is authenticated, traceable, and wrapped.
    *Builds on:* [Task 2.1 — identity-service: OAuth2 authorization server](#task-21--identity-service-oauth2-authorization-server--3h) — `client_credentials` is the service-to-service OAuth2 flow you set up there: a service presents its own id and secret and gets a token, no user involved; [Task 2.2 — Resource-server authorization and multi-tenancy](#task-22--resource-server-authorization-and-multi-tenancy--5h) — `payment-service` validates the incoming token exactly the way every service validates JWTs since then; [Task 1.8 — REST adapter, part 2: one error contract for the whole platform](#task-18--rest-adapter-part-2-one-error-contract-for-the-whole-platform--1h) — `traceId` is the per-request identifier you have carried in every response since then; [Task 4.5 — Redis operations and failure behaviour](#task-45--redis-operations-and-failure-behaviour--2h) — you already used Resilience4j there, wrapping the cache adapter in a circuit breaker (a switch that stops calling a failing dependency for a while instead of hammering it); [Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline) ([Task 10.4 — Resilience4j on every remote call](#task-104--resilience4j-on-every-remote-call--4h)) later makes this systematic — here you apply it to this one call.
    *Do this:*
    1. Give `order-service` a client registration in `identity-service`; on each call to `payment-service` it obtains a `client_credentials` token and sends it as the `Authorization: Bearer` header. `payment-service` rejects calls without a valid token.
    2. Propagate the `traceId` header on the outgoing call, so the same id appears in both services' logs for one request.
    3. Wrap the call in Resilience4j: a **timeout** (never wait forever), a **circuit breaker** (stop calling a dependency that keeps failing), and a **retry only for idempotent GETs** — a GET changes nothing, so repeating it is always safe; never auto-retry anything that moves money.
    *You know it worked when:* a call without a token gets 401; one request's `traceId` shows up in both services' logs; and with `payment-service` stopped, `order-service`'s read path fails fast with the breaker open instead of hanging.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Contract test, consumer side first: write the Pact test in `order-service`.**
    *What this step is:* Now you pin the synchronous boundary down so the two services can never silently break each other. A contract test records the exact request the consumer sends and the exact response shape it needs back — and it is owned by the *consumer* (`order-service`, the one doing the calling), because only the consumer knows which fields it actually reads. You write it with Pact, a library built for exactly this. Running the test produces the **pact file**: a JSON artifact recording the agreement. At the end of this step that file exists.
    *Builds on:* [Task 6.4 — Service decomposition: extract payment-service](#task-64--service-decomposition-extract-payment-service--5h) Step 4 above — `GET /payments/{orderId}` is the endpoint whose shape you are now pinning.

    2. Write a Pact consumer test for `GET /payments/{orderId}` declaring *exactly* the fields `order-service` reads — the payment status, the amount, when it was captured — **and nothing more**. Pact starts a tiny fake provider in the test; your real client code calls it; Pact checks the interaction and records it.
    3. Resist the urge to describe the provider's whole response. A contract that pins fields nobody reads just makes the provider needlessly rigid — every pinned field is a field `payment-service` can never change, so pin only what you consume.
    *You know it worked when:* the test passes and a generated pact JSON file appears (under `target/pacts/` by default) — open it and you can read your own recorded request and the three expected fields.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Commit the pact file: the repo is the broker.**
    *What this step is:* Both sides need to read the same agreement. Big teams exchange pact files through a broker service (a small server that stores and versions pacts); in a local-first project you get the same result with zero extra infrastructure by committing the file to the repository — both services read the same checked-in JSON.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.9 — REST adapter, part 3: pagination, caching, and the OpenAPI contract](#task-19--rest-adapter-part-3-pagination-caching-and-the-openapi-contract--15h) and [Task 6.2 — Event contract design and schema evolution](#task-62--event-contract-design-and-schema-evolution--2h) — the `contracts/` directory already holds your OpenAPI snapshots and Avro schemas; pacts are its third resident.
    *Do this:*
    1. Configure the consumer test to write (or copy) the generated pact file into `contracts/pacts/`, next to the Avro schemas.
    2. Commit it. No Pact Broker service — the repo *is* the exchange mechanism.
    *You know it worked when:* `git log` shows the pact JSON under `contracts/pacts/`, and a teammate (or you, in a fresh clone) can open it without running anything.

- [ ] **Step 9 — Provider side: verification in `payment-service`'s build.**
    *What this step is:* The consumer recorded what it needs; now the provider must prove it can deliver it — on every build, forever. Provider verification is a test in `payment-service` where Pact replays the consumer's recorded request against the real controller and checks the actual response satisfies the pact. Wired into `make ci`, it means a provider change that would break the consumer fails the provider's **own** build *before* deploy, instead of failing the consumer in production after it. That is the whole payoff of this task.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.4 — Git workflow, the remote, and a local CI pipeline](#task-04--git-workflow-the-remote-and-a-local-ci-pipeline--2h) — `make ci` is the local pipeline script from there, run before anything leaves your machine.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the dependency `au.com.dius.pact.provider:junit5spring` (test scope) to `payment-service`'s `pom.xml` — note it is a *different* artifact from the consumer one: Pact JVM splits the consumer and provider sides into separate artifacts.
    2. Write the verification test: point it at the committed pact file in `contracts/pacts/`, let it boot the real controller, replay the recorded `GET /payments/{orderId}`, and check the response against the pact. Use Pact's "provider states" hook to seed the payment row the recorded request expects to find.
    3. Wire the verification into `make ci` so it runs on every build.
    *You know it worked when:* `make ci` runs provider verification green — and you understand that from this moment, `payment-service` physically cannot ship a response change that violates the recorded agreement.

- [ ] **Step 10 — Break it on purpose: rename a field the consumer reads.**
    *What this step is:* You now stage, deliberately, the exact accident this machinery exists to catch — and watch it get caught. This is the moment the contract test stops being theory.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `payment-service`'s response for `GET /payments/{orderId}`, rename a field the consumer reads — say `capturedAt` → `captureTime`.
    2. Run `make ci`. Watch provider verification go red.
    3. Read the diff it prints, slowly — it names the pact, the interaction, and the exact field the consumer expected but did not get. That diff is the thing that would otherwise have been a production incident: the consumer deployed, reading a field that no longer exists.
    4. Rename the field back and watch `make ci` go green again.
    *You know it worked when:* you saw the red build **in the provider's pipeline**, before any deploy could happen — and you can explain why the consumer's build never even had to run for the breakage to be caught.

    *What this step is:* A half-page in `docs/patterns.md` connecting the two halves of your contract-testing story. Your services now talk two ways — async over Kafka and sync over HTTP — and each way has its own contract guard. The Avro compatibility gate from [Task 6.2 — Event contract design and schema evolution](#task-62--event-contract-design-and-schema-evolution--2h) *is* the contract test of the async channel: the registered schema plays the pact file's role (the recorded agreement), and the CI compatibility check plays provider verification's (the gate that rejects a breaking change before it ships). Pact is its synchronous-HTTP sibling. Together they cover both ways your services talk to each other — which is exactly the sentence to say in an interview.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.7 — The design pattern register](#task-07--the-design-pattern-register--1h) — `docs/patterns.md` is the living pattern register you created there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write the half-page in `docs/patterns.md`: the parallel (schema ↔ pact, compatibility check ↔ provider verification), one concrete example of each gate catching a break ([Task 6.2 — Event contract design and schema evolution](#task-62--event-contract-design-and-schema-evolution--2h)'s rejected rename; Step 10's `capturedAt` diff), and the one-sentence interview summary.
    *You know it worked when:* you can say the summary sentence out loud, from memory, and name which gate catches a broken event versus a broken HTTP response.

- [ ] **Step 12 — ADR-0014: record the extraction honestly.**
    *What this step is:* An Architecture Decision Record for the extraction — *Extracting payment-service*. The part that makes it credible is the "what got worse" section: a split always has costs, and naming them is what separates a considered decision from cargo-culting microservices.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.5 — Architecture Decision Records](#task-05--architecture-decision-records--1h) — the ADR format and numbering you have used since then.

    1. Write ADR-0014 covering: **why** (money-critical code sharing a database and deployment with workflow code), **the seam** (what moved, from Step 1), **the migration** (how the data moved, from Step 3), and **what got worse** — at minimum: one more network hop on the read path, eventual consistency in the order view (the order's payment status can lag reality by moments), and distributed debugging (one flow now spans two services' logs).

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. How did you identify the seam, and what would have told you it was in the wrong place?
2. What is shared between the two services now, and what is deliberately not shared?
3. What is an anti-corruption layer, and what specifically is it protecting `order-service` from?
4. Writes cross the boundary asynchronously, reads synchronously. Why that split?
5. Name three things that got *worse* after this extraction. If you cannot, you have not understood the trade-off.
6. You kill `payment-service` during checkout. What does the customer see, and what did you have to build for that to be true?
7. Who owns a contract test — the consumer or the provider — and why does it have to be that way round?
8. The provider renames a field in its response. What exactly breaks the build, in whose pipeline, and at what moment — before or after the change could reach a deploy?

#### Task 6.5 — Saga orchestration with compensation — 5h

**What:** The order fulfillment saga: reserve → authorize → capture → issue tickets → notify, with compensations.
**Why:** There are no distributed transactions, so every multi-service workflow is a saga. Being able to draw one, including compensation and the stuck-saga case, is a senior-interview staple.
**Solves:** partial failures that leave seats held but unpaid, or money captured with no tickets issued.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Saga** | A business workflow spanning several services, broken into steps where each has a compensating action. It exists because there is no transaction that can span services, so you build consistency out of ordinary business operations. |
| **Orchestration** | A coordinator that explicitly drives the steps. The workflow lives in one readable place and is debuggable; the cost is that the coordinator is a component you now own. |
| **Choreography** | Each service reacts to events with no coordinator. Very decoupled, but the business process exists nowhere explicitly, so understanding it means reading five codebases. |
| **Compensation** | The undo step — and it is not a rollback. A refund is a new, visible transaction that appears on the customer's statement; the original charge still happened. Getting this distinction right in an interview matters. |
| **Saga state** | The current step, attempt count, and last error, persisted in `order_saga`. In the database, never in memory, so a pod restart resumes rather than abandons. |
| **Step deadline** | A per-step timeout. Without one, a step whose answer never arrives leaves the saga alive forever, holding seats nobody can buy. |
| **Stuck saga** | One that has passed its deadline with no progress. A scheduled sweeper finds these, moves them into compensation, and alerts. This detail is most of the difference between a toy saga and a real one. |
| **Pivot step** | The point after which you can no longer compensate cleanly — typically once money is captured and tickets are issued. Knowing where yours is tells you which failures are recoverable. |
| **2PC (two-phase commit)** | The classic protocol for one transaction spanning several machines: a coordinator asks every participant to PREPARE (do the work, hold your locks, promise you can commit), and once all say yes, tells them all to COMMIT. It sounds like exactly what a saga replaces — and it is, but it is rejected here for concrete reasons, not fashion: it is **blocking** (every participant holds its locks while waiting for the coordinator's decision, so the slowest participant sets everyone's lock-hold time), a coordinator crash after PREPARE leaves participants **in-doubt** — frozen with locks held, unable to either commit or abort on their own — and, decisively, **Kafka and Stripe simply do not speak XA**, so two of your participants could never join the transaction at all. |
| **XA** | The standard distributed-transaction protocol family — the concrete spec that 2PC participants (databases, JTA transaction managers, some older message brokers) actually implement. "It doesn't support XA" is the practical way of saying a system cannot take part in a two-phase commit. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** that every step needs a **compensating action**, including the ones that cannot truly compensate. "We cannot un-send the email, so we send a correction" is a real design decision and belongs in the document.
- **When it works you will see:** a saga completing across four services, and every failure branch tested, including a deliberately stuck saga recovered by the timeout sweeper.
- **Where people get stuck:** only testing the happy path. The compensations are the entire point of a saga; an untested compensation is an assumption. Also: forgetting that a compensation can itself fail.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Choose orchestration, and write ADR-0015 rejecting 2PC.**
    *What this step is:* Two decisions, recorded before any code. First: your saga will be **orchestrated** — a coordinator inside `order-service` explicitly drives the steps — rather than **choreographed**, where each service just reacts to events with no coordinator. The trade-off to write down: orchestration centralises the workflow in one readable, debuggable place, but the coordinator is a component you now own; choreography is maximally decoupled, but the business process exists nowhere explicitly, so understanding it means reading five codebases. Second: record **2PC/XA as a considered-and-rejected option** — the interviewer *will* ask "why not just one distributed transaction?", and the strong answer names the failure modes rather than waving at fashion.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.5 — Architecture Decision Records](#task-05--architecture-decision-records--1h) — the ADR format you have used since then; [Task 5.1 — The oversell problem: four designs, measured](#task-51--the-oversell-problem-four-designs-measured--4h) — the contended-seat load you measured there is the workload that makes 2PC's lock-holding fatal here.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write ADR-0015 choosing orchestration, with the trade-off above stated in both directions.
    2. In the same ADR, write all three reasons 2PC is rejected — all three, not a summary: (1) 2PC **blocks** — every participant holds its database locks for the whole protocol round-trip, so the slowest participant sets everyone's lock-hold time, which under [Task 5.1](#task-51--the-oversell-problem-four-designs-measured--4h)'s contended-seat load would collapse throughput; (2) an **in-doubt crash freezes participants** — a coordinator dying between PREPARE and COMMIT leaves every participant locked and unable to decide alone, until recovery intervenes; (3) **your participants could never join anyway** — Kafka and Stripe do not speak XA (the standard protocol 2PC participants must implement), so the transaction could not span the two boundaries that matter most.
    3. End the ADR with the inversion sentence: a saga deliberately flips 2PC — each step commits locally and immediately, and failure is handled by explicit, visible business actions — compensations — instead of held locks.
    *You know it worked when:* you can answer "why not one distributed transaction?" out loud with the three failure modes and the participant that could never join, without looking at the ADR.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Persist the saga's state in the database.**
    *What this step is:* The coordinator needs memory that survives a crash. You create the `order_saga` table — `order_saga(order_id, state, step, attempts, last_error, updated_at)` — with an explicit, closed set of states and the legal transitions between them, implemented as the **State** pattern: each state is its own type behind one interface, every legal transition lives in exactly one place, and anything else throws. State lives in the database, never in memory, so a pod restart resumes the saga correctly instead of abandoning it mid-flight.
    *Builds on:* [Task 5.3 — Idempotency as a reusable platform capability](#task-53--idempotency-as-a-reusable-platform-capability--4h) — `order-service`, created there, was declared the owner of `order_saga` from the start; [Task 5.4 — Exactly-once money movement](#task-54--exactly-once-money-movement--3h) — you built exactly this kind of state machine there for payment status, where a late `authorized` webhook after `refunded` throws instead of corrupting state; [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — the table arrives as a Flyway migration like every schema change.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the Flyway migration creating `order_saga(order_id, state, step, attempts, last_error, updated_at)`.
    2. Define the states and legal transitions as State-pattern types; an illegal transition throws. Every saga step update writes the row — new state, incremented `attempts` on retry, `last_error` on failure, fresh `updated_at`.
    *You know it worked when:* you restart `order-service` while a saga row sits mid-workflow and, on startup, the coordinator picks the saga up from the persisted step — and a unit test proves an illegal transition throws.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Create `notification-service`, the thing the saga notifies.**
    *What this step is:* The saga's last step is "notify", so you build the seventh service — deliberately small. It consumes four events — `OrderConfirmed`, `OrderCancelled`, `PaymentFailed`, and `TicketsIssued` — renders an email template for each, and sends the mail. It owns two tables: `notification_template` and `delivery_attempt`. Two rules give it its interview value: it is **idempotent** — keyed on `event_id`, so a replayed event does not email the customer twice — and it is **allowed to fail** without blocking checkout, which is the whole reason it is a separate service rather than a method call inside `order-service`.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — Mailpit, the fake SMTP server from your Compose stack, accepts the mail and shows it in a web inbox instead of delivering it to a real person; [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) — the service template every new service is copied from; [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) — the idempotent-consumer mechanism (a `processed_event(consumer_group, event_id)` table with a unique constraint) that "keyed on `event_id`" reuses.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `notification-service` from the service template, with its own port, schema, and Compose entry; it owns `notification_template` and `delivery_attempt`.
    2. Add consumers for the four events; each one renders a template and sends via Mailpit over SMTP, recording the attempt in `delivery_attempt`.
    3. Make it idempotent the [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) way, keyed on `event_id`.
    *You know it worked when:* placing a test order makes an email appear in Mailpit's web inbox, replaying the same event twenty times produces exactly one email — and stopping `notification-service` entirely leaves checkout working (orders still complete; the mail arrives when the service comes back and reads the topic).

- [ ] **Step 4 — Wire the forward path: the happy day.**
    *What this step is:* The coordinator drives the success sequence, one event at a time: on `OrderPlaced` → confirm the seat hold; on `HoldConfirmed` → request payment authorization; on `PaymentCaptured` → issue the tickets; on `TicketsIssued` → mark the order `OrderConfirmed` and notify. Each arrow is an event consumed, a saga-state transition written to `order_saga`, and the next command sent.
    *Builds on:* [Task 5.5 — Transactional outbox](#task-55--transactional-outbox--3h) — events leave each service through the outbox, so a crash between "commit" and "publish" loses nothing; [Task 5.1 — The oversell problem: four designs, measured](#task-51--the-oversell-problem-four-designs-measured--4h) — the seat holds being confirmed live in `inventory-service`, built there; issuing tickets at this point means `inventory-service` converting the hold into a permanent `allocation` (the printable PDF ticket comes later, in [Phase 8 — File upload, download, and the media pipeline](#phase-8--file-upload-download-and-the-media-pipeline--12h-baseline)); [Task 6.4 — Service decomposition: extract payment-service](#task-64--service-decomposition-extract-payment-service--5h) — authorization and capture are requests to the `payment-service` you just extracted, over its async boundary.
    *Do this:*
    1. Implement the coordinator's four reactions, each one: consume the event → transition `order_saga` → emit the next command through the outbox.
    2. Run the whole flow locally and follow one order through the logs of all four services.
    *You know it worked when:* one checkout runs reserve → authorize → capture → issue tickets → notify across the services, the `order_saga` row ends in its final confirmed state, and the confirmation email sits in Mailpit.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Build the compensations: the undo for every step.**
    *What this step is:* Compensations are the entire point of a saga. When a step fails, the coordinator walks back through the steps already completed, undoing each with a compensating action — and each compensation must be idempotent, because it will be retried too. Two chains to build: on `PaymentFailed` → release the hold → cancel the order → notify; on `TicketIssuanceFailed` → refund → release the hold → cancel. And note the distinction that matters in interviews: compensation is **not** rollback — it is a new business action. A refund is a new, visible transaction on the customer's statement; the original charge still happened and does not disappear.
    *Do this:*
    1. Implement the `PaymentFailed` chain: release the seat hold in `inventory-service`, cancel the order, send the cancellation notification.
    2. Implement the `TicketIssuanceFailed` chain: refund through `payment-service`, release the hold, cancel the order.
    3. Make every compensating action idempotent — releasing an already-released hold, or refunding an already-refunded payment, is a no-op, never an error (the same rule the reaper followed in [Task 5.2 — Hold expiry and the reaper](#task-52--hold-expiry-and-the-reaper--2h)).
    4. Write the "compensation is not rollback" note, with the refund as the example, where you will find it again — `NOTES.md` or ADR-0015.
    *You know it worked when:* forcing each failure (make the mock provider decline; make ticket issuance throw) leaves the system clean — seats back in the pool, order cancelled, money refunded where it had been captured — and running the same compensation twice changes nothing the second time.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Step deadlines and the stuck-saga sweeper.**
    *What this step is:* Failure events are the easy case — the hard case is silence. Every step gets a deadline (a per-step timeout); a saga past its deadline with no progress is a **stuck saga**, and without handling it would hold seats forever that nobody can buy. A scheduled sweeper finds stuck sagas, moves them into compensation, and raises an alert. This detail is most of the difference between a toy saga and a real one.
    *Builds on:* [Task 5.2 — Hold expiry and the reaper](#task-52--hold-expiry-and-the-reaper--2h) — the sweeper is the reaper's shape again: a scheduled job scanning for rows past a time threshold, safe to run concurrently, with idempotent cleanup.
    *Do this:*

Write the scheduled sweeper: find sagas whose deadline has passed with no progress, transition them into the compensation path, and alert (log it loudly now, and queue the proper alert in `docs/alerts-todo.md` for [Task 11.4 — SLOs, alerting, and runbooks](#task-114--slos-alerting-and-runbooks--2h), as [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) did for the DLQ).

    *What this step is:* Integration tests for the happy path *and* for each failure branch: payment declined, provider timeout, inventory gone, ticket generation failure. An untested compensation is an assumption, and compensations are the entire point of a saga.

- [ ] **Step 10 — `[stretch]` Break it on purpose: crash mid-saga.**
    *What this step is:* The final proof that saga state in the database (Step 2) was worth it: kill the coordinator between steps and watch the saga resume instead of abandoning the order.

#### Task 6.6 — CQRS read model and eventual consistency — 3h

**What:** Build a denormalised read model fed by events, and handle the UX consequences of lag.
**Why:** CQRS is widely name-dropped and poorly understood. Building a projection, rebuilding it from the log, and reasoning about staleness is the real skill.
**Solves:** expensive multi-join read queries on the write schema, and cross-service joins that are impossible once data is split.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **CQRS** | Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate models for writing and reading. The write model protects invariants; the read model is shaped purely for how screens actually query. |
| **Projection** | A denormalised table built by consuming events. `order_summary` holds the customer name, event title, seat labels and totals already joined together. |
| **Denormalisation** | Deliberately duplicating data so reads need no joins. You trade storage and a little staleness for read speed — and across service boundaries it is the only option, because the join is impossible. |
| **Projection lag** | How far behind the projection is. A real metric with a real alert, because "my order is missing" is what lag looks like to a customer. |
| **Rebuild** | Resetting the consumer group to the earliest offset and regenerating the projection from the log. The capability that makes projections safe to change — and the single most impressive thing you can demo from this phase. |
| **Out-of-order event** | An event arriving after a later one, usually after a retry. Without a guard it overwrites newer data with older data. |
| **Applied-offset guard** | A version or offset column on the projection row, so an event older than what the row already reflects is ignored rather than applied. |
| **Read-your-writes** | The guarantee that a user sees their own change immediately, even though the system is eventually consistent generally. Usually solved by reading the authoritative aggregate for the owner and the projection for everyone else. |
| **Event sourcing** | Storing the events as the system of record rather than current state. Related to CQRS but a much bigger commitment — and a reasoned "no" here is worth as much as a yes. |
| **CAP** | A theorem about what you can promise *during a network partition* — the moment when machines that need each other cannot reach each other. While a partition is happening, you must pick one: **consistency** (refuse to answer rather than risk answering wrong) or **availability** (keep answering, accepting the answer may be stale). The common misreading is treating CAP as a permanent three-way dial for a whole system; it only speaks about partition moments, and it applies per component, not per system. |
| **PACELC** | The honest extension of CAP: if there is a **P**artition, choose **A**vailability or **C**onsistency — **E**lse, in normal operation (which is almost all of the time), the real trade-off is **L**atency versus **C**onsistency, because waiting for more replicas to confirm a write makes you more consistent and slower. PACELC matters because it describes every ordinary day of your system, not just the outage days. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** **eventual consistency** becoming visible to users. The order list may briefly lag the order you just placed, and read-your-own-writes is a decision you must make deliberately rather than discover.
- **When it works you will see:** the projection rebuilt from the log from scratch, with the time it took recorded.
- **Where people get stuck:** a user placing an order and not seeing it in their list. That is technically correct and feels broken. Decide how you handle it — read from the write model for your own recent orders is the usual answer.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Create the `order_summary` projection table.**
    *What this step is:* A projection is just an ordinary Postgres table that lives in `order-service`'s own database and holds, for each order, everything the order-list screen needs — customer name, event title, seat labels, totals, status — already joined together. You are defining that table plus the endpoint that reads it. The point: after Phase 6 split the data across services, no single database can perform this join any more — customer data, catalog data, seat data and payment data live in different services — so the only way to get a joined row is to *build* it, piece by piece, from the events those services publish. At the end of this step you have an empty table and an order-list endpoint that reads only it.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — Flyway versioned migrations, which is how you add any table. [Task 6.4 — Service decomposition: extract payment-service](#task-64--service-decomposition-extract-payment-service--5h) — you pulled payments into its own service there, which is exactly what made this join impossible with SQL. [Task 6.2 — Event contract design and schema evolution](#task-62--event-contract-design-and-schema-evolution--2h) — the versioned Avro events those services publish are the raw material this table is assembled from.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a Flyway migration in `order-service` creating `order_summary`: `order_id` (primary key), `customer_name`, `event_title`, `seat_labels`, `total_amount`, `status`, plus `applied_event_offset` and `updated_at` (those last two are used by Steps 2 and 3 — create them now so you migrate once).
    2. Add (or repoint) the order-list endpoint so it reads **only** `order_summary` — one single-table query, zero joins. That single-table read is the entire payoff of CQRS.
    3. Write one sentence in the code or `docs/` saying *why* no single service could perform this join: customer name belongs to identity, event title to `catalog`, seat labels to `inventory`, payment status to `payment` — four services, four databases, no shared SQL.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Build the idempotent, keyed projection consumer.**
    *What this step is:* A Kafka consumer inside `order-service` that listens to the `catalog`, `inventory` and `payment` event topics and upserts `order_summary` rows — "upsert" meaning insert the row if it does not exist, update it if it does, keyed on `order_id`. It must be idempotent (processing the same event twice changes nothing) and it must carry the applied-offset guard: a row remembers the offset of the newest event it reflects, and anything older is ignored. At the end of this step, placing an order makes a summary row appear on its own, a moment later.
    *Builds on:* [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) — the idempotent-consumer pattern (a `processed_event(consumer_group, event_id)` table with a unique constraint, written inside the processing transaction) that you reuse here unchanged, plus retries and the DLQ. [Task 6.1 — Kafka fundamentals, hands-on](#task-61--kafka-fundamentals-hands-on--3h) — consumer groups and offsets, which is what "keyed" and "offset" mean below. [Task 5.5 — Transactional outbox](#task-55--transactional-outbox--3h) — the Awaitility rule for testing things that happen eventually: a test never sleeps; it waits for a condition, with a deadline.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create a Kafka listener in `order-service` with its own consumer group named `order-projection`, subscribed to the `catalog`, `inventory` and `payment` topics.
    2. On each event, upsert the row for that `order_id` — in Postgres that is `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE`.
    3. Add the **applied-offset guard**: only apply the event if its offset (or version) is greater than the row's stored `applied_event_offset`; otherwise skip it silently. Update `applied_event_offset` in the same statement that updates the data.
    4. Make the consumer idempotent the [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) way: check-and-insert into `processed_event` inside the same database transaction as the upsert.
    5. Test the happy path: place an order through the API and assert the `order_summary` row appears — with Awaitility and a deadline, never a `Thread.sleep`.
    *You know it worked when:* the Awaitility test passes — an order placed through the API shows up as a projection row without you touching the table.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Break it on purpose: deliver an old event after a newer one.**
    *What this step is:* An out-of-order event — one that arrives *after* a later event, usually because of a retry — is the classic projection killer: without the guard it overwrites new data with old data. You are going to prove your guard works, and then watch what happens without it, so you never have to take this on faith.
    *Builds on:* [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) — retries are exactly where out-of-order delivery comes from, so this is not a theoretical case.

    2. Now comment out the guard and run the test again. Watch the row regress to `PENDING` — that silent overwrite of newer data with older data is the exact bug the guard exists to stop. Put the guard back.
    *You know it worked when:* the test is green with the guard in place, and you have personally watched it fail without it.

    *What this step is:* The superpower of a projection is that it is disposable: because every event is still sitting in the Kafka log, you can wipe the table and regenerate it from scratch by telling Kafka to rewind your consumer group to the beginning. At the end you have a one-command rebuild and a measured time for 2 million orders.

Define CAP (what you can promise *during a network partition*: consistency — refuse to answer rather than risk answering wrong — or availability — keep answering, accepting staleness) and PACELC (if **P**artition, **A** or **C** — **E**lse, **L**atency versus **C**onsistency on every ordinary day) in your own words.

Classify, component by component: **Postgres, single primary per aggregate: consistency-first** — there is exactly one writer, and if it is unreachable, writes stop rather than fork into two histories. **The CQRS projection and the [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) replica reads: availability/latency-first with bounded staleness** — you answer fast from a copy and accept that it may lag, which is precisely what your `projection_lag_seconds` metric from Step 5 measures and bounds. **Kafka with `acks=all` + `min.insync.replicas`: consistency-over-availability on produce** — when too few replicas are in sync, the producer gets an error instead of a silently under-replicated write.

**Phase 6 exit check — tick honestly:**

- [ ] `make up && make smoke` passes from a cold start, with the new assertions for this phase.
- [ ] A poison pill reaches the DLQ without stalling its partition.
- [ ] A 20× replay of one event produces exactly one side effect.
- [ ] Every saga failure branch has a passing test, and the sweeper recovers a deliberately stuck saga.
- [ ] I rebuilt the CQRS projection from the log and recorded how long it took.
- [ ] An incompatible schema change fails CI, and I have watched it happen.
- [ ] I can explain partitions, ordering, consumer groups, and rebalancing without looking anything up.
- [ ] Killing `payment-service` degrades checkout gracefully rather than returning 500s.

**Phase 6 deliverables:** seven services communicating over Kafka; versioned Avro contracts with a CI compatibility gate; retry/DLQ infrastructure with a replay tool; a fully tested compensating saga; a rebuildable CQRS projection; ADRs 0013–0016.

**Phase 6 pitfalls:** publishing internal domain objects as integration events; blocking retries inside a listener; forgetting consumer-side dedup; a saga with state in memory; no step timeouts; treating Kafka as a request/response RPC mechanism.

**Phase 6 interview talking points:** ordering vs throughput and the partition key choice; why exactly-once end-to-end still needs idempotent consumers; retry topics vs blocking retries and the ordering cost; orchestration vs choreography; compensation vs rollback; how you rebuild a projection; how you detect a stuck saga.

---

### Phase 7 — Background asynchronous and scheduled work — 15h baseline

**Scheduled:** Weeks 16–17

**Goal:** every non-request-path workload runs on the right mechanism, with bounded
resources, observability, and graceful shutdown.

**Why this phase exists:** "I used `@Async`" is the most common and most dangerous
background-work answer, because the default Spring executor historically had an unbounded
queue and `@Async` work vanishes on restart. Knowing *which* of five mechanisms to use,
and why, is the senior distinction.

#### Task 7.1 — Choosing the right mechanism — 2h

**What:** A decision table for in-process async vs Kafka vs database-queue vs scheduled vs batch, applied to your real workloads.
**Why:** Mechanism choice is the actual engineering decision; the implementation is mechanical afterwards.
**Solves:** losing work on deploy, unbounded memory growth, and jobs that silently run twice on two instances.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Durability** | Whether the work must survive a restart. This single question eliminates most of the options immediately, which is why it is first. |
| **`@Async`** | Spring's in-process background execution. It runs on a JVM thread pool, so the work exists only in memory and disappears on restart. Fine for a cache warm-up, catastrophic for a payment. |
| **Database-queue** | A table of pending work claimed with `SKIP LOCKED`. Durable, transactional with your other writes, and needs no new infrastructure. The right answer far more often than people expect. |
| **Fan-out** | One event needing several independent consumers. Kafka does this naturally; a queue or a thread pool does not. |
| **Latency budget** | How soon the work must finish. "Within the request" and "before tomorrow morning" are different mechanisms, not different settings. |
| **Fire-and-forget** | Work whose failure you are genuinely willing to never hear about. Rare, and it must be a deliberate decision written down, not an accident of using `@Async`. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** choosing the mechanism **consciously** for each workload. `@Async`, a Kafka consumer, a scheduled job and Spring Batch solve different problems, and "it was easiest" is only acceptable if you know the cost.
- **When it works you will see:** a written table in `docs/async-decision.md` with one line of justification per workload.
- **Where people get stuck:** `@Async` for something that must not be lost. It is fire-and-forget in memory: if the process dies, the work is gone with no record. Anything that matters needs a queue or a database row.
