### Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience — 12h baseline

**Scheduled:** Weeks 19–20

**Goal:** a real edge layer, three instances of each service behind it, and proof that
killing an instance under load loses zero requests.

**Why this phase exists:** you listed Nginx and load balancing, and most backend
engineers treat them as "someone else's config". Being the backend engineer who can
read and reason about the proxy layer is a genuine differentiator — and it is where
timeout and header bugs are debugged.

#### Task 10.1 — Nginx as a reverse proxy, properly configured — 3h

**What:** Write the Nginx config yourself rather than copying one, and understand each directive.
**Why:** Almost every "it works locally but not through the proxy" bug is a header, timeout, or buffering directive, and knowing them makes you the person who fixes it.
**Solves:** lost client IPs, wrong redirect schemes, truncated uploads, and premature timeouts.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **`upstream`** | A named group of backend servers. `proxy_pass` sends traffic to it, and the load-balancing method is chosen here. |
| **`X-Forwarded-For`** | The chain of client IPs added by proxies. A client can forge it, so you must not trust it blindly — `real_ip_module` with `set_real_ip_from` tells Nginx which proxies are yours and therefore which entries are believable. |
| **`X-Forwarded-Proto`** | Tells the application the original request was HTTPS even though the proxy forwarded it as HTTP. Without it Spring generates `http://` redirect URLs on an HTTPS site. |
| **`forward-headers-strategy`** | The Spring setting that makes it actually read those headers. Setting the headers without this does nothing, which is a confusing half-hour for most people. |
| **`proxy_buffering`** | Whether Nginx collects the whole response before sending it on. Good for slow clients, fatal for streaming and SSE, where it must be off. |
| **`proxy_request_buffering off`** | Streams the request body straight through instead of spooling the whole upload to disk first. What makes a 200 MB upload sane. |
| **`client_max_body_size`** | The request size cap. The default is 1 MB, so a large upload returns `413` — a bug essentially everyone hits exactly once. |
| **`keepalive` to upstreams** | Reusing backend connections. Without it every single request pays a new TCP handshake, which is pure, invisible latency. |
| **`proxy_cache_lock`** | When several requests miss the same cached entry, only one goes to the origin and the rest wait. Precisely the stampede protection from [Task 4.2 — Stampede protection and multi-level caching](#task-42--stampede-protection-and-multi-level-caching--3h) — where one expired hot key sending thousands of concurrent requests to the database was the problem — implemented at the edge. |
| **Timeout nesting** | Each layer's timeout must be shorter than the layer outside it. Violate it and the outer layer gives up and retries while the inner one is still working, multiplying load exactly when you can least afford it. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** writing the Nginx config **yourself**, line by line, so you can explain every directive. A copied config you cannot explain is worse than no Nginx at all.
- **When it works you will see:** the real client IP and scheme appearing correctly in your application logs through the proxy.
- **Where people get stuck:** forgetting `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`. Without them every request appears to come from the proxy and your application thinks it is on plain HTTP, which breaks redirect URLs and rate limiting at once.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Write the Nginx config file yourself.**
    *What this step is:* Nginx is a reverse proxy — a server that sits in front of your application, receives every request from the outside world, and forwards it to the right backend. In this step you create its configuration file by hand, line by line, instead of pasting one from a tutorial. Every line gets a comment explaining what it does and why you set it. At the end you will have a working config in which nothing is mystery copy-paste.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — you created the Docker Compose stack and its profiles there, including the `edge` profile that holds Nginx and 3 service replicas. [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) — you built the Spring Cloud Gateway that is the single entrance to all your services; Nginx now sits in front of that entrance.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create the file `deploy/compose/nginx/nginx.conf`.
    2. Inside it, write one `upstream` block per backend you proxy to (an `upstream` is just a named group of backend servers — for now each group has one entry, your gateway or a service). Then write a `server` block with `location` blocks, and in each `location` use `proxy_pass http://<upstream-name>;` to send traffic to the named group.
    3. Above every directive (a directive is one configuration instruction, like `proxy_pass http://gateway;`), write a comment saying in your own words what it does and why you chose its value. A copied config you cannot explain is worse than no Nginx at all.
    4. Add Nginx to the `edge` compose profile so it starts with `make up profile=edge`, then send a request through Nginx's port with `curl` and confirm it reaches your application.
    *You know it worked when:* a request through Nginx's port returns the same response as hitting the service directly, and you can read any line of `nginx.conf` out loud and explain it without looking anything up.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Forward the real client identity and scheme.**
    *What this step is:* once a proxy is in the middle, your application no longer sees the real client — every request appears to come from Nginx's own IP address, over plain HTTP. That breaks logging, rate limiting, and redirect URLs (Spring would generate `http://` links on an HTTPS site). The fix has two halves: Nginx must attach headers describing the original request, and Spring must be told to actually read them — setting the headers without the Spring half does nothing, which is a confusing half-hour for most people. At the end, your application knows the true client IP and the true scheme (http vs https) even though everything arrives via the proxy.
    *Builds on:* [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) — the request-identity headers you standardised there are exactly what goes wrong when a proxy is inserted without this step.
    *Do this:*
    1. In your `location` block, add the four forwarding headers:
    ```nginx
    proxy_set_header Host              $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    ```
    2. In the Spring application config, set `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework` — this is the switch that makes Spring read those headers instead of ignoring them.
    3. Verify both halves: log `request.getScheme()` in a controller and hit an endpoint that returns a redirect, then check that the scheme matches what Nginx received and the generated `Location` header uses the right scheme and host — not Nginx's internal address.
    *You know it worked when:* your application logs show the real client IP and the correct scheme for a request sent through the proxy, and a redirect's `Location` header is built from the original request, not from the proxy's view of it.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Understand why `X-Forwarded-For` can lie.**
    *What this step is:* `X-Forwarded-For` is just a request header, and any client can type one before sending the request — this is called spoofing. If you trust it blindly, an attacker can impersonate any IP address, which defeats IP-based rate limiting and poisons your logs. Nginx's `real_ip_module` fixes this: `set_real_ip_from` lists the proxy addresses you own, so only the entries appended by *your* proxies are believed and anything the client made up is discarded. At the end you will have proven the spoof and then closed it.
    *Do this:*
    1. Prove the problem first: send `curl -H "X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4" http://localhost:<nginx-port>/...` and watch your application log `1.2.3.4` as the client IP — a complete lie you just told it.
    2. Configure the fix in `nginx.conf`: `set_real_ip_from` with the address range your own proxy lives in (your Docker network range), plus `real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For;`, so Nginx only believes the parts of the chain added by proxies you control.
    3. Write a comment above these directives explaining the spoofing attack and why this configuration makes the header trustworthy — this is checkpoint question 1.
    *You know it worked when:* re-running the forged `curl` from action 1 no longer changes the client IP your application logs.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Layer every timeout deliberately.**
    *What this step is:* every layer of your system — Nginx, the gateway, the service, its HTTP clients — has its own timeout, and they must nest: each layer's timeout must be shorter than the layer outside it. Violate that and the outer layer gives up and retries while the inner one is still working, so you do the same work twice — stacked retries that multiply load exactly when the system is slowest, which is called tail-latency amplification. At the end you will have a written timeout budget where every inner number is smaller than the one outside it.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `nginx.conf`, set the three proxy timeouts explicitly: `proxy_connect_timeout` (how long Nginx waits to open a connection to the backend), `proxy_send_timeout` (how long it waits while sending the request), and `proxy_read_timeout` (how long it waits for the backend to respond).
    2. List your application's own timeouts next to them — the ones your services and their HTTP clients already use — and adjust until the nesting rule holds from the outside in: Nginx's timeouts are the outermost and everything inside is shorter.
    3. State the rule in a comment in `nginx.conf`: *each layer's timeout must be shorter than the layer outside it, or you get stacked retries and tail-latency amplification* — this is checkpoint question 2.
    *You know it worked when:* you can recite your timeout chain from outermost to innermost and every inner number is smaller than the one that wraps it.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Decide buffering for responses and uploads.**
    *What this step is:* `proxy_buffering` controls whether Nginx collects a backend's whole response before sending it to the client — good for slow clients (it frees your backend quickly), but fatal for streaming and SSE, where data must flow as it is produced. `proxy_request_buffering` is the same idea in the other direction: by default Nginx spools an entire upload to disk before forwarding it, so `proxy_request_buffering off` streams the request body straight through — what makes a 200 MB upload sane. And `client_max_body_size` is the request size cap. At the end, each location in your config has a deliberate, commented buffering decision.
    *Builds on:* [Task 8.3 — Streaming downloads, range requests, and caching](#task-83--streaming-downloads-range-requests-and-caching--3h) — the streaming download endpoints you built there are exactly the kind of response that response buffering would break.
    *Do this:*
    1. Leave `proxy_buffering` on for ordinary JSON API locations and write a comment saying why (slow clients should tie up Nginx, not your backend threads) — and a second comment noting it must be *off* for streaming and SSE locations.
    2. On the upload location, set `proxy_request_buffering off;` so large uploads stream through instead of being spooled to Nginx's disk first.
    3. Set `client_max_body_size` on the upload location to a value that fits your real uploads — the next step shows you what the default does.
    *You know it worked when:* every location block has a commented buffering decision, and you can say in one sentence when buffering helps and when it kills you — checkpoint question 4.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Break it on purpose: the 100 MB upload that returns 413.**
    *What this step is:* `client_max_body_size` defaults to 1 MB, so the first large upload through a fresh Nginx returns `413 Request Entity Too Large` — a bug essentially everyone hits exactly once in their career. You are going to hit it today, on purpose, so that when it happens in production you recognise it in five seconds instead of an afternoon.
    *Builds on:* [Task 8.3 — Streaming downloads, range requests, and caching](#task-83--streaming-downloads-range-requests-and-caching--3h) — [Phase 8 — File upload, download, and the media pipeline](#phase-8--file-upload-download-and-the-media-pipeline--12h-baseline) is where you built the upload/download flows you are now pushing a big file through.
    *Do this:*
    1. Temporarily remove (or comment out) your `client_max_body_size` line so the 1 MB default applies.
    2. Make a 100 MB file with `dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/big.bin bs=1m count=100` and upload it through Nginx with `curl` — watch the `413` come back without the request ever reaching your application.
    3. Restore your `client_max_body_size` setting, reload Nginx, and run the same upload again — it should now succeed.
    *You know it worked when:* you saw `413` with the default and a successful upload after restoring the directive — and you can answer checkpoint question 3 from memory.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Reuse upstream connections and compress JSON.**
    *What this step is:* by default Nginx opens a brand-new TCP connection to your backend for every single request, paying a fresh TCP handshake each time — pure, invisible latency on every request. The `keepalive` directive inside an `upstream` block keeps a pool of connections open for reuse. While you are in the config, you also turn on response compression (`gzip`, or `brotli` if your Nginx build has it) for JSON, and measure how much smaller the payloads get. At the end you have both improvements in place with a measured number for the compression win.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add `keepalive <n>;` inside each `upstream` block, and in the matching `location` set `proxy_http_version 1.1;` and `proxy_set_header Connection "";` — without these two lines Nginx still closes the connection after each request and the keepalive pool is never used.
    2. Write a comment stating the cost of omitting it: a new TCP handshake per request — checkpoint question 5.
    3. Enable `gzip on;` with `gzip_types application/json;` (use `brotli` as well if available) for your JSON responses.
    4. Measure the reduction: fetch a large JSON response once with `curl -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" -w '%{size_download}\n' -o /dev/null ...` and once without the header, and record both byte counts and the ratio.
    *You know it worked when:* you have two measured payload sizes written down — compressed and uncompressed — and your upstream blocks carry `keepalive` with the two companion directives.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Make WebSockets survive the proxy.**
    *What this step is:* a WebSocket starts life as a normal HTTP request that asks to be "upgraded" to a long-lived two-way connection. A proxy that does not pass the upgrade headers through silently breaks every WebSocket, and a proxy whose read timeout is shorter than your heartbeat interval silently kills idle connections — the very bug you were warned about in [Phase 9 — WebSockets and real-time delivery](#phase-9--websockets-and-real-time-delivery--9h-baseline). At the end, a WebSocket client connected through Nginx stays connected.
    *Builds on:* [Task 9.4 — Backpressure, coalescing, and reconnect](#task-94--backpressure-coalescing-and-reconnect--2h) — you set up STOMP heartbeats and WebSocket ping/pong there, with the rule that heartbeats must be more frequent than Nginx's `proxy_read_timeout`; this is the moment that rule becomes real configuration.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a dedicated WebSocket `location` block:
    ```nginx
    location /ws {
        proxy_pass http://<your-upstream>;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade    $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;  # long — but see the heartbeat reconciliation below
    }
    ```
    2. Reconcile the numbers: look up the heartbeat interval you configured in [Task 9.4 — Backpressure, coalescing, and reconnect](#task-94--backpressure-coalescing-and-reconnect--2h) and confirm it is comfortably shorter than this `proxy_read_timeout`; write the two values side by side in a comment so the relationship is explicit.
    3. Connect a WebSocket client through Nginx (websocat, or your [Phase 9 — WebSockets and real-time delivery](#phase-9--websockets-and-real-time-delivery--9h-baseline) test client) and leave it idle past your old timeout values to prove it is not silently dropped.
    *You know it worked when:* a WebSocket connection made through the proxy stays open through an idle period and still delivers messages afterwards.

- [ ] **Step 9 — Cache public catalog GETs at the edge.**
    *What this step is:* Nginx can store responses and serve repeats itself, so identical public catalog reads never reach your application at all — caching "at the edge", meaning at the outermost layer. `proxy_cache_lock` adds stampede protection: when several requests miss the same expired entry at once, only one goes to the origin and the rest wait for its answer. That is precisely the stampede protection you built in [Phase 4 — Redis and the caching layer](#phase-4--redis-and-the-caching-layer--12h-baseline), re-implemented one layer further out. At the end you will have an edge cache with a visible hit/miss header and a measured drop in requests reaching the application.
    *Builds on:* [Task 4.2 — Stampede protection and multi-level caching](#task-42--stampede-protection-and-multi-level-caching--3h) — you stopped one expired hot key from sending thousands of concurrent requests to the database there; `proxy_cache_lock` is the same idea at the proxy. [Task 4.1 — Cache-aside, key design, and TTL policy](#task-41--cache-aside-key-design-and-ttl-policy--2h) — the read-heavy catalog endpoints you cached there are the same ones you now cache at the edge, making this a third cache level.
    *Do this:*
    1. Define a cache with `proxy_cache_path` and enable `proxy_cache` on the public catalog GET locations only — never on anything authenticated or personalised.
    2. Add `proxy_cache_lock on;` (one request to the origin per missed key, everyone else waits) and serve stale entries while refreshing with `proxy_cache_use_stale updating;` — Nginx's version of `stale-while-revalidate`, meaning users get a slightly old answer instantly instead of waiting for the refresh.
    3. Add a cache-status response header: `add_header X-Cache-Status $upstream_cache_status;` so every response tells you whether it was a HIT or MISS.
    4. Measure the origin-request reduction: run the same catalog requests repeatedly, and compare how many reach the application (count its access log lines) with the cache off versus on. Record the numbers.
    *You know it worked when:* `X-Cache-Status` goes MISS on the first request and HIT on repeats, and your recorded numbers show origin traffic demonstrably reduced — plus you can answer checkpoint question 6.

- [ ] **Step 10 — Serve media downloads with X-Accel-Redirect.**
    *What this step is:* `X-Accel-Redirect` is a header your application returns *instead of* the file bytes. Nginx sees it, and serves the file itself from an `internal` location — your application does the authorization check (cheap) while Nginx does the byte-shovelling (what it is best at), freeing your application threads entirely. You then benchmark this against the application-streaming approach you built in [Phase 8 — File upload, download, and the media pipeline](#phase-8--file-upload-download-and-the-media-pipeline--12h-baseline) and record the difference — a strong, uncommon talking point, because most candidates have never heard of it.
    *Builds on:* [Task 8.3 — Streaming downloads, range requests, and caching](#task-83--streaming-downloads-range-requests-and-caching--3h) — you built media downloads there by streaming the bytes through your application without loading them into memory; that implementation is today's baseline to beat.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add an `internal` location in `nginx.conf` for the media files (`internal` means clients can never request it directly — only an `X-Accel-Redirect` from your application can route there).
    2. Change the download endpoint from [Task 8.3 — Streaming downloads, range requests, and caching](#task-83--streaming-downloads-range-requests-and-caching--3h) so that after its authorization check it returns an empty response carrying the `X-Accel-Redirect` header pointing into that internal location, instead of streaming the bytes itself.
    3. Benchmark both paths — the [Task 8.3 — Streaming downloads, range requests, and caching](#task-83--streaming-downloads-range-requests-and-caching--3h) application-streaming baseline and the new X-Accel-Redirect path — under the same load, and record throughput and application CPU/thread usage for each in your benchmarks notes. Write one paragraph on the difference.
    *You know it worked when:* a direct request to the internal location is refused, the download endpoint still serves the file through Nginx, and your recorded benchmark shows the difference against the [Task 8.3 — Streaming downloads, range requests, and caching](#task-83--streaming-downloads-range-requests-and-caching--3h) baseline.

**Done when:** a request's real IP and scheme are correct in application logs, a 100 MB upload succeeds, edge caching demonstrably reduces origin hits, and WebSockets work through the proxy.


**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Why must `X-Forwarded-For` not be trusted blindly, and what configuration makes it trustworthy?
2. State the timeout-nesting rule and explain what goes wrong when it is violated.
3. A 100 MB upload returns 413. Which directive, and what is its default?
4. What does `proxy_request_buffering off` change, and when would you want buffering left on?
5. Why configure `keepalive` to upstreams? What is the cost of omitting it?
6. What does `proxy_cache_lock` do, and which [Phase 4](#phase-4--redis-and-the-caching-layer--12h-baseline) concept is it the edge version of?
7. Your application is generating `http://` redirect URLs on an HTTPS site. Name the two settings involved.

#### Task 10.2 — Load balancing and failover — 3h

**What:** Three instances per service, balanced, health-checked, and proven to fail over.
**Why:** "Zero failed requests while I killed a pod under load" is a concrete, memorable claim with a graph behind it.
**Solves:** single points of failure, and uneven load distribution.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **`least_conn`** | Send the next request to the backend with the fewest active connections. Better than round robin when request costs vary a lot, because round robin keeps feeding a backend that is already stuck on slow work. |
| **`ip_hash`** | Pin a client to a backend by IP hash. Gives affinity, costs you even distribution, and rebalances badly when the topology changes. |
| **Consistent hashing** | A hashing scheme where adding or removing a backend remaps only a small fraction of keys instead of nearly all of them. The reason cache locality survives a deploy. |
| **`max_fails` / `fail_timeout`** | Passive health checking: after N failures in a window, stop sending traffic for a while. Passive because Nginx learns from real requests rather than probing. |
| **`proxy_next_upstream`** | Retry a failed request on another backend. Safe for reads, dangerous for `POST` — which is why you must exclude `non_idempotent` or risk charging someone twice. |
| **Readiness-before-shutdown race** | If the process starts shutting down before the load balancer notices, requests are routed to a dying instance. You close it by flipping readiness to DOWN first, waiting for the balancer to react, and only then shutting down. Nearly everyone misses this. |
| **`limit_req_zone`** | Edge rate limiting with `burst` and `nodelay`. Cheap and coarse, deliberately in front of the precise, business-aware limiter in your application. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** **zero dropped requests** when an instance dies. That requires readiness to be removed from rotation before the process starts shutting down, which is a genuine race.
- **When it works you will see:** one of three instances killed under sustained load with zero failed requests, and the graph saved as evidence.
- **Where people get stuck:** shutting down immediately on SIGTERM. The load balancer has not noticed yet and keeps sending traffic for a second or two. You need a brief pre-stop delay and then a graceful drain.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Start Prometheus and Grafana for one graph.**
    *What this step is:* to prove "zero failed requests while an instance died" you need a live graph, so you bring up Prometheus (a tool that scrapes and stores metrics from your services) and Grafana (a tool that draws dashboards from those metrics) now, ahead of schedule. [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline) teaches observability properly — for today you only need one graph of request rate and error count, which you will use for this task's failover demo and for the circuit-breaker panels in [Task 10.4 — Resilience4j on every remote call](#task-104--resilience4j-on-every-remote-call--4h).
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — you created the Compose profiles there, including the `observe` profile that holds Prometheus and Grafana.
    *Do this:*
    1. Bring up the `observe` compose profile (`make up profile=observe`).
    2. Open Grafana in your browser, import a stock (ready-made, community-published) Spring Boot dashboard, and point it at your services' metrics.
    3. Confirm you can see two panels: request rate and error count. That is all you need today.
    *You know it worked when:* you send a burst of curl requests at `catalog-service` and watch the request-rate panel in Grafana move.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Three replicas, `least_conn` versus `round_robin`.**
    *What this step is:* one instance of a service is a single point of failure, so you run three copies (replicas) of `catalog-service` — the read-heavy service you built in [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) — and let Nginx spread requests across them. Nginx's default method, round robin, deals requests out in turn like cards; `least_conn` instead sends each request to the backend with the fewest active connections. When request costs vary a lot, round robin keeps feeding a backend that is already stuck on slow work, so the two methods give different tail latencies — and you are going to measure that difference, not take it on faith.
    *Builds on:* [Task 10.1 — Nginx as a reverse proxy, properly configured](#task-101--nginx-as-a-reverse-proxy-properly-configured--3h) — the `upstream` blocks you wrote there are where the balancing method is chosen. [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — you learned k6, the JavaScript-scenario load-testing tool, there; it generates today's traffic.
    *Do this:*
    1. Scale `catalog-service` to 3 replicas in compose (the `edge` profile from [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) is sized for exactly this) and list all three in the Nginx `upstream` block.
    2. Build a k6 scenario with deliberately uneven request costs — mix a cheap endpoint with an expensive one (a heavy search or a large detail page) so some requests take far longer than others.
    3. Run it twice: once with the default round robin and once with `least_conn;` in the upstream block. Record p99 (the response time that 99% of requests beat) for both runs.
    4. Write down which method gave the better p99 and *why* — the answer should mention slow requests piling up behind round robin's blind rotation. This is checkpoint question 1.
    *You know it worked when:* you have two recorded p99 numbers, one per balancing method, and a written sentence explaining the difference.

- [ ] **Step 3 — When affinity is worth its cost.**
    *What this step is:* sometimes you *want* the same client to keep hitting the same backend — that is called affinity (or stickiness). `ip_hash` gives it by pinning each client IP to one backend, but costs you even distribution and rebalances badly when a backend is added or removed. Consistent hashing (`hash $arg_key consistent`) is the smarter version: adding or removing a backend remaps only a small fraction of keys instead of nearly all of them, which is the reason cache locality survives a deploy. This step is understanding, not building — at the end you can argue when affinity is needed and what it costs.
    *Builds on:* [Task 4.2 — Stampede protection and multi-level caching](#task-42--stampede-protection-and-multi-level-caching--3h) — the in-process L1 cache you added there is the "local cache locality" that affinity preserves. [Task 9.3 — Scaling across instances](#task-93--scaling-across-instances--2h) — you saw there that WebSocket connections live on one specific instance, the other classic reason to want affinity.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write a short note (a comment block in `nginx.conf` or a page in your docs) covering: what `ip_hash` does, what `hash $arg_key consistent` does, the two cases where affinity is needed (local cache locality, WebSockets), and the two costs (uneven distribution; a cache stampede on topology change, because every remapped client arrives at a backend whose local cache knows nothing about them).
    2. Optionally prove it to yourself: switch the upstream to `ip_hash`, send requests, and watch every one land on the same replica in the logs. Switch back afterwards.
    *You know it worked when:* you can answer checkpoint question 4 — what consistent hashing buys you, and what it still costs on a topology change — without notes.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Passive health checks and the retry caveat.**
    *What this step is:* open-source Nginx does not probe your backends; it learns from real traffic — that is a *passive* health check. `max_fails` and `fail_timeout` say: after N failures in a window, stop sending that backend traffic for a while. `proxy_next_upstream` adds retries: when a backend fails, try the request on another one. That retry is safe for reads but dangerous for `POST`s — replaying a non-idempotent request (one that is not safe to repeat) on another backend can charge someone twice. At the end, Nginx routes around a dead backend and retries only what is safe to retry.
    *Builds on:* [Task 5.3 — Idempotency as a reusable platform capability](#task-53--idempotency-as-a-reusable-platform-capability--4h) — idempotency (an operation being safe to repeat) was defined and built there; it is exactly the property that decides what a proxy may retry.
    *Do this:*
    1. In the upstream block, set `max_fails` and `fail_timeout` on each server entry, and write a comment explaining "passive": Nginx learns from real requests rather than probing.
    2. Configure retries safely: `proxy_next_upstream error timeout;` — and make sure `non_idempotent` is **excluded** (never listed), so `POST`s are never replayed on another upstream. Write the charging-someone-twice reason in a comment; it is checkpoint question 2.
    3. Test it: stop one replica, keep sending requests, and watch Nginx mark it failed and route everything to the survivors.
    *You know it worked when:* with one replica stopped, requests keep succeeding, and your config contains `proxy_next_upstream error timeout;` with a comment explaining why non-idempotent requests are excluded.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Active health checks: document the honest gap.**
    *What this step is:* an *active* health check is the opposite of Step 4 — the load balancer probes each backend on a schedule instead of waiting for real requests to fail. Open-source Nginx cannot do this; it is a paid Nginx Plus feature. You have two honest options, and either is acceptable as long as you write the decision down — pretending the gap does not exist is the only wrong answer.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — a forward pointer: Kubernetes has first-class readiness probes, which is where this gap gets properly closed in [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline).
    *Do this:*
    1. Pick one: (a) implement an app-level approximation — have Nginx probe each replica's `/actuator/health/readiness` endpoint via a dedicated upstream check you build yourself; or (b) acknowledge in writing that active checks are an Nginx Plus feature and that you will rely on the Kubernetes readiness probe when you reach [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h).
    2. Document the gap honestly in your docs: what open-source Nginx cannot do, which option you chose, and why.
    *You know it worked when:* a written note exists naming the limitation, your choice, and the [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline) plan — something you could hand an interviewer.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Graceful shutdown that closes the readiness race.**
    *What this step is:* when you stop a container, the process receives SIGTERM — the operating system's polite "please shut down" signal. If the process starts shutting down immediately, there is a race: the load balancer has not noticed yet and keeps sending traffic to the dying instance for a second or two, and those requests fail. You close the race with three ordered moves: flip the readiness endpoint (the health URL a balancer checks to decide "send this instance traffic?") to DOWN *first*, wait long enough for the balancer to react, and only then begin the graceful drain. This is the detail nearly everyone misses — and the entire mechanism behind the zero-failed-requests demo in the next step.
    *Builds on:* [Task 10.1 — Nginx as a reverse proxy, properly configured](#task-101--nginx-as-a-reverse-proxy-properly-configured--3h) — Nginx is the load balancer that must notice the instance is going away before its socket closes.
    *Do this:*
    1. Set `server.shutdown=graceful` in the Spring config, so in-flight requests are finished before the server closes (a "graceful drain").
    2. Make the readiness endpoint flip to DOWN *before* shutdown begins — react to the shutdown signal by changing readiness state first, while the server still accepts and serves traffic.
    3. Add a `preStop`-equivalent delay (a deliberate pause of a few seconds between readiness going DOWN and the socket actually closing) so the load balancer stops sending traffic before the instance disappears. `preStop` is the Kubernetes name for this hook — here you build its moral equivalent yourself.
    4. Write the race down in your own words — what goes wrong without each of the three moves. This is checkpoint question 3, and it must come out in order: readiness DOWN, wait, then drain.
    *You know it worked when:* you can state the three ordered actions from memory and point to the line of code or config implementing each one.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Break it on purpose: kill an instance under load.**
    *What this step is:* the payoff. You run steady load against the three replicas, kill one mid-flight, and watch the dashboard prove that not a single request failed and p99 barely moved. "Zero failed requests while I killed a pod under load" is a concrete, memorable claim — but only with the graph behind it, so the screenshot is the deliverable.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — k6, learned there, generates the sustained load. Step 1 of this task — the Grafana request-rate and error-count graph is where the proof appears.
    *Do this:*
    1. Start a k6 scenario at steady load against the proxied `catalog-service`.
    2. While it runs, kill one of the three replicas (`docker compose kill` on one container — a hard kill is the honest test).
    3. Watch Grafana: the error count must stay at zero and p99 should barely move while the survivors absorb the traffic. If errors appear, revisit Steps 4 and 6 — a failed retry config or the readiness race is almost always the culprit.
    4. Save the Grafana screenshot — it belongs in your performance report.
    *You know it worked when:* the saved screenshot shows the kill moment with the error count flat at zero, and you can explain the mechanism (checkpoint question 6): passive health checks route around the corpse, safe retries absorb in-flight errors, and graceful shutdown never let the race happen.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Rate limit at the edge, defence layer 1.**
    *What this step is:* you already built a rate limiter inside your application in [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline). Now you add a second, cruder one in front of it at Nginx — `limit_req_zone` caps request *rate* per client (with `burst` allowing short spikes and `nodelay` serving the burst immediately instead of queueing it), and `limit_conn` caps concurrent *connections*. The reasoning is layered defence: the edge limiter is cheap and coarse and shields everything behind it from floods; the application limiter is precise and business-aware (it knows who the user is and what their plan allows). Each does what the other cannot.
    *Builds on:* [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) — the application-level rate limiter you built there (returning 429 with `Retry-After`) is defence layer 2, which this Nginx limiter now sits in front of. [Task 4.4 — Redis as a data structure server](#task-44--redis-as-a-data-structure-server--3h) — where that limiter got its Redis-backed, multi-instance-correct implementation.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `nginx.conf`, define a `limit_req_zone` keyed by client IP, and apply it on the API locations with a `burst` value and `nodelay`.
    2. Add `limit_conn` with its own zone to cap concurrent connections per client.
    3. Prove the layering: hammer an endpoint with a tight curl loop and watch Nginx reject the excess itself (HTTP 503 by default for `limit_req`) without those requests ever reaching the gateway limiter from [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h).
    4. Write the layered-defence reasoning in a comment: cheap and coarse at the edge, precise and business-aware in the application — checkpoint question 5.
    *You know it worked when:* a flood is rejected by Nginx before touching your application, a polite request rate still passes through to be judged by the application limiter, and you can explain what each layer does better than the other.

**Done when:** the kill-one-instance-under-load test shows zero failed requests, with a saved graph.


**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. `least_conn` versus round robin: under what conditions does the difference actually show up?
2. Why must you never retry a `POST` on another upstream, and what is the directive that controls it?
3. Describe the readiness-before-shutdown race precisely, and the three things you did to close it.
4. What does consistent hashing buy you, and what does it still cost when the topology changes?
5. Why rate limit at both the edge and the application? What does each layer do better?
6. You killed one of three instances under load and errors stayed at zero. Explain the mechanism that made that true.

#### Task 10.3 — TLS and the gateway's role — 2h

**What:** Terminate TLS at Nginx, understand the handshake, and settle the Nginx-vs-gateway division of labour.
**Why:** "Where do you terminate TLS and why?" and "why do you have both Nginx and Spring Cloud Gateway?" are both fair questions you should be able to answer crisply.
**Solves:** plaintext internal traffic, and duplicated/conflicting cross-cutting logic in two layers.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **TLS termination** | The point where encryption ends and plaintext begins. Here it is Nginx, so certificates live in one place rather than in nine services. |
| **SNI** | Server Name Indication — the client names the host it wants during the handshake, so one IP can serve many certificates. Without it, virtual hosting over HTTPS would be impossible. |
| **Certificate chain** | Your certificate, signed by an intermediate, signed by a root the client already trusts. Omitting the intermediate works in browsers that cache it and fails elsewhere — which is why the bug looks random. |
| **OCSP stapling** | The server presents a recent proof that its certificate is not revoked, so the client does not have to ask the authority itself. Faster and more private. |
| **HTTP/2** | Multiplexes many requests over one connection, removing head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer. |
| **mTLS** | Both sides present certificates, so the server authenticates the client too. The usual way to secure internal service-to-service traffic. |
| **Service mesh** | Sidecar proxies that provide mTLS, retries, and telemetry without application code. Genuinely useful at scale, and overkill for nine services — being able to say why you did *not* adopt one is the point. |
| **mkcert** | A small tool that creates a certificate authority your own machine trusts, then issues certificates from it — real HTTPS locally with no browser warnings. Installed in [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h), where the whole toolchain went in; one-time setup is `mkcert -install`, then `mkcert localhost` makes the certificate Nginx will serve. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** which responsibilities belong at the edge and which must not be delegated there. TLS terminates at the edge; authorization does not.
- **When it works you will see:** HTTPS working end to end with HTTP/2, and a written split of edge versus service responsibilities.
- **Where people get stuck:** assuming TLS at the edge means traffic is safe everywhere. Between the proxy and your services it is plain HTTP — fine locally, a decision you must make consciously anywhere else.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Create a certificate your machine trusts.**
    *What this step is:* HTTPS needs a certificate — a file that proves to a client "this server really is localhost". Real certificates come from public authorities; locally you use `mkcert`, a small tool that creates a private certificate authority (CA — an issuer of certificates) on your machine, tells your Mac to trust it, and then issues certificates from it. At the end of this step you will have two files on disk: a certificate and its private key, ready for Nginx to serve.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — `mkcert` was installed there as part of the toolchain, so there is nothing new to install.
    *Do this:*
    1. Run `mkcert -install` once. This creates the local CA and registers it in your Mac's trust store — it is one-time setup and you never run it again.
    2. In `deploy/compose/nginx/` (next to the `nginx.conf` you wrote), run `mkcert localhost`. It writes two files, typically `localhost.pem` (the certificate) and `localhost-key.pem` (the private key).
    *You know it worked when:* both `.pem` files exist, and `mkcert -install` reported the CA was created and installed with no error.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Serve HTTPS from Nginx, hardened properly.**
    *What this step is:* You now point Nginx at those two files so it terminates TLS — meaning encryption from the browser ends at Nginx, and everything behind it stays plain HTTP. While you are in the config you also switch on the modern settings a reviewer would expect: HTTP/2 (many requests multiplexed over one connection), TLS 1.3 + 1.2 with a modern cipher suite, HSTS (the header that tells a browser to keep using HTTPS — you met it in [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline)), and OCSP stapling (the server attaches a recent "not revoked" proof to its certificate so clients do not have to check themselves). At the end, `https://localhost` works with no browser warning.
    *Builds on:* [Task 10.1 — Nginx as a reverse proxy, properly configured](#task-101--nginx-as-a-reverse-proxy-properly-configured--3h) — the hand-written `nginx.conf` you are now editing, reached by a bind mount so edits on your Mac appear in the container. [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) — where HSTS and response-header hardening were first explained.
    *Do this:*
    1. In your `server` block, change `listen 80;` to `listen 443 ssl;` and enable HTTP/2, then add `ssl_certificate` and `ssl_certificate_key` pointing at the two files from Step 1 (bind-mount them into the container the same way as `nginx.conf`, and use the paths as seen *inside* the container).
    2. Add `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;` and a modern cipher suite (a cipher suite is the exact set of encryption algorithms a connection uses — ask AI for a current recommended `ssl_ciphers` line and read what each part means before pasting it).
    3. Add the HSTS response header (`add_header Strict-Transport-Security ...`) and the OCSP stapling directives (`ssl_stapling on; ssl_stapling_verify on;`). One honest note: your mkcert CA has no revocation service, so Nginx may log a warning that it cannot actually staple — that is expected locally; the point is that you know the directive and what it does.
    4. Reload Nginx (`docker exec <nginx-container> nginx -s reload`) and open `https://localhost` in your browser.
    *You know it worked when:* the browser shows a padlock with no warning, and `curl -sI https://localhost` shows a response that starts `HTTP/2` and includes your `strict-transport-security` header.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Watch the TLS handshake happen.**
    *What this step is:* The handshake is the short negotiation at the start of every HTTPS connection: the client says which host it wants, the server presents its certificate chain, and both agree on a protocol version and cipher. You will watch one happen in plain text instead of taking it on faith, using `openssl s_client` (openssl ships with macOS, so there is nothing to install).
    *Do this:*
    1. Run `openssl s_client -connect localhost:443` and read the output top to bottom: the certificate chain section, the negotiated protocol (expect TLSv1.3) and cipher, and the `Verify return code` line at the end.
    2. Run it again with `-showcerts` to see every certificate in the chain printed in full.
    *You know it worked when:* the output ends with `Verify return code: 0 (ok)` and names the protocol and cipher you configured in Step 2.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Understand the chain, SNI, and the random-looking bug.**
    *What this step is:* A certificate is trusted through a chain: *your* certificate is signed by an **intermediate** certificate, which is signed by a **root** certificate the client already ships with. The server is supposed to send its own certificate *plus* the intermediate. You also pin down **SNI** (Server Name Indication — the client names the host it wants during the handshake, so one IP address can serve many different certificates; without it, hosting several HTTPS sites on one IP would be impossible). At the end you can explain, from memory, the classic bug: a server that forgets to send the intermediate works in some clients and fails in others.
    *Builds on:* Step 3 — the `-showcerts` output you just read is the chain you are now explaining.
    *Do this:*
    1. From the Step 3 output, identify the three roles: your `localhost` certificate, the issuer (locally that is the mkcert CA playing both intermediate and root — in production they are separate), and the root in the client's trust store.
    2. Write down, in your own words, why a missing intermediate looks random: browsers often *cache* intermediates from earlier visits to other sites (and can even fetch them on the fly), so they still succeed — while strict clients like `curl`, Java's HTTP client, or a fresh machine have never seen that intermediate and fail with an untrusted-certificate error. Same server, different clients, different results.
    3. State what SNI solves in one sentence, and verify you can see the client sending it: `openssl s_client -connect localhost:443 -servername localhost` sets it explicitly.
    *You know it worked when:* you can answer checkpoint questions 3 and 4 out loud without looking anything up.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Write the edge responsibility split.**
    *What this step is:* You now have two pieces of infrastructure in front of your services — Nginx at the very edge, and Spring Cloud Gateway behind it — and "why do you have both?" is a question you must answer crisply. This step writes the division of labour down in `docs/architecture/edge.md` so the split is a decision, not an accident.
    *Builds on:* [Task 10.1 — Nginx as a reverse proxy, properly configured](#task-101--nginx-as-a-reverse-proxy-properly-configured--3h) — edge caching and media offload (`X-Accel-Redirect`) were built there. [Task 10.2 — Load balancing and failover](#task-102--load-balancing-and-failover--3h) — coarse IP rate limiting at the edge (`limit_req_zone`) was built there. [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) — the Spring Cloud Gateway with per-route routing, JWT pre-validation, per-principal rate limiting, and request IDs was built there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/architecture/edge.md` with two lists. **Nginx owns:** TLS termination, static/media offload, coarse IP rate limiting, edge caching, and connection handling. **The gateway owns:** per-route routing, JWT pre-validation, per-principal rate limiting, request IDs, and request/response shaping.
    2. Add a paragraph explaining why you would *not* put business logic in Nginx — it has no tests, no types, and no deploy pipeline: config lives outside your build, so a mistake there is invisible to every quality gate you built in [Phase 0 — Repository, tooling, standards](#phase-0--repository-tooling-standards--15h-baseline).
    *You know it worked when:* someone who has never seen your project (or you, next month) can read the file and answer "why both Nginx and Spring Cloud Gateway?" with a clean division — and nothing appears on both lists.

- [ ] **Step 6 — `[stretch]` mTLS inside, and the service-mesh answer.**
    *What this step is:* TLS currently stops at Nginx, so gateway-to-service traffic is plain HTTP — fine on your laptop, a conscious decision anywhere else. **mTLS** (mutual TLS) closes that gap: *both* sides present certificates, so the server also authenticates the client. You wire it between the gateway and one internal service, then write the honest note about service meshes — sidecar proxies (a small proxy container running next to each service) that provide mTLS, retries, and telemetry without application code.
    *Builds on:* Step 1 — `mkcert` issues the extra certificates. [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) — the gateway whose outbound calls you are now securing.
    *Do this:*
    1. Issue a server certificate for one internal service and a client certificate for the gateway with `mkcert`, enable TLS on that service, and set it to *require* a client certificate; configure the gateway's outbound HTTP client to present its certificate. Verify a plain, certificate-less call to the service is now rejected while the gateway's call succeeds.
    2. Add a note to `docs/architecture/edge.md`: a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) replaces this hand-wiring by moving mTLS, retries, and telemetry into sidecars — genuinely useful at scale — and state why you did *not* adopt one: the operational cost of a mesh is not worth it for 9 services.
    *You know it worked when:* `curl` straight at the internal service fails the handshake, the gateway's call still works, and the mesh paragraph answers checkpoint question 6 in writing.

**Done when:** HTTPS works end to end with HTTP/2, and the edge responsibility split is documented.


**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Where do you terminate TLS, and what are the two main reasons for choosing that point?
2. Why do you have both Nginx and Spring Cloud Gateway? Divide the responsibilities cleanly.
3. What problem does SNI solve?
4. A missing intermediate certificate breaks some clients and not others. Explain why.
5. Why would you not put business logic in Nginx? Give three reasons.
6. What would a service mesh give you here, and why did you decide against it?

#### Task 10.4 — Resilience4j on every remote call — 4h

**What:** Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and bulkheads on all cross-service and third-party calls.
**Why:** The default `RestClient` has no timeout, which means one slow dependency can consume every request thread in your service. Cascading failure is the most important distributed-systems failure mode to be able to discuss.
**Solves:** cascading failures, retry storms, and thread exhaustion caused by a slow dependency.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Cascading failure** | One slow dependency consuming all your request threads, so your service fails, so *its* callers fail. The most important distributed-systems failure mode to be able to discuss. |
| **Timeout budget** | A table showing every layer's timeout nesting correctly from client down to database. Without it, timeouts are set independently and contradict each other. |
| **Retry storm** | Three layers each retrying three times is twenty-seven calls to a dependency that is already struggling. The fix is to retry at exactly one layer. |
| **Circuit breaker** | After a failure-rate threshold it stops calling and fails fast (*open*), waits, then lets a trial call through (*half-open*) before resuming (*closed*). It gives a struggling dependency room to recover instead of hammering it. |
| **Sliding window** | The recent-calls window the failure rate is computed over. Too small and it trips on noise; too large and it reacts too slowly. |
| **Semaphore bulkhead** | A simple cap on concurrent calls to one dependency. Cheap, and it runs on the calling thread so context propagates naturally. |
| **Thread-pool bulkhead** | Full isolation on a separate pool, so a hung dependency cannot block callers at all — at the cost of context propagation and overhead. |
| **Honest fallback** | Degrading in a way that tells the truth: stale availability clearly marked stale, a queued notification. Never a fake success on anything that moves money. |
| **toxiproxy** | A proxy that injects latency, bandwidth limits, and failures on demand, so you can test what your system does when a dependency misbehaves rather than guessing. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** the **timeout nesting rule**: an inner timeout must always be shorter than the outer one containing it. Violate it and you do work nobody is waiting for, which is how one slow dependency collapses everything.
- **When it works you will see:** a circuit breaker visibly opening and recovering in Grafana, and a complete chaos matrix with no cell reading "500 for everything".
- **Where people get stuck:** retrying without backoff and jitter. Every client retries in unison and you have built a thundering herd that finishes off the service that was only briefly struggling.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Give every outbound call a timeout.**
    *What this step is:* An outbound call is any moment your service waits on something else over the network. Today, many of those waits are unbounded — the default `RestClient` will wait forever — and an unbounded wait is how one slow dependency eats every request thread you have. You audit every outbound call in the whole system and give each one an explicit **connect timeout** (how long to wait for the connection to open) and **read timeout** (how long to wait for the response). At the end, no call anywhere can wait forever.
    *Builds on:* [Task 4.5 — Redis operations and failure behaviour](#task-45--redis-operations-and-failure-behaviour--2h) — you already set timeouts on every Redis call there (Lettuce's defaults were too generous); this step extends that discipline to everything else. [Task 5.4 — Exactly-once money movement](#task-54--exactly-once-money-movement--3h) — the payment provider you call is the WireMock stand-in added there. [Task 8.1 — Object storage and the presigned upload flow](#task-81--object-storage-and-the-presigned-upload-flow--2h) — the S3 calls go to the MinIO client configured there.
    *Do this:*
    1. List every outbound call in the system: HTTP calls to other services, the payment provider, Redis, S3 (MinIO), and SMTP (Mailpit). Grep for every place a `RestClient` or other client bean is built.
    2. For each, set an explicit connect and read timeout in configuration — no call may keep the library default.
    *You know it worked when:* your list has a timeout value written next to every single entry, and no outbound client in the codebase is constructed without one.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Write the timeout budget in `docs/timeouts.md`.**
    *What this step is:* Individually sensible timeouts can still contradict each other. The **timeout nesting rule** — each inner timeout must be shorter than the outer one containing it — only holds if you can see all the layers at once, so you build one table, the *timeout budget*, showing the chain from the user's client down to the database. Violate the rule and an outer layer gives up and retries while the inner one is still working: effort nobody is waiting for, exactly when you can least afford it.
    *Builds on:* [Task 10.1 — Nginx as a reverse proxy, properly configured](#task-101--nginx-as-a-reverse-proxy-properly-configured--3h) — the nesting rule was stated there when you layered Nginx's `proxy_*_timeout` directives against the application's own timeouts; this table is that rule made visible end to end.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/timeouts.md` with one row per layer and verify the budget nests correctly: client 10 s > Nginx 9 s > gateway 8 s > service 5 s > downstream 2 s. Every value in the table must match what is actually configured — fix the config where it disagrees.
    *You know it worked when:* reading the table top to bottom, every layer's timeout is strictly shorter than the layer above it, and each number traces to a real config line you can point at.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Add retries that follow the rules.**
    *What this step is:* A retry re-sends a failed call, which can rescue a request from a brief network blip — and can also double-charge a customer or pile load onto a struggling service if done carelessly. You add Resilience4j's retry (Resilience4j is the resilience library you have already used twice) with three safety rules baked in: wait longer between attempts with **exponential backoff** plus **full jitter** (randomising the whole wait so a thousand clients do not all retry in the same instant), keep the max-attempt count low, and retry *only* idempotent operations — never a 4xx, because a 4xx says *your request* is wrong and resending the same wrong request can never succeed.
    *Builds on:* [Task 7.3 — Distributed scheduling](#task-73--distributed-scheduling--3h) — the webhook dispatcher there used exponential backoff with full jitter; this is the same idea applied to synchronous calls. [Task F4.2 — Methods, and the promise each one makes](#task-f42--methods-and-the-promise-each-one-makes--1h) — where you learned which operations are idempotent (safe to repeat because repeating changes nothing).
    *Do this:*
    1. Configure a Resilience4j `Retry` on the idempotent outbound calls (GETs and other repeat-safe operations): exponential backoff, full jitter enabled, and a low max-attempt count (2–3).
    2. Encode the rules in config, not in your memory: no retry on any non-idempotent operation, and an exception predicate that never retries a 4xx response.
    *You know it worked when:* a test that makes a dependency fail once then recover shows the call succeeding on a retry — and a test returning a 400 shows exactly one attempt, no retries.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Break it on purpose: the retry storm.**
    *What this step is:* Now you manufacture the classic outage. If three layers each retry three times, one user click becomes 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls to a dependency that is *already struggling* — you have built a machine that finishes off a briefly-sick service. You demonstrate the arithmetic for real, then fix it with the rule: retry at exactly **one** layer.
    *Builds on:* Step 3 — the retry configuration you are about to deliberately over-apply. [Task 5.4 — Exactly-once money movement](#task-54--exactly-once-money-movement--3h) — WireMock, added there, plays the failing dependency and counts the hits for you.
    *Do this:*
    1. Temporarily configure 3 attempts at each of three layers on one call path (for example: the gateway, the calling service, and an inner client wrapper), point the path at a WireMock stub that always returns 500, and send one request.
    2. Count the requests WireMock received (its request journal shows them) — you should see 27 from your single request.
    3. Fix it: remove retries from every layer except one (the layer closest to the failure is the usual choice), re-run, and count again.
    *You know it worked when:* the WireMock request count drops from 27 to 3 for the same single user request, and you can state the fix in one sentence: retry at exactly one layer.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Circuit breakers that visibly open and recover.**
    *What this step is:* A circuit breaker watches recent calls to a dependency and, past a failure-rate threshold, stops calling and fails fast — that is the *open* state. After a wait it moves to *half-open* and lets a few trial calls through; if they succeed it *closes* and traffic resumes. The point is to give a struggling dependency room to recover instead of hammering it. You put breakers on the payment provider and on inter-service calls, and you watch one open and recover with your own eyes.
    *Builds on:* [Task 4.5 — Redis operations and failure behaviour](#task-45--redis-operations-and-failure-behaviour--2h) — your first circuit breaker, around the cache adapter. [Task 6.4 — Service decomposition: extract payment-service](#task-64--service-decomposition-extract-payment-service--5h) — the inter-service call you wrapped in Resilience4j there now gets fully-tuned breaker settings. [Task 5.4 — Exactly-once money movement](#task-54--exactly-once-money-movement--3h) — WireMock supplies the induced failures.
    *Do this:*
    1. Configure a Resilience4j `CircuitBreaker` on the payment-provider call and on each inter-service call, setting each knob deliberately: the **sliding window** (how many recent calls the failure rate is computed over — too small trips on noise, too large reacts slowly), the failure-rate threshold, `waitDurationInOpenState` (how long to stay open before trying again), and the number of half-open trial calls.
    2. Make WireMock return failures until the breaker opens — calls now fail instantly without touching the dependency — then let WireMock recover and watch the breaker go half-open, pass its trial calls, and close.
    3. Write down how a breaker and retries interact badly if misconfigured: each retry attempt is recorded as another failure, so retries *feed the failure counter* and can slam the breaker open far earlier than your threshold suggests. Decide and document the order you want (breaker outside, retry inside — or the reverse — and why).
    *You know it worked when:* you have watched the full open → half-open → closed cycle in your logs or actuator endpoint, and can name what caused each transition.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Bulkheads: cap concurrent calls per dependency.**
    *What this step is:* A bulkhead (named after a ship's watertight compartments) caps how many calls may be in flight to one dependency at once, so a slow provider can occupy at most N threads instead of all of them. You add **semaphore bulkheads** — a simple counter-based cap that runs on the calling thread, so request context (like trace IDs) propagates naturally — and you learn the contrast with the **thread-pool bulkhead**, which isolates calls on a separate pool so a hung dependency cannot block callers at all, at the cost of context propagation and extra overhead.
    *Builds on:* Step 5 — the same Resilience4j configuration files; a bulkhead is one more named instance next to your breakers.
    *Do this:*
    1. Configure a semaphore `Bulkhead` per dependency with a deliberate concurrency cap, and verify the cap bites: hold the dependency slow (point it at a WireMock stub with a fixed delay) and fire more concurrent requests than the cap — the excess should be rejected fast, not queued forever.
    2. Write the contrast in a short note: semaphore = cheap, context propagates, but the calling thread is still the one waiting; thread-pool = full isolation, a hung dependency cannot block callers, but context must be copied across threads and you pay pool overhead. This contrast is a direct bridge to [Phase 12 — The concurrency track: 30 incremental levels](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner), where you will build a semaphore-based limiter with your own hands.
    *You know it worked when:* with the cap set to N, firing N+5 concurrent requests at a slowed dependency shows exactly N in flight and 5 rejected immediately.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Fallbacks that tell the truth.**
    *What this step is:* A fallback is what you serve when the real dependency is unavailable. The trap is a fallback that lies — a fake success. Yours must be honest: degraded, and saying so. You implement three, and then write the rule that generalises them: **fall back on reads, fail on writes that move money.**
    *Builds on:* [Task 4.1 — Cache-aside, key design, and TTL policy](#task-41--cache-aside-key-design-and-ttl-policy--2h) — the cached data that lets a read degrade gracefully. [Task F7.9 — Compose, and your first Dockerfile](#task-f79--compose-and-your-first-dockerfile--15h) — Mailpit, the fake SMTP server from your compose stack, is the "SMTP" you make fail here. [Task 5.4 — Exactly-once money movement](#task-54--exactly-once-money-movement--3h) — why payment must hard-fail rather than pretend.
    *Do this:*
    1. When `inventory-service` is down: serve cached availability, *clearly marked stale* (a field or header the caller can see — never silently pass old data off as fresh).
    2. When SMTP fails: queue the notification for later delivery instead of dropping it or erroring the whole request.
    3. When the payment provider fails: hard failure, surfaced to the user. Never fake success on anything that moves money.
    4. Write the rule — fall back on reads, fail on writes that move money — into your resilience notes alongside the bulkhead contrast.
    *You know it worked when:* killing each of the three dependencies produces the designed degraded behaviour (visible staleness, a queued email, an honest payment error) and never a fabricated success.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Idempotency plus retries: the safety proof.**
    *What this step is:* Here the two halves of the plan click together. An automatic retry re-sends a request — so what stops a retried "create order" from creating two orders? The `Idempotency-Key` mechanism you built in [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline): the retry carries the same key, the server recognises it, and the second attempt returns the first attempt's result instead of acting twice. You demonstrate both directions — safe with the key, duplicate without it. This connection is the single best way to demonstrate systems thinking.
    *Builds on:* [Task 5.3 — Idempotency as a reusable platform capability](#task-53--idempotency-as-a-reusable-platform-capability--4h) — the `Idempotency-Key` mechanism, usable by any endpoint with one annotation, that makes this demo possible.
    *Do this:*
    1. Configure a retry on the order-creation call *with* the idempotency key flowing through, make the first attempt fail after the server has processed it (WireMock or toxiproxy can cut the response), and show the retry returns the original result — one order in the database.
    2. Repeat the same experiment with the idempotency key removed, and show the retry creates a duplicate order. Save both results side by side.
    *You know it worked when:* the same failure-plus-retry sequence yields exactly one order with the key and two without it, and you can narrate why from memory.

- [ ] **Step 9 — Put circuit-breaker state on a Grafana panel.**
    *What this step is:* A breaker that opens silently teaches you nothing. Resilience4j publishes its state as metrics through Micrometer (the metrics library already in your services); you expose them and build one Grafana panel showing each dependency's breaker state over time, so Step 11's chaos runs are *visible* — you will literally watch a breaker open and recover on a graph.
    *Builds on:* [Task 10.2 — Load balancing and failover](#task-102--load-balancing-and-failover--3h) — the `observe` compose profile (Prometheus + Grafana) you brought up there for the failover graph; this panel lives in the same Grafana.
    *Do this:*
    1. Confirm Resilience4j metrics (such as `resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state`) appear on each service's Prometheus endpoint, and that Prometheus is scraping them.
    2. Build a Grafana panel of circuit-breaker state per dependency — one line or state block per breaker, labelled by dependency name.
    *You know it worked when:* forcing one breaker open (repeat Step 5's WireMock failures) moves that dependency's line on the panel within a scrape interval, and recovery moves it back.

- [ ] **Step 10 — Set up toxiproxy between you and every dependency.**
    *What this step is:* Killing a container only tests the "dependency is dead" case; the nastier case is "dependency is *slow*". toxiproxy is a proxy that injects latency, bandwidth limits, and failures on demand, so you can test what your system does when a dependency misbehaves rather than guessing. You slot it between your services and each dependency now, so the next step's matrix can delay as well as kill.
    *Builds on:* [Task F7.9 — Compose, and your first Dockerfile](#task-f79--compose-and-your-first-dockerfile--15h) — adding a container to the compose file and re-pointing ports is exactly the skill practised there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a `ghcr.io/shopify/toxiproxy` container to the compose file, and install the command-line client on your Mac: `brew install shopify/shopify/toxiproxy` gives you `toxiproxy-cli`.
    2. For each dependency (Postgres, Redis, Kafka, MinIO, and the payment provider's WireMock), create a toxiproxy listener that forwards to the real container's port, and re-point the consuming services' configuration at the toxiproxy listener instead of the dependency directly.
    3. Smoke-check the plumbing: with no toxics (toxiproxy's word for an injected fault) configured, `make up && make smoke` must still pass — toxiproxy at rest is invisible.
    *You know it worked when:* `toxiproxy-cli list` shows one proxy per dependency, and the whole stack behaves exactly as before while traffic flows through them.

- [ ] **Step 11 — Break it on purpose: the chaos matrix.**
    *What this step is:* The graduation exercise. For every dependency you run two experiments — kill it, and slow it down — and record what a *user* actually experiences in each case. The output is a table, the chaos matrix: rows are dependencies, columns are failure modes, cells are observed user-visible behaviour. Any cell where the answer is "500 for everything" is a bug to fix — it means some resilience work from Steps 1–8 is missing or mis-wired for that path.
    *Builds on:* Step 10 — toxiproxy provides the delays; `docker stop` provides the kills. Steps 1–8 — the timeouts, retries, breakers, bulkheads, and fallbacks whose combined behaviour you are now grading. Step 9 — the Grafana panel where each run should be visible.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/chaos-matrix.md` with one row per dependency: Postgres, Redis, Kafka, MinIO, payment provider.
    2. For each, first kill it (`docker stop` the container), exercise the main user flows, and write down exactly what the user sees — then restart it. Next, delay it (add a latency toxic with `toxiproxy-cli`), and do the same.
    3. Wherever a cell reads "500 for everything", treat it as a bug: find the missing timeout, breaker, or fallback, fix it, re-run that cell, and update the matrix. Repeat until no unintended total outage remains.
    *You know it worked when:* every cell describes a deliberate, degraded behaviour you designed (stale reads, queued work, an honest error on payments) — and not one cell reads "500 for everything".

**Done when:** the chaos matrix is complete with no unintended total outages, and a circuit breaker visibly opens and recovers in Grafana.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. The default `RestClient` has no timeout. Walk through exactly how that becomes a total outage.
2. Show the retry-storm arithmetic for three layers retrying three times, and state the fix.
3. Name the three circuit-breaker states and what causes each transition.
4. Semaphore versus thread-pool bulkhead: what does each give you and cost you?
5. State your fallback rule for reads versus writes that move money, and justify it.
6. How does [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline)'s idempotency key ([Task 5.3 — Idempotency as a reusable platform capability](#task-53--idempotency-as-a-reusable-platform-capability--4h) — the `Idempotency-Key` mechanism any endpoint can adopt with one annotation) make an automatic retry safe? What happens without it?
7. A cell in your chaos matrix says "500 for everything". What does that tell you, and what do you do?


**Phase 10 exit check — tick honestly:**

- [ ] `make up && make smoke` passes from a cold start, with the new assertions for this phase.
- [ ] The real client IP and scheme appear correctly in application logs through the proxy.
- [ ] Killing one of three instances under load produces zero failed requests, and I saved the graph.
- [ ] I can state the timeout-nesting rule and show `docs/timeouts.md` obeying it.
- [ ] A circuit breaker visibly opens and then recovers in Grafana.
- [ ] The chaos matrix is complete, with no cell reading "500 for everything".
- [ ] I can describe the readiness-before-shutdown race from memory.
- [ ] I wrote the Nginx config myself and can explain every directive in it.

**Phase 10 deliverables:** a hand-written, understood Nginx config with edge caching and WebSocket support; a zero-downtime failover demo; a TLS-terminated edge; a full timeout budget; Resilience4j everywhere; a chaos matrix.

**Phase 10 interview talking points:** the timeout-nesting rule; why retrying at every layer is dangerous; circuit breaker vs retry vs bulkhead; the readiness-before-shutdown race; why sticky sessions are a last resort; Nginx vs gateway responsibilities.
