### Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting — 16h baseline

**Scheduled:** Weeks 20–21

**Goal:** be able to answer "what is wrong with checkout right now?" in under 60 seconds,
from a dashboard, for a system you did not touch for two weeks.

**Why this phase exists:** observability is the clearest proxy for production
experience. An engineer who has been on call instruments differently: correlation IDs,
business metrics, SLO-based alerts, and runbooks. This phase also retroactively makes
every earlier phase measurable.

#### Task 11.1 — Structured logging and correlation — 2h

**What:** JSON logs with trace correlation that survives async and Kafka hops.
**Why:** Grep-able text logs across 9 services are unusable. One `traceId` that follows a request through HTTP → thread pool → Kafka → another service is the single most valuable debugging tool you can build.
**Solves:** being unable to reconstruct what happened to one specific failed order.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Structured logging** | Emitting logs as JSON with named fields rather than sentences. It means you can query `tenantId = X AND level = ERROR` instead of writing a regular expression against prose. |
| **MDC** | Mapped Diagnostic Context — a per-thread map Logback merges into every log line. It is per-*thread*, which is exactly why it needs explicit help to cross a thread pool or a Kafka hop. |
| **`traceId` / `spanId`** | The trace is the whole journey of one request; a span is one step within it. Both belong on every log line so logs and traces can be cross-referenced. |
| **Context propagation** | Deliberately carrying MDC across the three places it would otherwise be lost: into a thread pool, out through a Kafka producer header, and back in at the consumer. |
| **Log-and-throw** | Logging an exception and then rethrowing it, so it gets logged again higher up. Pick one: handle it and log, or throw it and let the handler log. Doing both triples your log volume and your confusion. |
| **Async appender** | Logging on a background thread so request threads are not blocked by disk or network. |
| **`neverBlock`** | What the async appender does when its queue is full. `false` blocks the application to preserve every line; `true` drops lines to protect latency. A real trade-off, and you must know which you chose. |
| **LogQL** | Loki's query language. Writing five queries you actually need is worth more than a dashboard you never open. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** the **correlation id**. Without one identifier threaded through everything, debugging across nine services is guesswork, and with one it is a single query.
- **When it works you will see:** one `traceId` retrieving the complete story of a request across HTTP, a thread pool, Kafka and two services.
- **Where people get stuck:** MDC not propagating into async code. It is thread-local, so the moment work hops to a pool thread or a Kafka consumer the context is gone unless you deliberately carry it. [Task 7.2 — Thread pools done properly](#task-72--thread-pools-done-properly--4h) set this up — the `TaskDecorator` there copies MDC into every pool thread and clears it afterwards — verify it still holds.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Make every service log JSON, not sentences.**
    *What this step is:* Today your services write log lines meant for human eyes — free-form sentences. You will reconfigure Logback (the logging library Spring Boot already uses — it has been writing your console output since your first app) so that every log line comes out as one JSON object with named fields. That is what "structured logging" means, and it is what lets a log database later answer a query like `tenantId = X AND level = ERROR` instead of you writing a regular expression against prose. At the end of this step, all nine services emit identical-shaped JSON log lines.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — the shared `platform-*` modules you created there; this config goes in `platform-observability` once so every service inherits it instead of nine copies drifting apart.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the `logstash-logback-encoder` dependency to `platform-observability` and create a `logback-spring.xml` there that uses its JSON encoder instead of the default pattern layout.
    2. Make sure every log line carries this exact standard field set: `timestamp`, `level`, `logger`, `thread`, `message`, `service`, `version`, `env`, `traceId`, `spanId`, `requestId`, `tenantId`, `userId`. The first five come from Logback itself; `service`, `version` and `env` you set as fixed fields per service; the last four come from MDC (Step 2 fills them in).
    3. Adopt one rule for extra data: any value you want in a log line goes in as a named key-value pair (the encoder's structured-arguments feature), **never** string-concatenated into the message. `"hold created" + holdId` is banned; `kv("holdId", holdId)` is the way.
    *You know it worked when:* you start one service, hit any endpoint, and every line in the console is a single JSON object containing all the fields above (the MDC-sourced ones may still be empty — Step 2 fixes that).

- [ ] **Step 2 — A filter that fills MDC and always empties it.**
    *What this step is:* MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) is a per-thread map that Logback automatically merges into every log line — put `tenantId` in it once at the start of a request, and every log statement during that request carries it for free. You will write a servlet filter (a class that sees every HTTP request before your controllers do) that fills MDC as early as possible and — critically — clears it in a `finally` block. The `finally` matters because web servers reuse threads: without it, the next request on that thread would log the *previous* request's ids, which is both a lying log and a data leak between tenants.
    *Builds on:* [Task 2.3 — edge-gateway: routing, rate limiting, request identity](#task-23--edge-gateway-routing-rate-limiting-request-identity--5h) — the gateway already stamps every request with an `X-Request-Id` header, which this filter now reads. [Task 2.2 — Resource-server authorization and multi-tenancy](#task-22--resource-server-authorization-and-multi-tenancy--5h) — the `TenantContext` filter there extracts `org_id` and the user from the JWT; your MDC values for `tenantId` and `userId` come from it.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `platform-observability`, write a servlet filter registered to run very early (before security has rejected anything, if possible after `TenantContext` is populated for the tenant fields) that does `MDC.put` for `requestId` (from the `X-Request-Id` header), `tenantId`, and `userId`.
    2. Wrap the rest of the filter chain in `try { chain.doFilter(...) } finally { MDC.clear(); }` — the clear must run even when the request throws.
    *You know it worked when:* two consecutive requests as two different tenants each log their own `tenantId`, and a request made right after one that threw an exception shows no trace of the previous request's ids.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Carry MDC across the three hops where it dies.**
    *What this step is:* MDC is per-*thread*. The moment work leaves the request thread — into a thread pool, out through a Kafka producer, or into a Kafka consumer on another service — the context is silently gone unless you carry it by hand. Those are exactly the three hops, and this step wires and tests all three. This is the heart of the whole task: after it, one `traceId` follows a request through HTTP → thread pool → Kafka → another service.
    *Builds on:* [Task 7.2 — Thread pools done properly](#task-72--thread-pools-done-properly--4h) — the `TaskDecorator` you wrote there already copies MDC into pool threads and clears it in a `finally`; hop 1 is verifying it still does. [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) — the Spring Kafka producers and consumers you built there are what hops 2 and 3 attach to.
    *Do this:*
    1. Hop 1 (thread pool): confirm the [Phase 7 — Background asynchronous and scheduled work](#phase-7--background-asynchronous-and-scheduled-work--15h-baseline) `TaskDecorator` propagates MDC into your executors — write or re-run a test that submits a task and asserts the pool thread logs the caller's `traceId`.
    2. Hop 2 (Kafka out): add a producer interceptor that copies `traceId` from MDC into a Kafka message header.
    3. Hop 3 (Kafka in): add a consumer interceptor that reads that header and puts it back into MDC before your listener runs — and clears it after.
    4. Test all three hops together: one request that fans into async work and publishes a Kafka event consumed by another service.
    *You know it worked when:* that test's log output shows the **same** `traceId` on the HTTP thread's lines, the pool thread's lines, and the consuming service's lines.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Write the logging rulebook.**
    *What this step is:* A one-page team standard that says what each log level means, so "ERROR" is a pager-worthy signal rather than noise. You will write it in `docs/logging-standards.md` and then apply it to your own code. The two habits it bans — logging inside tight loops, and log-and-throw — are the two biggest sources of useless log volume in real codebases.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/logging-standards.md` with these rules, each with one Zenith example: `ERROR` only for things a human must act on; `WARN` for degraded-but-handled (a retry that eventually succeeded); `INFO` for business state transitions (order placed, hold expired); `DEBUG` off in production.
    2. Add the ban on logging inside tight loops — one log line per item in a 10,000-item batch is 10,000 lines saying nothing.
    3. Add the ban on log-and-throw (logging an exception and *then* rethrowing it, so a handler higher up logs it again — the same failure appears two or three times and triples your confusion). The rule: pick one — handle it and log it, or throw it and let the handler log it.
    4. Sweep your own `catch` blocks and fix every violation you find.
    *You know it worked when:* the document exists with an example per level, and you can point at a `catch` block you changed because it was logging *and* throwing.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Log exceptions once, and log the whole exception.**
    *What this step is:* Two discipline rules for exceptions. First: pass the exception *object* to the logger (`log.error("payment failed", e)`), never `e.getMessage()` — the message alone loses the stack trace and the chained causes, which are exactly what you need at 3 a.m. Second: log it **once**, at the boundary that actually handles it, not at every layer it passes through.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.8 — REST adapter, part 2: one error contract for the whole platform](#task-18--rest-adapter-part-2-one-error-contract-for-the-whole-platform--1h) — the `@RestControllerAdvice` you built there is that handling boundary for HTTP requests; it is where the one log call belongs.
    *Do this:*
    1. Audit every `log.error`/`log.warn` call that mentions an exception; replace any `e.getMessage()` argument with the exception object itself.
    2. Remove exception logging from intermediate layers so each failure is logged exactly once, at the handler.
    *You know it worked when:* one deliberately failed request produces exactly **one** stack trace in the logs — not zero, not three.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Prove PII is redacted, and cap the hot paths.**
    *What this step is:* Two protections for your log pipeline. First, verify by test that the PII masking you built earlier still works — logs get shipped, copied and retained, so an email or card number in a log line is a data breach waiting to happen. Second, add volume control: without it, one hot endpoint can generate 80% of your log bill while saying nothing new.
    *Builds on:* [Task 2.4 — Application security hardening and auditing](#task-24--application-security-hardening-and-auditing--3h) — the `@Sensitive` annotation plus Logback masking converter you built there is the redaction mechanism this step verifies.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write (or re-run) a test that logs an email address and a card-like number through the normal logging path and asserts both come out masked in the rendered JSON.
    2. Add a Logback `TurboFilter` (a filter that runs before the log event is even built, so it is cheap enough for hot paths) or a sampling filter on your highest-volume logging paths, so a hot endpoint emits a bounded fraction of its lines instead of all of them.
    *You know it worked when:* the redaction test is green, and hammering a hot endpoint in a loop shows visibly fewer log lines than requests.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Async appender, and a trade-off you choose on purpose.**
    *What this step is:* By default Logback writes logs on the thread that made the request — meaning a slow disk or log network hop slows your users down. An async appender moves log writing to a background thread with a queue in between. But every queue can fill up, and then you must pick a side: `neverBlock=false` makes request threads *wait* so no line is lost; `neverBlock=true` *drops* lines so latency is protected. Both are defensible — what is not defensible is not knowing which one you shipped.
    *Do this:*
    1. Wrap your JSON appender in Logback's `AsyncAppender` with an explicit, bounded `queueSize`.
    2. Set `neverBlock` explicitly — do not leave it to the default — and write one paragraph next to the config (or in `docs/logging-standards.md`) stating which you chose and what you traded away: blocking protects log completeness and can stall request threads; dropping protects latency and loses lines.
    *You know it worked when:* the config shows an explicit `queueSize` and `neverBlock`, and you can answer "what happens to a log line when the queue is full?" in one sentence without looking.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Loki plus Grafana, and five queries you will actually run.**
    *What this step is:* Loki is a log database (think "Prometheus, but for logs") and Grafana is the UI you query it from. You will add Loki to your local stack, ship your JSON logs into it, and save the five LogQL (Loki's query language) queries you will genuinely reach for during an incident. Five queries you actually need are worth more than a dashboard you never open. This is the payoff step: the "one `traceId`, whole story" query becomes real here.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — the `deploy/compose` stack you add Loki to, and where you rehearsed the bind-mount trick for editing Grafana files from your Mac. [Task 10.2 — Load balancing and failover](#task-102--load-balancing-and-failover--3h) — the `observe` compose profile you started there already runs Grafana; you are adding Loki as a data source, not starting from zero.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a Loki container to the compose stack, ship each service's JSON logs to it, and register Loki as a data source in Grafana.
    2. Write and save five LogQL queries you actually need — including at least: "all ERROR in order-service last 15m grouped by logger" and "everything for traceId X across all services"; good candidates for the rest: all WARN-and-above for one tenant, all logs for one `requestId`, error rate per service over time.
    *You know it worked when:* you place one order, grab its `traceId` from any log line, run the traceId query in Grafana — and get back the complete story of that order across HTTP, the thread pool, Kafka, and two services. That is this task's Done-when, working.

**Done when:** a single `traceId` query in Loki returns the full story of one order across HTTP, a thread pool, Kafka, and two services.


**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Why JSON logs rather than formatted text? Give the concrete thing it lets you do.
2. Name the three hops where MDC must be propagated manually, and what carries it across each.
3. Why is log-and-throw an anti-pattern, and what should you do instead?
4. `neverBlock` true or false — which did you choose, and what did you trade away?
5. Why log the exception object rather than `e.getMessage()`?
6. State your rule for ERROR versus WARN, and give one example of each from Zenith.

#### Task 11.2 — Metrics that answer real questions — 3h

**What:** Micrometer + Prometheus with RED dashboards per service and business metrics.
**Why:** Technical metrics tell you a service is slow; business metrics tell you that you are losing money. Senior engineers instrument both.
**Solves:** "the dashboards are all green but customers cannot buy tickets."

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Counter** | A number that only increases — requests served, orders placed. You never read it directly; you take its `rate()`. |
| **Gauge** | A value sampled at a point in time — queue depth, active connections. One honest warning: Micrometer holds only a *weak* reference to the object a gauge samples, so the classic bug is that object getting garbage collected and the gauge silently reporting `NaN` forever. The fix is keeping a strong reference to the gauged object yourself — store it in a field, not a local variable. |
| **Timer** | Records how long things took, as a distribution rather than a single number. |
| **Client-side percentile** | A p99 computed inside one instance. It **cannot be averaged across instances** — the average of two p99s is not a p99. This is a frequent interview gotcha and a frequent real-world dashboard bug. |
| **Histogram** | Bucketed counts exported to Prometheus, where `histogram_quantile()` computes the percentile *after* aggregating across instances. The correct choice for anything you will aggregate. |
| **Cardinality** | The number of distinct label combinations. Every combination is a separate time series, so a `userId` label with a million values creates a million series and takes Prometheus down. |
| **RED** | Rate, Errors, Duration — the three things to measure for every service. |
| **USE** | Utilisation, Saturation, Errors — the three things to measure for every resource. RED is for things that serve requests; USE is for things that get consumed. |
| **Business metric** | `tickets_sold_total`, `oversell_attempts_total`. These catch the incident where every technical dashboard is green and nobody can buy a ticket. |
| **Dashboards as code** | Grafana JSON committed to the repository, so dashboards are reviewable and survive the machine they were drawn on. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** **cardinality**. Putting a user id or an order id in a metric label creates millions of time series and will take down your metrics backend before it helps you.
- **When it works you will see:** a dashboard where a deliberately injected failure becomes visible within thirty seconds.
- **Where people get stuck:** averaging percentiles. You cannot average p99 across instances — the result is meaningless. Export histograms and let Prometheus compute the quantile.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Expose a metrics endpoint and scrape it.**
    *What this step is:* Micrometer is the metrics library already sitting inside Spring Boot — your services have been *collecting* numbers (request counts, pool usage, JVM memory) all along; nothing has been *reading* them. You will expose those numbers on an HTTP endpoint in Prometheus's text format, and configure Prometheus (a time-series database that works by *pulling* — it visits each service's endpoint every few seconds and stores what it finds; that visit is called a "scrape") to scrape all nine services.
    *Builds on:* [Task F6.9 — Auto-configuration: removing the magic](#task-f69--auto-configuration-removing-the-magic--1h) — you added Spring Boot Actuator there and learned endpoint exposure is opt-in; this adds one more endpoint. [Task 10.2 — Load balancing and failover](#task-102--load-balancing-and-failover--3h) — the `observe` compose profile you started there already runs Prometheus and Grafana; you are now pointing Prometheus at every service instead of a stock dashboard.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add the `micrometer-registry-prometheus` dependency to `platform-observability` and add `prometheus` to `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`.
    2. Open `/actuator/prometheus` on one service and read a few lines — each is `metric_name{label="value"} number`.
    3. In the Prometheus config inside your compose stack, add a scrape job for every service.
    *You know it worked when:* Prometheus's own UI → Status → Targets shows every service as `UP`.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Confirm every metric family is actually arriving.**
    *What this step is:* Spring Boot auto-instruments the libraries you already use — but only if the wiring is right, and a missing family is invisible until the incident where you needed it. So you verify, one by one, that all six families you will depend on in Phase 11 are flowing: JVM, Tomcat, Hikari, Kafka, cache, and Resilience4j.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.4 — Transactions, MVCC, locking, and connection pooling](#task-34--transactions-mvcc-locking-and-connection-pooling--6h) — Hikari is the database connection pool you tuned there. [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) — your Kafka producers/consumers emit the Kafka metrics. [Task 4.1 — Cache-aside, key design, and TTL policy](#task-41--cache-aside-key-design-and-ttl-policy--2h) and [Task 4.5 — Redis operations and failure behaviour](#task-45--redis-operations-and-failure-behaviour--2h) — the cache counters and Redis metrics you exposed there. [Task 10.4 — Resilience4j on every remote call](#task-104--resilience4j-on-every-remote-call--4h) — circuit breaker and retry metrics come from the resilience layer you built there.
    *Do this:*
    1. In the Prometheus UI, run one query per family and confirm each returns data: `jvm_memory_used_bytes` (JVM), `tomcat_sessions_active_current` or an `http_server_requests` query (Tomcat/HTTP), `hikaricp_connections_active` (Hikari), a `kafka_` metric (Kafka), your cache hit/miss counters (cache), and a `resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state` metric (Resilience4j).
    *You know it worked when:* all six queries return at least one time series each; write down any family that was missing and what you fixed to get it flowing.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Learn the four instrument types — and the two classic traps.**
    *What this step is:* Everything you will ever record is one of four instruments, and two of them have famous pitfalls. A `Counter` only goes up (requests served) — you never read it directly, you take its rate. A `Gauge` is a sampled value (queue depth) — and Micrometer holds only a *weak* reference to the object it samples, so if your code drops its own reference, the garbage collector eats it and the gauge silently reports `NaN` forever; keep the gauged object in a field, not a local variable. A `Timer`/`DistributionSummary` records a distribution of durations or sizes. And for percentiles: a p99 computed inside one instance (`publishPercentiles`) **cannot be averaged across instances** — the average of two p99s is not a p99 — so for anything you will aggregate, publish a histogram (`publishPercentileHistogram`) and let Prometheus compute the quantile with `histogram_quantile()` *after* summing across instances.
    *Do this:*
    1. Register one of each by hand in a service you own: a `Counter`, a `Gauge` (stored correctly, in a field), and a `Timer` with `publishPercentileHistogram` enabled.
    2. Demonstrate the gauge pitfall once on purpose: gauge a local variable, force GC or wait, and watch the value go `NaN` — then fix it.
    3. In Prometheus, compute a p99 from your histogram with `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(..._bucket[5m])))` and note that this works across instances precisely because the buckets are summed first.
    *You know it worked when:* you can say out loud, without notes, why averaging p99s is meaningless and what the weak-reference gauge bug looks like — both are frequent interview questions because both are frequent production bugs.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Cardinality discipline: the label budget.**
    *What this step is:* Every distinct combination of label values on a metric is a *separate time series* that Prometheus must store and index. A label like `status` (a handful of values) is fine; a label like `userId` (a million values) creates a million series and takes your metrics backend down — the monitoring system dies first, exactly when you need it. This step turns that into a written rule you cannot drift away from.
    *Do this:*
    1. Adopt the hard rule: **never** a user id, order id, or raw URL path (which embeds ids) as a metric label. Use templated paths (`/events/{id}`) and bounded enums only.
    2. Write a cardinality budget into a doc (e.g. `docs/metrics-standards.md`): for each custom metric, list its labels, each label's possible values, and the resulting series count — and one paragraph explaining *why* a label with 1M values destroys Prometheus (1M series × every scrape, forever).
    3. Audit the labels on everything you registered in Steps 3 and 5 against the budget.
    *You know it worked when:* every label on every custom metric has a bounded, written-down value set, and no metric's series count exceeds its budget.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Business metrics: the numbers that catch real incidents.**
    *What this step is:* Technical metrics say "the service is slow"; business metrics say "you are losing money". [Task 5.3 — Idempotency as a reusable platform capability](#task-53--idempotency-as-a-reusable-platform-capability--4h) — duplicate-request detection (`idempotency_duplicate_hits_total`). [Task 5.4 — Exactly-once money movement](#task-54--exactly-once-money-movement--3h) — payment authorization (`payment_failures_total`). [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) — the dead-letter queue (`dlq_depth`). [Task 6.5 — Saga orchestration with compensation](#task-65--saga-orchestration-with-compensation--5h) — the order saga (`saga_stuck_total`, and ticket issuance for `tickets_sold_total`). [Task 6.6 — CQRS read model and eventual consistency](#task-66--cqrs-read-model-and-eventual-consistency--3h) — projection lag (`projection_lag_seconds`). [Task 8.4 — The async media processing pipeline](#task-84--the-async-media-processing-pipeline--3h) — the signed QR tickets whose gate-scan checks produce `scan_rejections_total`.
    *Do this:*

Add each of these, at the point in the code where the business fact happens: `tickets_sold_total{event}`, `checkout_conversion`, `oversell_attempts_total`, `idempotency_duplicate_hits_total`, `holds_expired_total`, `payment_failures_total{provider,reason}`, `saga_stuck_total`, `dlq_depth`, `projection_lag_seconds`, `scan_rejections_total{reason}`.
    2. Check every label against the Step 4 budget (`event` is bounded by your catalog; `provider`, `reason` are enums — all fine).
    *You know it worked when:* you run one order through the system, one duplicate request, and one failed payment — and the matching counters visibly increase in Prometheus.

    *What this step is:* Two standard dashboard recipes, applied everywhere. RED — Rate, Errors, Duration — is what you measure for every thing that *serves requests* (each of your services). USE — Utilisation, Saturation, Errors — is what you measure for every thing that *gets consumed* (the Hikari pool, thread pools, Kafka consumer lag, Redis memory). And the dashboards live as Grafana JSON files committed to the repository — "dashboards as code" — so they are reviewable in a PR and survive the machine they were drawn on, instead of being hand-drawn and lost.

    2. Export each as JSON and commit the files to `deploy/grafana/dashboards/`, loaded into the Grafana container via a bind-mounted provisioning directory.
    *You know it worked when:* you destroy the Grafana container, run `docker compose up`, and every dashboard is back — because they live in git, not in the container.

    *What this step is:* The single screen you would put on a wall during an on-sale: it answers "is the business working right now?" at a glance. It combines the Step 5 business metrics with a few capacity numbers.

    2. Rehearse this task's Done-when against it: deliberately inject a failure — slow the database with toxiproxy (the failure-injection proxy you set up in [Task 10.4 — Resilience4j on every remote call](#task-104--resilience4j-on-every-remote-call--4h)), let the DLQ grow, or force a cache miss spike — and time how long until the dashboard shows it.
    *You know it worked when:* each injected failure is visible on your committed dashboards within 30 seconds of starting it.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Enough PromQL to be dangerous.**
    *What this step is:* PromQL is Prometheus's query language — the dashboards above are just saved PromQL. You need five constructs and one "why", and you will be able to improvise any panel you need during an incident.
    *Do this:*
    1. Work through each against your live data: `rate()` (per-second rate of a counter over a window), `increase()` (total growth over a window), `histogram_quantile()` (percentile from histogram buckets, as in Step 3), `sum by (...)` (aggregate series, keeping chosen labels), `topk()` (the k biggest series — "top 5 endpoints by error rate").
    2. Answer, in writing, why `rate()` on a gauge is meaningless: `rate()` assumes a monotonically increasing counter and treats any decrease as a counter reset — a gauge goes up *and* down by nature, so the result is garbage. For "how fast is this gauge changing", `deriv()` or `delta()` exist instead.
    *You know it worked when:* you can write "p99 latency of order-service" and "top 3 services by error rate" from memory, and explain the gauge answer in one sentence.

**Done when:** you have committed dashboards that make a deliberately injected failure (slow database, DLQ growth, cache miss spike) visible within 30 seconds.

#### Task 11.3 — Distributed tracing — 3h

**What:** End-to-end traces through gateway, services, Kafka, and thread pools.
**Why:** With a saga spanning 4 services and 2 async hops, logs alone cannot show you where the 3 seconds went. Tracing can, and being able to read a flame-graph-style trace is a strong signal.
**Solves:** latency attribution in a distributed call path, and discovering an unexpected N+1 or a serial loop of remote calls.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Trace** | The complete journey of one request across every service it touched. |
| **Span** | One timed operation within a trace, with a parent. Spans nest into a tree, which is what lets you see where the three seconds actually went. |
| **`traceparent`** | The W3C standard header carrying trace context between services. Standardised so tools from different vendors interoperate. |
| **OTLP** | The OpenTelemetry protocol — the standard wire format your services use to ship trace data to a backend like Tempo or Jaeger. One exporter speaks it; any compliant backend can receive it. |
| **Async propagation** | Carrying trace context across thread pools and Kafka. The genuinely hard part — synchronous HTTP propagation is nearly free, and a trace that stops at the first async hop is not much use. |
| **Head-based sampling** | Deciding at the start whether to record a trace. Cheap, but you may discard the one that turned out to be interesting — which is why you also always-sample on error. |
| **Tail-based sampling** | Deciding after the trace completes, so you can keep all the slow and failed ones. More useful and more expensive, since everything must be buffered. |
| **Exemplar** | A link from a point on a metric graph to one specific trace. Turns "p99 is bad" into "here is a request that was bad", which is the gap between a dashboard and a diagnosis. |
| **Critical path** | The chain of spans that actually determined total duration. Optimising anything off the critical path changes nothing — which is the usual reason an optimisation disappoints. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** tracing finding a problem you did not already know about. A trace that merely confirms what you expected has not earned its keep; the goal is a genuine surprise you then fix.
- **When it works you will see:** one trace showing a full order saga across four services including the async hops, and a real problem found and fixed with before/after numbers.
- **Where people get stuck:** traces that stop at the first async boundary. Context propagation through Kafka needs explicit header injection and extraction — without it the trace silently ends and you conclude nothing is wrong.

At the end of this step you can open one request's trace in Grafana.

A trace that stops at the first async boundary silently ends, and you wrongly conclude nothing is wrong there. This step carries the context across all of them, so one trace shows the whole order saga — `OrderPlaced` → payment → ticket issuance — as a single connected tree. This is the genuinely hard part, and the part worth demonstrating in an interview.

[Task 6.5 — Saga orchestration with compensation](#task-65--saga-orchestration-with-compensation--5h) — the order fulfillment saga whose journey this trace must show end to end. [Task 11.1 — Structured logging and correlation](#task-111--structured-logging-and-correlation--2h) — you already carried MDC across these same three hops there; this is the same exercise for trace context, and the two must agree.
    *Do this:*
    1. Make trace context survive `@Async` and `CompletableFuture` by wrapping your executors with the tracing library's context-propagating wrapper (or extending your `TaskDecorator`).
    2. On the Kafka producer, inject the trace context into message headers; on the consumer, extract it before processing so the consumer's spans attach to the producer's trace.
    3. Place one order and follow it: `OrderPlaced` event → payment-service → ticket issuance.
    *You know it worked when:* one single trace in Tempo shows the full saga as a connected tree including the Kafka hops — if payment or issuance appears as its own separate trace, a hop is still broken.

    *What this step is:* Auto-instrumented spans tell you "an HTTP call took 400 ms"; they do not tell you *which saga step* or *how many seats*. You now add your own spans and attributes (named key-value pairs attached to a span) at business-meaningful points — with one hard rule: **no PII in span attributes**, ever, because traces are shipped, stored, and browsed by anyone with Grafana access.
    *Builds on:* [Task 6.5 — Saga orchestration with compensation](#task-65--saga-orchestration-with-compensation--5h) — the saga steps you name in `saga.step`.     *You know it worked when:* you can open a saga trace and say which business step took longest without reading any code — and a search of span attributes for an email address finds nothing.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Sampling: choose what to keep, on purpose.**
    *What this step is:* Recording every trace at production volume is expensive, so you sample. Head-based sampling decides at the *start* of a request whether to record — cheap, but it may discard the one trace that turned out to be interesting. Tail-based sampling decides *after* the trace completes, so it can keep all the slow and failed ones — more useful, more expensive, because everything must be buffered until the decision. You implement the standard pragmatic mix.
    *Do this:*
    1. Configure head-based sampling at a low rate (e.g. a few percent) for normal traffic.
    2. Add always-sample on error, and always-sample when a debug header is present — so you can force a full trace for any request you are actively investigating.
    3. Write a short explanation (in `docs/`, or next to the config) of the cost/visibility trade-off you made and what tail-based sampling would buy you over this setup.
    *You know it worked when:* a loop of normal requests yields only the sampled fraction in Tempo, while a forced error and a request with the debug header each show up every single time.

- [ ] **Step 6 — Make tracing earn its keep: find one real problem.**
    *What this step is:* A trace that merely confirms what you expected has not earned its keep — the goal is a genuine surprise you then fix. You will read your own traces looking for the critical path (the chain of spans that actually determined total duration — optimising anything off it changes nothing, which is why most optimisations disappoint) and hunt for the classic finds: a serial loop of remote calls that should be parallel, or an unexpected N+1.
    *Builds on:* [Phase 12 deliverables](#phase-12-deliverables) — the concurrency track ahead; its `CompletableFuture` fan-out levels are where you will build the *proper* parallel fix, so the serial loop you find here is deliberate setup, not a loose end.
    *Do this:*
    1. Pull traces for your slowest endpoints and the saga; look at the span waterfall for stair-step patterns (calls running one after another that have no reason to wait for each other).
    2. Pick one real problem, record the *before* latency, fix it (or, for the serial-loop find, apply the simplest safe improvement now and note that [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner)'s fan-out work completes it), and record the *after*.
    *You know it worked when:* you have before/after numbers written down for one problem that tracing — not guesswork — revealed.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Exemplars: from a bad graph to the bad request.**
    *What this step is:* An exemplar is a link from a point on a metric graph to one specific trace that contributed to it. It closes the gap between a dashboard and a diagnosis: "p99 is bad" becomes "here is an actual request that was bad — click it".

#### Task 11.4 — SLOs, alerting, and runbooks — 2h

**What:** Define SLIs/SLOs, write burn-rate alerts, and write a runbook per alert.
**Why:** Threshold alerts on CPU are noise; SLO burn-rate alerts are what mature teams run. And an alert without a runbook is a 3 a.m. guessing game.
**Solves:** alert fatigue, and alerts nobody knows how to action.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **SLI** | Service Level Indicator — the measurement itself, such as the fraction of checkout requests under 800 ms. |
| **SLO** | The target you set for that indicator, such as 99.9% monthly. Internal, chosen by you. |
| **SLA** | A contractual promise to a customer with consequences attached. Always looser than your SLO, because you want to find out before they do. |
| **Error budget** | The failure you are allowed. 99.9% monthly is about 43 minutes. It converts reliability from an argument into arithmetic: budget left means ship, budget gone means stabilise. |
| **Burn rate** | How fast you are consuming the error budget relative to the allowed pace. A burn rate of 1× means you are failing at exactly the rate the SLO permits, so the budget lasts the whole 30-day month — which is 720 hours. At 14.4× you are spending it 14.4 times faster, so it would last 720 ÷ 14.4 = 50 hours. The useful way to hold the number in your head: 14.4× burns exactly 2% of the month's budget every hour (14.4 ÷ 720 = 2%). That 2%-per-hour pace is *why* 14.4 is the standard fast-burn threshold — a one-hour alert window at that rate pages you when only about 2% of the budget is gone: early enough to act, severe enough to be a real outage rather than noise. |
| **Multi-window multi-burn-rate** | Two alerts: a fast one (14.4× over an hour) that pages for real outages, and a slow one (6× over six hours) that opens a ticket for steady degradation. Catches both shapes of problem without paging on noise. |
| **Alert fatigue** | So many alerts that people stop reading them. At that point your alerting system has negative value, and the fix is deleting alerts, not adding dashboards. |
| **Liveness vs readiness** | Liveness asks "is this process broken and in need of a restart?". Readiness asks "can it serve traffic right now?". Putting a database check in liveness means a database blip restarts every pod — turning a brief degradation into a total outage. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** alerting on **burn rate** rather than raw thresholds. A threshold alert pages you for one slow request at 3 a.m.; a burn-rate alert pages you when the error budget is genuinely at risk.
- **When it works you will see:** an alert firing with a runbook link, and that runbook actually leading you to a cause.
- **Where people get stuck:** alerts nobody acts on. Every alert that fires and gets ignored trains you to ignore the next one. If an alert would not wake you, it should be a ticket, not a page.

    *What this step is:* An error budget is the amount of failure your SLO permits — it turns reliability from an argument into arithmetic. Derive 14.4 on paper, then copy the derivation into `docs/slo.md`: a 30-day month is **720 hours**; at burn rate 1× the budget lasts exactly those 720 hours; at 14.4× it lasts 720 ÷ 14.4 = 50 hours; and 14.4 ÷ 720 = **2% of the month's budget per hour** — so a one-hour alert window at 14.4× pages you when only about 2% of the budget is gone: early enough to act, severe enough to be a real outage rather than noise.
    3. Do the same arithmetic for the slow window — 6× over 6 hours burns 6 × 6 ÷ 720 = 5% of the budget — and note what it is for: steady degradation too slow to page on.

    ```yaml
    groups:
      - name: slo-checkout-availability
        rules:
          - alert: CheckoutAvailabilityFastBurn
            expr: |
              (
                sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{uri="/api/orders", status=~"5.."}[1h]))
                /
                sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{uri="/api/orders"}[1h]))
              ) > 14.4 * 0.001
            labels:
              severity: page
            annotations:
              summary: "Checkout is burning its monthly error budget at 14.4x — ~2% of the budget per hour."
              runbook: docs/runbooks/checkout-availability-burn.md
          - alert: CheckoutAvailabilitySlowBurn
            expr: |
              (
                sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{uri="/api/orders", status=~"5.."}[6h]))
                /
                sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{uri="/api/orders"}[6h]))
              ) > 6 * 0.001
            labels:
              severity: ticket
            annotations:
              summary: "Checkout error budget burning at 6x over 6h — steady degradation, not an outage."
              runbook: docs/runbooks/checkout-availability-burn.md
    ```
    (Adjust the metric name and `uri` label to whatever your [Task 11.2 — Metrics that answer real questions](#task-112--metrics-that-answer-real-questions--3h) dashboards actually use — copy from a query you already trust.)

    *You know it worked when:* no line in `docs/alerts-todo.md` is still an open IOU, and each closed line names the rule that settled it.

- [ ] **Step 6 — A runbook for every alert.**
    *What this step is:* An alert without a runbook is a 3 a.m. guessing game. A runbook is a short document that tells the half-asleep reader what the alert means and exactly what to do — written now, while you are calm and the system is fresh in your head. At the end, every alert from Steps 3–5 has one file in `docs/runbooks/`.
    *Do this:*
    1. For every alert, create `docs/runbooks/<alert>.md` with exactly these sections: **what it means**, **likely causes**, **the first three things to check** (with the exact PromQL query or shell command for each — "check the database" is not a runbook line, `kubectl`-free `docker compose logs postgres --since 10m` is), **how to mitigate**, and **how to escalate**.
    2. Make each rule's `runbook` annotation point at its file, so the firing alert carries the link.
    3. Test one honestly: trigger a fault you know (stop a scheduled job, or pause a Kafka consumer), wait for the alert, then follow your own runbook's three checks *as written* — no improvising — and see whether they actually lead you to the cause. Fix the runbook where they do not.
    *You know it worked when:* a deliberately injected fault fires an alert whose annotation links a runbook, and following that runbook verbatim gets you to the cause.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Set severity and routing deliberately.**
    *What this step is:* Not every alert deserves to wake a human. You now sort every alert into **page** (wake someone now), **ticket** (handle during working hours), or **dashboard-only** (visible, never notifies) — because every alert that fires and gets ignored trains you to ignore the next one, which is alert fatigue, the failure this whole task exists to prevent.
    *Do this:*
    1. Give every rule from Steps 3–5 a `severity` label: `page`, `ticket`, or `dashboard`.
    2. In Alertmanager's config, create one route per severity (locally, each route can simply be a distinct receiver you inspect in the `localhost:9093` UI — you have no PagerDuty, and do not need one to prove the routing).
    3. Say out loud, alert by alert, which ones you would genuinely accept being woken at 3 a.m. for — **if the answer is "all", your alerts are wrong**; demote until the page list contains only alerts where minutes matter.
    4. Record the final page/ticket/dashboard split, with one sentence of justification each, in `docs/slo.md`.
    *You know it worked when:* a fired `page` alert and a fired `ticket` alert land under different routes in the Alertmanager UI, and your page list is short enough to defend out loud.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Split liveness from readiness, and add custom `HealthIndicator`s.**
    *What this step is:* Your services expose one `/actuator/health` endpoint that mixes two different questions. **Liveness** asks "is this process broken and in need of a restart?" — for a Spring service that means "is the JVM alive?", nothing more. **Readiness** asks "can it serve traffic right now?" — which legitimately checks that Kafka, Redis, and the database are reachable. You now split them, because putting a database check in liveness means a database blip restarts every instance — turning a brief degradation into a total outage. At the end, each service has two endpoints answering the two questions separately.
    *Builds on:* [Task F6.9 — Auto-configuration: removing the magic](#task-f69--auto-configuration-removing-the-magic--1h) — where you added Spring Boot Actuator and first met `/actuator/health`.
    *Do this:*
    1. Configure Actuator health *groups* in each service's `application.yml`: the `liveness` group includes only the JVM/process state (`livenessState`, plus disk if you must); the `readiness` group includes the database, Redis, and Kafka indicators.
    2. Add a custom `HealthIndicator` (a small bean implementing Spring's `HealthIndicator` interface, returning `UP`/`DOWN` with details) for any dependency Actuator does not already cover — Kafka reachability is the usual gap.
    3. Prove the split — break it on purpose: stop Postgres, then curl both endpoints. `/actuator/health/readiness` must flip to `DOWN` (stop sending traffic) while `/actuator/health/liveness` stays `UP` (do not restart me).
    4. Write down, in the service's runbook or `docs/slo.md`, *why* mixing them causes restart loops when a dependency blips: the restarter kills a healthy JVM, the replacement comes up, still cannot see the database, gets killed again — and a 30-second blip becomes a rolling outage. This exact trap is what [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h)'s probes will exploit, so the explanation you write now is the one you will reuse there.
    *You know it worked when:* with Postgres stopped, readiness reports `DOWN` while liveness stays `UP` — and you can explain the restart-loop mechanism without notes.

**Done when:** a deliberately injected fault fires the right alert with the right severity, and the runbook you wrote actually leads you to the cause.


**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Define SLI, SLO, and SLA, and say which one you choose and which one you are held to.
2. 99.9% monthly is how many minutes, and what is an error budget actually *for*?
3. Why do burn-rate alerts beat a static error-rate threshold?
4. Why two windows rather than one? What does each catch?
5. Liveness versus readiness: what happens if you put a database check in the liveness probe?
6. Which of your alerts would you genuinely accept being woken at 3 a.m. for? If the answer is all of them, what is wrong?

#### Task 11.5 — Load testing, chaos, and your first postmortem — 6h

**What:** Run a realistic on-sale load test, break things on purpose, hunt down a flaky test the way you will have to on a real team, and write up what you learned.
**Why:** The numbers from this task are what you will quote for the rest of your career, a self-written postmortem is a rare and credible artifact — and every real team is haunted by a flaky test nobody has had the discipline to diagnose. Arriving with that skill already built is a quiet superpower.
**Solves:** having no evidence for any performance claim, and never having diagnosed a flaky test until the day a real one blocks your team's releases.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Virtual user** | k6's simulated client. Ramping VUs is how you build a spike. |
| **Spike test** | A sudden steep ramp, modelling the on-sale moment. Finds what breaks under sudden load. |
| **Soak test** | Moderate load held for hours. Finds what a spike cannot: memory leaks, connection churn, `ThreadLocal` retention, slowly filling disks. |
| **Threshold as gate** | Pass/fail criteria written inside the k6 script, so the load test fails the build rather than producing a graph someone interprets optimistically. |
| **Saturation point** | The load at which some resource runs out and latency turns sharply upward. Knowing yours, and which resource it was, is the whole output of this exercise. |
| **Bottleneck iteration** | Measure, find the limiting resource, fix it, measure again — and the bottleneck moves somewhere new. Two or three documented rounds of this is the real deliverable. |
| **Chaos engineering** | Deliberately breaking things to learn how the system behaves, in controlled conditions, while you are watching. |
| **Blameless postmortem** | A write-up attacking the system rather than the person. It matters because a culture that assigns blame gets fewer honest postmortems and therefore learns less. |
| **Five whys** | Asking why repeatedly until you reach a cause worth fixing. "The pod restarted" is not a root cause; "the liveness probe checked a dependency" is. |
| **Flaky test** | A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change in between. It is never "just unlucky" — either the test makes a hidden assumption (about time, ordering, or speed) or the code genuinely has a race. Both are worth finding. |
| **Quarantine (a test)** | Moving a flaky test out of the blocking build (into a separate tag or CI job) the day it first flakes, so it stops blocking the team — on the strict condition that it is diagnosed within the week and then fixed or deleted. Quarantine without a deadline is deletion in slow motion. |
| **Retried-until-green** | Configuring the build to rerun a failing test and accept the result if any attempt passes. It feels pragmatic and it is poison: the test still catches the bug on some runs, and you have told the build to ignore it when it does. Retries teach the suite to lie. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** writing a **blameless** postmortem — attacking the system rather than yourself. "There was no mechanism requiring a timeout" has a fix that works; "I forgot" does not.
- **When it works you will see:** two genuine write-ups in `docs/postmortems/`, each with a timeline, a five-whys, and at least one action item of type *detect*.
- **Where people get stuck:** action items that are all "be more careful". If the only outcome is increased vigilance, you have not learned anything durable. Aim for a default, a template, or a lint rule.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Write the four k6 traffic scenarios.**
    *What this step is:* You script the realistic traffic shapes this platform must survive, as k6 scenarios (k6 is the JavaScript load-testing tool that has been your only "client" since [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline)). At the end, `load/` holds four runnable scenarios modelling the on-sale day.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — where k6 was introduced, `load/` got its first scenarios, and you recorded the baseline numbers these runs will be compared against. [Task 5.3 — Idempotency as a reusable platform capability](#task-53--idempotency-as-a-reusable-platform-capability--4h) — the `Idempotency-Key` mechanism your checkout scenario must exercise, so retried requests do not create duplicate orders.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `load/`, create `browse.js` — constant moderate load on search and event-detail, the read-only 95% of real traffic.
    2. Create `on-sale-spike.js` — a ramp from **50 to 5,000 virtual users in 30 seconds**, modelling the moment tickets go on sale; use a `ramping-vus` executor stage of 30 s.
    3. Create `checkout.js` — the full purchase flow, with each logical purchase sending a fresh `Idempotency-Key` header (and the occasional deliberate retry of the *same* key, which must not double-charge).
    4. Create `scan-rush.js` — a burst against the ticket-scan endpoint, modelling gate staff scanning thousands of QR codes in minutes when venue doors open (step 12 of the user journey, served by `inventory-service`).
    5. Smoke-run each one briefly (low VUs, one minute) to prove the script itself works before any real measurement.
    *You know it worked when:* all four scripts complete a short run with 0% script errors — failures, when they come later, should be the system's, not the test's.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Write the soak scenario and schedule its unattended run.**
    *What this step is:* A soak test is moderate load held for hours — it finds what a spike cannot: memory leaks, connection churn, `ThreadLocal` retention, slowly filling disks. You script it now and plan to run it while you are away from the desk. This is also how this task's six-hour budget fits its own contents: the soak's **two hours are wall-clock, not desk time** — the same trick [Phase 12](#phase-12-deliverables)'s long JMH runs will use (JMH is the Java microbenchmark harness you will meet there).
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `load/soak.js`: **2 hours at moderate load** (roughly your browse + occasional checkout mix — well below the spike, well above idle), designed to expose leaks and connection churn rather than saturation.
    2. Plan the unattended run: start it before dinner, leave the stack and Prometheus running, and read the graphs afterwards (Step 7 is that reading).
    *You know it worked when:* `load/soak.js` exists, runs clean in a 2-minute smoke run, and you have an actual plan (a time this week) for the full 2-hour run.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Put pass/fail thresholds inside the scripts.**
    *What this step is:* A load test whose output is a graph gets interpreted optimistically; a load test with thresholds is a **gate** — it exits non-zero and fails the build when the numbers are bad. You now define pass/fail criteria inside the k6 scripts themselves, so the verdict is the tool's, not your mood's.
    *Builds on:* [Task 11.4 — SLOs, alerting, and runbooks](#task-114--slos-alerting-and-runbooks--2h) — where you wrote `docs/slo.md`; the thresholds here are those same targets, enforced by the load tool.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a `thresholds` block to each scenario's `options`, mirroring the SLOs — for example in `checkout.js`:
    ```javascript
    export const options = {
      thresholds: {
        http_req_failed:   ['rate<0.001'],   // checkout availability 99.9%
        http_req_duration: ['p(99)<800'],    // checkout p99 < 800 ms
      },
    };
    ```
    2. Use the matching numbers for the others (search p99 < 200 ms in `browse.js`, and sensible failure-rate gates in `scan-rush.js` and `soak.js`).
    3. Prove the gate gates: temporarily set an absurd threshold (`p(99)<1`), run, and watch k6 finish with a non-zero exit code; then restore the real values.
    *You know it worked when:* `echo $?` after a deliberately failed run prints non-zero — the test can fail a build without a human reading a graph.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Run the spike and iterate on the bottleneck.**
    *What this step is:* This is the heart of the task: the measure → find the limiting resource → fix → re-measure loop. You run the on-sale spike with every dashboard open, watch which resource saturates first (the saturation point — where some resource runs out and latency turns sharply upward), fix the top bottleneck, and run again — and the bottleneck moves somewhere new. **Two or three documented iterations of this loop are the whole deliverable**, not the final number.
    *Builds on:* [Task 11.2 — Metrics that answer real questions](#task-112--metrics-that-answer-real-questions--3h) — the RED/USE Grafana dashboards you watch during the run. [Task 11.3 — Distributed tracing](#task-113--distributed-tracing--3h) — the traces that tell you *where inside a slow request* the time went. [Task 3.4 — Transactions, MVCC, locking, and connection pooling](#task-34--transactions-mvcc-locking-and-connection-pooling--6h) — the Hikari pool that is a prime suspect. [Task 7.2 — Thread pools done properly](#task-72--thread-pools-done-properly--4h) — the bounded executors that are the other prime suspect.
    *Do this:*
    1. Open the RED dashboards, the Hikari pool panel, and the thread-pool panels side by side, then run `k6 run load/on-sale-spike.js`.
    2. Record which resource saturated **first** — expect database connections or a thread pool — identified by the saturation signal (pool usage pinned at max, queue depth climbing, latency hockey-sticking) rather than by guesswork; pull one slow trace to confirm where the time went.
    3. Fix only the top bottleneck (pool size, a missing index, a serial remote call — whatever the evidence says), and note the before number.
    4. Re-run the identical spike and record the after number — and the *new* first-saturating resource, because the bottleneck will have moved.
    5. Repeat for two or three total iterations, keeping per-round notes (bottleneck, change, number) — Step 8 turns them into the report.
    *You know it worked when:* you have at least two completed rounds, each with a named bottleneck, a specific change, and a before/after number.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Break it on purpose: the chaos round.**
    *What this step is:* Chaos engineering means deliberately breaking things in controlled conditions, while you are watching, to learn how the system actually behaves. You now injure every major dependency in turn, record the user-visible result, and fix anything unacceptable. At the end, the [Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline) chaos matrix is fully filled in.
    *Builds on:* [Task 10.4 — Resilience4j on every remote call](#task-104--resilience4j-on-every-remote-call--4h) — where you started `docs/chaos-matrix.md`, put toxiproxy (the proxy that injects latency and failures on demand) in front of each dependency, and wrote the timeouts and circuit breakers this round now stress-tests.
    *Do this:*
    1. With moderate k6 load running and dashboards open, inject each fault in turn: **kill the Postgres primary** (`docker compose stop` its container), **kill Redis**, **pause Kafka** (`docker compose pause` — the broker freezes but the port stays open, a nastier failure than a clean kill), **add 500 ms latency to the payment provider** (via `toxiproxy-cli`, as in [Task 10.4 — Resilience4j on every remote call](#task-104--resilience4j-on-every-remote-call--4h)), **fill the disk** (e.g. `docker exec` into a container and `dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/fill bs=1M` until the volume is full), and **OOM one service instance** (lower its container memory limit until the JVM is killed).
    2. For each, record the observed user-visible behaviour in the [Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline) chaos matrix (`docs/chaos-matrix.md`) — what the customer saw, how long until recovery, which alert fired.
    3. Fix any unacceptable behaviour — any cell reading "500 for everything" is a bug, because [Task 10.4 — Resilience4j on every remote call](#task-104--resilience4j-on-every-remote-call--4h) gave every remote call a fallback path; keep at least one genuine failure for Step 6's postmortems.
    *You know it worked when:* every one of the six faults has a filled matrix cell, and no cell reads "500 for everything".

- [ ] **Step 6 — Write two blameless postmortems.**
    *What this step is:* A postmortem is the write-up a team produces after an incident; *blameless* means it attacks the system, not the person — "there was no mechanism requiring a timeout" has a fix that works, "I forgot" does not. You write two, for genuine failures you caused in Steps 4–5. A self-written postmortem is a rare and credible interview artifact.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/postmortems/`, one file per incident, each with exactly these sections: **impact** (who saw what, for how long), **timeline** (timestamped, from your logs and dashboards), **root cause with a five-whys** (ask why repeatedly until the cause is worth fixing — "the pod restarted" is not a root cause; "the liveness probe checked a dependency" is), **what went well**, **what did not**, and **action items with owners** (the owner is you, but write the column anyway — it is the format real teams use).
    2. Make at least one action item of type *detect* (an alert or dashboard change that would catch the recurrence) — and ban "be more careful" items: if the only outcome is increased vigilance, aim instead for a default, a template, or a lint rule.
    3. Re-read both for blame: every sentence that names you as the cause gets rewritten to name the missing mechanism.
    *You know it worked when:* two write-ups exist, each with a timeline, a five-whys, and at least one *detect* action item — and neither contains the phrase "be more careful" or any equivalent.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Read the soak results for slow leaks.**
    *What this step is:* The 2-hour soak from Step 2 has run; now you read its graphs for the slow-motion failures a spike can never show. At the end you have written findings — even "no leak found" is a finding, but look hard, because [Phase 12](#phase-12-deliverables) will hunt whatever you find here.
    *Builds on:* [Task 7.2 — Thread pools done properly](#task-72--thread-pools-done-properly--4h) — where you learned `ThreadLocal` retention (a pooled thread keeping a previous request's data because nobody cleared it) and built the `TaskDecorator` that is supposed to prevent it.
    *Do this:*
    1. In Grafana, inspect the full 2-hour window for: a **slow heap climb** that GC never fully reclaims (sawtooth floors trending upward), **growing connection counts** (Hikari active/idle, Postgres `pg_stat_activity`, Redis clients — churn or leak), and signs of **`ThreadLocal` retention** (per-request data surviving across requests in logs, or heap dominated by request-scoped objects).
    2. Check the boring one too: disk usage trending upward (logs, Kafka segments) — the "slowly filling disk" from this task's New words.
    3. Write the findings into the load report (Step 8), each with the graph evidence and a one-line hypothesis.
    *You know it worked when:* the report has a soak-findings section where every claim points at a specific graph over the 2-hour window.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Write `docs/benchmarks/load-report.md` with the iteration history.**
    *What this step is:* You assemble the evidence file — the numbers you will quote for the rest of your career. Its core is the **iteration history**: for each Step 4 round, the bottleneck you hit, what you changed, and the number afterwards. That history is the document, not the final figure; it is the evidence that you found bottlenecks by measuring rather than by guessing.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.1 — Realistic data volume and a measured baseline](#task-31--realistic-data-volume-and-a-measured-baseline--2h) — the baseline numbers in `docs/benchmarks/` that make your after-numbers meaningful.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/benchmarks/load-report.md` with: the **spike results** (p50/p95/p99, RPS, error rate, against the thresholds), the **soak results** (Step 7's findings), and the **iteration history** — one row per round: bottleneck, evidence, change, number after.
    2. State the conditions honestly (your laptop, Docker, synthetic k6 traffic), as every benchmark in this plan does — a number without its conditions is not evidence.
    *You know it worked when:* a stranger reading only this file could retell your bottleneck story round by round, with numbers.

- [ ] **Step 9 — Break it on purpose: author two flaky tests.**
    *What this step is:* A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change in between — and it is never "just unlucky": either the test makes a hidden assumption (about time, ordering, or speed) or the code has a real race. The glossary condemns flaky tests in one line; this is where you build the skill of actually hunting one — by planting two on purpose, so you know the ground truth before you practise the diagnosis.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h) — where you made `Clock` an injected port precisely so time-based logic is testable; flake #1 is what happens when code bypasses it. [Task 5.5 — Transactional outbox](#task-55--transactional-outbox--3h) — where you learned Awaitility (`await().atMost(...).untilAsserted(...)`) and killed the assert-immediately-after-async anti-pattern; flake #2 resurrects exactly that anti-pattern.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write the *time-dependent* flake: an integration test that asserts something about "today" by calling `LocalDate.now()` directly instead of using the injected `Clock` from [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h), and seed it with data dated near a day boundary (e.g. an event stamped 23:59 UTC) — it passes or fails depending on *when* it runs, not on what the code does.
    2. Write the *async race*: publish an event and assert the Kafka consumer's side effect **immediately**, with no Awaitility wait — the exact anti-pattern [Task 5.5 — Transactional outbox](#task-55--transactional-outbox--3h) killed — so it passes only when the consumer happens to win the race.
    3. Commit both on a branch, labelled as the drill — you are about to hunt them as if you did not know what they were.
    *You know it worked when:* both tests exist, both pass at least sometimes, and each contains exactly one planted assumption you could name (but will pretend not to know in Step 10).

- [ ] **Step 10 — Hunt them from the outside.**
    *What this step is:* On a real team a flake arrives as a red CI run on someone else's change, and the failure output is all you get at first. You now recreate that: run the suite repeatedly, and diagnose each failure **from its failure output alone** — before you allow yourself to open the test's source code. That constraint is the whole exercise.
    *Do this:*
    1. Run the suite 20 times with a shell loop — something like `for i in $(seq 1 20); do mvn -q test > run-$i.log 2>&1 || echo "run $i FAILED"; done` — and record exactly which runs failed.
    2. For each failing run, read only the log: the assertion message, the stack trace, the timestamps — and write down your diagnosis of the cause *before* opening the test's source.
    3. Notice how the two flakes *smell* different — the time-dependent one fails consistently within a bad window (every run in the window red, every run outside it green), while the race fails a random scattering of runs. Write that contrast down; it is the pattern-recognition you came for.
    4. Only now open the source and check your diagnoses against the planted causes.
    *You know it worked when:* you have the list of failed run numbers, a written output-only diagnosis for each flake, and both diagnoses survived contact with the source code.

- [ ] **Step 11 — Fix both properly and write the team policy.**
    *What this step is:* You repair both flakes the right way, prove determinism with the same 20-run loop, and then write down the team policy for the next flake — because the policy, not the fix, is what you carry to a real team. The policy's enemy is *retried-until-green*: configuring the build to rerun a failing test and accept any pass. It feels pragmatic and it is poison — the test still catches the bug on some runs, and you have told the build to ignore it when it does. Retries teach the suite to lie.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h) — the injected `Clock` is fix #1. [Task 5.5 — Transactional outbox](#task-55--transactional-outbox--3h) — the Awaitility wait is fix #2.
    *Do this:*
    1. Fix the time-dependent test by injecting the `Clock` (the test hands in a fixed one), and the race by adding the Awaitility wait (`await().atMost(...).untilAsserted(...)` on the consumer's side effect).
    2. Rerun the 20-run loop and confirm zero failures — the fixes made the tests deterministic, not merely luckier.
    3. Write the policy into a new `docs/testing-notes.md`: a flaky test is **quarantined the day it flakes** (moved to a separate tag or CI job so it stops blocking the team), **diagnosed within the week, and fixed or deleted** — quarantine without a deadline is deletion in slow motion — and **never retried-until-green**, because retries teach the suite to lie.
    *You know it worked when:* 20 consecutive green runs, and `docs/testing-notes.md` states the quarantine-deadline-fix-or-delete policy and the ban on retries in your own words.

**Done when:** `docs/benchmarks/load-report.md` has spike/soak results with the bottleneck iteration history, two postmortems exist, both deliberately flaky tests were diagnosed from their failure output and properly fixed, and the flaky-test policy is written down in `docs/testing-notes.md`.

**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. What does a soak test find that a spike test never will?
2. Why put pass/fail thresholds inside the k6 script rather than reading the graph afterwards?
3. Describe one complete measure-fix-remeasure loop you ran, with the actual numbers.
4. Which resource saturated first, and did that surprise you? What did you expect?
5. What makes a postmortem blameless, and why does that produce better engineering?
6. Run the five whys on one of your real failures, out loud, to a cause worth fixing.
7. Tell me about a flaky test you diagnosed — the cause, the evidence in its failure output that pointed to it, and the fix. You now have a real story; practise telling it as one.


**Phase 11 exit check — tick honestly:**

- [ ] `make up && make smoke` passes from a cold start, with the new assertions for this phase.
- [ ] One `traceId` query returns the full story of an order across HTTP, a thread pool, Kafka, and two services.
- [ ] My committed dashboards make a deliberately injected failure visible within 30 seconds.
- [ ] One trace shows a complete order saga across four services, including the async hops.
- [ ] Tracing revealed a real problem in my own system and I fixed it, with before/after numbers.
- [ ] Every alert has a runbook, and at least one runbook has actually led me to a cause.
- [ ] I can explain why client-side percentiles cannot be averaged across instances.
- [ ] `docs/postmortems/` holds two genuine write-ups, each with a five-whys.
- [ ] I authored two flaky tests on purpose, diagnosed both from their failure output alone before reading the code, fixed them, and the flaky-test policy is written down in `docs/testing-notes.md`.

**Phase 11 deliverables:** JSON logs with full trace correlation; committed Grafana dashboards; end-to-end traces across async hops; SLOs with burn-rate alerts; a runbook per alert; load and chaos reports; two postmortems; a flaky-test diagnosis drill with a written quarantine policy in `docs/testing-notes.md`.

**Phase 11 interview talking points:** client-side percentiles vs histograms; metric cardinality; how you propagate trace context through Kafka and thread pools; why burn-rate alerts beat static thresholds; liveness vs readiness; a real bottleneck you found and fixed with numbers; a flaky test you diagnosed from its failure output — cause, evidence, fix.
