10. A build needs a token for a private Maven repository. Why is `ARG TOKEN` wrong, where exactly does it leak, and what do you use instead?

#### Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing — 16h

**What:** Deploy the full stack to a local kind cluster (kind — Kubernetes-in-Docker: a real, conformant local cluster whose nodes are Docker containers) using raw manifests first — then move observability into the cluster, because a cluster you cannot see into is not deployed, it is abandoned.
**Why:** Starting with Helm hides what the objects actually do. Write the YAML once by hand and the abstractions make sense forever.
**Solves:** "Kubernetes works by magic", which collapses the moment a pod is in `CrashLoopBackOff` — and the quieter failure where everything *seems* fine because nothing is measuring it any more.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Pod** | The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network namespace. You rarely create one directly. |
| **Deployment** | Declares the desired state; it creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pods. Rolling updates work by shifting Pods between two ReplicaSets. |
| **Service** | A stable name and virtual IP in front of a changing set of Pods. `ClusterIP` is internal only, `NodePort` opens a port on every node, `LoadBalancer` asks the cloud for one. |
| **Ingress** | HTTP routing into the cluster. `ingress-nginx` is literally Nginx, so your [Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline) knowledge transfers directly — the same directives, expressed as annotations. |
| **`startupProbe`** | Protects a slow starter. Until it passes, liveness is not checked at all — which is how you give a JVM 60 seconds to boot without a generous liveness timeout forever after. |
| **`readinessProbe`** | Can this pod serve traffic right now? Failing removes it from the Service endpoints but does **not** restart it. |
| **`livenessProbe`** | Is this pod broken beyond recovery? Failing restarts it. Never check a dependency here — if the database blips, every pod restarts simultaneously and a brief degradation becomes a full outage. |
| **Requests vs limits** | A request is what the scheduler reserves; a limit is the hard ceiling. Requests decide placement, limits decide throttling and killing. |
| **QoS class** | `Guaranteed` (requests equal limits), `Burstable` (requests below limits), `BestEffort` (neither). Under node pressure, BestEffort is evicted first and Guaranteed last. |
| **CPU throttling** | Exceeding a CPU limit does not kill you, it *slows* you — visible only in `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total`. This is why latency can be terrible while CPU usage looks modest. |
| **`preStop`** | A hook that runs before SIGTERM. A short sleep here gives the control plane time to remove the pod from the Service endpoints before the process starts shutting down — the same race as Phase 10, one layer up. |
| **`StatefulSet`** | For workloads needing stable identity, ordered rollout, and per-pod storage — databases, Kafka. The honest production answer is usually a managed service instead. |
| **Helm** | A package manager for Kubernetes: a *chart* bundles the YAML for a whole system, and `helm install` applies it in one move. [Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies](#task-133--scaling-configuration-and-deployment-strategies--8h) teaches Helm properly — in this task you only run install commands for ready-made charts. |
| **Operator / Strimzi** | An *operator* is a controller that runs and manages a stateful system inside Kubernetes for you, doing the work a human admin otherwise would. **Strimzi** is the Kafka operator used in this phase; Bitnami's plain Helm charts are the simpler route used here for Postgres and Redis. |
| **`NetworkPolicy`** | Firewall rules between pods. Default-deny plus explicit allows is the only configuration worth having. One sharp truth: a `NetworkPolicy` is a *request to the CNI*, not a guarantee — if the cluster's network plugin does not enforce policies, Kubernetes accepts the object, `kubectl` shows it looking healthy, and traffic flows straight through it with no error anywhere. |
| **CNI** | Container Network Interface — the cluster's network plugin, the component that actually moves packets between pods and therefore the thing that implements (or silently ignores) your `NetworkPolicy` objects. kind's built-in CNI (kindnet) only began enforcing NetworkPolicy in kind v0.23 (May 2024); heavier CNIs such as Cilium or Calico have always enforced it, and add richer policy on top. |
| **kube-prometheus-stack** | A Helm chart that installs the whole in-cluster monitoring kit in one move: Prometheus, Grafana, kube-state-metrics and node-exporter, already wired together. The standard way to make a cluster observable without assembling five parts by hand — and it runs entirely on your laptop's kind cluster, like everything else in this plan. |
| **kube-state-metrics** | A small service that turns Kubernetes *object state* — pod restarts, replica counts, pending pods — into Prometheus metrics. Without it, "how many times did this pod restart?" has no metric at all; `kubectl` can tell you, but nothing can alert on it. |
| **cAdvisor** | The per-container stats collector built into the kubelet on every node. It is where container CPU and memory metrics — including the throttling counter above — are actually born. Only a Prometheus running inside the cluster can scrape it, which is the whole reason for the observability move in this task. |
| **DaemonSet** | "Run exactly one copy of this pod on every node." The natural shape for node-level agents — here, the log shipper that reads every pod's log files off the node and sends them to Loki. |
| **Replication factor** | How many brokers hold a copy of each partition. `replication.factor=3` means every record lands on three brokers — lose one broker and nothing is lost. Until now you ran a single broker, so this number was silently 1 and a dead broker meant dead data. |
| **ISR (in-sync replicas)** | The copies of a partition that are currently caught up with the leader. With `acks=all`, the leader only confirms a write once at least `min.insync.replicas` of those copies have it — that is the actual durability guarantee, not the replication factor on its own. |
| **Leader election** | When the broker leading a partition dies, one of the in-sync followers takes over as the new leader. Producers and consumers find the new leader automatically — it looks like a brief hiccup, not an outage. |
| **UnderReplicatedPartitions** | The broker metric that says "some copies are missing right now". The first Kafka alert any real team pages on, because it means you are one more failure away from losing data. |
| **kube-apiserver** | The cluster's front door and the only component anyone ever talks to — kubectl, controllers and kubelets alike all read and write through it. |
| **etcd** | The database of desired state. Everything you `kubectl apply` is stored here, and the rest of the cluster works to make reality match what it says. |
| **kube-scheduler** | Decides *where* each new Pod runs — which node — using requests, taints and affinity. It only places; the kubelet does the starting. |
| **controller-manager** | The reconciliation engines in one process: the Deployment, ReplicaSet, Job and other controllers, each forever comparing desired state with actual state and fixing the difference. |
| **kube-proxy** | Runs on every node and programs that node's Service routing rules. A Service's virtual IP works because kube-proxy wrote forwarding rules on the node your traffic starts from — not because anything is listening on that IP. |
| **CoreDNS** | The cluster's DNS server, running as ordinary pods in `kube-system`. When a pod looks up `catalog-service`, CoreDNS answers. |
| **kubelet** | The node agent — the one piece that is not a pod. It watches the apiserver for Pods assigned to its node, pulls their images, starts their containers, and keeps reporting their state. |
| **Reconciliation** | The loop every controller runs: compare desired state (what etcd says) with actual state (what exists), fix the difference, repeat forever. You will watch it happen in this task. |
| **metrics-server** | The component that answers `kubectl top` and the HPA's CPU and memory questions. It is not Prometheus, and kind does not ship it — until you install it, `kubectl top` fails with "Metrics API not available". |
| **Endpoints** | The live list of pod IPs currently behind a Service, maintained from readiness. `kubectl get endpoints` shows exactly who would receive traffic right now. |
| **FQDN** | A service's fully qualified in-cluster name: `catalog-service.zenith.svc.cluster.local` reads *service*.*namespace*.svc.*cluster domain*. The short name works inside the same namespace; a cross-namespace call needs more of the name. |
| **Headless Service** | A Service with `clusterIP: None`: DNS returns the pod IPs themselves instead of one virtual IP — how stateful clients address a *specific* replica such as `postgres-0`. |
| **ExternalName** | A Service that is only a DNS alias to a name outside the cluster — no virtual IP, no endpoints, just a CNAME. |
| **securityContext** | Pod and container YAML that pins down what the process may do at runtime: which user it runs as, whether the root filesystem is writable, which kernel capabilities it keeps. The manifest twin of Task 13.1's image hardening. |
| **Pod Security Standards** | Three built-in policy levels — `privileged`, `baseline`, `restricted` — that the cluster enforces per namespace via a label. Under `restricted`, a pod that runs as root is rejected at creation, with a message naming the broken rule. |
| **PV / PVC / StorageClass** | A PersistentVolume is an actual piece of disk; a PersistentVolumeClaim is a workload's request for one; a StorageClass is the factory that makes PVs on demand. A PVC is a claim ticket; the StorageClass is the factory. kind ships the `local-path` provisioner, which hands out directories on the node's own disk. |
| **Access modes** | What a volume permits: `ReadWriteOnce` (one node), `ReadOnlyMany`, `ReadWriteMany` (many nodes). Databases want ReadWriteOnce. |
| **Taint / toleration** | A taint is the *node refusing* pods ("stay away unless you tolerate this"); a toleration is a pod accepting it. How real clusters fence off GPU or spot nodes. |
| **Affinity / anti-affinity** | The *pod preferring*: run me with these pods (affinity) or away from them (anti-affinity) — the tool for spreading replicas across nodes. Keep the split straight: the taint is the node refusing, affinity is the pod preferring. |
| **Ephemeral debug container** | A container `kubectl debug` attaches to a *running* pod, sharing its namespaces, so you can bring a shell and tools to an image that deliberately has none. The answer to "how do you debug distroless". |
| **CRD / operator, revisited** | A CustomResourceDefinition teaches the apiserver a new noun — after Strimzi installs its CRDs, `kind: Kafka` is a real object on your cluster. An *operator* (the Operator row above, now made precise) is a CRD plus the controller that reconciles objects of that kind — the same control loop, running on a type Kubernetes was not born with. |
| **Role / RoleBinding** | A Role is a named list of permissions in a namespace ("may get and list pods"); a RoleBinding attaches it to someone — usually a ServiceAccount. ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding are the cluster-wide forms. |
| **`restartPolicy`** | What the kubelet does when a container exits — `Always` for anything a Deployment runs. Each successive crash doubles the wait before the next try: 10s → 20s → 40s → … capped at 5 minutes. That doubling is the "BackOff" in `CrashLoopBackOff`, and the arithmetic behind a forty-second blip taking eleven minutes to recover. |
| **kubeconfig / context** | The file — `~/.kube/config` — where kubectl's cluster addresses and credentials live; a *context* is one cluster-plus-user pair, and `kind create cluster` added yours. `kubectl config get-contexts` lists them; this file is how one kubectl talks to many clusters. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** writing the YAML **by hand** before touching Helm. Helm templating an object you do not understand is how Kubernetes stays magic, and magic fails badly at 3 a.m.
- **When it works you will see:** the full stack running on a local kind cluster from manifests you wrote, and you diagnosing `CrashLoopBackOff` and `OOMKilled` from memory.
- **Where people get stuck:** a liveness probe that checks the database. A brief database blip then restarts every pod simultaneously, startup also needs the database so it fails too, and a forty-second blip becomes an eleven-minute outage. Cause it on purpose, then fix it.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Create the kind cluster and install ingress-nginx.**
    *What this step is:* kind runs a real, conformant Kubernetes cluster on your laptop where each "node" is a Docker container. You create a multi-node cluster whose control-plane node is prepared for ingress (HTTP routing into the cluster), install the `ingress-nginx` controller, and look at the kubeconfig file kubectl now uses to talk to it. At the end you have a running local cluster and know where its credentials live.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.1 — Local infrastructure in one command](#task-01--local-infrastructure-in-one-command--3h) — you installed `kind`, `kubectl` and `helm` there, precisely so this phase is about the work and not installation; [§5.2 — Your machine, and how to not melt it](#52-your-machine-and-how-to-not-melt-it) — its kind sizing applies now (give OrbStack 8 CPUs and 16 GB; run a 3-node cluster); [Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline) — your Nginx knowledge applies directly to the ingress controller: `ingress-nginx` is literally Nginx, the same directives expressed as annotations.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write a kind config with one ingress-ready control-plane node (the standard `kindest` ingress setup: a node label plus port mappings for 80/443) and two workers, then `kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml`.
    2. Install `ingress-nginx` (the kind-flavoured manifest or Helm chart).
    3. One housekeeping fact while the cluster is fresh: `kind create cluster` just wrote a *context* into `~/.kube/config` — the file where kubectl's cluster addresses and credentials live; a context is one cluster-plus-user pair. Run `kubectl config get-contexts` and `kubectl config current-context` to see it (the kubeconfig row in the New words table says what that file is).
    *You know it worked when:* `kubectl get nodes` lists three nodes `Ready`, the ingress-nginx controller pod is `Running`, and `kubectl config current-context` names your kind cluster.

- [ ] **Step 2 — The cluster's anatomy, by observation.**
    *What this step is:* Before writing any YAML, meet the thing you just created. Kubernetes' own control machinery runs as ordinary pods in the `kube-system` namespace — you are going to find each one and say its job out loud. These seven names are half of every Kubernetes interview.
    *Do this:*
    1. Run `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` and find each resident, saying its one-line job out loud: **kube-apiserver** (the cluster's front door — the only thing anyone, kubectl included, ever talks to), **etcd** (the database of desired state), **kube-scheduler** (decides *where* pods go), **controller-manager** (the reconciliation engines), **kube-proxy** (one per node, programming Service routing on that node), and **CoreDNS** (the cluster's DNS server).
    2. Note that they are all just pods — and that the one piece that is *not* a pod is the **kubelet**, the node agent that actually pulls images and starts containers.
    *You know it worked when:* you can name all seven components and their one-line jobs from memory, with the kubectl output closed.

- [ ] **Step 3 — THE interview question, answered by doing it.**
    *What this step is:* "What happens when you run `kubectl apply`?" is the single most common Kubernetes interview question, and you answer it by watching it happen. `kubectl apply` is just HTTP to the kube-apiserver — nothing more — and everything after that is the components from Step 2 doing their jobs in a chain. Run this drill the moment your first Deployment manifest exists (you write it in Step 6).
    *Builds on:* Step 2's kube-system tour — every actor in the chain is one you just met.
    *Do this:*
    1. Apply your first Deployment manifest with verbose logging: `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --v=7`, and READ the output: those lines are REST calls — HTTP verbs, paths, response codes.
    2. Narrate the chain that follows, pointing at each actor from the tour: the apiserver validates the object and writes the desired state to etcd → the deployment controller makes a ReplicaSet → the ReplicaSet controller makes Pods → the scheduler assigns each Pod to a node → that node's kubelet pulls the image and starts the containers → kube-proxy updates Service routing.
    3. Write that chain from memory into `docs/runbooks/k8s-triage.md` — it is the runbook's first entry, because every triage walks some part of it.
    *You know it worked when:* the chain is in the runbook, written without looking anything up, and you can recite it out loud.

- [ ] **Step 4 — The reconciliation loop, felt.**
    *What this step is:* Reconciliation is the loop every controller runs: compare desired state (what etcd says) with actual state (what exists), fix the difference, repeat forever. You are going to trigger it both ways and watch it work.
    *Builds on:* Step 3's Deployment — the object whose desired state you are about to fight with.
    *Do this:*
    1. `kubectl delete pod` one of your Deployment's pods and watch it come back in seconds (`kubectl get pods -w`). Nothing "restarted" it: you changed *actual* state, but the *desired* state in etcd still said two replicas, and the ReplicaSet controller reconciled the difference.
    2. Scale the Deployment to 5 (`kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=5`) and watch the same loop run the other way.
    3. Say the sentence to own, because it is the entire system in one line: **Kubernetes is a control loop driving actual state toward desired state — everything else is detail.**
    *You know it worked when:* you watched a deleted pod resurrect and a scale-up fan out, and you can explain both as the same loop running in different directions.

- [ ] **Step 5 — Install metrics-server now, before anything needs it.**
    *What this step is:* metrics-server is the component that answers `kubectl top` and the autoscaler's CPU and memory questions. It is not Prometheus, and stock kind does not ship it — until you install it, `kubectl top` fails with "Metrics API not available". Installing it now removes a wall you would otherwise hit later.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies](#task-133--scaling-configuration-and-deployment-strategies--8h) reads from it too — its CPU-based autoscaling (HPA) queries this exact component, so skipping this step plants a wall you will hit there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Install metrics-server with Helm, adding the args kind needs: `--kubelet-insecure-tls` (because kind's kubelets use self-signed certificates that metrics-server would otherwise refuse).
    2. Verify: `kubectl top pods` and `kubectl top nodes` return real numbers.
    *You know it worked when:* both `kubectl top` commands print CPU and memory figures instead of "Metrics API not available".

- [ ] **Step 6 — Write the raw manifests, one object at a time.**
    *What this step is:* This is the heart of the task: hand-written YAML for one service, so every object is something you understand rather than something a tool generated. A manifest is a YAML file describing one Kubernetes object's desired state. At the end, your service runs on the cluster from files you wrote.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.1 — Production-grade container images](#task-131--production-grade-container-images--6h) — the hardened image you built there is what these manifests deploy (load it into kind with `kind load docker-image`, since the cluster cannot see your local Docker images otherwise).
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `deploy/k8s/` and write raw manifests for one service, understanding each object as you write it: `Namespace` (a named compartment for the app's objects), `Deployment` (and the `ReplicaSet` it creates — run `kubectl get rs` and see it), `Service` (ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer, and what `kube-proxy` does with each), `Ingress` (the HTTP route in from outside), `ConfigMap` (non-secret config as an object), `Secret` (the base64-encoded sibling), `ServiceAccount` (the identity the pod runs as).
    2. Apply them, and for each object run `kubectl describe` on it once, reading what the cluster filled in.
    *You know it worked when:* `curl` through the Ingress reaches your service, and you can say in one line what each of the seven object kinds is for, without notes.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Probes, tuned for Spring Boot.**
    *What this step is:* Kubernetes asks your pod three different questions, through three probes. `startupProbe` protects a slow starter — until it passes, liveness is not checked at all, which is how you give a JVM 60 seconds to boot without a generous liveness timeout forever after. `readinessProbe` asks "can this pod serve traffic right now?" — failing removes it from the Service endpoints but does **not** restart it. `livenessProbe` asks "is this pod broken beyond recovery?" — failing restarts it.
    *Builds on:* [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline) — the actuator health endpoints these probes call were wired there, including the separate liveness and readiness groups.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a `startupProbe` on `/actuator/health` with a generous `failureThreshold` (JVM start is slow — budget a minute or more).
    2. Add a `readinessProbe` on `/actuator/health/readiness` and a `livenessProbe` on `/actuator/health/liveness`.
    3. Roll out and confirm the pod passes startup, then readiness, then serves traffic.
    *You know it worked when:* `kubectl describe pod` shows all three probes configured, the pod reaches `Ready` without a single liveness failure during boot, and you can state from memory what happens when each probe fails.

- [ ] **Step 8 — Break it on purpose: the liveness probe that checks the database.**
    *What this step is:* The classic Kubernetes incident, demonstrated on your own cluster. Never check a dependency in a liveness probe — if the database blips, every pod fails liveness simultaneously, all of them restart, startup also needs the database so it fails too, and a forty-second blip becomes an eleven-minute outage. This is the best Kubernetes story you can tell.
    *Builds on:* Step 7's probes — you are about to mis-point one of them deliberately.
    *Do this:*
    1. Point the liveness probe at a health check that includes the database.
    2. Take the database down and watch (`kubectl get pods -w`): every pod restart-loops, and a dependency blip turns into a total outage.
    3. Fix it: liveness back to `/actuator/health/liveness` (process-only), readiness keeps the dependency awareness — a pod that cannot reach the database should stop *receiving traffic*, not be *killed*.
    *You know it worked when:* you caused the outage, watched it, fixed it, and can narrate the whole chain — blip, simultaneous restarts, startup failures, backoff — from memory.

- [ ] **Step 9 — Requests and limits, from measured numbers.**
    *What this step is:* A request is what the scheduler reserves for a pod; a limit is the hard ceiling. Requests decide placement, limits decide throttling and killing — and the two resources fail differently: exceeding a CPU limit does not kill you, it *slows* you (visible only in the metric `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total`), while exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOMKilled.
    *Builds on:* [Phase 12 deliverables](#phase-12-deliverables) — the measured resource behaviour from your concurrency work is what makes your requests informed numbers instead of guesses; [Task 13.1 — Production-grade container images](#task-131--production-grade-container-images--6h) — you already met OOMKilled and `MaxRAMPercentage` there, at the Docker layer.
    *Do this:*
    1. Set requests from observed usage (what the service actually consumed under load), and set limits deliberately.
    2. Work out your pod's QoS class and write down the eviction order: `Guaranteed` (requests equal limits), `Burstable` (requests below limits), `BestEffort` (neither) — under node pressure, BestEffort is evicted first and Guaranteed last.
    3. Consider running with no CPU limit but a correct CPU request, and write down the trade-off (no throttling cliff, but a noisy pod can eat idle CPU).
    4. One honest note on ordering: the throttling counter `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total` is produced by cAdvisor *inside* the cluster, so you cannot actually query it until the observability move in Step 15 is done — set your numbers now, and come back to verify throttling right after that move.
    *You know it worked when:* `kubectl describe pod` shows your chosen requests/limits and QoS class, and your notes state which limit kills, which throttles, and which metric reveals the throttling.

- [ ] **Step 10 — Graceful termination, end to end.**
    *What this step is:* When Kubernetes replaces a pod during a rolling update, there is a race: the pod can start shutting down *before* every node has stopped sending it traffic. A `preStop` hook (a short sleep that runs before SIGTERM) gives the control plane time to remove the pod from the Service endpoints first. This is the same race you solved at the Nginx layer, now one layer up — and you prove the fix with a load test, not an assertion.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.1 — Production-grade container images](#task-131--production-grade-container-images--6h) — exec-form `ENTRYPOINT` means SIGTERM actually reaches the JVM, which is what makes any of this possible; [Task 10.2 — Load balancing and failover](#task-102--load-balancing-and-failover--3h) — the drain-before-removal race you met behind Nginx is the same race here; [Task 11.5 — Load testing, chaos, and your first postmortem](#task-115--load-testing-chaos-and-your-first-postmortem--6h) — k6, your load generator for the proof.
    *Do this:*
    1. Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` greater than your measured drain time.
    2. Add a `preStop` sleep (a few seconds) so endpoints are removed from the Service before the process starts shutting down.
    3. Set `server.shutdown=graceful` in the Spring config so in-flight requests finish.
    4. Prove zero dropped requests during a rolling update with k6 running: start a steady k6 load, trigger `kubectl rollout restart`, and check the k6 summary for errors.
    *You know it worked when:* the k6 run across a full rolling update reports zero failed requests.

- [ ] **Step 11 — Stateful dependencies in the cluster.**
    *What this step is:* Move Postgres, Redis and Kafka into the cluster. A `StatefulSet` is the workload shape for things that need stable identity, ordered rollout, and per-pod storage — databases and Kafka. Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes (a *chart* bundles the YAML for a whole system; `helm install` applies it in one move — [Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies](#task-133--scaling-configuration-and-deployment-strategies--8h) teaches Helm properly; here you only run install commands for ready-made charts). An *operator* is a controller that runs and manages a stateful system inside Kubernetes for you; **Strimzi** is the Kafka operator used in this phase.
    *Builds on:* [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) — the Kafka you have run in compose since then is what moves in here.
    *Do this:*
    1. Install Postgres and Redis via the Bitnami **Helm** charts.
    2. Install Kafka via the **Strimzi operator** (both terms are in the New words table above) — Strimzi is pinned here, not optional, because the replication drill in Step 17 scales this same Strimzi Kafka to 3 brokers.
    3. Look at what the charts created: `StatefulSet`s and `PersistentVolumeClaim`s (`kubectl get statefulset,pvc`).
    4. Write down why a `StatefulSet` exists (stable identity, ordered rollout, per-pod storage) — and that in production you would use managed services instead, and why (backups, patching, failover and on-call are someone else's full-time job).
    *You know it worked when:* your services connect to the in-cluster Postgres, Redis and Kafka, and the managed-services paragraph is written.

- [ ] **Step 12 — DNS and discovery: how a pod finds a service by name.**
    *What this step is:* Inside the cluster, services find each other by DNS names that CoreDNS answers. A service's full name (FQDN) reads *service*.*namespace*.svc.*cluster domain* — `catalog-service.zenith.svc.cluster.local` — and the short name works only inside the same namespace. You also watch the Endpoints list — the live list of pod IPs currently behind a Service, maintained from readiness.
    *Builds on:* Step 7's probes — you reuse them here to push a pod out of the endpoint list on purpose.
    *Do this:*
    1. Start a throwaway pod with a shell: `kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- sh`, and run `nslookup catalog-service`. It resolves — CoreDNS answered.
    2. Resolve the full name, `catalog-service.zenith.svc.cluster.local`, and name the parts out loud: *service*.*namespace*.svc.*cluster domain*. The short form works because your pod's own namespace is searched first; a cross-namespace call needs the longer form.
    3. Run `kubectl get endpoints catalog-service -w` while you make a pod fail its readiness probe (the probes drill above gave you the tools) — watch its IP leave the list and come back when readiness recovers. That list *is* the Service's truth: readiness decides who is on it, and the preStop race you closed in Step 10 is exactly a pod leaving this list in time.
    *You know it worked when:* both name forms resolve, you can name the FQDN's four parts, and you have watched an IP leave and rejoin the endpoints list live.

- [ ] **Step 13 — What a Service really is: kube-proxy, headless, ExternalName.**
    *What this step is:* One honest paragraph on the routing itself, plus two more Service shapes. A Service is not a process, and nothing listens on its virtual IP — **kube-proxy programs iptables (or IPVS) rules on every node**, so "traffic to this virtual IP goes to one of these pod IPs" is rewritten on the very node that sent the packet. A Service is rules on every node, not a box in the middle.
    *Builds on:* [§5.2 — Your machine, and how to not melt it](#52-your-machine-and-how-to-not-melt-it) — it promised an `ExternalName` bridge for pointing a cluster at services still living in Compose; this is that bridge.
    *Do this:*
    1. Say the kube-proxy paragraph above out loud until it stops sounding strange — nothing listens on a ClusterIP; the rules on your own node rewrite the packet.
    2. Run `kubectl get svc` and find the Postgres StatefulSet's companion Service showing `CLUSTER-IP: None` — a **headless Service** (`clusterIP: None`). `nslookup` it from the busybox pod: DNS returns the pod IPs directly instead of one virtual IP, which is how stateful clients address a *specific* replica like `postgres-0`.
    3. Create one **ExternalName** Service pointing at a name outside the cluster and resolve it — a pure DNS alias (a CNAME, no virtual IP, no endpoints), and exactly the bridge that [Your machine, and how to not melt it](#52-your-machine-and-how-to-not-melt-it) promised for pointing a cluster at services still living in Compose.
    *You know it worked when:* the headless lookup returns pod IPs, the ExternalName lookup returns the outside name, and you can explain why neither needed kube-proxy rules.

- [ ] **Step 14 — Storage mechanics: where your data actually is.**
    *What this step is:* Three objects cooperate to give a pod a disk: a PersistentVolume (PV — an actual piece of disk), a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC — a workload's request for one), and a StorageClass (the factory that makes PVs on demand). The sentence to keep: **a PVC is a claim ticket; the StorageClass is the factory.** You follow one chain end to end and then prove — and break — the StatefulSet's storage promise.
    *Builds on:* Step 11's Postgres StatefulSet — its PVC is the chain you follow.
    *Do this:*
    1. Run `kubectl get pv,pvc,storageclass` and follow one chain end to end: the Postgres PVC (the claim ticket), the PV it is bound to (the actual disk), and the StorageClass that made the PV — kind ships `local-path`, which provisions a directory on the node's own disk, and `docker exec` into the kind node will show you that directory. Your orders are files on a disk, not magic.
    2. Prove the promise: write a marker row into a Zenith table, `kubectl delete pod` the Postgres pod, and watch the replacement pod come up attached to the SAME PVC — the marker row is still there.
    3. Then, on a throwaway PVC (not your database!), delete the PVC itself and watch the data go with it: the claim ticket, not the pod, is what owns the disk.
    *You know it worked when:* you have seen the data directory on the node with your own eyes, the marker row survived a pod delete, and the throwaway data did not survive a PVC delete.

- [ ] **Step 15 — Move observability into the cluster.**
    *What this step is:* Until now Prometheus, Grafana, Loki and Tempo have lived in docker-compose, scraping services they could reach directly, and that was exactly right for Phases 11 and 12. But the moment your services move into kind, that compose stack goes blind — and it goes blind *silently*: no error, just dashboards that quietly stop updating. Metrics are born where the workload lives, so observability follows the workload — the rule to internalise and to say in interviews.
    *Builds on:* [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline) — the compose observability stack and the committed Grafana dashboards you are about to re-point; Step 11's Helm installs — this is the same move.
    *Do this:*
    1. Understand the three separate reasons before fixing them, and write them down: first, cluster metrics such as the CPU-throttling counter are produced by cAdvisor (the per-container stats collector built into the kubelet) inside the cluster, which a Prometheus outside cannot reach; second, object-state facts such as "this pod restarted four times" only become metrics if kube-state-metrics exists — and nothing has installed it; third, pod logs are now files on cluster nodes, and nothing is shipping them to Loki.
    2. Install **kube-prometheus-stack** with Helm — Prometheus, Grafana, kube-state-metrics and node-exporter, already wired together, entirely on your laptop, no cloud account anywhere.
    3. Install a **Promtail (or Grafana Alloy) DaemonSet** (a DaemonSet runs exactly one copy on every node — the natural shape for a log shipper that reads every pod's log files off the node) pointed at your Loki.
    4. Re-point the Grafana dashboards you committed in Phase 11 at the in-cluster Prometheus.
    *You know it worked when:* the in-cluster Grafana loads your Phase 11 dashboards and they are updating — but do not trust it yet; Step 16 is the proof.

- [ ] **Step 16 — Verify the move before building anything on it.**
    *What this step is:* Three checks, one per pillar (metrics, alerts, logs), all mandatory. A monitoring stack you have not tested is a monitoring stack you merely hope works.
    *Builds on:* Step 15's installs; [Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies](#task-133--scaling-configuration-and-deployment-strategies--8h) — its custom-metric HPA and KEDA scaling both work by querying *this* Prometheus, so skipping this verification means hitting an unexplained wall there.
    *Do this:*
    1. *Metrics:* query `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total` in the new Prometheus and get actual data back — this also closes the throttling verification you deferred in Step 9.
    2. *Alerts on object state:* `kubectl delete pod` on one service and watch the restart show up via kube-state-metrics, with one alert firing.
    3. *Logs:* open Grafana, query Loki, and find that same pod's log lines.
    *You know it worked when:* all three checks pass. Only then do you move on.

- [ ] **Step 17 — Break it on purpose: the replication drill a single broker could never teach you.**
    *What this step is:* Every Kafka exercise so far — Phase 6 included — ran one broker, where `min.insync.replicas` can do nothing observable because there is only ever one copy of anything. Replication factor is how many brokers hold a copy of each partition; the ISR (in-sync replicas) are the copies currently caught up; with `acks=all` the leader only confirms a write once at least `min.insync.replicas` copies have it. You scale to 3 brokers and then kill them one at a time to watch each guarantee earn its keep.
    *Builds on:* Step 11's Strimzi Kafka — you are already running Strimzi for the single broker, so this is a size change in one field, fully local on kind; [Task 6.1 — Kafka fundamentals, hands-on](#task-61--kafka-fundamentals-hands-on--3h) — the `kafka-topics.sh` CLI you drive the drill with; [Task 6.6 — CQRS read model and eventual consistency](#task-66--cqrs-read-model-and-eventual-consistency--3h) — the CAP essay you wrote there is about to run live in front of you.
    *Do this:*
    1. Scale your Strimzi Kafka to **3 brokers**, create a topic with `replication.factor=3` and `min.insync.replicas=2`, and start a producer with `acks=all` writing continuously.
    2. **Kill one broker:** watch leader election happen (`kafka-topics.sh --describe` shows the new leader and a shrunken ISR) and watch `UnderReplicatedPartitions` rise — in the in-cluster Prometheus if you have wired Kafka's metrics into it, or simply in the shrinking ISR list if not — while produces *keep succeeding*, because 2 of 3 copies in sync still meets the minimum of 2.
    3. **Kill a second broker:** produces now fail with `NotEnoughReplicas`. That failure is **Kafka choosing consistency over availability** — it would rather refuse your write than accept one it might lose — and you should say that sentence out loud, because it is the CAP essay from [Task 6.6 — CQRS read model and eventual consistency](#task-66--cqrs-read-model-and-eventual-consistency--3h) running live in front of you.
    4. **Restart the brokers** and watch the ISR heal and the under-replicated count fall back to zero, with no data lost and no action from you.
    5. (If you took the descoping lever in [§11 — Weekly cadence and how to not fall behind](#11-weekly-cadence-and-how-to-not-fall-behind) and kept Kafka in compose instead of moving it to Strimzi, the same drill runs against three compose brokers instead — nothing about the lesson changes.)
    *You know it worked when:* you watched all three stages — survived failure, refused writes, self-healing — and can narrate what each one proves about `replication.factor`, ISR and `min.insync.replicas`.

- [ ] **Step 18 — Name the thing you have been doing: CRDs and operators.**
    *What this step is:* A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) teaches the apiserver a new noun — after Strimzi installs its CRDs, `kind: Kafka` is a real object on your cluster. An *operator* is a CRD plus the controller that reconciles objects of that kind — the same control loop you watched in Step 4, running on a type Kubernetes was not born with. You have been operating custom resources without the word.
    *Builds on:* Step 11's Strimzi install — its CRDs are the ones you are about to list; Step 4 — the reconciliation loop that operators reuse; [Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies](#task-133--scaling-configuration-and-deployment-strategies--8h) — the `ExternalSecret` object you will create there is the next custom resource in your life.
    *Do this:*
    1. Run `kubectl get crds` — dozens appear, and the Kafka ones are Strimzi's. `kind: Kafka` is not built-in Kubernetes, and neither is the `ExternalSecret` object you will create in [Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies](#task-133--scaling-configuration-and-deployment-strategies--8h); a CRD is the only reason `kubectl get kafka` works on your cluster and fails on a fresh one.
    2. Recognise what Step 17 was: scaling Kafka to 3 brokers was you editing a custom resource and the Strimzi controller doing the work.
    3. Run `kubectl explain kafka.spec` and watch the apiserver answer questions about a type it only just learned.
    *You know it worked when:* you can define CRD and operator in one sentence each, and name the custom resource you already operate.

- [ ] **Step 19 — Scheduling placement: telling the scheduler where things may go.**
    *What this step is:* Your kind cluster is multi-node, so placement is finally observable. Three mechanisms, three drills: a *taint* is the node refusing pods ("stay away unless you tolerate this"), a *toleration* is a pod accepting it, and *affinity/anti-affinity* is the pod preferring to run with or away from other pods. Keep the split straight: the taint is the node refusing, affinity is the pod preferring.
    *Builds on:* Step 1's multi-node cluster — you need more than one worker for any of this to be visible.
    *Do this:*
    1. **nodeSelector:** label one worker node (`kubectl label node <node> disk=fast`), pin a Deployment to it with `nodeSelector`, then change the selector to a label no node has and watch the pods sit `Pending` — `kubectl describe pod` names the reason, and this is the second everyday cause of `Pending` beside insufficient resources.
    2. **Taints:** `kubectl taint` one worker (`dedicated=batch:NoSchedule`) and watch new pods avoid it until you add the matching toleration — exactly how real clusters fence off GPU or spot nodes. Untaint when done.
    3. **podAntiAffinity:** catalog-service runs 2 replicas — add anti-affinity so they must land on different nodes, and prove it with `kubectl get pods -o wide`. Two replicas on one node is one node failure away from zero replicas; anti-affinity is the fix, and the same reasoning is what keeps your 3 Kafka brokers from secretly sharing a node.
    *You know it worked when:* you caused and diagnosed a selector-`Pending`, watched a taint repel and a toleration admit, and `kubectl get pods -o wide` shows the two replicas on different nodes.

- [ ] **Step 20 — Job and CronJob for migrations and the rollup.**
    *What this step is:* A `Job` runs a pod to completion once; a `CronJob` does it on a schedule. Your two candidates: the Flyway database migration (must run before the new app version starts) and the nightly rollup. You also make a real design decision and defend it.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.10 — Persistence adapter: Flyway migrations and JPA mapping](#task-110--persistence-adapter-flyway-migrations-and-jpa-mapping--1h) — the Flyway migrations being run; [Task 7.3 — Distributed scheduling](#task-73--distributed-scheduling--3h) — the nightly rollup job you built there, now getting a Kubernetes schedule.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write a `Job` for the Flyway migration and a `CronJob` for the nightly rollup, and run both.
    2. Decide: migration as an `initContainer` (a container that runs to completion inside each pod, before the app container starts) or as a pre-upgrade `Job` — with reasoning written down: a Job is better for multi-replica deploys, because an initContainer runs per pod, so three replicas means the migration races itself three times.
    *You know it worked when:* the migration has run exactly once per deploy under your chosen design, the CronJob fires on schedule, and the reasoning paragraph exists.

- [ ] **Step 21 — Break it on purpose: the five failure states, diagnosed until fluent.**
    *What this step is:* Debugging drills. You deliberately cause the five classic pod failure states, then diagnose each one with the standard toolkit until the moves are muscle memory. Every diagnosis goes into the triage runbook.
    *Builds on:* Step 5's metrics-server — `kubectl top` works because you installed it; Step 19 — where you already met the taint-caused variant of `Pending`.
    *Do this:*
    1. Learn the toolkit on your healthy pods first: `kubectl describe` (events are where the answer usually is), `logs -p` for a crashed container, `exec` (works on fat images with a shell — the distroless case is the next step), `port-forward`, `top`, `get events --sort-by`.
    2. Deliberately create and then diagnose each of: `ImagePullBackOff` (misspell the image tag), `CrashLoopBackOff` (run `kubectl get pods -w` and note the restart delays doubling — 10s, 20s, 40s — exactly the `restartPolicy` backoff from the New words table, and the arithmetic behind a forty-second blip becoming the eleven-minute outage in the Step 8 liveness story), `OOMKilled` (memory limit too low), `Pending` (insufficient resources — and you met the taint-caused variant in the placement step), and a failing readiness probe.
    3. Write each diagnosis in `docs/runbooks/k8s-triage.md`: the symptom, the command that revealed the cause, the fix.
    *You know it worked when:* all five states are in the runbook and you can diagnose each from memory, starting from nothing but `kubectl get pods` output.

- [ ] **Step 22 — Break it on purpose: `kubectl debug`, the distroless answer.**
    *What this step is:* Your images are distroless: no shell. So `kubectl exec` has nothing to run — and the fix is an *ephemeral debug container*, a container `kubectl debug` attaches to a running pod, sharing its namespaces, so you can bring a shell and tools to an image that deliberately has none.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.1 — Production-grade container images](#task-131--production-grade-container-images--6h) — you hardened the image by removing the shell; this is how you debug it anyway.
    *Do this:*
    1. `kubectl exec -it` into catalog-service and watch it fail — there is no `sh` to run.
    2. Attach an ephemeral debug container: `kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container>` starts a busybox beside your container, sharing the pod's namespaces, so you can inspect its processes and filesystem with tools the image deliberately refuses to carry. That is the whole point: [Task 13.1 — Production-grade container images](#task-131--production-grade-container-images--6h) hardened the image, and this is how you debug it anyway — say that sentence in interviews.
    3. Add the row to `docs/runbooks/k8s-triage.md`: "exec fails, no shell in image → `kubectl debug`".
    *You know it worked when:* you saw exec fail, got a shell via the debug container, and the runbook row exists.

- [ ] **Step 23 — securityContext and Pod Security Standards: the platform enforcing what 13.1 started.**
    *What this step is:* A `securityContext` is pod/container YAML that pins down what the process may do at runtime; Pod Security Standards are three built-in policy levels (`privileged`, `baseline`, `restricted`) the cluster enforces per namespace via a label. Each securityContext line is a promise the image already keeps — now the *cluster* holds you to it, and then enforces it for everyone.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.1 — Production-grade container images](#task-131--production-grade-container-images--6h) — the non-root `USER` and read-only-filesystem hardening these manifest fields are the twin of; [Task 2.4 — Application security hardening and auditing](#task-24--application-security-hardening-and-auditing--3h) — `docs/security-review.md`, started there, records this posture.
    *Do this:*
    1. Harden one Deployment's YAML with a `securityContext`: `runAsNonRoot: true` (the manifest twin of 13.1's non-root `USER`), `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` plus an `emptyDir` volume mounted at `/tmp` for the scratch space the JVM still needs, `capabilities: {drop: [ALL]}`, and `seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}`.
    2. Make the cluster enforce it for everyone: label the namespace `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted`, deliberately apply a pod that runs as root, and read the rejection — the apiserver refuses it *at creation*, with a message naming the exact rule it broke. Same lesson as Step 25: a security control you have watched reject something is worth ten you merely configured.
    3. Record the posture in `docs/security-review.md`.
    *You know it worked when:* the hardened pod runs, the root-running pod was rejected in front of you with the rule named, and the security review file records both.

- [ ] **Step 24 — RBAC made real: a denial you have watched happen.**
    *What this step is:* A `Role` is a named list of permissions in a namespace ("may get and list pods"); a `RoleBinding` attaches it to someone — usually a `ServiceAccount`, the identity a pod runs as (ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding are the cluster-wide forms). You build least privilege for one real workload and then *prove* it both ways instead of asserting it.
    *Builds on:* Step 20's nightly-rollup `CronJob` — the workload getting the least-privilege identity; [Task 7.3 — Distributed scheduling](#task-73--distributed-scheduling--3h) — where that rollup job was originally built.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create a ServiceAccount for the nightly-rollup `CronJob`, a Role granting only what the job needs, and the RoleBinding joining them.
    2. Prove it both ways: `kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:zenith:rollup-job` answers yes; `kubectl auth can-i delete deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:zenith:rollup-job` answers no.
    3. Attempt the denied action for real to see the `Forbidden` error. Least privilege is not a Role that exists; it is a denial you have watched happen.
    *You know it worked when:* the allowed check says yes, the denied check says no, and you have the real `Forbidden` error in your terminal history.

- [ ] **Step 25 — NetworkPolicy: prove the deny before trusting it.**
    *What this step is:* A `NetworkPolicy` is firewall rules between pods, and default-deny plus explicit allows is the only configuration worth having. But here the *order of proof* is the whole lesson: a NetworkPolicy is a *request to the CNI* (the cluster's network plugin — the component that actually moves packets between pods), not a guarantee. If the CNI does not enforce policies, Kubernetes accepts the object, `kubectl` shows it looking healthy, and traffic flows straight through it with no error anywhere.
    *Builds on:* [Task 2.4 — Application security hardening and auditing](#task-24--application-security-hardening-and-auditing--3h) — `docs/security-review.md`, where this lesson gets written down.
    *Do this:*
    1. **Step 1 of the proof, before trusting any policy: prove your cluster enforces policies at all.** Apply a default-deny-all-ingress policy to one namespace, then `kubectl exec` into a pod and `curl` another pod's ClusterIP. If that call *still succeeds*, your CNI is not enforcing NetworkPolicy — the API accepted your object, `kubectl get networkpolicy` shows it looking perfectly healthy, and it is doing absolutely nothing.
    2. This is not hypothetical — check `kind version` first (see the CNI row in the New words table: kindnet enforces NetworkPolicy only from v0.23). On an older kind (or a cluster built from an older tutorial's config), either upgrade, or create the cluster with `disableDefaultCNI: true` in the kind config and install Cilium with one Helm install — fully local, like everything else here.
    3. **Step 2 of the proof, only after the deny provably denies:** build the real posture — default-deny ingress plus explicit allows for exactly the calls your services make — and prove it both ways: the allowed call succeeds, an un-allowed one times out.
    4. Write the one-sentence lesson into `docs/security-review.md`, because it is interview-grade: *a NetworkPolicy is a request to the CNI, not a guarantee — "our policies turned out to be unenforced" is a real incident class, and proving a security control actually does something before trusting it is the skill this subtask exists to build.*
    *You know it worked when:* you watched the deny actually deny (or caught your CNI not enforcing and fixed it), the allowed call succeeds while the un-allowed one times out, and the lesson sentence is in the security review file.

**Done when:** the full stack runs on kind with observability running beside it — the throttling metric queryable in the in-cluster Prometheus, a pod-restart alert fired on purpose, and pod logs visible in Loki — a rolling update loses zero requests under load, you have watched a 3-broker Kafka lose its leader without losing a write and refuse writes rather than risk them when a second broker died, and you can diagnose all five failure states from memory. Also: you can recite the kubectl-apply chain from apiserver to kube-proxy without notes; `nslookup` resolves catalog-service by both its short name and the full `catalog-service.zenith.svc.cluster.local` form, and you can name the parts; the `restricted`-labelled namespace has rejected a root-running pod in front of you; `kubectl get pods -o wide` shows catalog-service's replicas on different nodes because your anti-affinity put them there; and `kubectl top pods` returns numbers.


**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Name the three probes, say what each is for, and describe what happens when each one fails.
2. Describe the liveness-probe-with-a-database-check outage from start to finish. Why is it so destructive?
3. Name the three QoS classes and the order in which they are evicted.
4. CPU limit versus memory limit: describe the different failure mode of each, and the metric that reveals the CPU one.
5. Your compose Prometheus served Phase 11 perfectly. Name the three separate reasons it goes blind the moment the workloads move into kind, and what fixes each one.
6. Where does a pod's log physically live, and what ships it to Loki? Why is a DaemonSet the right shape for that job?
7. What race is the `preStop` hook closing, and which Phase 10 problem is it the same as?
8. Migrations as a `Job` or as an `initContainer`: which did you choose, and why does replica count decide it?
9. You applied a default-deny `NetworkPolicy` and the cross-pod `curl` still succeeded. What does that tell you, why was there no error anywhere, and what are your two fixes on kind?
10. A pod is stuck `Pending`. Name the first three things you check, with commands.
11. A broker dies in your 3-broker cluster. Describe what happens, in order — to the partitions it was leading, to the ISR, to `UnderReplicatedPartitions`, and to your running `acks=all` producer.
12. Killing the first broker did not stop produces; killing the second did, with `NotEnoughReplicas`. Why the difference, and which side of the CAP trade-off is Kafka taking in that moment?
13. Walk through what happens, component by component, when you run `kubectl apply` on a Deployment — from the HTTP call to the running container.
14. A pod calls `http://catalog-service:8080`. How is that name found — what answers the lookup, and why does the short name work inside the same namespace but not across namespaces?
15. Nothing listens on a Service's virtual IP. What actually forwards the traffic, and where does it run?
16. Taint versus affinity: which one is the node refusing and which is the pod preferring? Give a real use of each.
17. What is a CRD? Name the custom resource you already operate and the one [Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies](#task-133--scaling-configuration-and-deployment-strategies--8h) is about to add — and say who acts on them.
18. `kubectl exec` into catalog-service failed. Why did you build the image that way, and what did you use instead?

#### Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies — 8h

**What:** HPA, KEDA, Helm packaging, and a rehearsed canary plus rollback.
**Why:** Autoscaling on the right signal and having actually rolled back a bad deploy are both strong operational signals.
**Solves:** manual scaling, config duplicated across environments, and risky all-at-once deploys.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **HPA** | HorizontalPodAutoscaler — adds and removes pods based on a metric. CPU out of the box, custom metrics with an adapter. |
| **Custom metric scaling** | Scaling on something that actually correlates with load. CPU is a poor signal for a connection-bound service, which can be at 10,000 connections and 5% CPU while being completely saturated. |
| **KEDA** | Event-driven autoscaling, including on Kafka consumer lag and including scale-to-zero. Lag is the correct signal for a consumer, because it measures the backlog rather than the symptom. |
| **Flapping** | Scaling up and down repeatedly around a threshold. `stabilizationWindowSeconds` damps it. |
| **`PodDisruptionBudget`** | A floor on how many pods may be available during *voluntary* disruption such as a node drain. It does not protect against crashes, only against your own operations. |
| **Helm** | Templated, versioned Kubernetes packaging with per-environment values files and a one-command rollback. |
| **Checksum annotation** | A hash of the ConfigMap placed on the Deployment's pod template. Without it, changing a ConfigMap changes nothing — pods keep the old values until something unrelated triggers a restart. A subtle and very common bug. |
| **Canary** | Running a small number of pods on the new version beside the stable one and comparing error rates before proceeding. |
| **Build once, promote many** | Deploy the *same image digest* to every environment rather than rebuilding per environment. Rebuilding means staging and production ran different bytes, which defeats the purpose of staging. |
| **Secret store** | A system whose entire job is holding secrets: access-controlled, audited, rotatable. Everything a base64 Kubernetes `Secret` is not — a `Secret` only *encodes*, and anyone who can read the object can decode it with one command. |
| **Vault dev mode** | HashiCorp Vault running locally in a single container with no unseal ceremony — it starts already unlocked, keeps everything in memory, and prints an all-powerful root token at startup. Fine for learning, never for production, and you should be able to say why: nothing survives a restart, nothing is sealed, and one token opens everything. |
| **External Secrets Operator (ESO)** | A controller that syncs secrets *from* a store (Vault here) *into* ordinary Kubernetes `Secret`s. Pods keep their normal env-var and volume mounting while the store stays the single source of truth — delete the k8s `Secret` and ESO quietly recreates it. |
| **Rotation** | Changing a credential while everything keeps working. The hard part is never the change itself — it is the order of operations, because at every instant during the change something is still using the old value. |
| **Namespace** | A named slice of the cluster with its own RBAC, quotas and DNS suffix. You have been *using* one as a label since [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h); here it becomes a governed boundary. |
| **ResourceQuota** | A hard cap on what an entire namespace may consume in total — CPU, memory, pod count. The apiserver refuses anything that would cross the line. This is how platform teams stop one team eating the cluster. |
| **LimitRange** | Per-container defaults and bounds inside a namespace. A container that declares no requests gets the defaults injected, so nothing lands in `BestEffort` by accident. |
| **Admission controller** | A gatekeeper the apiserver consults *before* persisting an object — it can reject or mutate what you apply. Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper are the policy engines teams build on top of it. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** scaling on the **right signal**. CPU is the wrong metric for a Kafka consumer; consumer lag is the right one, which is exactly what KEDA is for.
- **When it works you will see:** a rolling update under k6 load dropping zero requests, and KEDA scaling consumers on lag during a spike.
- **Where people get stuck:** the checksum annotation. You change a ConfigMap, nothing restarts, and pods keep serving stale config until some unrelated rollout picks it up days later — which looks exactly like "my change did nothing". The annotation in the New words table is the cure; wire it in from the start. The other classic: scaling a Kafka consumer on CPU instead of lag, so the backlog grows while CPU sits low and the HPA sees no reason to act.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Your first autoscaler: HPA on CPU.**
    *What this step is:* A `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` (HPA) is a Kubernetes object that watches one metric and adds or removes pods to keep that metric near a target you set. You start with CPU because it works out of the box — no extra install, no custom wiring — which makes it the right place to see the mechanism before you argue with it. At the end of this step, `catalog-service` grows under load and shrinks afterwards without you touching anything.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — you installed metrics-server there (the component that answers `kubectl top` and the HPA's CPU questions) and deployed all your services into the `zenith` namespace on kind. [Task 11.5 — Load testing, chaos, and your first postmortem](#task-115--load-testing-chaos-and-your-first-postmortem--6h) — the k6 load scripts in `load/` are how you will generate the load that makes the HPA act.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `k8s/hpa-catalog.yaml`: an `autoscaling/v2` HPA targeting the `catalog-service` Deployment with `minReplicas: 2`, `maxReplicas: 6`, and a CPU target of `averageUtilization: 70` (meaning: keep average pod CPU at 70% of its *request* — the request you set in [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) is the denominator, which is why an HPA is useless on a pod with no CPU request). Apply it.
    2. Run `kubectl get hpa -w` in one terminal while a k6 `browse` run pushes traffic in another. Watch the `TARGETS` column climb past 70% and the `REPLICAS` column follow.
    *You know it worked when:* `kubectl get hpa` shows a real percentage (not `<unknown>` — that means metrics-server is not answering), replicas climb under load, and fall back to 2 a few minutes after the load stops.

- [ ] **Step 2 — HPA on a custom metric via prometheus-adapter.**
    *What this step is:* CPU is the wrong signal for most of your services, so now you scale on metrics that actually mean "busy": requests-per-second for `catalog-service` and active WebSocket connections for `realtime-service`. The HPA cannot read Prometheus directly — it asks the Kubernetes *custom metrics API*, and **prometheus-adapter** is the translator that answers the HPA's "what is the current value?" question by querying Prometheus. You will also tune `stabilizationWindowSeconds` so the autoscaler does not flap — scale up and down repeatedly around the threshold. Be ready to say out loud why CPU is a terrible signal for a connection-bound service: `realtime-service` can hold 10,000 open connections at 5% CPU and be completely saturated — the resource it exhausts is connections and memory, not compute, so a CPU-based HPA would watch it drown and see no reason to act.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — you installed the in-cluster Prometheus (kube-prometheus-stack) there, and this step is the dependency that observability move existed for. [Task 11.2 — Metrics that answer real questions](#task-112--metrics-that-answer-real-questions--3h) — your services already export request-rate and connection-count metrics via Micrometer; those are the numbers the adapter will serve. [Task 9.5 — Connection load testing](#task-95--connection-load-testing--2h) — the active-WebSocket-connections gauge you watched there is exactly the metric `realtime-service` scales on now.
    *Do this:*
    1. Install the adapter with Helm from the same prometheus-community repo kube-prometheus-stack came from: `helm install prometheus-adapter prometheus-community/prometheus-adapter -n monitoring`, with a `rules:` value that maps your Prometheus request-rate query (a `rate(...)` over the Micrometer request counter) and your WebSocket-connections gauge into named custom metrics.
    2. Confirm the translation works before touching any HPA: `kubectl get --raw "/apis/custom.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1" | jq .` must list your two metrics. If it does not, no HPA built on them can work — debug here, not there.
    3. Replace the catalog HPA's CPU target with the requests-per-second metric, and write a second HPA for `realtime-service` on active WebSocket connections.
    4. Add `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` (start at 120) to both HPAs: the autoscaler then acts on the *highest* desired replica count seen in that window instead of the instantaneous value, which damps the up-down-up flapping a noisy metric causes.
    *You know it worked when:* under a k6 run, `kubectl describe hpa` shows the custom metric's live value and the replica count tracks it — and when the load oscillates, replicas do not thrash up and down with it.

- [ ] **Step 3 — KEDA scales your Kafka consumers on lag.**
    *What this step is:* For a Kafka consumer, even requests-per-second is the wrong signal — the right one is **consumer lag**, the number of messages waiting in the topic that the consumer group has not yet processed, because lag measures the backlog itself rather than a symptom of it. KEDA (event-driven autoscaling) reads lag straight from Kafka and scales your consumers on it, including down to **zero** pods when there is nothing to do. Install KEDA with Helm — one chart, fully local, the same move as Vault and ESO below. At the end you have a screenshot of replica counts tracking lag during a spike — an excellent demo.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — the 3-broker Strimzi Kafka running in your cluster is what KEDA measures lag against. [Task 8.4 — The async media processing pipeline](#task-84--the-async-media-processing-pipeline--3h) — the `media-service` consumer you built there is one of the two you scale now. [Task 6.3 — Producer and consumer implementation with real failure handling](#task-63--producer-and-consumer-implementation-with-real-failure-handling--4h) — the consumer-group mechanics (and the group ids you will name in the trigger) come from there; the notification consumer is the other scaling target. [Task 7.5 — Spring Batch for bulk processing](#task-75--spring-batch-for-bulk-processing--4h) — the batch worker from there is the scale-to-zero candidate: it only has work when a bulk job arrives, so zero idle pods is the honest size. [Task 11.5 — Load testing, chaos, and your first postmortem](#task-115--load-testing-chaos-and-your-first-postmortem--6h) — the `on-sale-spike` k6 scenario (50 → 5,000 virtual users in 30 s) is "the Phase 11 spike test" you re-run here.
    *Do this:*
    1. `helm repo add kedacore https://kedacore.github.io/charts && helm install keda kedacore/keda -n keda --create-namespace`.
    2. Write a KEDA `ScaledObject` for the `media-service` consumer and one for the notification consumer, each with a `kafka` trigger naming the bootstrap servers, the consumer group, the topic, and a `lagThreshold` (start at 50 — one more pod per 50 messages of backlog).
    3. Write a third `ScaledObject` for the batch worker with `minReplicaCount: 0`, and watch its pods disappear when the topic is empty.
    4. Run the [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline) `on-sale-spike` test, keep `kubectl get pods -w` and the consumer-lag panel from your Grafana dashboards side by side, and **screenshot the replica count tracking the lag**.
    *You know it worked when:* you have the screenshot — lag rises, replicas follow, lag drains, replicas fall — and the batch worker sits at 0 replicas whenever it has no work.

- [ ] **Step 4 — Know the two scaling axes you are not running.**
    *What this step is:* An honesty checkpoint, not a build. Real clusters scale on two axes: HPA and KEDA add **pods**; the **cluster-autoscaler** adds **nodes** when pods sit `Pending` for lack of room, and the VerticalPodAutoscaler resizes a pod's own requests instead of adding copies. A laptop has no nodes to add, so there is nothing honest to rehearse here — know the concept, have the sentence ready, and move on.
    *Do this:*
    1. Say the sentence out loud until it is yours: "pod autoscaling I have run; node autoscaling needs an environment that can produce nodes."
    *You know it worked when:* you can explain, without notes, which component solves "my pods are overloaded" (HPA/KEDA), which solves "my cluster has no room for more pods" (cluster-autoscaler), and which solves "this pod's requests are sized wrong" (VPA).

- [ ] **Step 5 — Break it on purpose: scale past a ResourceQuota and read the quiet failure.**
    *What this step is:* You make the `zenith` namespace a *governed* boundary instead of just a label: a `ResourceQuota` caps what the whole namespace may consume in total, and a `LimitRange` injects default requests and limits into any container that declares none. Then you deliberately crash into the quota — because its failure shape is *quiet* and you need to have seen it before it happens for real. This is how platform teams stop one team eating the cluster.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — the `zenith` namespace everything is deployed into, and the `docs/runbooks/k8s-triage.md` runbook you started there, which gets a new row now.
    *Do this:*
    1. Apply a `ResourceQuota` to `zenith` — say 2 CPU, 4Gi memory, 10 pods — and a `LimitRange` with default requests and limits.
    2. Create a pod that declares no resources at all, then read `kubectl get pod -o yaml` and find the defaults the LimitRange injected — nothing lands in the `BestEffort` QoS class by accident any more.
    3. Now scale `catalog-service` past the quota and *read the rejection*. The surprise: the pods do **not** go `Pending` — the Deployment just sticks below its desired replica count while the ReplicaSet records `FailedCreate` events. Find them with `kubectl describe rs` (and `kubectl get events`).
    4. Add the new row to `docs/runbooks/k8s-triage.md`: "stuck below desired replicas, no Pending pods → check the quota."
    5. Set the quota generously enough that the Step 3 KEDA spike still fits — or delete it after the drill. The lesson is the rejection event, not a permanent ceiling.
    *You know it worked when:* you have read a `FailedCreate` event with your own eyes, can say why no pod ever showed `Pending`, and the runbook row exists.

- [ ] **Step 6 — PodDisruptionBudget and spreading, proven with a drain.**
    *What this step is:* A `PodDisruptionBudget` (PDB) is a floor on how many pods must stay available during *voluntary* disruption — your own operations, like draining a node for maintenance. It does not protect against crashes. `topologySpreadConstraints` spread a service's replicas across nodes so one node dying cannot take every replica at once. You prove both with a real drain.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — your kind cluster is multi-node (each node is a Docker container), which is what makes draining one node a meaningful drill.
    *Do this:*
    1. Add a PDB with `minAvailable` (the availability floor — e.g. `minAvailable: 1` for a 2-replica service) and `topologySpreadConstraints` to your service manifests.
    2. Drain a worker node with `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets` and watch: evictions that would take the service below `minAvailable` are refused until replacement pods are ready elsewhere — the drain waits rather than breaking you.
    3. Uncordon the node afterwards (`kubectl uncordon <node>`).
    *You know it worked when:* during the drain the service never dropped below the PDB's `minAvailable`, and you saw the drain pause while it waited.

- [ ] **Step 7 — Package everything as a Helm umbrella chart.**
    *What this step is:* So far your Helm use has been *installing other people's charts*; now you write your own. Helm is templated, versioned Kubernetes packaging: one **umbrella chart** that lists every Zenith service as a subchart, a shared **library chart** holding the common Deployment/Service/HPA template (so ten services do not mean ten copies of the same YAML), and per-environment values files — `values-local.yaml` and `values-staging.yaml` — so configuration differs per environment without duplicating manifests.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — the raw manifests you wrote there are the source material; this step turns them into templates rather than inventing anything new.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create the umbrella chart with a library chart for the common Deployment/Service/HPA template and `values-{local,staging}.yaml`.
    2. Run `helm lint` (catches template errors), then `helm template` and *diff-review the rendered output* against your [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) manifests — the rendered YAML should say exactly what your hand-written YAML said.
    3. Deploy with `helm upgrade --atomic --timeout` — `--atomic` rolls the release back automatically if it does not become healthy within the timeout, which turns a failed deploy into a non-event.
    *You know it worked when:* `helm upgrade --install` brings up the whole stack from nothing, and the `helm template` diff showed no surprises you could not explain.

- [ ] **Step 8 — ADR-0021: Helm versus Kustomize.**
    *What this step is:* A short written decision. Kustomize is a template-free alternative built into kubectl that patches base YAML with per-environment overlay files — no templating language, but also no packaging, versioning, or one-command rollback. You compare the two, pick one, and record why.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.5 — Architecture Decision Records](#task-05--architecture-decision-records--1h) — the ADR format (Context / Options considered / Decision / Consequences, one page, a named rejected alternative) and the `docs/adr/` home for it.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write `docs/adr/0021-helm-vs-kustomize.md`: compare Helm with Kustomize overlays, pick one, and say why — naming at least one real cost of your choice.
    *You know it worked when:* the ADR exists, names the rejected alternative, and you can argue the trade-off out loud in under a minute.

- [ ] **Step 9 — Configuration that actually rolls out: ConfigMap, Secret, and the checksum annotation.**
    *What this step is:* Move configuration where Kubernetes wants it: a `ConfigMap` (a Kubernetes object holding plain key-value configuration) for Spring profiles, a `Secret` for credentials, both injected into pods as environment variables. Then fix the trap: changing a ConfigMap changes **nothing** by itself — running pods keep the old values until something unrelated triggers a restart, which looks exactly like "my change did nothing" and is a subtle, very common bug. The cure is a **checksum annotation**: a hash of the ConfigMap's content placed on the Deployment's pod template, so any config change changes the template and forces a rollout.
    *Builds on:* [Task F6.5 — Profiles and secrets](#task-f65--profiles-and-secrets--05h) — Spring profiles and why secrets never live in a profile file; the ConfigMap now carries the profile selection into the cluster. Step 7's Helm chart — the annotation is one template line there.
    *Do this:*
    1. Move the Spring profile configuration into a `ConfigMap` and the credentials into a `Secret`, both injected as env vars in the Deployment template.
    2. In the library chart's Deployment template, add the checksum annotation to the pod template:

    ```yaml
    annotations:
      checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
    ```

    3. Prove it both ways: change a ConfigMap value *without* the annotation and watch nothing restart; then with the annotation, run `helm upgrade` after the same change and watch the rollout happen.
    *You know it worked when:* a ConfigMap-only change triggers a visible `kubectl rollout status` rollout, and you can explain why it would not have without the annotation.

- [ ] **Step 10 — See the secrets problem with your own eyes.**
    *What this step is:* Before building the proper path, you look at why it must exist. A Kubernetes `Secret` only *encodes* — base64 is a reversible text encoding, not encryption — so anyone who can read the object can decode it with one command. This step is thirty seconds long and changes how you talk about secrets forever.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — the Secrets your in-cluster Postgres install created there are the ones you now decode.
    *Do this:*
    1. Run `kubectl get secret <name> -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d` — the plaintext password prints to your terminal. Anyone with read access gets the same.
    2. Say the capstone sentence that frames the whole drill: a Kubernetes `Secret` is base64 **plaintext** sitting in etcd (the cluster's own database), gated by nothing but RBAC on who may read it — "base64 is not encryption" is the interview line, and everything Vault and ESO are about to do exists because of it.
    *You know it worked when:* you have watched a cluster credential print in plaintext from one command, and the capstone sentence comes out of you without notes.

- [ ] **Step 11 — Install Vault and give it one real secret.**
    *What this step is:* Real teams keep secrets in a **secret store** — a system whose entire job is holding secrets: access-controlled, audited, rotatable — and let the cluster *consume* them. You build that path locally: HashiCorp Vault in **dev mode**, one container inside your kind cluster, installed with Helm, no cloud account anywhere. Dev mode means it starts already unlocked, keeps everything in memory, and prints an all-powerful root token at startup — and you should be able to say why that is fine for learning and never for production: nothing survives a restart, nothing is sealed, and one token opens everything. This is a drill, not a discussion, and all of it is local.
