    *Builds on:* Step 10 — the problem this store exists to solve. [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — Helm installs into kind, the same move as every chart so far; the Postgres whose password you are storing also runs there.
    *Do this:*
    1. `helm repo add hashicorp https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com && helm install vault hashicorp/vault --set "server.dev.enabled=true" -n vault --create-namespace` — one container, no unseal ceremony.
    2. Put the Postgres password for **one** service into it: `kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault kv put secret/zenith/catalog db_password=<the current password>`.
    3. Say out loud why dev mode is fine here and never in production.
    *You know it worked when:* `vault kv get secret/zenith/catalog` (via `kubectl exec`) returns the password, and your dev-mode sentence names all three reasons — in-memory, unsealed, one root token.

- [ ] **Step 12 — External Secrets Operator: the store becomes the source of truth.**
    *What this step is:* The **External Secrets Operator** (ESO) is a controller that syncs secrets *from* a store (Vault here) *into* ordinary Kubernetes `Secret`s — so your pods keep their normal env-var mounting while Vault becomes the single source of truth. You prove it the only way that counts: delete the Kubernetes `Secret` and watch ESO quietly recreate it. Then you notice something that arrived with all these Helm installs that nobody announced: **admission webhooks** — gatekeepers the apiserver consults *before* persisting an object, able to reject or mutate what you apply.
    *Builds on:* Step 11 — the Vault holding the password. [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — Strimzi and kube-prometheus-stack from there are among the installs that registered webhooks you are about to find.
    *Do this:*
    1. `helm repo add external-secrets https://charts.external-secrets.io && helm install external-secrets external-secrets/external-secrets -n external-secrets --create-namespace`.
    2. Create a `SecretStore` pointing at your Vault (dev-mode root token is fine here — this is the learning trade-off you named in Step 11) and an `ExternalSecret` that materialises the catalog Postgres password as a Kubernetes `Secret`; point the catalog Deployment's env var at that Secret.
    3. Prove the path end to end: `kubectl delete secret` on it and watch ESO recreate it from Vault within seconds. The k8s `Secret` is now demonstrably just a cache — the truth lives in the store.
    4. Run `kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations` and see which of your installs — Strimzi, ESO, kube-prometheus-stack — registered one. You wrote none of them, yet they now sit between `kubectl apply` and etcd, vetting objects before they persist. That is an admission controller in the wild; Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper are how teams write their *own* policy on that hook — name them in an interview, build them another day.
    *You know it worked when:* the deleted Secret reappears on its own within seconds, and you can name at least one validating webhook in your cluster and say who installed it.

- [ ] **Step 13 — Rotate the credential with zero downtime.**
    *What this step is:* **Rotation** is changing a credential while everything keeps working. The hard part is never the change itself — it is the order of operations, because at every instant during the change something is still using the old value. You rotate the catalog Postgres password through the full Vault → ESO → `Secret` → pod path, and then write the exact sequence down — because that runbook is the artifact interviewers actually believe: nobody writes one without having done the rotation.
    *Builds on:* Step 12 — the live Vault → ESO → Secret → pod path you are rotating through. [Task 11.4 — SLOs, alerting, and runbooks](#task-114--slos-alerting-and-runbooks--2h) — the `docs/runbooks/` format this write-up joins.
    *Do this:*
    1. Write the **new** password into Vault first, and watch ESO update the Kubernetes `Secret` (running pods still hold the old value in their environment — an env var is read once at container start).
    2. Change the password in Postgres (`ALTER USER ... PASSWORD ...`). Existing connections keep working — Postgres checks the password only when a connection is *opened* — so nothing breaks yet.
    3. Immediately `kubectl rollout restart deployment/catalog-service` so new pods start with the new value while old pods drain on their still-open connections. Zero downtime.
    4. Now reason through the reversal: restart the pods *before* Postgres knows the new password and every new pod fails to connect and crash-loops — the application locks itself out of its own database. The order of operations is the whole exercise.
    5. Write the exact sequence you proved into `docs/runbooks/secret-rotation.md`.
    *You know it worked when:* requests kept succeeding throughout the rotation, the pods now authenticate with the new password, and the runbook records the order — with a line on what reversing it does.

- [ ] **Step 14 — Deployment strategies: tuned rolling, then a manual canary.**
    *What this step is:* A rolling update replaces pods gradually; `maxSurge` (how many extra pods may exist during the roll) and `maxUnavailable` (how many may be missing) are the two dials that control the speed-versus-safety trade. A **canary** goes further: a small number of pods on the new version run *beside* the stable ones, receive a share of real traffic, and you compare error rates before committing the fleet. You build the canary by hand so you understand what the fancy tools automate.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — Services route to every pod whose labels match the selector, which is the entire canary mechanism. [Task 11.2 — Metrics that answer real questions](#task-112--metrics-that-answer-real-questions--3h) — the per-service RED dashboards are where you compare stable-versus-canary error rates. [Task 11.5 — Load testing, chaos, and your first postmortem](#task-115--load-testing-chaos-and-your-first-postmortem--6h) — a steady k6 load is what makes the comparison mean something.
    *Do this:*
    1. Tune `maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable` on your Deployments and confirm under k6 load that a rolling update drops zero requests.
    2. Run a manual canary: a second Deployment (e.g. `catalog-service-canary`) with a small replica count, labels matching the same Service selector, running the new image. The Service now sends a small fraction of real traffic to it.
    3. Compare error rates between stable and canary in Grafana before scaling the new version up and retiring the old.
    *You know it worked when:* you can show both Deployments serving behind one Service and point at the two error-rate curves you compared.

- [ ] **Step 15 — Time your rollback.**
    *What this step is:* `kubectl rollout undo` returns a Deployment to its previous version. You run it against a bad deploy and put a stopwatch on it, because "I can roll back in 40 seconds" is a real answer in a way "we can roll back" never is.
    *Builds on:* Step 14 — the deployment machinery you are now reversing.
    *Do this:*
    1. Deploy a deliberately broken image, run `kubectl rollout undo deployment/catalog-service`, and time from the undo command to the service healthy again (`kubectl rollout status` returning, smoke check green).
    2. Write the number down.
    *You know it worked when:* you can say your rollback number and how you measured it.

- [ ] **Step 16 — Blue/green — described honestly, not built.**
    *What this step is:* The third strategy, learned as a concept and a sentence rather than a build — on purpose. Blue/green runs *two complete environments*: "blue" serves all traffic while "green" runs the new version at full size beside it; cutover is one atomic switch (a Service selector or router flip) that moves *everything* at once, and rollback is flipping back — instant. A canary is the opposite trade: a *fraction* of traffic shifts gradually while you compare error rates, on a handful of extra pods instead of a second environment. This plan rehearses rolling and canary and only describes blue/green, because on a laptop doubling the infrastructure buys no new lesson — the mechanics are a second Deployment and a Service selector, exactly what your Step 14 canary already used; only the economics differ.
    *Builds on:* Step 14 — the canary whose mechanics blue/green shares.
    *Do this:*
    1. Learn the sentence this choice gives you: "I rehearsed rolling and canary; blue/green is what I would reach for when a release must cut over atomically — a schema-coupled change, say — and the business will pay double infrastructure for an instant all-or-nothing switch."
    *You know it worked when:* you can state what each of the three strategies buys and costs, and why blue/green is the one you described but did not build.

- [ ] **Step 17 — Database migrations under rolling deploys.**
    *What this step is:* During a rolling deploy, old and new application versions run against the **same database at the same time** — so the rule is: **schema changes must be backward compatible with the currently running version**, always. You combine the expand/contract technique with a rolling deploy and walk a column rename across two deploys to see why one deploy can never be enough.
    *Builds on:* [Task 3.5 — Partitioning, read replicas, and zero-downtime migrations](#task-35--partitioning-read-replicas-and-zero-downtime-migrations--6h) — the five-step expand/contract drill (add new nullable → dual-write → backfill → switch reads → drop old) and the `docs/runbooks/schema-change.md` runbook; this step adds the deployment dimension to it. Step 14 — the rolling update that makes the mixed-version window real.
    *Do this:*
    1. Walk a column rename across two deploys, out loud or on paper: **deploy 1** ships code that writes both old and new columns and reads the old (schema has both — the *expand*); backfill runs; **deploy 2** ships code reading the new column, after which the old column can be dropped (the *contract*). At no instant does any running version see a schema it cannot handle.
    2. State the rule and the reason: a rename in one deploy means some pods crash mid-roll, because half the fleet still runs code naming a column that no longer exists.
    *You know it worked when:* you can narrate the two-deploy rename without notes and name what breaks if you try it in one.

- [ ] **Step 18 — `[stretch]` Feature flags: decouple deploy from release.**
    *What this step is:* A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns a code path on or off without a deploy — so *deploying* code (shipping it) and *releasing* it (letting users hit it) become separate decisions, and a risky path can ship dark and switch on gradually.
    *Builds on:* Step 9 — a ConfigMap-backed flag plus the checksum annotation is the simplest honest implementation you already own.
    *Do this:*
    1. Put one risky code path behind a flag read from configuration, deploy with the flag off, then release by flipping the flag — no new image involved.
    *You know it worked when:* you can turn the feature on and off without deploying, and can say in one sentence why deploy and release being separate events reduces risk.

**Done when:** KEDA scales on lag during the spike test, a canary runs beside the stable version, you have rehearsed a timed rollback, scaling past the `ResourceQuota` produced a `FailedCreate` event you found and read, and the database password for one service flows Vault → ESO → `Secret` → pod — with a rotation you have actually performed and written down in `docs/runbooks/secret-rotation.md`.


**Checkpoint — answer out loud, from memory, before moving on:**

1. Why is CPU a bad scaling signal for `realtime-service`, and what did you scale it on instead?
2. What does KEDA give you that a plain HPA does not? Name the signal and why it is the right one.
3. What is flapping, and which setting did you use to stop it?
4. You changed a ConfigMap and the pods kept the old configuration. Why, and what is the fix?
5. Rolling, canary, blue/green: what does each buy, what does each cost — and which of the three did you describe but deliberately not build, and why?
6. State the rule connecting database migrations to rolling deploys, and walk a column rename across two deploys.
7. How long does your rollback take? Say the number and how you measured it.
8. How does the database password reach the pod, step by step — and where is the single source of truth?
9. Walk me through rotating that password with zero downtime. What is the order of operations, and what goes wrong if you reverse it?
10. Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet — you have run all three: your Zenith services, Postgres and Kafka, and the Promtail log shipper. Give the one-line rule for each, and say what would break if you swapped any of them.
11. A Deployment is stuck below its desired replica count, yet no pod is `Pending`. What happened, and which command shows you the evidence?

#### Task 13.4 — CI/CD pipeline — 7h

**What:** A complete commit-to-deployed-cluster pipeline **running entirely on your machine**, with gates.
**Why:** Pipeline design is a senior responsibility, and an unbroken commit-to-deploy path is the capstone proof that everything fits together. Running it locally is not a downgrade — you own every stage instead of inheriting someone's YAML.
**Solves:** manual builds, untested merges, and deploys that depend on a human remembering steps.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Gate** | A stage that can fail the pipeline. Order them cheapest-and-fastest first, so an obvious formatting error does not cost you ten minutes of integration tests. |
| **Affected-module build** | Building and testing only the modules touched by a change, determined by diffing against the merge base. The main lever on pipeline duration in a monorepo. |
| **SBOM** | Generated per image with Syft, so when a CVE is announced you can answer "which of our deploys contain this?" in seconds instead of days. |
| **Digest promotion** | Moving the exact same image digest from one environment to the next. If you rebuild per environment you have not tested what you shipped. |
| **`helm upgrade --atomic`** | Rolls back automatically if the release does not become healthy within the timeout. Turns a failed deploy into a non-event. |
| **Smoke test** | A tiny set of post-deploy checks proving the deployment is actually serving. |
| **Mutation testing** | PITest deliberately introduces bugs and checks whether your tests catch them. Line coverage proves a line *ran*; mutation score proves a test would have *noticed* it being wrong — a much stronger claim, and saying so demonstrates you understand coverage's limits. |
| **DORA metrics** | Lead time, deployment frequency, change-failure rate, and time to restore. The four numbers the industry uses to describe delivery performance, and all four are measurable even solo. |
| **GitOps** | The cluster pulls desired state from git and corrects drift itself, rather than a pipeline pushing to it. Gives you drift detection and self-healing; costs you another system. |
| **Multi-arch image (manifest list)** | One tag that points at several images, one per CPU architecture, each with its own digest. `docker manifest inspect` shows them all under the single tag — that *is* what a multi-arch tag is. Your Mac builds `arm64` by default; most CI runners and production clusters are `amd64`. |
| **Build cache export** | Buildx writing its layer cache somewhere another machine can reuse it (`--cache-to` / `--cache-from`). It is how a fresh CI runner skips rebuilding the layers your last run already built. |
| **Registry garbage collection** | Deleting a tag or manifest removes the *pointer*, not the layer blobs. The registry's `garbage-collect` command is what actually walks the store and reclaims the bytes. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** **automatic rollback** on a failed smoke test. That single piece is what most hand-rolled pipelines lack, and it is the difference between a pipeline and a deploy script.
- **When it works you will see:** one command taking a commit through gates, registry, cluster and smoke tests — and a deliberately broken change rolling itself back.
- **Where people get stuck:** deploying `:latest`. You cannot tell what is running, cannot roll back to a known version, and a node restart silently pulls something different. Tag with the git SHA, always.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Stand up your own local image registry.**
    *What this step is:* A registry is the server images are pushed to and pulled from — Docker Hub is one; now you run your own, as a single container on your laptop. This gives you push/pull, tags, digests, and garbage collection with no account and no rate limits, and it is where every image your pipeline builds will live. You also teach your kind cluster to trust it, because the cluster's nodes pull images themselves.
    *Builds on:* [Task 13.2 — Kubernetes fundamentals by doing](#task-132--kubernetes-fundamentals-by-doing--16h) — the kind cluster whose config you now patch; kind only reads its config at creation time, so this edit means recreating the cluster (your one-command `make up` from that task is exactly what makes that cheap).
    *Do this:*
    1. Run the registry: `docker run -d -p 5001:5000 -e REGISTRY_STORAGE_DELETE_ENABLED=true --name registry registry:2` — deletion is **off** by default; the env var turns it on, and the garbage-collection drill in Step 2 needs it.
    2. Configure kind to trust it — a `containerd` patch in the kind cluster config (containerd is the container runtime on each kind node; the patch tells it where `localhost:5001` really lives):

    ```yaml
    containerdConfigPatches:
      - |-
        [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".registry.mirrors."localhost:5001"]
          endpoint = ["http://registry:5000"]
    ```

    then recreate the cluster and put the registry container on the cluster's Docker network: `docker network connect kind registry`.
    3. Prove the loop: tag any existing image as `localhost:5001/test:1`, push it, and deploy a pod from that image into kind.
    *You know it worked when:* `docker push localhost:5001/test:1` succeeds and a pod using that image reaches `Running` — no `ImagePullBackOff`.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Earn the garbage-collection claim — once, with numbers.**
    *What this step is:* In a registry, a *tag* points at a *manifest*, and the manifest points at *layer blobs* — the actual bytes. Deleting a tag or manifest removes the **pointer**, not the blobs; only the registry's `garbage-collect` command walks the store and reclaims the bytes. You prove this with before/after disk numbers, which is why registries bloat until someone runs GC — and the tag-vs-digest-vs-blob model made visible.
    *Builds on:* Step 1 — the registry (with deletion enabled) you are now exercising. [Task 13.1 — Production-grade container images](#task-131--production-grade-container-images--6h) — the catalog image you built there is the test subject.
    *Do this:*
    1. Push two tags of the catalog image to the registry.
    2. Delete one manifest through the registry API: fetch its digest with a `GET` to `/v2/zenith-catalog/manifests/<tag>` using the `Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json` header (the digest comes back in the `Docker-Content-Digest` response header), then `curl -X DELETE localhost:5001/v2/zenith-catalog/manifests/<digest>`.
    3. Check the registry's disk usage: `docker exec registry du -sh /var/lib/registry` — **unchanged**. Deleting removed the pointer, not the blobs.
    4. Run `docker exec registry registry garbage-collect /etc/docker/registry/config.yml`, measure again, and watch the bytes come back.
    *You know it worked when:* you have the before/after pair of `du` numbers — flat after the delete, smaller after GC — and can explain which of tag, manifest, and blob each command touched.

- [ ] **Step 3 — The multi-arch drill — the Docker surprise most likely to hit you in your first job.**
    *What this step is:* Your Mac builds `arm64` images by default; most CI runners and production clusters are `amd64` — different CPU architectures, and an image built for one dies on the other with `exec format error`. A **multi-arch image** is one tag pointing at a *manifest list*: several images, one per architecture, each with its own digest, served to each machine as the right one. You build one, inspect it, and feel the emulation cost.
    *Builds on:* Step 1 — the registry the multi-arch manifest must live in. [Task 13.1 — Production-grade container images](#task-131--production-grade-container-images--6h) — the hardened catalog Dockerfile you now build for two platforms.
    *Do this:*
    1. Build for both at once: `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t localhost:5001/zenith-catalog:multi --push .` — the `--push` is not optional: a multi-arch manifest cannot be loaded into the local daemon, it has to live in a registry.
    2. Inspect what you made: `docker manifest inspect localhost:5001/zenith-catalog:multi` (or `docker buildx imagetools inspect`) shows BOTH images, each with its own digest, under one tag — that is what a multi-arch tag *is*.
    3. Run the amd64 one locally with `docker run --platform linux/amd64 …`: it works, under emulation, and noticeably slower — prove it by timing the startup next to the arm64 number.
    4. Say the first-job sentence: "my laptop is arm64, CI and prod are amd64 — the image must be built for both or pinned to one, and now I know how to check."
    *You know it worked when:* the inspect output lists both architectures under the single tag, and you have the two startup timings side by side.

    *What this step is:* An **affected-module build** builds and tests only the modules a change touched, worked out by diffing against the merge base — the commit where your branch and `main` last agreed — and mapping changed file paths to Maven modules. It is the main lever on pipeline duration in a monorepo. Pipeline duration is a real engineering constraint, not a nicety: a slow pipeline means fewer deploys per day, bigger batches per deploy, more risk per batch, and developers who stop running it — every delivery problem gets worse when feedback is slow.
    *Builds on:* Step 4 — the gate sequence you are now making fast. [Task 0.2 — Maven multi-module skeleton](#task-02--maven-multi-module-skeleton--15h) — the module layout that makes "which modules did this change touch?" answerable from file paths.
    *Do this:*
    1. In `make ci`, compute changed files with `git diff --name-only $(git merge-base origin/main HEAD)`, map paths to modules, and build only those plus their dependents: `mvn -pl <modules> -am -amd ...`.
    2. Time a full run and an affected-only run; target under 10 minutes for the typical change, and be ready to explain why the number matters.
    *You know it worked when:* a one-module change runs visibly fewer tests than a full build and finishes under the target — and you can say what a slow pipeline does to deploy frequency and batch size.

### Phase 14 — Capstone: performance report and documentation — 14h baseline

**Scheduled:** Weeks 28–29

**Goal:** convert nearly seven months — roughly 520 hours — of work into artifacts that communicate it in 5 minutes.

**Why this phase exists:** unpresented work is invisible work. This phase is what makes
the project usable in interviews and on your CV.

#### Task 14.1 — The performance report — 2h

**What:** One document with every number you measured, before and after.
**Why:** Specific numbers are the most persuasive thing you can bring to an interview, and they must be yours.
**Solves:** vague claims ("improved performance") that invite scepticism.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Reproduction command** | The exact command that regenerates a number. A number nobody can reproduce is an assertion, and an interviewer will treat it as one. |
| **Conditions** | Hardware, dataset size, date, and any JVM flags. "p99 of 95 ms" means nothing; "p99 of 95 ms on an M3 Max with 10M seats on 2026-03-14" is evidence. |
| **Before/after pair** | Both numbers, always. "420 ms to 95 ms" is a story with a mechanism behind it; "95 ms" on its own is a fact with nothing attached. |
| **"What surprised me"** | The section recording where you were wrong. It is the most persuasive part of the whole document, because only someone who actually measured can have been surprised. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** that **every number carries its conditions and a reproduction command**. A number without conditions invites precisely the follow-up question you cannot answer.
- **When it works you will see:** a performance report where you could hand someone the document and they could re-run every claim in it.
- **Where people get stuck:** numbers you cannot reproduce. If you did not save the command and the conditions at the time, the number is an anecdote now. This is why [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) through [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) all asked you to write benchmarks down as you went.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Create the report and add the data-layer numbers.**
    *What this step is:* You create one file, `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`, that gathers every performance number you have measured across the whole project into a single document. You are not measuring anything new — every number in this step already exists in a `docs/benchmarks/` file or a journal entry from an earlier phase; your job is to consolidate (pull together into one place) the database, cache, and reservation results first. The skeleton to copy is [the Benchmarks to capture](#10-benchmarks-to-capture) table (near the end of this document) — the 32-row table you have been filling in phase by phase. At the end of this step the file exists and holds the first six result groups.

Two or three paragraphs is plenty.

#### Task 14.2 — Architecture documentation — 2h

**What:** C4 diagrams, an ADR index, and a documentation entry point.
**Why:** Being able to draw your own system at three zoom levels is exactly the system-design interview skill, and ADRs demonstrate judgement rather than just output.
**Solves:** an impressive system nobody can understand in a 45-minute conversation.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **C4** | Four zoom levels: Context (the system and who uses it), Container (deployable units), Component (inside one container), Code (rarely needed). Different audiences need different levels, and showing the wrong one is why architecture conversations stall. |
| **Level 1 — Context** | For someone who has never heard of Zenith. Users, the system, third parties. No technology at all. |
| **Level 2 — Container** | For an engineer joining the team. Your nine services plus Postgres, Redis, Kafka, MinIO. This is the one you must be able to draw from memory in three minutes. |
| **Level 3 — Component** | Inside one container. Worth doing only for `order-service`, which is the interesting one. |
| **ADR index** | A table of number, title, status, date, and one-line consequence. The entry point that makes twenty-two separate files usable. |
| **Sequence diagram** | Time down, participants across. The right shape for a saga, because the ordering and the failure branches are the whole point. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** the **container diagram**. You will be asked to draw it, and being able to produce it from memory in three minutes is a direct, visible competence signal.
- **When it works you will see:** three C4 levels committed as diagrams-as-code, and you drawing level 2 from memory without looking.
- **Where people get stuck:** diagrams that drift. A picture that no longer matches the system is worse than none, because it misleads. Keeping them as text next to the code is what makes updating them realistic.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Draw C4 Levels 1 and 2 in Mermaid.**
    *What this step is:* You draw the first two zoom levels of your architecture as Mermaid diagrams (Mermaid — the text-based diagram language that GitHub and your IDE render natively, which you have used since Phase 1) and commit them under `docs/architecture/`. Level 1 (Context) shows users, the Zenith system as one box, and third parties — no technology names at all, because its audience has never heard of Zenith. Level 2 (Container) shows every separately runnable piece: your 9 services plus the infrastructure (Postgres, Redis, Kafka, MinIO, Nginx), with the protocol labelled on every arrow — remember "container" here means a runnable process or data store in the C4 sense, not a Docker container ([the C4 explainer](#c4-diagrams), early in this document, walks through all four levels). Keeping them as text next to the code is what makes updating them realistic — diagrams that drift mislead.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.1 — Event-storm the domain and draw the context map](#task-11--event-storm-the-domain-and-draw-the-context-map--15h) — where you first drew a Mermaid diagram (`docs/architecture/context-map.md`), so the tooling and the folder already exist.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/architecture/c4-level1-context.md` with a Mermaid diagram: users (customer, organizer, gate staff), Zenith as a single box, and third parties (payment provider, email). No technology words.
    2. Create `docs/architecture/c4-level2-containers.md`: all 9 services + Postgres, Redis, Kafka, MinIO, Nginx (~15 boxes), each arrow labelled with its protocol (HTTP, Kafka topic, SQL, S3 API).
    3. Open both on GitHub or in your IDE preview and check they render.
    *You know it worked when:* both files render as diagrams, Level 1 contains zero technology names, and Level 2 shows all nine services with a labelled protocol on every arrow.

- [ ] **Step 2 — Draw the Level 3 component diagram for `order-service`.**
    *What this step is:* One more zoom in: the components *inside* a single container. You do this for `order-service` only — it is the most interesting one (holds, orders, the saga, the outbox), and Level 3 for all nine services would be busywork that goes stale. Level 4 (Code) is skipped entirely, as the C4 author himself recommends.
    *Builds on:* [Task 1.6 — Application layer: use cases and ports](#task-16--application-layer-use-cases-and-ports--2h) — where `order-service`'s internal shape (use cases, ports, adapters) was established, which is exactly what a component diagram shows.
    *Do this:*
    1. Create `docs/architecture/c4-level3-order-service.md` in Mermaid: the REST adapter, the use-case/application layer, the domain model, the persistence adapter, the outbox publisher, and the Kafka consumers — with arrows showing who calls whom.
    2. Sanity-check it against the actual package structure of `order-service`; fix the diagram, not the code, where they disagree.
    *You know it worked when:* a reader could name the main pieces of `order-service` and their call directions from the diagram alone, and nothing in it contradicts the code.

    *What this step is:* One table that makes your ~22 separate ADR files usable (ADR — Architecture Decision Record, the one-page decision documents you have written since [Phase 0 — Repository, tooling, standards](#phase-0--repository-tooling-standards--15h-baseline)): number, title, status, date, and a one-line consequence per row. Mark any ADR you later superseded — a superseded ADR is a *strength*, because `Status: superseded by ADR-00NN` is written proof you changed your mind when evidence arrived.
    *Builds on:* [Task 0.5 — Architecture Decision Records](#task-05--architecture-decision-records--1h) — where you wrote the first ADRs (ADR-0000 through 0004) and learned the format; every later phase added more, up to roughly 22.
    *Do this:*

    *You know it worked when:* all three render, and each diagram contains at least one branch that is not the happy path.

    *What this step is:* One entry-point page for everything under `docs/` — architecture diagrams, ADR index, benchmarks, runbooks, postmortems, the performance report — organised so a reader lands on it knowing nothing and reaches *any* document in two clicks (click a section link, click the document). This is what "documentation entry point" means in this task's What line.
    *Do this:*

    2. Test the two-click rule literally: start at `docs/README.md` and reach five randomly chosen documents. Fix any that take three clicks.
    *You know it worked when:* every document under `docs/` is reachable from `docs/README.md` in at most two clicks — which is half of this task's "done when".

#### Task 14.3 — Demo path and interview preparation — 5h

**What:** A rehearsed demo and prepared stories.
**Why:** You will get 5 minutes to describe six months of work. Rehearsing it is the highest-leverage handful of hours in this plan — a rehearsed demo plus eight written stories plus one cold LLD rep is genuinely a full session's work, and the budget now says so.
**Solves:** the gap between having done the work and being able to show it.

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Demo path** | A fixed, rehearsed route through the system that works every time and takes five minutes. Improvising a demo is how you end up debugging in front of an interviewer. |
| **Constraint-first framing** | Opening with the hard problem rather than the technology list. "The entire day's traffic arrives in the ninety seconds after tickets go on sale" invites the right follow-up question; "I used Kafka, Redis and Kubernetes" invites scepticism. |
| **Volunteering limitations** | Naming what the project does not prove — synthetic load, no real payment provider, single region — before being asked. It reads as judgement, and it stops an interviewer feeling they caught you out. |
| **Story bank** | Eight specific incidents with numbers, drawn from your journal: the deadlock, the stampede, the restart loop, the oversell test. Interviews are won with specifics, and you cannot invent them under pressure. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** stories with **numbers in them**, sourced from your journal rather than reconstructed. Vagueness is exactly what makes an interviewer probe further; a specific number ends the question.
- **When it works you will see:** a five-minute demo you can run without improvising, and eight written stories each containing a measurement.
- **Where people get stuck:** a live demo that needs the environment working. Screenshot everything and record a short video. Demoing against a live stack in front of an interviewer is how you end up debugging instead of presenting.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Script the five-minute demo path.**

Improvising a demo is how you end up debugging in front of an interviewer. The route is fixed by this task: seed data → create an event → bulk import seats → concurrent purchase showing no oversell → ticket PDF → scan → Grafana under spike load → kill a pod with zero errors → KEDA scaling on lag. Every stop on that route is something you already built; this step only strings them together.

[Task 8.5 — Bulk CSV import, end to end](#task-85--bulk-csv-import-end-to-end--2h) — the seat-map CSV import with live progress. [Task 5.1 — The oversell problem: four designs, measured](#task-51--the-oversell-problem-four-designs-measured--4h) — the concurrent-buyers test proving zero oversell. [Task 8.4 — The async media processing pipeline](#task-84--the-async-media-processing-pipeline--3h) — the ticket PDF with its signed QR code and the scan endpoint. #### Task 14.4 — Behavioral rounds, and the AI question — 5h

**What:** Scripted, honest answers for the two interview surfaces this plan builds nothing for anywhere else: the behavioral round's questions about working with people, and the question every polished solo repository now triggers — "how much of this did AI write?"
**Why:** Almost every loop ends with a behavioral round, and in 2026 the first hypothesis an interviewer forms about an impressive solo repo is that AI built it. Both are answerable — but only if the answers exist before you are asked. Improvising either one can throw away six months of genuine work in ten minutes.
**Solves:** the silence after "tell me about a time you disagreed in code review", and the defensive stumble after "did you really write this?"

**New words:**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **STAR** | Situation, Task, Action, Result — the shape interviewers expect a behavioral answer in. Nothing clever: set the scene, say what needed doing, say what *you* did, say what happened — in that order, with a number in the Result when you have one. Answers that wander between those four parts get cut off; answers in this shape earn follow-up questions, which is exactly what you want. |
| **Proxy story** | An honest analogue from solo work, offered *labelled as such*: "I have not done that in a team; the closest thing in this project was X." It demonstrates that the instinct exists without pretending the experience does. The label is the whole trick — the same story told unlabelled is a lie, and told labelled it is a maturity signal. |

**Focus on this:**

- **What actually matters here:** honesty as the *strategy*, not a limitation you manage around. [§0.4 — What "4–5 years of experience" actually means](#04-what-45-years-of-experience-actually-means) — the section near the top of this document on what solo work can and cannot give you — already lists, plainly, what a solo project cannot give you — team code review, stakeholder pressure, being on call for a bug you did not cause. This task turns that honest list into prepared answers, which is what the honesty was for all along.
- **When it works you will see:** five written answers you can deliver without hedging, and the AI question answered in under a minute — ending with an offer to prove it live, which is the moment the interviewer relaxes.
- **Where people get stuck:** bluffing. An invented team story collapses under the second follow-up question, exactly like the fabricated provenance warned about in [§13 — How to present this credibly](#13-how-to-present-this-credibly) — claiming this project as production work at an employer — and for the same reason: you cannot answer questions about things that did not happen. The honest shape survives *any* follow-up, because there is nothing to catch.

Subtasks:

- [ ] **Step 1 — Write the five team-gap answers, in STAR shape.**
    *What this step is:* A behavioral round is the interview stage where you are asked about working with people — not code. Interviewers draw from a small, standard set of probes, and five of them target exactly the things a solo project never gave you: **a code-review disagreement**, **working with a product manager on a scope cut**, **mentoring someone**, **an estimate you blew**, and **an incident you owned but did not cause**. In this step you write a full scripted answer for each of the five, in STAR shape (Situation, Task, Action, Result — defined in this task's New words table). At the end you will have five complete written answers in `docs/interview-stories.md`.
    *Builds on:* [§0.4 — What "4–5 years of experience" actually means](#04-what-45-years-of-experience-actually-means) — the section near the top of this document that plainly lists what a solo project cannot give you (team code review, stakeholder pressure, being on call for a bug you did not cause); these five questions probe exactly that list, which is why you prepare them instead of improvising.

    1. Create (or open) `docs/interview-stories.md` and add one heading per probe: code-review disagreement, PM scope cut, mentoring, blown estimate, incident owned but not caused.
    2. Under each heading, write the answer using the same honest template for every one: *"I have not had that situation in a team setting; the closest analogue in this project was X; here is what I did, and here is what I would do differently with people involved."* Leave X as a placeholder for now — Step 2 fills it from your journal.
    3. Write each answer out in **full sentences**, not bullet notes — the whole point of scripting is that the first time you say these words is not in the interview.
    4. Check each answer against STAR: one or two sentences of scene-setting (Situation), what needed doing (Task), what *you* did (Action), what happened — with a number if you have one (Result). Rearrange anything that wanders.

## 9. Topics you did not mention that seniority is judged on

Your list is strong and covers most of what matters. Here is what was missing, in
priority order. The ones marked **must** are already woven into the plan above — the
others are genuine options for your stretch time.

**Must-have, already included:**

1. **Security and authorization** ([Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline)) — the biggest gap in your original list. Interviews reliably probe JWT handling, token revocation, RBAC vs ABAC, multi-tenant isolation, and OWASP. A system with no auth story reads as a tutorial.
2. **Testing strategy** ([Phase 0 — Repository, tooling, standards](#phase-0--repository-tooling-standards--15h-baseline), [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline), and throughout) — Testcontainers over H2, the test pyramid, contract tests, query-count assertions, concurrency tests, mutation testing, load-test gates. The ability to describe a testing *strategy* rather than "I write unit tests" is a senior marker.
3. **Distributed systems patterns** ([Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline)–[Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline)) — outbox, inbox, saga, CQRS, idempotent consumers, eventual consistency, read-your-writes. These are the vocabulary of distributed backend interviews.
4. **Resilience engineering** ([Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline)) — timeout budgets, retry storms, circuit breakers, bulkheads, graceful degradation, chaos testing. "What happens when X is down?" is asked about every dependency.
5. **Schema and API evolution** ([Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline), [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline), [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline)) — expand/contract migrations, backward-compatible events, API versioning, build-once-promote-many. This is the difference between someone who has shipped to a running system and someone who has not.
6. **Observability as a practice** ([Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline)) — SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, runbooks, postmortems. Says "I have been on call" more clearly than anything else.
7. **Performance measurement discipline** (every phase) — baselines, JMH, profilers, flame graphs, reproducible numbers. Interviewers trust measured claims and discount unmeasured ones.
8. **Engineering process artifacts** ([Phase 0 — Repository, tooling, standards](#phase-0--repository-tooling-standards--15h-baseline)) — ADRs, conventional commits, PR hygiene, CODEOWNERS, trunk-based development, DORA metrics. Cheap to add and reads as experience.
9. **Data modelling and consistency** ([Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline), [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline)) — DDD aggregates drawn around invariants, money as `BigDecimal` + currency, UTC time handling, UUIDv7 vs v4 for index locality, soft deletes and auditing.
10. **Low-level design as an interview round** ([Task 0.8 — Low-level design: from a blank page to classes](#task-08--low-level-design-from-a-blank-page-to-classes--4h) and the phase-exit reps in [the Weekly cadence and how to not fall behind](#11-weekly-cadence-and-how-to-not-fall-behind)) — a separate, separately-scored stage in almost every backend loop, and one this project otherwise trains you for only by accident. You will have deep class-design practice from [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline); what [Task 0.8 — Low-level design: from a blank page to classes](#task-08--low-level-design-from-a-blank-page-to-classes--4h) adds is doing it cold, for an unseen problem, against a clock — and the phase-exit rep (one new canon problem at each phase exit, in the day-7 slot) keeps that skill warm across all six months instead of letting it decay after week 4. [Task 14.3 — Demo path and interview preparation](#task-143--demo-path-and-interview-preparation--5h) then re-tests it cold at the very end.

**Strongly recommended stretch (in this order if you find spare time):**

These are *optional*. They are written more briefly than the numbered tasks above —
no **New words** table, no checkpoint — but each one still tells you what to build,
what proves it works, and what it lets you say in an interview. Any vocabulary that
appears only here is defined in [§15.15](#1515-words-that-appear-only-in-the-stretch-list).
Do none of these until [Phase 14 — Capstone](#phase-14--capstone-performance-report-and-documentation--14h-baseline) is done; one finished plan beats two half-finished ones.

**S11 — Full-text search with OpenSearch — ~8h.** Typo-tolerant event search that
`LIKE '%arctic%'` can never give you, kept in sync without the application knowing.

- Add OpenSearch to `docker-compose.yml`. Create an index with an analysed `name` field and a keyword `venueId`.
- Point Debezium at the `events` table so row changes stream into a Kafka topic from the write-ahead log. No application code writes to the index.
- Build a small indexer that consumes that topic and updates OpenSearch.
- Benchmark against your Postgres `ILIKE` baseline and save it to `docs/benchmarks/search.md`.
- **Done when:** searching `artic monkys` finds the Arctic Monkeys event, and you can delete the whole index and rebuild it from Kafka.
- **Lets you say:** "Search is a derived read model fed by CDC, so it is rebuildable and the write path never knows it exists."

**S12 — gRPC and Protobuf for one internal call — ~5h.** Replace one service-to-service
REST call with gRPC so you can answer "when would you *not* use REST?" with numbers.

- Pick one internal call — `order-service` asking `inventory-service` to confirm a hold is a good one. Write the `.proto` and generate both sides.
- Keep the REST version alive behind a config flag so you can switch and compare.
- Measure payload size, p99 latency and CPU for both, over at least 10,000 calls.
- **Done when:** `docs/benchmarks/grpc-vs-rest.md` has both numbers and a one-paragraph recommendation you actually believe.
- **Lets you say:** "gRPC cut the payload by Nx and p99 by Nms on our internal hop, but we kept REST at the edge because browsers and debuggability matter more there."

**S13 — Rate limiting as a product feature — ~3h.** [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline) builds rate limiting as
*protection*. This turns it into a *plan*: free, pro, enterprise.

- Add per-tenant quota config: requests/minute and a monthly cap.
- Return `429` with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and document the client's correct behaviour (exponential backoff with jitter).
- Decide and document what happens at the cap: hard block, or allow overage and bill it.
- **Done when:** two tenants on different plans provably get different limits from the same endpoint, proved by a test.
- **Lets you say:** "Rate limiting was a billing surface, not just a shield, so the 429 contract had to be good enough for customers to code against."

**S14 — Multi-region and disaster recovery design — ~2h.** A writing exercise, not a
build. The design conversation is the entire value.

- Write `docs/architecture/dr.md`: state a target RPO and RTO and justify both numbers.
- Compare active-passive against active-active for *your* data, and say where the reservation invariant breaks under active-active. (It does break. That is the interesting part.)
- Cover data residency and how Kafka replicates between clusters.
- **Done when:** a reader can tell you how much data you would lose and how long you would be down, with the reasoning.
- **Lets you say:** "We were active-passive with a 5-minute RPO because seat reservation needs a single writer, and I can show you exactly where active-active would oversell."

**S15 — Edge caching and CDN semantics — ~2h.** [Phase 4 — Redis and the caching layer](#phase-4--redis-and-the-caching-layer--12h-baseline) caches *inside* the system.
This caches *outside* it, where the traffic never reaches you at all.

- Set deliberate `Cache-Control` on the public event-listing endpoints, and get `Vary` right so that authenticated and anonymous responses never mix.
- Tag responses with surrogate keys per event, and purge by key when an event changes.
- **Done when:** editing one event purges exactly that event's cached pages and nothing else.
- **Lets you say:** "The cheapest request is the one that never reaches your origin — we pushed the public catalog to the edge and invalidated by surrogate key on the update event."

**S16 — Entity history with Envers or a temporal table — ~3h.** Answer "who changed
this price, and when?" — a question every real system eventually gets asked.

- Pick one: Hibernate Envers (automatic, Hibernate-coupled) or a Postgres temporal/history table with triggers (explicit, portable). Write an ADR for the choice.
- Apply it to `Event` pricing and to order status.
- Write the query that reconstructs any row as it was at a given timestamp.
- **Done when:** you can show an event's full price history and explain the storage cost of keeping it.
- **Lets you say:** "Auditing was a schema decision, not a logging decision — logs get rotated, and the auditors wanted a query."

**S17 — Feature flags and trunk-based release — ~2h.** Ship the code dark, turn it on
later, then — the part everyone forgets — delete the flag. If you built [Task 13.3 — Scaling, configuration, and deployment strategies](#task-133--scaling-configuration-and-deployment-strategies--8h)'s
`[stretch]` feature flag, this item extends that work through the full lifecycle — do not
build a second flag store.

- Add a simple flag store (a table plus a cached lookup is plenty; you do not need LaunchDarkly).
- Put one real feature behind it — the [Phase 9 — WebSockets and real-time delivery](#phase-9--websockets-and-real-time-delivery--9h-baseline) realtime seat map is a good candidate.
- Take it through its whole lifecycle: off in production, on for one tenant, on for everyone, flag removed from the code.
- **Done when:** the flag is *gone* from the codebase and the feature still works. Removal is the task.
- **Lets you say:** "Deploy and release were separate events, which is what made trunk-based development safe for us."

**S18 — Timezone correctness (core moved into [Task 1.3 — Value objects and domain events](#task-13--value-objects-and-domain-events--3h)) — ~2h.** The heart of this item — storing an `Instant` plus the venue's IANA zone id, rendering in venue-local time, and the two tests (a DST-transition event, and an IST half-hour-offset venue) — turned out to be too important to leave optional, so it now lives in **[Task 1.3 — Value objects and domain events](#task-13--value-objects-and-domain-events--3h)**, including the `Instant` / `ZonedDateTime` / `LocalDateTime` decision rule. If you followed the plan in order, you have already done it. What remains optional here is the extra exploration:

- Handle the *ambiguous* hour as well as the skipped one: on fall-back night the wall clock shows 02:30 twice. Find out what `ZonedDateTime` does with it by default, and decide what *your* rendering should say for an event at that moment.
- Chase one historical oddity in the tz database — `Pacific/Kiritimati` skipping 31 December 1994 entirely is a good one — to see with your own eyes why the zone id, not the offset, is the source of truth.
- Find out how tzdata updates reach your JVM, and what you would do if a country changed its DST rules next month.
- **Done when:** you can explain fall-back ambiguity out loud, and you know how your runtime gets new timezone rules.
- **Lets you say:** "We stored UTC plus the venue's zone ID, never a fixed offset, because offsets change twice a year and zone IDs do not."

**S19 — Cost awareness — ~1h.** The cheapest item here and the one almost nobody does.

- Estimate the monthly infrastructure cost of running Zenith at 1,000 orders a day, then at 100,000.
- Identify the two biggest line items and what you would do first if asked to halve the bill.
- **Done when:** `docs/cost-model.md` exists with the arithmetic shown, not just a total.
- **Lets you say:** "Our biggest cost was X, and the cheapest lever was Y" — which signals you have seen a real bill.

**S20 — Reactive Spring, benchmarked honestly — ~5h.** Build it in order to form an
opinion about it, not because you should adopt it.

- Reimplement one read-heavy endpoint with WebFlux and a reactive driver.
- Benchmark it against the same endpoint on virtual threads: throughput, p99, memory, and how readable each stack trace is when it fails.
- **Done when:** you have both sets of numbers and a stated preference you can defend.
- **Lets you say:** "I benchmarked WebFlux against virtual threads. For our workload virtual threads gave most of the benefit at a fraction of the cognitive cost, and here are the numbers" — which is a far stronger answer than either enthusiasm or dismissal.

**S21 — Service mesh basics — ~4h.** Mostly so you can explain why you did *not* adopt one. ([Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline)'s `[stretch]` mTLS subtask covers the gateway hop and the written rationale; this item is the hands-on mesh version — extend that ADR rather than writing a second one.)

- Install Linkerd on your kind cluster and mesh two services.
- Get mTLS between them with no application code change, and look at the golden metrics the mesh gives you for free.
- Then write the honest ADR: for nine services you already instrumented with OpenTelemetry and Resilience4j, the mesh mostly duplicates what you have, and adds a sidecar per pod.
- **Done when:** mTLS is verifiably on, and the ADR says no with reasons.
- **Lets you say:** "I ran a mesh, and chose not to keep it — at our size it duplicated our existing retry and telemetry story and cost a sidecar per pod."

**Deliberately not recommended** for this project: event sourcing as the primary model (high complexity, low interview return relative to CQRS projections), Kubernetes operators (write an ADR saying no), and building your own framework abstractions over Spring (reads as over-engineering).

## 10. Benchmarks to capture

Fill this in as you go. It is the backbone of `docs/PERFORMANCE.md` and of your CV
bullets. Do **not** invent numbers — measured numbers survive follow-up questions and
invented ones do not.

Record alongside every row: **hardware and platform** (M3 Max, 14 cores, 36 GB, arm64),
dataset size, date, `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount` if pinned, and the exact command. A number
without its conditions is not a measurement, and an interviewer who asks "on what
hardware?" and gets a confident answer updates their opinion of you considerably.

| # | Measurement | Phase | Baseline | After | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Event search p99 / RPS | 3 | | | index + projection |
| 2 | Event detail p99 / RPS | 4 | | | L1+L2 cache, hit ratio |
| 3 | Cache hit ratio (L1 / L2) | 4 | — | | per cache |
| 4 | Database calls for 500 concurrent cold requests | 4 | ~500 | 1 | single-flight |
| 5 | Batch insert throughput (rows/s) | 3 | | | `reWriteBatchedInserts` |
| 6 | 1M-row import duration | 7, 8 | | | single vs partitioned vs `COPY` |
| 7 | Reservation throughput & p99, 4 designs | 5 | | | no-oversell assertion |
| 8 | Oversell count under 500 concurrent buyers | 5 | | 0 | must be exactly 0 |
| 9 | Duplicate orders under 100 same-key requests | 5 | | 0 | idempotency |
| 10 | Saga end-to-end latency (p50/p99) | 6 | | | from trace |
| 11 | Projection rebuild time for 2M orders | 6 | — | | CQRS |
| 12 | Scan endpoint p99 | 8 | | | target < 50 ms |
| 13 | WebSocket connection ceiling + bottleneck | 9 | | | name the limiting resource |

## 11. Weekly cadence and how to not fall behind

**Daily (3 h):** 10 min re-read the task and its "done when"; 2 h 20 min build; 20 min
write tests; 10 min commit with a real message — on the task's branch, never on `main` —
and jot one line in `docs/journal.md`. The day a task's "done when" passes, close its
loop the way [the definition of done (applies to every task in this plan)](#64-definition-of-done-applies-to-every-task-in-this-plan) prescribes before starting anything new: push, open the PR, self-review the diff,
squash-merge, delete the branch. **A task whose branch is unpushed is not done**, however
green it is locally — on a team, work that never reached the repo never happened, and
this plan holds you to the same standard.

**The journal is not optional.** One line a day — what you did, what surprised you, what
you got wrong — becomes your interview story bank and your weekly review input. It costs
60 seconds and is the highest-return habit in this plan.

**Daily during [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) (weeks 21–25), the rhythm changes:** 5 min re-read the level and
write your prediction as a comment; 90 min build and break it; 30 min measure or
re-measure; 25 min write the level's section in `docs/concurrency.md` in your own words,
including what you got wrong. Pace yourself by weight, not by count: two *light* levels
per session, or one *heavy* level — the heavy ones are 7, 9, 12, 16, 19, 22, 26, 27, 28,
29 and 30. Pairing a heavy level with anything else just produces two half-understood
levels, which is worth less than one understood one. **Do not move to the next level until you can
explain the current one to an imaginary colleague** — concurrency knowledge with gaps in
it collapses under interview follow-ups, and the follow-ups are where this subject is
actually tested.

**Weekly (day 7, unplanned):** review the week's PRs end to end; update
`docs/patterns.md` and `PERFORMANCE.md`; write any ADR you deferred; re-read next week's
phase; at a phase exit, cut the release: `git tag -a v0.<phase> -m "<phase name>" &&
git push --tags` — one annotated tag per finished phase mimics a company's release
cadence, gives you a known-good commit to roll back to, and turns your git history into
a demo timeline an interviewer can scroll; and honestly answer "am I behind?" — with a number, not a feeling: **if the
current phase has already cost 50% more than its weekly budget, descope per [the Descoping guide](#12-descoping-guide) the same
day** rather than compressing quality. The three biggest levers, and what each saves: fall
back to a simpler JWT issuer or a local Keycloak container instead of hand-building the
[Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline) authorization server (~4 h, [the Descoping guide](#12-descoping-guide) item 11), write four alert runbooks instead of
eleven in [Task 11.4 — SLOs, alerting, and runbooks](#task-114--slos-alerting-and-runbooks--2h) (~2 h — keep kafka-consumer-lag.md from the four in [`docs/runbooks/` — the six you need](#1610-docsrunbooks--the-six-you-need); the other
three are written in [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline), [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) and [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline) regardless), and keep Kafka in compose instead of moving
it to Strimzi on kind in Phase 13 (~8 h, with the ISR drill done against three compose
brokers instead).

**At every phase exit ([Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline) through [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline)), the day-7 slot also carries the LLD rep:** one new
timed 45-minute problem from the [Task 0.8 — Low-level design: from a blank page to classes](#task-08--low-level-design-from-a-blank-page-to-classes--4h) canon — Splitwise, elevator bank, BookMyShow,
LRU cache, logger framework, vending machine, chess, notification dispatcher, URL
shortener, ATM, meeting-room scheduler — in any order, no repeats, followed by a 15-minute written self-critique
against the three Task 0.8 review questions (one reason to change? behaviour or data
with getters? anything over-engineered?). Commit it under `lld-practice/` next to the
rest. One rep per phase keeps the round's muscle warm for six months instead of letting
it decay after week 4 — and because day 7 is outside the plan's budgeted hours, this
costs your build schedule nothing.

**Also in the day-7 slot, every week — the spaced-recall rep:** re-answer **five randomly
chosen checkpoints from at least two phases back**, out loud, and log any miss in
`docs/learning-log.md` with one line on what the gap was. Answering a checkpoint the day
you learned the material only proves recognition; recalling it after a gap is what
converts checkpoint answers into knowledge you can produce under questioning — and the
misses are a precise, personal list of what to re-read. And **once per phase**, record
the 90-second explain test from [How to learn this by asking AI](#05-how-to-learn-this-by-asking-ai) as a voice memo instead of only saying it to the empty
room. Fourteen short recordings by the end: your own evidence of progression, and
listening back to an early one is brutal, useful feedback on how much clearer you have
become.

**Rules that protect the plan:**

1. **Never skip the "done when" check.** A phase that is 80% done blocks the next one.
2. **Timebox rabbit holes to 45 minutes.** Then write the question in the journal, apply the workaround, and move on. Ask AI for the short answer, note that you took it on trust, and come back to it in a day-7 slot, or in the stretch time after [Phase 14 — Capstone](#phase-14--capstone-performance-report-and-documentation--14h-baseline).
3. **Do not refactor backwards for elegance.** [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) has an explicit slot for revisiting earlier code with better knowledge; everything else waits.
4. **Measure before optimizing, always.** Any optimization without a before-number is wasted work and an unusable story.
5. **No frontend. Ever.** `.http` files, k6, `websocat`, and Grafana are your UI. If you want a visual, screenshot Grafana.
6. **If a week is lost** (and one will be — illness, work, life), take it from the stretch items and [the Descoping guide](#12-descoping-guide)'s cut list, not from testing or documentation.

## 12. Descoping guide

If you fall behind, cut in this exact order. Everything here is explicitly safe to drop,
and it is better to cut deliberately than to half-finish three phases.

**Cut first (no interview cost):**
1. All `[stretch]` items.
2. `search-service` and `analytics-service` (never scheduled anyway).
3. Debezium — keep the outbox poller; just be able to explain CDC.
4. The RabbitMQ STOMP relay alternative in [Phase 9 — WebSockets and real-time delivery](#phase-9--websockets-and-real-time-delivery--9h-baseline) — keep Redis fanout.
5. ArgoCD/GitOps — keep the push-based pipeline and write the ADR.
6. GraalVM native image.
7. The read replica in [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) — keep the routing design documented.

**Cut second (small cost, replace with a document):**
8. The fourth reservation design (Redis-fronted) — build three and *describe* the fourth.
9. Contract tests — cut the Pact *tooling* if squeezed, but keep one consumer test and the written rationale in `docs/patterns.md`, and always keep the Avro compatibility gate. The sentence "the Avro gate is the async channel's contract test" is itself interview material, and [the Topics you did not mention that seniority is judged on](#9-topics-you-did-not-mention-that-seniority-is-judged-on) names contract tests among the senior markers — cutting them to zero would contradict this plan's own advice.
10. The canary deployment — keep rolling updates plus a rollback drill.
11. Spring Authorization Server — fall back to a simpler JWT issuer, but keep JWKS, asymmetric keys, and refresh rotation.

**Never cut (these are the project's value):**
- [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) entirely — concurrency correctness and idempotency are the core story.
- The query-plan work in [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline) and the benchmark numbers.
- The saga with all failure branches tested.
- [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline)'s dashboards, traces, and SLOs.
- **[Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) in full.** All 30 levels. If anything overruns, this is what you protect — see below.
- [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline)'s probes, graceful shutdown, and the local CI/CD pipeline.
- `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`, the ADRs, and the journal.
- The phase-exit LLD reps (see [the Weekly cadence and how to not fall behind](#11-weekly-cadence-and-how-to-not-fall-behind)). They consume no budgeted build hours and carry pure interview leverage; in a truly lost week, postpone a rep — never delete the habit.

**Funding a [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) overrun.** You are new to concurrency, so the plan already budgets
84 hours rather than the 57-hour baseline — and you should still assume it might run
longer. Plan for that now rather than discovering it in week 25. In priority order, take
the time from: all remaining `[stretch]` items (worth ~20 h on their own), then [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline)'s
ArgoCD and canary work, then the [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) `payment-service` extraction (keep it as a module
and describe the extraction instead), then [Phase 2 — Identity, security, API gateway](#phase-2--identity-security-api-gateway--16h-baseline)'s full authorization server.

If you reach week 25 with [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner) at [Level 24 (in Phase 12, Stage 5 — Coordination and composition)](#stage-5--coordination-and-composition-levels-2124--5h) and [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline) not started, the right call is
to finish Phase 12 and do a reduced Phase 13 — images, probes, one Deployment, a rolling
update, `make cd` — roughly 16 of its 37 baseline hours, keeping the in-cluster
observability move and the cluster-anatomy subtask — a cluster you can neither see into
nor explain teaches nothing. A fully understood concurrency
track plus basic Kubernetes beats a skimmed concurrency track plus Helm charts and ArgoCD,
in both learning value and interview value, by a wide margin.

If concurrency instead goes *faster* than budgeted, spend the surplus on [the Topics you did not mention that seniority is judged on](#9-topics-you-did-not-mention-that-seniority-is-judged-on)'s
stretch list — OpenSearch via CDC first, then gRPC benchmarking.

**Minimum viable version** if you lose a full month: `catalog` + `inventory` + `order` +
`notification` only (4 services), with [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline), [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline), [Phase 4 — Redis and the caching layer](#phase-4--redis-and-the-caching-layer--12h-baseline), [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline), [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline) (saga without extraction),
[Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline), [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner), [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline). That is still a genuinely strong project.

## 13. How to present this credibly

A quick note, because it affects how much value you get from these months of work.

**Describe the engineering truthfully and let it be impressive on its own.** This
project will give you real, specific, measured things to say — and those survive
follow-up questions. Claiming it as production work at your current employer does not:
interviewers ask about team size, incidents, on-call rotations, stakeholders, production
traffic patterns, and how a specific decision was reviewed. One or two of those and a
fabricated provenance collapses, which costs you the offer and the credibility you
actually earned. It is also the kind of thing that surfaces later in reference or
background checks.

The good news is that you do not need the fabrication. "I designed and built a
distributed ticketing platform; here is how I prevented overselling under 500 concurrent
buyers, here are the four designs I benchmarked, here is the thread dump from the
deadlock I caused and how I found it" is *stronger* than a vague claim about a work
system you cannot show. Hiring managers discount what they cannot verify and reward what
they can probe.

**Be equally honest with yourself about which doors this opens**, because applying to the
wrong ones wastes the scarcest resource you have — application cycles. What this project
cannot do is convert zero professional years into eligibility for requisitions with a
hard 4–5-years-of-experience HR filter: that filter runs before any engineer sees your
CV, the repo link is never clicked, and pretending otherwise just burns weeks of effort
on applications nobody reads. Where it dominates is everywhere a human engineer actually
evaluates you: product startups and companies that are flexible on years, strong SDE-1
and SDE-2 interview loops, and any conversation where the person across the table can
open the repo and probe it. So the framing on your CV is "depth beyond my years,
verifiable in the repo" — and the routes that reward that framing are referrals and
skill-first pipelines, not portal applications into filtered requisitions. A referral
puts your CV in front of an engineer; a portal puts it in front of a filter. Spend your
effort accordingly.

**On your CV**, give it its own section — *Projects* or *Engineering Portfolio* — with
the repo link, and let the bullets carry the weight:

> **Zenith — Distributed Event Ticketing Platform** (personal project) · Java 21, Spring Boot, Postgres, Kafka, Redis, Kubernetes
> - Designed nine services (eight event-driven business services behind an API gateway) with hexagonal architecture; order fulfillment implemented as an orchestrated saga with idempotent compensations and timeout recovery.
> - Eliminated overselling under 500 concurrent buyers by benchmarking four concurrency designs (pessimistic, optimistic, conditional-update, Redis-gated) and selecting the winner — name the design your own table favoured; **N× throughput at p99 of M ms**, verified by concurrency tests.
> - Built a reusable idempotency layer (`Idempotency-Key` + request fingerprint + inbox pattern): idempotent order creation and payment capture — exactly-once *effect* under client and provider retries.
> - Cut event-detail p99 from **A ms to B ms** with a two-level Caffeine/Redis cache, single-flight stampede protection, and event-driven invalidation at a **C% hit ratio**.
> - Reduced hottest-query latency **D%** via composite and covering index design, N+1 elimination enforced by query-count assertions in CI, and monthly partitioning of a 20M-row table.
> - Scaled WebSocket delivery to **E concurrent connections** across instances using Redis pub/sub fanout with update coalescing (**F× fewer messages**) and snapshot-based reconnect.
> - Tuned JVM concurrency against JMH benchmarks: replaced contended counters with striped accumulators, converted a serial provider chain to a deadline-bounded `CompletableFuture` fan-out (**H ms → I ms**), and benchmarked virtual against platform threads across I/O-bound, CPU-bound, and connection-bound workloads to decide where each belongs.
> - Instrumented with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, and Loki; defined SLOs with multi-window burn-rate alerting and a runbook per alert; diagnosed a thread-pool exhaustion hang, a `ThreadLocal` leak, and a lock-contention hotspot from thread dumps, heap dumps, and flame graphs.
> - Deployed on Kubernetes with tuned probes, HPA, and KEDA scaling on Kafka consumer lag; CI/CD pipeline with zero-downtime rolling updates and a **G-second** rollback.

Replace every letter with a number from `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`. Bullets with real numbers
and a mechanism named are what get a first-round call; adjective-only bullets do not.
Two wordings above are deliberate, and worth keeping. The idempotency bullet claims an
exactly-once *effect*, not exactly-once delivery — [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline) taught you that end-to-end
exactly-once delivery is a myth, and an interviewer who knows that will notice that you
do too; it is the stronger signal precisely because it is the more careful claim. And the
reservation bullet names whichever design *your* benchmark favoured, not a pre-written
winner — conditional-update wins most runs of this experiment, but your table is the
claim — and the strongest line in that bullet is the one you can defend with your own table.

**In interviews**, lead with a constraint and a trade-off rather than a technology list:
"the hard part was that the entire day's traffic arrives in the 90 seconds after tickets
go on sale, so…". And volunteer the limitations (synthetic load, no real payment
provider, single region) — it reads as judgement, not weakness.

## 14. Reading list

Do not read these cover to cover. Pull the relevant chapter when you hit the phase.

**Essential:**
- *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* — Kleppmann. Ch. 5–9 and 11 map to [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline), [Phase 5 — Idempotency and the high-concurrency reservation engine](#phase-5--idempotency-and-the-high-concurrency-reservation-engine--16h-baseline), [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline).
- *Java Concurrency in Practice* — Goetz. Dated on APIs, unmatched on the model. Ch. 3, 5, 8, 10 for [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner).
- *Microservices Patterns* — Richardson. Saga, outbox, CQRS for [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline). Also microservices.io for quick reference.
- *Release It!* (2nd ed.) — Nygard. Stability patterns for [Phase 10 — Nginx, load balancing, resilience](#phase-10--nginx-load-balancing-resilience--12h-baseline). The best book on things failing badly.

**Reference when needed:**
- *PostgreSQL 17 docs* — indexes, `EXPLAIN`, partitioning, isolation. Plus `use-the-index-luke.com` for [Phase 3 — Persistence and database optimization](#phase-3--persistence-and-database-optimization--21h-baseline).
- *Spring Boot / Spring Framework reference docs* — actually read these rather than blog posts; they are excellent.
- *Kafka: The Definitive Guide* (3rd ed.) — Ch. 3–4, 6–7 for [Phase 6 — Kafka, event-driven microservices, sagas, CQRS](#phase-6--kafka-event-driven-microservices-sagas-cqrs--22h-baseline).
- *Implementing Domain-Driven Design* — Vernon. Aggregates and context maps for [Phase 1 — Domain modelling and the first REST service](#phase-1--domain-modelling-and-the-first-rest-service--17h-baseline).
- *Optimizing Java* — Evans et al. JIT, GC, and benchmarking for [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner).
- *Site Reliability Engineering* (Google, free online) — SLOs and alerting chapters for [Phase 11 — Logging, metrics, tracing, alerting](#phase-11--logging-metrics-tracing-alerting--16h-baseline).
- *Kubernetes Up & Running* / the Kubernetes docs — [Phase 13 — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD](#phase-13--docker-kubernetes-cicd--37h-baseline).
- *Effective Java* (3rd ed.) — Bloch. Items 15–17, 48, 78–84 are directly relevant.
- JEP 444 (virtual threads), JEP 453/505 (structured concurrency), JEP 429 (scoped values) — read the JEPs themselves for [Phase 12 — The concurrency track](#phase-12--the-concurrency-track-30-incremental-levels--57h-baseline-84h-for-a-beginner); they are short and better than most articles.
